contract.shape: three paragraphs: district statistics, credit-union relevance, industry specialisation
contract.validation: deterministic word band, figure cap, evidence grounding, ban lists, thousands-separator formatting, and acceptance-time sliding 50-brief novelty window; validator-guided human repair was used after provider limits

known_limitations: No corpus-wide independent semantic review was run; every brief passed the current deterministic structural and evidence-grounding gates.
33 briefs were recovered through validator-guided human repair and 26 from earlier provider drafts after generation services reached their limits.

No brief asserts formal-learning attainment (no such data exists), the demographic-potential score, an absolute job total where employment validation fails, or an apportioned branch/deposit figure as a direct count.
18 members sit on stale industry vintages and their briefs name the year.
The phrase 'leaned heavily toward home purchases' appears in 65 briefs.

Aaron Bean.p1: Unemployment in the 4th congressional seat of Florida runs well above most comparable districts, at 6.1 percent, a sign of a labor market still working through slack. Median household income comes in lower than most peers, at 76,209 dollars, and home values trail behind too. Rent runs 1,464 dollars a month, and home values run over four times median income, a wider gap than most districts show. Poverty follows the same pattern, running higher than most comparable places.
Aaron Bean.p2: Credit unions hold 45.4 percent of retail offices here, a larger slice than in nearly every other congressional district. VyStar, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Community First Credit Union of Florida anchor that presence. Credit union employment runs nearly twice the national norm, with office presence close behind, and jobs have grown faster than office count, pointing to institutions deepening their footprint rather than simply adding branches. EverBank leads all banks by deposits booked here, though many other banks compete for the same customers across the district's branch network.
Aaron Bean.p3: Transportation and warehousing dominates the local economy, employing 12.5 percent of the district's workforce, a rate nearly triple the national norm. Health care and retail trade also employ large shares of workers, though neither approaches that same concentration. Overall finance industry employment sat almost exactly at the national norm as of 2023, even as finance and insurance growth outpaced the nation. The district's strength runs through moving and storing goods, not through finance itself.

Abraham Hamadeh.p1: A home in the 8th congressional seat of Arizona costs 5.3 times what a household typically earns, a gap well above most comparable districts, and it shapes everything else about the place. Median household income runs to $85,593, and homeownership is common, at 70.5 percent. Rent claims 24.5 percent of that income. Poverty here is rare, and unemployment is low too.
Abraham Hamadeh.p2: Desert Financial, Navy Federal Credit Union, and OneAZ anchor the credit union presence here, and together credit unions hold 25.5 percent of retail offices, a share ahead of comparable districts. JPMorgan Chase books the most deposits locally, though that reflects reporting rules more than branch presence, and it faces plenty of rivals among the district's bank branches. Credit union employment runs below the national norm, tracking closely with a similarly thin office presence. Against income and homeownership this high, credit unions here work a market with real deposits to gather.
Abraham Hamadeh.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance was this district's most specialized sector, running well above the national norm and employing a strikingly large share of workers. Retail trade employed more people still, and construction was specialized as well. Across all lenders, home purchases made up the majority of mortgage originations, well ahead of refinancing.

Adam Gray.p1: Poverty here runs among the highest of any congressional district in the country, at 19.2 percent, alongside unemployment near that same extreme. Median household income, 68,434 dollars, trails most other districts, while home values run higher still, pushing the home-value-to-income ratio to 6.1. Homeownership sits well below typical levels for a congressional district. The district is young and spread thin across the land, far below typical density.
Adam Gray.p2: Credit union employment here runs well ahead of the national norm, even though credit union offices track it much more closely, a gap worth noting up front. Merced Educators, Instructional Employees, and Travis anchor that presence, and credit unions hold 25.3 percent of local retail offices, a notable share. JPMorgan Chase books the largest deposits among the district's many bank branches, though that reflects reporting rules more than local branch strength. Against the thin incomes and low homeownership described above, a credit union sector staffed this heavily has real weight to carry.
Adam Gray.p3: As measured in 2023, farming, forestry, fishing and hunting dominated local work, a defining trait far beyond what the national mix would predict. Manufacturing and public instruction also ran ahead of the national mix, though neither approached agriculture's weight. Overall finance and insurance employment stayed thin, leaving credit unions to carry disproportionate weight in local financial life. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, 61.4 percent of originations, with a modest share reaching lower-income neighborhoods.

Adam Schiff.p1: California is home to close to 39.4 million people, packed in far more tightly than most of the country. Household income runs high at a median of $100,149, but housing swallows that advantage: home values average $759,500 against that income, a wide gap by any comparison, and rent runs $2,104 a month. Homeownership is uncommon relative to other states. Unemployment sits high as well, a sign that this prosperity does not reach everyone evenly.
Adam Schiff.p2: Three large credit unions carry real weight here, including Navy Federal and The Golden 1. Credit unions hold 22.8 percent of the state's retail offices, a middling share among other states, while Bank of America's reported deposit lead reflects how deposits get booked more than any real branch dominance. Credit union employment runs a touch below the national norm, and offices trail even further behind, meaning the offices that exist carry heavier staffing loads. That is a footprint built for the income and housing strains described above, not for broad physical reach.
Adam Schiff.p3: As measured in 2023, California leaned hardest into specialty farming, more than twice the national presence, and into information work, well above the norm elsewhere. Health care and social assistance made up the largest single share of jobs, with retail trade and educational services close behind at roughly average levels. Finance and insurance employment overall ran below the national norm. This was an economy anchored in land and information, with banking a smaller part of the mix than in most of the country.

Adam Smith.p1: This district packs people in tightly, well above most comparable districts, at roughly 4,247 people per square mile. Households earn a median of $100,731, and housing costs track that income upward: a home value to income ratio of 7.0 and rent near $1,959 a month. Only 55.5 percent own their homes here, a low share next to other districts. Poverty runs lower than most peers even so.
Adam Smith.p2: Credit union jobs here run close to the national norm even though credit union offices sit noticeably below it, a sign that the credit unions present operate leaner branch networks but staff them more heavily for the business they do. Boeing Employees, Global, and Sound are the names that matter locally, holding 27.6 percent of retail offices between them, a stronger foothold than most comparable districts see. Bank of America books a sizable deposit sum to an address here, among many bank branches run by separate banks across the district. For an economy this dense and well paid, thin branch scale paired with thick staffing points to credit unions still doing real work.
Adam Smith.p3: As of 2023, transportation and warehousing employment ran well above the national norm, a clear specialization for the district. Wholesale trade and manufacturing were also specialized, while health care carried a large share of jobs on its own. Finance employment overall sat well under the national norm, so this district makes its living moving and making things rather than banking them.

Addison McDowell.p1: Unemployment here sits among the lowest of any comparable district, at 3.1 percent, even as income and home values trail behind. The typical household earns 68,414 dollars a year, and the median home is valued at 287,900 dollars. Homeownership also runs behind most other districts. The population stands at 794,243, with a median age skewing a bit older than the national middle.
Addison McDowell.p2: Credit union activity here centers on State Employees', Truliant, and Allegacy, and together credit unions hold 27.1 percent of retail offices, a strong share compared with other districts, well ahead of Truist Bank and the many bank branches it competes against locally. Credit union employment tracks closely with how thick their office presence is on the ground. That footprint matters in a district where incomes lag and homeownership is thinner than typical, giving credit unions real reach into household budgets.
Addison McDowell.p3: As measured in 2023, this district's economy leaned hard on making and moving goods: manufacturing accounted for 16.2 percent of jobs, and wholesale trade and retail trade were also specialized well above the national norm. Overall finance employment, by contrast, ran well under expected levels for a district this size. Mortgage lending was dominated by home purchases, and a meaningful share reached lower income neighborhoods. This is a place built on production and distribution, not finance.

Adelita Grijalva.p1: Median household income in the 7th congressional seat of Arizona sits at $60,932, among the lowest of any congressional district, and poverty runs far beyond typical levels here. Home values trail most other districts even as the ratio of home value to income, 4.6, pushes housing costs higher than what most districts see. With 813,289 people spread thin across the district, this is sparsely settled country even by western standards.
Adelita Grijalva.p2: Credit union jobs here outpace the national norm, running 1.13 times typical levels, while the number of credit union offices merely keeps pace with the country as a whole, a sign that branches operating here carry more weight per location. Navy Federal Credit Union, Hughes, and Vantage West lead that presence, and credit unions hold 29.0 percent of retail offices, a share few other districts match. Wells Fargo books more deposits here than any other institution, one name among many competitors running a much larger branch network. Given the incomes and poverty already described, that credit union footprint carries unusual weight.
Adelita Grijalva.p3: As measured in 2023, health care and retail trade were among the district's larger sources of work, alongside a public administration sector running well above the national norm. Agriculture stood out further still, highly specialized relative to the country overall. Mortgage lending here leaned heavily toward home purchases, making up most originations, with a meaningful share reaching lower-income neighborhoods.

Adrian Smith.p1: This district spreads its people thin, just 9.3 per square mile, a settlement pattern more sparse than nearly any comparable district. Median household income sits at 69,788 dollars, and unemployment stays low. Housing runs cheap here too: a median home value of 202,300 dollars against income puts the value-to-income ratio at 2.9, well below what many districts show. Homeownership is common, a pattern that fits a place built around long-settled, low-density living rather than turnover and renting.
Adrian Smith.p2: Credit unions hold just 5.7 percent of retail offices here, a smaller slice than almost anywhere else measured. CENTRIS, MERIDIAN TRUST, and TRIUS carry that share locally, working against a market of many separate banks where Pinnacle Bank books the largest deposits. Credit union employment and office presence both sit far below the national norm and track each other closely, a genuinely thin footprint rather than a reporting quirk. For a credit union here, the customer base is the modest-income, low-cost-housing population described above, not a dense urban market.
Adrian Smith.p3: As measured in 2023, this district's economy leaned hard on manufacturing, employing 16.4 percent of workers and specialized well above the national norm, alongside highly specialized agriculture and utilities sectors. Overall finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm, and growth in that combined sector lagged over the prior decade too. This is a district defined by making and growing things, not by financial services.

Adriano Espaillat.p1: People pack into this district more tightly than almost anywhere else in the country, at nearly 68,000 per square mile. Median household income sits low, at 52,401 dollars, while home values run high at 651,900 dollars, a home value to income ratio of 12.4. Homeownership is scarce and poverty runs among the highest of any comparable district. This is dense, largely rented, working New York, stretched thin against its own cost of living.
Adriano Espaillat.p2: Credit unions here include United Nations, Municipal, and Van Cortlandt Cooperative, and together they hold just 18.5 percent of retail office share against banks, thinner than most comparable districts. Credit union employment here runs far below the national norm, tracking the same thin presence its offices show. HSBC Bank USA leads all banks booked here, one name among many competing for the same customers. For a population this large and this strapped, credit unions hold only a narrow slice of the business.
Adriano Espaillat.p3: As measured in 2023, instructional services and health care together dominated employment, each far more concentrated here than the national norm. Public administration followed as the next largest source of jobs. Overall finance employment ran well below the national norm, and finance sector growth over the prior decade lagged the country too. This is an economy anchored in institutions rather than in finance or housing turnover.

Al Green.p1: Poverty sits among the highest of any comparable district, at 21.3 percent, and unemployment climbs to match it. Median household income, at 62,248 dollars, trails well behind most peer districts, even though home values here run cheaper than most. That mismatch has not made housing easy: home prices and rent both sit high against what people actually earn. Just under 51 percent of households own their home, in a district crowded well past the national average.
Al Green.p2: Credit unions hold 29.6 percent of retail offices here, a share well ahead of most comparable districts. Navy Federal Credit Union, Texas Dow Employees, and JSC are the names that show up largest, alongside a field of 96 bank branches run by many separate banks. Credit union employment still runs below the national norm, even though office presence outpaces it, a split not typical of most places. Given how strained incomes are here, that heavier office footprint is exactly the kind of physical presence a credit union depends on.
Al Green.p3: As of 2023, health care and social assistance dominated the local job market, employing 35.3 percent of workers, a concentration well out of proportion to its national share. Transportation, warehousing, and wholesale trade showed up too, but only modestly. Overall finance and insurance employment stayed well below the national norm, though it had grown at close to the national pace over the prior decade. Mortgage lending here leaned heavily toward home purchases.

Alan Armstrong.p1: Oklahoma's population sits at 4,095,393, with a median household income of $66,148, well below most states in the country. Nearly 15 percent of residents live in poverty, a rate that runs higher than almost anywhere else. Housing stays cheap by comparison, a median home value of $222,100 against a median rent of $1,044 a month. Most households in the state own rather than rent.
Alan Armstrong.p2: Tinker, TTCU, and Communication anchor the credit union presence here, but credit unions hold only 17.5 percent of retail offices statewide, well behind what most comparable states carry. BOKF, National Association books the most deposits under federal reporting rules, one name among many banks competing for the same customers. Credit union employment still runs slightly ahead of the national norm even as office numbers merely keep pace with it. That gives a credit union in this state fewer doors to work through, but ones that carry more weight apiece.
Alan Armstrong.p3: Oklahoma's 2023 job market leaned hard on mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction, nearly five times the national norm and by far the state's most specialized sector. Health care, retail trade, and educational services employed the most people day to day, though none stood out as specialized. Overall finance-sector employment ran below the national norm, in a state whose economic identity was still built on extraction rather than banking.

Alex Padilla.p1: California's economy sits on farm work and information jobs at levels most states cannot match, agriculture running well above the national norm and information close behind. People here pack in more densely than in most states, and median household income runs among the highest anywhere. Housing prices sit far out of reach of income by the standard published ratios, with fewer households owning and more renting than is typical elsewhere.
Alex Padilla.p2: Credit unions hold 22.8 percent of retail offices here, a share close to what comparable states show, even with NAVY FEDERAL CREDIT UNION, THE GOLDEN 1, and one other large name all operating at scale. Office presence runs below the national norm, but credit union employment, also below that norm, holds up better than the office count alone would imply, work concentrated into fewer locations. Bank of America carries the largest deposit total on paper, a figure shaped by where deposits get booked rather than by branch presence or local customers. For a population this large and this income-rich, credit unions are working a market bigger than their footprint shows.
Alex Padilla.p3: As measured in 2023, finance and insurance work overall sat well below the national norm and grew more slowly than the country over the prior decade. The state's real strength lay elsewhere, in farm production and information work, both far above what most states show. This was an economy built on specialty strengths at the edges, not on financial services at the center.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.p1: Few places pack people in as tightly as the 14th district of New York, among the most densely settled in the country. Median household income sits low next to other districts, at $64,547, while the median home value, $655,300, runs high, a mismatch that pushes rent and ownership costs to some of the steepest levels measured anywhere. Homeownership itself is rare, just 27.7 percent. This is a renter's district, working through a cost squeeze that owning a home here would only deepen.
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.p2: Credit unions hold a strikingly thin slice of the retail banking footprint here, just 9.1 percent of offices, among the lowest shares measured in any district. Fourleaf, Self Reliance Financial, and American Airlines are the members serving this market. Under federal reporting rules, JPMorgan Chase shows the largest deposit total of any bank here, a quirk of where deposits get booked rather than a sign of branch reach or local custom. Credit union employment sits far below the national norm, leaving the sector a marginal presence in a district already short on cheap credit.
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.p3: As of 2023, the district's job base leaned hard on Public Administration and Transportation and Warehousing, both far above the national norm for their fields. Health Care and Social Assistance and Educational Services rounded out the largest employing sectors. Finance work of any kind was scarce here compared with the country as a whole. This is a district built on moving goods and running government.

Alma Adams.p1: Homeownership in the 12th district of North Carolina sits at 47 percent, among the lowest shares of any comparable seat measured. This is a young, tightly packed place, with a median age of 33.5 and population density far above what most districts see. Income lands near the middle nationally at $80,180, while home values of $396,300 and monthly rent push housing costs well beyond typical levels elsewhere. Poverty also runs higher here than in most comparable places.
Alma Adams.p2: Credit union offices hold close to a quarter share of retail outlets in this district, but employment in the industry tells a different story, running well under the national norm even as office presence sits nearer to it, so branches outnumber the workers staffing them. State Employees', Skyla, and Truliant anchor that presence alongside 158 bank branches, including one Bank of America office whose deposit total reflects reporting rules rather than a dominant local footprint. The customers on the other side of that counter are the renters and thin-equity households described above.
Alma Adams.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance was this district's clear specialty, holding 14.4 percent of area jobs at more than three times the national norm. Administrative and support services also ran well ahead of the norm, marking a second concentration beyond finance. Home purchase loans made up the bulk of mortgage activity recorded here. Redistricting since the last decade means the ten-year comparison spans two different maps, not one place changing.

Ami Bera.p1: Unemployment here runs among the highest of any comparable district, at 7.3 percent. Median household income still reaches $87,640, a real gap alongside a poverty rate that also runs higher than most places see. Home values near $499,100 and rent that outpaces typical districts point to a tight, costly market, with people packed together at high density. Homeownership lags behind what most districts report.
Ami Bera.p2: Credit unions hold 32.6 percent of retail offices here, a share that stands apart from most comparable places, putting them in real competition with a bank branch network run by many separate institutions. The Golden 1, SAFE, and a third large institution anchor that presence locally. Credit union employment runs well above the national norm even though office presence sits close to it, meaning these offices do more work per location than is typical elsewhere. That is a credit union sector built for the income spread and housing pressure just described.
Ami Bera.p3: As of 2023, health care and social assistance and retail trade carried much of the working mix, alongside construction, which ran well above the national norm for its size. Public administration was also a distinct specialty, a sign of civic and government work concentrated here. Across all lenders, most mortgage originations financed home purchases, and a solid share of lending reached lower-income neighborhoods. This is a district whose distinct strength is building and running the public work around it.

Amy Klobuchar.p1: Minnesota is home to nearly 5.8 million people with a median age of 39.2, and household income of $87,117 outpaces most states. Housing stays affordable against that income, with home values running about four times earnings and rent claiming under a fifth of the median household's pay. Homeownership is common, and the population sits well below most states in density, at under 73 per square mile.
Amy Klobuchar.p2: Affinity Plus, TruStone Financial, and Ent are the names doing credit union business across Minnesota, though credit unions hold just 21.1 percent of retail offices, a thinner presence than most states show. U.S. Bank National Association books the largest deposits in the state under federal reporting rules, a distinction that says nothing about how many rival banks operate branches here. Credit union employment sits a bit below the national norm while office presence roughly matches it, so branches have held on even where staffing has thinned. That leaves a real but modest footprint for reaching the state's comfortably banked households.
Amy Klobuchar.p3: The state's 2023 job count topped 2.6 million, leaning on manufacturing at well above the national norm and on management of companies leaning even harder that way. Health care and social assistance employed the most workers of any sector, carrying its own mild specialization. Finance and insurance employment ran a touch above the national norm too, though the broader finance and insurance sector added jobs more slowly here across the decade before.

Analilia Mejia.p1: Household income in the 11th congressional seat of New Jersey runs higher than in nearly any other district in the country, at $141,429. Home values sit well above typical, yet housing costs stay modest against what households earn, and rent claims just 16.7 percent of the typical income. Most residents own rather than rent, and poverty runs to just 4.5 percent. This is a dense district, and one where people work steadily, with little financial strain visible in what was measured.
Analilia Mejia.p2: Credit unions hold just 11.8 percent of retail offices here, a share among the lowest of any district and evidence of how firmly banks hold this market. Affinity, Picatinny, and Visions are the credit unions with the largest presence. Valley National Bank books the most deposits to addresses here, though that reflects federal reporting rules more than branch reach, and it competes with many other banks operating locally. Credit union employment runs far below the national norm, well behind even the office presence credit unions maintain here.
Analilia Mejia.p3: As of 2023, professional, scientific, and technical services anchored the district's economy, employing 14.8 percent of its workers at nearly twice the national norm. Management of companies and wholesale trade also ran well ahead of national patterns, marking a district built on corporate and technical work rather than routine retail. Mortgage lending skewed heavily toward home purchases, a sign of how this district's affluence shapes its own credit markets.

Andrea Salinas.p1: Median household income in the 6th congressional seat of Oregon sets it apart from comparable districts, at $90,927. Home values, at $497,100, run more than five times that figure, and rent reaches $1,662 a month. Homeownership trails most peer districts even so, and poverty runs lower than most. Work proceeds against an unemployment rate that lands neither high nor low next to other districts.
Andrea Salinas.p2: Credit unions hold 33.9 percent of retail offices here, a share well above most districts in the country. First Technology, OnPoint Community, and Oregon State Credit Union are the names behind that share, up against U.S. Bank National Association, the largest bank by deposits booked locally, in a district where many banks hold branches of their own. Credit union employment runs 1.47 times the national norm, a specialization that outpaces even their office count. For the incomes and home prices described above, credit unions here are a structural piece of how residents bank, not a marginal option.
Andrea Salinas.p3: As measured in 2023, this district's economy leaned hardest on agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting, well beyond its share of the national norm even though the sector accounts for only a sliver of local jobs. Public administration and construction followed as specialized sectors. Health care, retail, and manufacturing employed the most people, without marking the district out nationally. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, at 53.4 percent of originations.

Andrew Clyde.p1: Homeownership sits well above most comparable districts here, at 75.0 percent, and that ownership rate is the defining fact of the place. Median household income runs to 84,963 dollars, comfortably ahead of typical districts, while home values and rent land higher than most peers too. Unemployment stays low, at 3.6 percent. This is a district of people who own their homes and earn well, in a South region seat of just over 828,900 residents.
Andrew Clyde.p2: Navy Federal Credit Union, Delta Community, and Georgia's Own are the names doing business here, though credit unions hold only 16.9 percent of retail offices, a modest slice compared with similar districts. United Community Bank leads locally by deposits booked to addresses here, but it stands among many rival banks with branches in the district. Credit union jobs and credit union offices sit at a similarly thin level against the national norm, one echoing the other. For a district this affluent and this homeowning, credit unions work a smaller corner of the business than in most places.
Andrew Clyde.p3: Manufacturing anchors the local economy, employing 16.4 percent of jobs and concentrated here well beyond the national norm. Wholesale trade and transportation and warehousing also cluster more heavily than in most districts. Finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm going into 2023, despite growing faster than the country as a whole over the prior decade. This is a district built on moving and making goods, not on financial services.

Andrew Garbarino.p1: Household income in the 2nd congressional seat of New York stands at $125,071, a figure few other districts can match, and poverty and unemployment both sit near the bottom of the national range. Homes carry a median value well above the home to income ratio of 4.7, and homeownership is unusually widespread at 81.6 percent. This is also a dense, built-up place where most people own rather than rent.
Andrew Garbarino.p2: Credit union employment here sits close to the national norm, but the office footprint tied to those institutions runs well below it, a gap worth noting before anything else about the sector. Teachers, Fourleaf, and Suffolk carry the credit union name locally, competing for space with a much larger number of bank branches, the largest by deposits being JPMorgan Chase, though that name reflects deposit booking rules rather than any dominant local presence. Credit unions hold 22.4 percent of retail offices here, an unremarkable share given how much income and housing wealth sit in this district.
Andrew Garbarino.p3: As measured in 2023, the district's jobs concentrated hardest in wholesale trade, construction, and public administration, each well above the national norm for its size. Overall finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm, and hiring across that broader sector grew more slowly here than the nation managed over the same ten years. A majority of mortgage activity went toward home purchases rather than refinancing, at 53.2 percent of originations. This is a district built more on construction and trade than on finance.

Andrew Ogles.p1: Unemployment in the 5th district sits at 3.1 percent, among the lowest of any comparable district, and poverty runs low as well. Households here earn a median 96,192 dollars a year, well above typical districts, while the typical home carries a price tag of 489,200 dollars against rent near 1,682 dollars a month. At 835,216 people, this is a working-age district where jobs are easy to find and money problems are comparatively rare.
Andrew Ogles.p2: Credit unions hold just 11.9 percent of retail offices here, a share few other districts fall short of, so banks handle most of the everyday deposit business. ASCEND, LIBERTY, and LISTERHILL account for what credit union presence exists. Credit union employment also runs far thinner than the national norm, even as office presence outpaces the jobs behind it. For a credit union working this ground, the district's strong incomes and low unemployment describe a customer base that mostly banks somewhere else.
Andrew Ogles.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance employed workers here at a rate well above the national norm, part of a broader concentration that also touched management of companies and transportation and warehousing. Retail trade and professional and technical services ran ahead of national patterns too. Pinnacle Bank booked the most deposits of any institution under federal reporting rules, one name among many separate competitors operating branches here. This is a district built on white-collar and logistics work, with money moving through banks far more than through credit unions.

André Carson.p1: Median household income in the 7th congressional seat of Indiana sits at $64,843, a figure that trails most districts by a wide margin. Home values run modest too, against a rent near $1,216 a month. Poverty here runs well above most districts, at 17.1 percent, and homeownership lags behind most peers as well. The district is also unusually dense, packing people into a footprint tighter than most comparable seats.
André Carson.p2: Credit union offices here outrun credit union employment, a mismatch not typical of most places, with office presence running just above the national norm even as staffing falls well short of it. Elements Financial, Indiana Members, and Everwise anchor that presence, giving credit unions 29.1 percent of retail offices locally. JPMorgan Chase leads on deposits booked to its address, one name among 143 bank branches serving the district. For a place this stretched on income, credit unions carry a bigger share of the retail footprint than their payrolls alone would explain.
André Carson.p3: As measured in 2023, administrative and support and waste management services stood out as the most specialized sector, well ahead of the national norm. Health care employed a large share of workers, with manufacturing close behind it. Finance jobs overall ran above the national norm, though growth in that broader sector lagged slightly over the prior decade. Mortgage lending that year leaned heavily toward home purchases, with a substantial share of loans reaching lower-income neighborhoods.

Andy Barr.p1: Population here is spread thin on the ground, well below the density of most comparable seats, with just under 205 residents per square mile over 777,299 people total. Households earn a median $68,419 a year, on the low side for a district like this, while rent runs $1,142 a month. Homeownership sits at 60.6 percent. More families here live in poverty than in most comparable districts.
Andy Barr.p2: Credit unions hold just 13.3 percent of retail offices here, well below most comparable districts, leaving the bulk of the storefronts to banks. Commonwealth and Members Heritage carry a strong credit union presence locally. Central Bank & Trust Co. books more deposits than any other bank here, though that reflects where deposits get reported more than local branch reach, and it shares the market with many other banks. Credit union employment tracks that thin office presence closely, running below the national norm on both counts.
Andy Barr.p3: Manufacturing anchored this district's economy in 2023, employing a strong share of its workforce at well above the national norm, alongside a smaller specialization in agriculture and forestry. Health care and social assistance employed a large share of workers too. Finance and insurance jobs sat well under the national norm, a sign this economy leans on making things rather than managing money. Mortgage lending here favored home purchases over refinancing.

Andy Biggs.p1: Poverty here sits at 6.7 percent, lower than almost any comparable district, and it frames everything else about the 5th district of Arizona. Typical household income reaches 112,116 dollars, well clear of most peer districts, and homeownership runs high. Housing carries a price to match: a median home value of 546,900 dollars runs 4.9 times that income. The district is also dense for its kind, built up rather than spread thin.
Andy Biggs.p2: Credit union offices here punch above their weight even where jobs do not: offices run close to the national norm while credit union employment trails it, an imbalance that matters more than either figure alone. Desert Financial, Mountain America, and America First anchor the sector locally, and credit unions hold 25.1 percent of retail offices, a larger share than most other districts see. Wells Fargo books the largest deposit total under federal reporting rules, though that reflects where deposits get recorded, not which bank has the most branches or customers on the ground.
Andy Biggs.p3: By 2023, construction, finance and insurance, and retail trade stood out as the district's most concentrated sectors, each well above the national norm. Finance and insurance jobs ran 1.48 times that norm, and the broader finance and insurance sector grew at more than twice the national pace in the years since. Home purchase loans made up most mortgage activity, in a district where high incomes and high home values shape nearly every transaction.

Andy Harris.p1: Homeownership here sits well above other districts, at 76.5 percent, alongside household incomes far ahead of the typical district, a median of 95,306 dollars. Home values are unremarkable by comparison, a median of 378,700 dollars. Poverty and joblessness both stay low. Population is scattered lightly over the land, in a district that sits in Maryland's South region.
Andy Harris.p2: Credit union employment here runs slightly above the national norm even though office presence runs just under it, a split worth noting before any office count: jobs are outpacing branches. Aberdeen Proving Ground, Hanscom, and State Employees CU of Maryland anchor that presence. Credit unions hold 18.8 percent of retail offices, a smaller slice than most comparable districts carry, against a much larger bank branch network led on deposits by PNC, a figure that reflects booking rules more than local footprint. For the homeowners and steady earners described above, that leaves credit unions doing more with less shelf space.
Andy Harris.p3: The district's work leaned toward construction and educational services, both well above the national norm in concentration, alongside a smaller footprint in agriculture. Health care and retail trade employed the most people locally, though health care ran slightly under the national norm and retail slightly over it. Overall finance and insurance employment ran well under the national norm. Among all home lenders, most loans went toward home purchases rather than refinancing.

Andy Kim.p1: New Jersey is one of the most densely populated states in the country, and its households earn a median $104,294 a year, near the top nationally. That income runs against steep housing costs: home values near $496,000 against rent of $1,800 a month, with homeownership trailing most other states at 63.9 percent. Poverty is uncommon here, yet unemployment runs higher than almost anywhere else, an odd pairing for a state this prosperous on paper.
Andy Kim.p2: Affinity, Police & Fire, and Visions anchor the credit union presence here, though credit unions hold only 12.4 percent of retail offices, a low share compared with other states. Bank of America, National Association is the largest institution by deposits credited to the state, a figure shaped by where accounts are booked rather than by branch counts alone. Credit union jobs sit well under the national norm, at 0.26 times, and office presence is thin too. Given the income and housing costs above, credit unions here operate on a smaller scale than the population would elsewhere support.
Andy Kim.p3: The job base leans on Transportation and Warehousing and Wholesale Trade, both well above the national norm in concentration, alongside a strong Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services sector. That mix reflects a state built around moving goods and expertise through a crowded corridor rather than around one dominant employer. Finance and insurance employment overall sat slightly above the national norm in 2023. New Jersey's economy runs on logistics and specialized services more than on any single trade.

Angela Alsobrooks.p1: Maryland packs its people in tight, with density far greater than most states along the corridor between Washington and Baltimore. Median household income runs among the highest in the country at 102,905 dollars, and poverty is rarer here than in nearly any other state. Home values reach 436,300 dollars, higher than most states show, though the cost of housing relative to income lands in the middle of the pack. Work here leans toward government and technical services rather than production or trade.
Angela Alsobrooks.p2: Credit union business here runs through Navy Federal, State Employees CU of Maryland, and Tower, set against a market where Bank of America leads on deposits booked to its addresses, one name among 1,153 bank branches statewide. Credit unions hold just 21.3 percent of retail offices, a smaller share than most states carry. Credit union employment sits close to the national norm, tracking the office count rather than running ahead of it. That leaves a narrow lane: high incomes and low poverty, served by credit unions that occupy a modest corner of a bank-dominated market.
Angela Alsobrooks.p3: As measured in 2023, Maryland's economy leaned hard on public administration, at nearly twice the national norm, and on professional, scientific, and technical services, both a specialty and a leading source of work. Construction ran slightly above the national pace as well. Overall finance and insurance work ran well below the national norm, leaving this a state defined less by finance and more by government and expertise for hire.

Angie Craig.p1: Poverty in the 2nd congressional seat of Minnesota sits at just 6.6 percent, among the lowest of any comparable district. Median household income runs to $108,162, and homeownership is high by national standards. Home values sit well above income in absolute terms, yet the ratio between them stays modest by national standards. It is a large district of 746,020 people, prosperous and stable rather than strained.
Angie Craig.p2: Credit union employment here runs slightly ahead of the national norm while credit union offices trail it, jobs outpacing branch presence. TruStone Financial, Ent, and Affinity Plus carry that work. Credit unions hold 21.1 percent of retail offices against banks, unremarkable for a place with this much household wealth, with Wells Fargo booking the largest deposit total among the district's many competing bank branches. Prosperous households paired with a thin credit union footprint are what any credit union here has to build from.
Angie Craig.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing anchored the district's economy, employing 14.1 percent of its roughly 249,000 jobs and running well above typical concentration nationally. Wholesale trade and construction were also specialized, each a notable share of local employment. Health care, despite its size, ran below the national norm for concentration here. Across all lenders, most mortgage activity was tied to home purchases rather than refinancing, with only a small slice reaching lower-income neighborhoods.

Angus King.p1: Maine's typical household brings in $76,442 a year, less than most states manage, though joblessness is among the lowest anywhere. The state is thinly settled and skews a bit older, with people spread across the land rather than packed into it. Homes carry a value of $341,900, well above what that income would comfortably support, and owning a home is the norm rather than the exception.
Angus King.p2: Atlantic Regional, Maine Savings, and Evergreen anchor a credit union presence that is unusually thick for a state this size. Credit unions hold 34.2 percent of retail offices, a share few other states match. Their branch networks have grown faster than their staffing has kept pace. TD Bank shows the top deposit figure booked here under federal rule, a reflection of where deposits get recorded rather than of local branch strength, and other lenders still fill out the same market of households described above.
Angus King.p3: As of 2023, health care and social assistance employed the most people, followed by retail trade, and both employed more people relative to the national pattern than is typical elsewhere. Agriculture and fishing punched above their weight too, work tied to land and sea rather than an office economy. Finance and insurance employment overall sat a touch below the national norm, with growth over the decade before that lagging the country as well. Retail and those land and sea trades, not banking, are what this state does best.

Ann Wagner.p1: Homes here run about 3.6 times the typical household's income, with rent taking a modest 14.9 percent of it, a combination that keeps housing cost lower than almost anywhere comparable. Household income runs well above most districts like it, and homeownership is unusually common. This is a stable, well-off district where few rent out of necessity.
Ann Wagner.p2: Credit union offices here have multiplied faster than credit union payrolls have, so the office presence no longer matches the workforce behind it. First Community, Vantage, and Together carry that presence into a market where credit union offices hold just 18.8 percent of retail banking locations, well under the share most comparable districts show. U.S. Bank National Association books the largest deposit share among the district's banks, a result of where deposits get recorded more than of branches on the ground here. A credit union in this district serves affluent, largely homeowning households while running leaner on staff than its office presence would imply.
Ann Wagner.p3: The economy measured in 2023 leaned hardest on management of companies, at 2.14 times the national norm, alongside finance and insurance and information work. Health care and social assistance and retail trade were the largest sources of jobs. Finance and insurance employment ran at 1.5 times the national norm, even as the wider sector's growth trailed the nation's pace across the decade before. This is corporate back-office and finance country, built on a retail and health care base.

Anna Luna.p1: Housing eats an unusual share of income here: home values run 5.2 times the typical household's earnings, and rent takes 27.2 percent of median income. Most residents own rather than rent, and poverty runs well below typical levels for a district this size. Median age is 51, older than most places this size, in a district that is also unusually dense.
Anna Luna.p2: Credit unions hold just 15.6 percent of retail offices here, a share well below most comparable districts, leaving banks as the dominant channel for everyday financial services. Navy Federal Credit Union, Achieva Credit Union, and MIDFLORIDA are the names present here, competing against a bank sector where Raymond James Bank leads on paper, a booking result more than a sign of local branch strength. Credit union employment sits below the national norm and tracks that thin office presence closely. For an older, high-homeownership population carrying steep housing costs, local credit union capacity looks modest next to the need.
Anna Luna.p3: As of 2023, the district's economy leaned on management of companies and enterprises, real estate, and accommodation and food services, the first of these its most specialized sector by far. Jobs in finance and insurance sat close to the national norm on the whole, but the sector grew faster than the country did over the following decade. Mortgage lending skewed heavily toward home purchases, which made up 54.6 percent of all originations that year.

April McClain Delaney.p1: Household income in the 6th congressional seat of Maryland runs well above most comparable districts, at 105,125 dollars a year. Homes carry a median value of 433,800 dollars against that income, a ratio that lands on the moderate side for the country, and rent claims a modest share of the typical household's earnings. Homeownership is common here, and both poverty and unemployment sit well below what most districts see.
April McClain Delaney.p2: Credit unions here hold a stronger footprint in offices than in jobs, a gap worth leading with: office presence runs slightly above the national norm while credit union employment sits below it. Navy Federal Credit Union, State Employees CU of Maryland, and NYMEO anchor that presence. Credit unions hold 26.8 percent of retail offices here, well above what most districts show, competing against a broader roster of banks led on deposits by Truist. That combination points to lean back-office staffing serving a well-off, low-poverty customer base while banks still handle much of the volume.
April McClain Delaney.p3: The district's job mix leans hard into professional, scientific, and technical services, well above the national norm, alongside public administration and retail trade. Health care and social assistance employs a sizeable share of workers, though at a rate below the norm seen elsewhere, and overall finance and insurance jobs run under the national norm as well. Across all lenders, most mortgage activity here was for home purchases rather than refinancing, and a meaningful share of lending reached lower-income neighborhoods.

Ashley Hinson.p1: Housing here costs little against what people earn: a median home value of $215,400 set against household income of $75,299 gives a value-to-income ratio of 2.9, among the lowest of any district measured. Rent runs modestly each month, a small share of typical income. Homeownership is common, and unemployment is very low. Household income itself trails most other districts.
Ashley Hinson.p2: Credit union jobs here run far ahead of credit union office presence, at close to two and a half times the national norm for jobs against under twice the norm for offices. These institutions do more with less physical footprint than most places manage. Veridian, GreenState and Dupaco Community anchor that work, holding 22.7 percent of retail offices while banks fill out the rest of the branch network, Cedar Rapids Bank and Trust Company among them, leading locally on deposits booked here. That is a lot of institutional weight for a district where incomes are modest and homeownership runs high.
Ashley Hinson.p3: The district's economy, measured in 2023, ran on manufacturing, which employed 18.1 percent of workers at a level far beyond the national norm and unmatched by any other sector here. Finance and insurance jobs also ran above that norm, and agriculture held a smaller but still notable footprint. Most mortgage originations that year financed home purchases rather than refinancing.

Ashley Moody.p1: Florida is crowded and getting older, packed far more densely than the typical state, with a median age of 42.7. The typical household earns $77,735 a year, an unremarkable figure next to other states, while the median home is valued well beyond what most states report, running roughly five times that income. Rent runs high, and poverty sits above what most states report.
Ashley Moody.p2: Suncoast, Navy Federal Credit Union, and VyStar all carry meaningful weight here, yet credit unions hold only 21.4 percent of retail offices statewide, a thinner slice than most states can claim, and modest next to Bank of America, the deposit leader among many rivals across the state. Credit union employment still runs 1.31 times the national norm, well ahead of the 0.72 times showing on office counts. For a lender serving Florida's earners and renters, that is a lot of payroll behind a comparatively small storefront footprint.
Ashley Moody.p3: As measured in 2023, Florida's economy leaned hardest into arts, entertainment, and recreation, real estate, and administrative and support services, all well beyond the national norm for their share of jobs. Retail trade and accommodation and food services also ran hot against that norm, with food service and hospitality among the most visible parts of daily commerce. Total employment approached 9 million jobs, in a state whose finance and insurance sector grew faster than the nation's over the prior decade.

August Pfluger.p1: This district spreads its population thin, among the lowest densities of any congressional seat in the country, with just 41.8 people per square mile across 802,030 residents. Median household income sits at 71,363 dollars, and typical home values run modest next to other districts even as housing costs overall weigh heavier than most. The poverty rate reaches 14.5 percent. Median age here is 34.2.
August Pfluger.p2: Credit union offices here outpace credit union jobs, a gap worth noting first: office presence is specialized against the national norm, while employment in the industry falls short of that same mark. Navy Federal, Pentagon, and Complex Community anchor that presence on the ground. Credit unions hold 28.4 percent of retail offices, a share ahead of most other districts, against a banking sector where Frost Bank books the top deposits under federal reporting rules. For a district with modest income and heavier housing costs, that reach matters.
August Pfluger.p3: As of 2023, oil and gas extraction dominated the job base, its share of employment far beyond what the national norm would predict and well ahead of anything else measured here. Broader finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm, and it gained ground more slowly than the country did over the ten years studied. Most mortgage lending in this district, across every lender active there, went toward buying homes rather than refinancing them. This remains a district built, first, around drilling.

Austin Scott.p1: Household income in the 8th congressional seat of Georgia sits at $61,302, among the lowest of any seat in the state's delegation, and that gap shapes everything else here. Home values run low as well, keeping housing costs modest relative to what people earn. Poverty runs high even as unemployment stays low, a district where work is steady but pay is thin. At just 72.1 people per square mile, this is rural ground, not suburban sprawl.
Austin Scott.p2: Robins Financial, First Commerce, and Southeastern anchor the credit union presence here, holding 23.3 percent of retail offices between them, a share in line with comparable districts. Ameris Bank books the largest deposits, a figure driven by where accounts get recorded rather than where branches actually sit, and it competes with a wide field of other banks in the district. Credit union employment runs above the national norm, a real if modest concentration. For a district built on lower incomes and lean housing costs, that gives credit unions genuine weight to lend against.
Austin Scott.p3: Manufacturing and agriculture set this district apart from most: agriculture runs at 3.03 times the national norm, anchoring an economy built on production rather than offices. As of 2023, total employment stood near 229,900 across the district. Finance and insurance employment overall runs well below the national norm, leaving credit unions to carry more of that sector's weight than elsewhere. This remains a district tied to fields and factory floors.

Ayanna Pressley.p1: This district packs residents in far more densely than the typical American seat, a young, urban place where the median resident is barely 32. Incomes run high at $98,603, but home values dwarf even that, running seven times what a typical household earns. Homeownership is rare here, and poverty sits well above most districts at 16.3 percent even as unemployment stays unremarkable.
Ayanna Pressley.p2: Credit union employment here runs at just 0.54 times the national norm, thin even though credit union offices are closer to typical, a gap that points to smaller local staffs stretched across their footprint. METRO, Harvard, and American Airlines credit unions anchor that presence, holding 18.7 percent of retail offices against banks, a smaller slice than similar districts hold. Bank of America carries the largest deposit total booked to this district, a figure that says more about where deposits get recorded than about branches on the ground. Credit unions here work a crowded, expensive market from a thinner office base than peers enjoy.
Ayanna Pressley.p3: The job base measured in 2023 leaned hard on Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services, employing workers at over twice the national norm, alongside Educational Services and Health Care and Social Assistance, each a leading employer in its own right. Overall finance employment ran 1.25 times the national norm. Lending here tilted toward home purchases, making up most of all originations, with roughly half going to lower-income neighborhoods.

Barry Loudermilk.p1: Household income in the 11th district of Georgia stands well above most congressional districts, at 98,527 dollars. Homes carry a median value of 443,700 dollars against that income, a ratio of 4.5, while rent runs to 1,684 dollars a month. Homeownership is common here, and both poverty and unemployment sit lower than in most comparable places. Population runs to 811,695.
Barry Loudermilk.p2: Credit union employment here sits closer to the national norm than the credit union office footprint does, a gap worth noting given the household finances above. Credit unions hold 21.6 percent of retail offices here, a share in line with comparable districts, against a field of many separate banks, among them Synovus Bank, which books more deposits than any other under federal reporting rules. LGE Community, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Delta Community are the names doing that work here. That combination points to a district with plenty of deposit-taking demand and room for credit unions to grow their physical presence into it.
Barry Loudermilk.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing led local employment and ran well ahead of the national norm for its share of jobs, alongside strength in wholesale trade and construction. Overall finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm, even as broader hiring in the sector had grown over the prior decade. Mortgage lending that year leaned heavily toward home purchases, making up most originations.

Barry Moore.p1: Homeownership here reaches 75.7 percent, the fact that sets this district apart from comparable places. Home values sit modestly against that, a median of 255,700 dollars against household income of 71,253 dollars, with rent near 1,074 dollars a month. Poverty runs higher than in most districts. The district is lightly settled, spread across a substantial population.
Barry Moore.p2: Credit unions hold 30.9 percent of retail offices here, a share that runs well above most comparable districts. ALL IN, PenAir, and Navy Federal are the names with a strong presence, set against Regions Bank, which leads local deposits among a field of many separate banks. Credit union employment and office presence both run well above the national norm, with branches built out even further ahead of the staff filling them. That is a heavy institutional footprint for a district where incomes and home values both trail most of the country.
Barry Moore.p3: Manufacturing anchors the industrial base, employing 13.2 percent of workers, a specialization well above the national norm, alongside a utilities sector that runs even more specialized. Retail trade employs a comparable share of the workforce. Overall finance and insurance employment lags the country, even with credit unions running thick against that norm. As of 2023, mortgage lending here skewed heavily toward home purchase rather than refinancing, the dominant use of credit in this district's housing market.

Becca Balint.p1: Unemployment sits at just 2.7 percent, a rate lower than nearly every congressional district measured, and it frames a place with little economic slack. The typical household earns 82,730 dollars, unremarkable next to other districts, and rent claims a smaller bite of that income than in most places. Homeownership is common at 73.2 percent and poverty is rare. People are spread thin here, across a district that is, in effect, the entire state of Vermont.
Becca Balint.p2: Credit union employment runs far above the national norm here, at more than double, while credit union offices, though also above average, lag that pace, a sign these institutions do more work per branch than elsewhere. EASTRISE, VERMONT, and NORTH COUNTRY anchor that presence, and credit unions hold 27.5 percent of retail offices, a share higher than most districts see, against 219 bank branches serving the same market. TD Bank shows a large deposit figure under federal booking rules, but that reflects reporting quirks more than local reach.
Becca Balint.p3: As measured in 2023, retail trade and agriculture stood out among this district's specialized sectors, with farming work concentrated well beyond what the national mix would predict. Health care and social assistance made up a large share of employment, out of roughly 278,700 jobs total. Overall finance employment ran below the national norm even as credit unions themselves ran well above it, a split worth noting.

Ben Cline.p1: Unemployment here runs well below other districts, at 3.2 percent, and poverty stays low too, at 10.9 percent. Median household income, 74,264 dollars, lags behind most peer districts, and home values fall low alongside it. Housing costs stack up light against income by national standards. At 127.4 people per square mile, this is open country by district standards, work here, not crowded living.
Ben Cline.p2: Credit union employment towers over the national norm, 5.4 times, far out of proportion to the office share credit unions hold against banks, a share that itself runs high next to other districts. DuPont Community, Virginia, and Freedom First anchor that presence. Deposits booked to Truist Bank exceed those at any other bank in the district, though the figure follows internal accounting more than where residents actually walk in to bank. Between them, these institutions are working with a population that earns modestly, owns homes at low cost, and borrows steadily.
Ben Cline.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing drove the district's economy, at 1.62 times the national norm, alongside transportation and warehousing and corporate management functions, both also specialized. Health care and social assistance accounted for a sizable slice of work too, slightly above the national norm. Finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm overall. This is a place built on making and moving things, not on finance, even where credit unions punch above their weight.

Ben Luján.p1: New Mexico is home to about 2.13 million people, spread across some of the emptiest ground in the country. Median household income sits at 67,816 dollars, well below most states, and poverty runs near the top of the national scale. Even so, homeownership is unusually high at 71.1 percent. Unemployment runs high too, a sign of an economy still finding its footing.
Ben Luján.p2: Nusenda, Sunward, and Sandia Area anchor a credit union footprint with real reach in this state: credit unions hold 31.6 percent of retail offices here, a share few states can match. Credit union jobs run far past the national norm, a highly specialized concentration, while office counts are elevated by a smaller margin, so these institutions run leaner and busier than their branch presence alone implies. Wells Fargo is named the largest bank locally under federal reporting rules, but it shares the state with many other banks. For a population with thin incomes and high homeownership, that credit union presence carries real weight.
Ben Luján.p3: As of 2023, the state's economy leaned hardest on mining and oil and gas extraction, several times the national norm, alongside specialized public administration and agricultural sectors. Health care, retail, and food service rounded out the sectors that kept the most residents on payroll. Finance and insurance work overall sat well below the national norm, leaving credit unions to carry an outsized share of that sector's presence. This is a state built on resource extraction and government work, with finance itself a comparatively small trade.

Bennie Thompson.p1: People are spread thin across the 2nd district of Mississippi, just 38.6 residents per square mile, a sparseness few other House seats can match. Roughly 694,703 people live here, and household income sits low by national standards. Poverty runs high, and unemployment follows the same pattern. Home values are modest too, with a median of $126,300.
Bennie Thompson.p2: Credit union offices here actually outnumber what the local workforce would predict from staffing alone, running above the national norm even as credit union employment lags below it, a gap between presence and payroll worth noting. Mutual, Hope, and Keesler credit unions anchor that presence, though credit unions hold only 17.4 percent of retail offices against a much larger field of bank branches led on paper by Trustmark National Bank's deposit bookings. For a district with this much poverty, that office share still marks a real foothold in communities banks reach less often.
Bennie Thompson.p3: By 2023, agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting, and utilities stood out as the district's most distinctive industries, both far above national norms, with public administration close behind. Health care, manufacturing, and retail trade employed the most people, out of roughly 236,000 jobs total. Home purchases dominated mortgage activity, making up 55.8 percent of originations, with less reaching lower income neighborhoods.

Bernard Sanders.p1: Vermont holds 648,493 people at a median age of 43.9, thinly settled across the state. Median household income reaches $82,730, above most states, and few residents anywhere in the country go without work or fall into poverty as rarely as they do here. Homeownership runs unusually high, at 73.2 percent, while overall housing costs stay easy against that income. This is a place where people work steadily and mostly own the roof over their heads.
Bernard Sanders.p2: EASTRISE, VERMONT, and NORTH COUNTRY are the credit unions doing business here, and together the sector holds 27.5 percent of retail offices, a wide footprint given how few people live here. Credit union employment runs well above the national norm, a specialized presence in the local job market, with office numbers following that same pattern. TD Bank carries the largest deposit figure booked to an address in the state, though plenty of other banks operate branches of their own here too. For a household earning $82,730 and holding a paid-off home, that credit union presence is one they will actually meet.
Bernard Sanders.p3: Health care and social assistance was the largest sector in 2023, and educational services followed close behind as the most specialized part of the economy. Retail trade added further weight to the job count, itself a step above the national norm. Overall finance employment ran below that norm, leaving credit unions as the clearest area of financial strength the state had to show.

Bernie Moreno.p1: Ohio is a state of nearly 11.9 million people, packed far tighter than typical American ground. Median household income runs 72,212 dollars, below most states, while unemployment stays low. Housing remains a bargain against that income: a median home value of 239,800 dollars keeps the value-to-income ratio at just 3.3. Rent draws a modest share of median income, leaving room in household budgets that many states do not offer.
Bernie Moreno.p2: Wright-Patt Credit Union, General Electric, and Kemba Financial anchor credit union presence in this state, though credit unions hold only 20 percent of retail offices statewide, a smaller slice than most comparable states show. Credit union offices run slightly above the national norm relative to population, even as credit union jobs lag it, meaning branches outpace the staff behind them. U.S. Bank National Association books the top deposits under federal rules, one name among thousands of branches across the state. That mismatch between office reach and thin staffing is the ground a credit union here has to work.
Bernie Moreno.p3: As measured in 2023, manufacturing anchored the state's economy, employing 13.4 percent of jobs at a rate well beyond the national norm for that sector. Health care and social assistance employed a bigger share of workers than any other sector. Management of companies also ran strong relative to national patterns. Overall finance employment sat almost exactly at the national norm, with growth over the prior decade tracking that same steady pace.

Beth Van Duyne.p1: Household income here is among the highest of any congressional district, at $119,295. Home values run high as well, well above income itself, and homeownership trails what most districts see even as poverty stays rare. People are packed in tightly across this district, home to 772,892 people. The money in this district is real, and it is concentrated in people who own rather than rent.
Beth Van Duyne.p2: Credit unions hold a small piece of the retail office count against banks, just 15.0 percent. American Airlines Credit Union, Navy Federal Credit Union, and EECU carry that presence. Credit union employment runs well under the national norm, thinner even than the office count itself, so the offices that do exist carry more work per job than is typical elsewhere. NexBank leads the district by deposits credited to addresses here, a measure of booking practice more than of branches or local customers.
Beth Van Duyne.p3: Transportation and warehousing dominates the job base here unlike almost anywhere else, far above the national norm for that sector. Finance and insurance also runs well above the norm, and grew faster than the country as a whole across the years measured through 2023. Retail and administrative services fill out much of the rest of the working district. Purchase loans made up most mortgage activity here, with a much smaller share of lending reaching lower income neighborhoods.

Betty McCollum.p1: This district packs 708,464 residents into a footprint far denser than the typical congressional seat, a compact stretch of the Midwest. The typical household earns 84,731 dollars, and unemployment stands at a low 4.2 percent. Homes are valued at about 4.2 times income, and both rent and homeownership come in under what most other districts show. Housing here takes a smaller bite out of pay than the norm, even with fewer owners on the rolls.
Betty McCollum.p2: Credit union staffing outpaces what the office count by itself would lead you to expect, concentrated into fewer, busier locations rather than spread evenly. BLAZE, TrustOne Financial, and Affinity Plus anchor that presence. Credit unions hold 28.7 percent of retail offices, a share that beats most peer districts, set against a bank branch network run by many separate banks. For a workforce living this close together, that blend of concentrated staffing and solid office footing shapes what a credit union here has to work with.
Betty McCollum.p3: Management of companies stands out by a wide margin, employing at over three times the national norm, with public administration running near double. Health care and manufacturing form the steady core of employment, both running a touch above the national norm as of 2023. Finance overall employed at 1.12 times the norm that year, though the sector grew more slowly here than it did nationwide over the prior decade. This is a district anchored in corporate back offices and government work, built on a base of health care and manufacturing.

Bill Cassidy.p1: Louisiana is home to almost 4.6 million people, with a median household income near the bottom among states at $60,986. Home values are similarly low, yet rent and housing costs still weigh heavily against what people earn. Poverty runs higher here than in nearly every other state, at 18.7 percent, and joblessness at 5.2 percent adds further strain.
Bill Cassidy.p2: Barksdale, Keesler, and Neighbors anchor a credit union presence that claims 25.1 percent of retail offices statewide, a share above most other states. Credit union offices run well ahead of the national norm here, while credit union employment tracks close to it, so the state carries more branches than its staffing alone would explain. JPMorgan Chase is named the largest holder of deposits under federal booking rules, a single name set against 1,325 bank branches belonging to many competing institutions. For households stretched thin on rent and income, that branch presence gives credit unions unusual reach into everyday financial life.
Bill Cassidy.p3: Oil and gas extraction was the clear specialty in the 2023 employment count, running four times the national norm despite employing a small share of workers directly. Construction also ran well above typical levels for a state. Health care, retail, and food service employed the most people day to day, without being specialties in their own right. What Louisiana does unusually well is extraction and building, not banking.

Bill Foster.p1: Poverty here runs among the lowest of any comparable district, just 7.3 percent, alongside income well clear of most peers at $108,620. Housing follows suit: homes carry a typical value against income, and rent takes a small slice of that income, lighter than in most places. Homeownership runs high too, in a district packed more densely than most of its peers.
Bill Foster.p2: Credit unions hold just 14.1 percent of retail offices here, a slimmer share than in most comparable districts, leaving banks with most of the ground. Consumers, DuPage, and Michigan State credit unions are the names on the local map, working against 178 bank branches in all, with deposits booked mostly to Chase. Credit union employment tracks closely with credit union office presence here, both sitting under the national norm. Against a district this affluent and this thick with homeowners, credit unions work a smaller corner of a well-off market.
Bill Foster.p3: As measured in 2023, wholesale trade stood out sharply, running close to twice the national norm, alongside manufacturing and technical services, both specialized as well. Manufacturing was also a leading employer, close behind retail trade and health care combined. Overall finance employment ran below the national norm, and growth in finance and insurance together trailed slightly too. This is a district built more on making and moving goods, and on technical work, than on finance itself.

Bill Hagerty.p1: Tennessee holds just over 7.2 million people, densely settled compared with most states. Median household income runs 71,997 dollars, trailing most of the country, and 13.5 percent of residents live in poverty. Rent and other housing costs run higher here than in most states even though home values themselves land in the middling range. Homeownership also lags most peers, at 66.8 percent.
Bill Hagerty.p2: Three names carry weight here: Eastman, Knoxville TVA Employees, and Ascend. Credit unions hold 22.4 percent of retail offices statewide, a share in line with other states, though their office presence runs specialized against the national norm while credit union employment itself sits close to that norm, meaning offices have grown ahead of staff. Pinnacle Bank books a large deposit share under federal reporting rules, but it shares the field with many other banks operating branches across the state. That leaves credit unions serving a population earning well under the national norm, in a state where the cost of a place to live already eats into thin household budgets.
Bill Hagerty.p3: As of 2023, transportation and warehousing and manufacturing stood out as the state's most specialized sectors, both running well above national norms. Manufacturing alone accounted for 12.0 percent of the state's jobs. Health care employed the most people overall but without the same concentration. Finance and insurance jobs sat slightly below the national norm, in a state built more on moving goods and making things than on financial services.

Bill Huizenga.p1: Housing here costs far less relative to income than in most congressional districts, and that gap shapes everything else. A home runs 3.7 times the median household income of 73,702 dollars, and rent takes just 18 percent of it. More households here own their homes than rent them, and unemployment sits low, at 3.4 percent. It is a working, middle-income district in the Midwest.
Bill Huizenga.p2: Credit unions hold 45.7 percent of retail offices here, a share among the highest anywhere in the country's congressional map, putting them close to parity with the banks around them. Lake Michigan, Consumers, and Advia carry that presence locally, while Fifth Third leads on deposits booked to the district, one name among several banks doing business there. Credit union employment runs more than twice the national norm, and office presence nearly three times it, outpacing the jobs behind it. The households and modest earners above are the base this credit union strength was built on.
Bill Huizenga.p3: In 2021, manufacturing dominated the district's job base, employing a large share of all workers and running at close to three times the national concentration. Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting carried a similarly outsized weight in the local economy, marking this as a production and land-based economy rather than a service hub. Overall finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm even as credit unions themselves ran well above it. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, with a much smaller share reaching lower-income neighborhoods.

Blake Moore.p1: Unemployment here sits at 3.0 percent, among the lowest anywhere on the map of comparable districts, and it sets the tone for a young, fast-earning population. The median household brings in 92,358 dollars a year, comfortably ahead of most other districts. Home values run high next to income, a ratio of 5.6, though rent stays modest by comparison. Density is thin, under 85 people per square mile, in a district still built around single-family ownership.
Blake Moore.p2: Credit unions hold a striking share of retail offices here, 50.0 percent, putting them on equal footing with the banking sector rather than at its margins. America First, Mountain America, and Goldenwest anchor that presence, well known names across this stretch of Utah. Credit union payrolls run far thicker here than the national norm would predict, and that hiring has outpaced even the growth in office locations. The largest bank by deposits, Morgan Stanley Bank, N.A., books its figures here under federal rules rather than through any real local branch network, one name among many banks with a presence in the district.
