Blake Moore.p3: Manufacturing and public administration stood out in the 2023 job counts, both employing well beyond their national share. Health care added real weight to the payroll too, a steady source of work locally. Mortgage activity skewed toward home purchases, and a smaller slice of lending reached lower-income neighborhoods.

Bonnie Watson Coleman.p1: Household income in the 12th district sits among the highest of any congressional seat, at $117,099. Home values run high too, at $529,100, against rent of $1,932 a month, though housing costs overall land in the middle range once measured against comparable places. Poverty runs low, at 9.1 percent, even as unemployment sits a touch higher than in most districts. Compared with its peers, this is also a tightly packed district, its population settled closer together than most.
Bonnie Watson Coleman.p2: Credit unions hold just 14.9 percent of retail offices here, a thin slice next to what banks control elsewhere. Credit Union of New Jersey, Affinity, and Financial Resources carry that smaller footprint. Credit union employment runs thin against the national norm, and office presence lags it too, though offices still hold up better than jobs do in relative terms. Set against the income and low poverty described above, this is a district where credit unions work a small corner of a wealthy lending market that banks otherwise dominate.
Bonnie Watson Coleman.p3: As of 2023, Public Administration made up 11.2 percent of jobs, more than two and a half times what the national norm would predict, well clear of every other sector measured here. Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services followed, both a large employer and a specialized one in its own right. Mortgage activity that year tilted strongly toward buyers purchasing homes rather than refinancing, with a smaller share reaching lower-income neighborhoods.

Brad Finstad.p1: Housing here is unusually affordable next to income, the sharpest thing distinguishing this district from its peers: a typical home costs about 3.5 times what a typical household earns, and rent claims only 16 percent of median income. Homeownership runs well above most districts, at 74.3 percent, alongside low poverty and low unemployment. Density is thin, just 58.7 people per square mile, consistent with a place built around owned homes rather than rented ones.
Brad Finstad.p2: Credit unions hold a comparatively small footprint here, just 15.3 percent of retail offices in a district where banks otherwise dominate the shelf space. Mayo Employees, Affinity Plus, and Altra carry the credit union name locally, up against a Wells Fargo operation that tops the deposit figures for this area, in a market crowded with other lenders as well. Jobs and offices tied to credit unions both fall short of what the national picture would predict. That leaves a modest base to build on, given a population of homeowners with steady incomes and little debt stress.
Brad Finstad.p3: The 2023 employment picture shows a district built on making and healing: manufacturing and health care are the two sectors that most set this place apart nationally, and health care alone accounts for 26.2 percent of the jobs here. Agriculture is similarly overrepresented relative to national patterns. Finance employment here is thin by comparison, and has grown slowly. This is a place defined by production and care work, not by finance.

Brad Knott.p1: Housing here costs strikingly little against what people earn: the median home runs about four times the median household income, and rent claims just 17.2 percent of it, well below most comparable districts. Household income clears $85,183, ahead of most peer districts, and homeownership stands far above the norm at 75.9 percent of households. Owning outright, rather than renting, is simply how most people here live.
Brad Knott.p2: Credit union employment runs slightly above the national norm even though credit union office presence runs below it, a gap worth noting first: these institutions employ more than their office presence alone would imply. State Employees', Navy Federal Credit Union, and URW Community are the names on the ground. Credit unions hold just 20.0 percent of retail offices here, trailing most comparable districts, and Truist Bank leads locally on deposits, a name that reflects where deposits get booked rather than who serves customers nearby. For a district with this much income and homeownership behind it, the credit union presence runs thinner than the office count alone shows.
Brad Knott.p3: Manufacturing and retail trade each account for 14.1 percent of the district's roughly 174,800 jobs measured in 2023, with manufacturing running well above the national norm. Construction also runs strong here. Finance and insurance employment overall sits below the national norm, even though that combined sector had grown faster than the national pace over the decade to 2023, a decade across which the district's lines were redrawn.

Brad Sherman.p1: Home values in the 32nd district sit near the top of the national range, with a median close to $1,135,000 against a typical household income of $108,176. Home prices run over ten times income here, a gap that marks this place apart more than any other number attached to it. Rent runs a median $2,351 a month, and homeownership falls short of what most other districts see. Density here runs high too, shaped by people working in offices and classrooms rather than on factory floors or in warehouses.
Brad Sherman.p2: Credit unions hold just 14.4 percent of retail offices here, a thin share next to the district's 152 bank branches. LOGIX, PREMIER AMERICA, and a third named institution carry a strong presence locally among them. Credit union employment trails the national norm, though it outpaces the office count, pointing to leaner branches doing more work per location. For a credit union, the customers here are high earners carrying expensive homes, in a market where credit unions themselves hold comparatively little ground.
Brad Sherman.p3: As measured in 2023, work in the district leaned on real estate, arts and entertainment, and professional and scientific services, all running well above the national norm. Finance and insurance employment overall ran a bit above the national norm too, though its growth over the prior decade lagged the national pace. Services and expertise carry this economy far more than production does, with money concentrated in property and knowledge work.

Bradley Schneider.p1: Household income in the 10th district of Illinois runs well above most comparable districts, at 103,955 dollars a year. Homes carry a modest value against that income, and rent claims just 17.3 percent of the median household's earnings. Homeownership runs high, and poverty stays low. This is a dense Midwest district, more crowded than most of its counterparts.
Bradley Schneider.p2: Credit union employment sits nearly at the national norm, 0.8 times the typical rate, but the office count falls further short at 0.65, a sign that fewer branches here carry a fuller staffing load. Navy Federal, Consumers, and Baxter anchor the credit union presence, holding 23.4 percent of retail offices against banks. Lake Forest Bank & Trust books the top deposit total under federal rules, though it competes with many other banks and their branches across the district. Credit unions here operate out of fewer storefronts than a district this affluent might otherwise carry.
Bradley Schneider.p3: Manufacturing was the dominant force in this district's economy as of 2023, taking in 16.6 percent of jobs at close to twice the national concentration. Wholesale trade and corporate management showed similarly outsized shares, pointing to an economy weighted toward production and distribution over services. Overall finance employment landed almost exactly at the national norm, and its growth over the prior decade lagged behind typical rates elsewhere.

Brandon Gill.p1: Median household income in the 26th congressional seat of Texas is among the highest anywhere in the country, at 122,953 dollars. Home values run well ahead of income, yet the gap between the two is modest and rent claims a small slice of that income. Most households own rather than rent here. Pay in this district clears the cost of living with room to spare.
Brandon Gill.p2: Credit unions here employ far below the national norm, at 0.36 times expected levels, even as their office footprint sits closer to typical, offices outpacing jobs on the ground. DATCU, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Texans Credit Union anchor that presence, though credit unions hold only 19.4 percent of retail offices in the district. Charles Schwab Bank, SSB carries the top deposit figure booked locally, a function of reporting rules rather than branch reach, among many competing banks nearby. The high-earning households described above are thin ground for credit union jobs compared with what banks book.
Brandon Gill.p3: As of 2023, the district leaned on mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction, running more than twice the national norm, alongside wholesale trade and transportation and warehousing, each well above typical levels. Retail trade and health care carried large shares of jobs, though neither strayed far from national norms. Finance and insurance employment ran 1.43 times the national norm, well above typical levels nationally. Oil, trade, and logistics sit at the center of an economy built on a high-income workforce.

Brendan Boyle.p1: This district crowds people onto the land more tightly than nearly anywhere else in the country, with close to 738,540 residents packed into the Northeast's tightest quarters. Household income sits low compared with other districts, and poverty runs high alongside unemployment. Homes here cost far less than in most districts, yet rent and monthly housing costs push higher anyway, a mismatch that squeezes household budgets from both ends. Homeownership trails most comparable places too.
Brendan Boyle.p2: Credit union employment here runs below the national norm while credit union offices hold closer to it, so the offices carry more weight locally than the staffing behind them. Police & Fire, American Heritage, and Philadelphia are the names doing that work, running branches that make up 25.2 percent of retail offices, a share above most other districts. Wells Fargo lands on top under federal rules for booking deposits, one name among 116 bank branches split across many competing banks. For the people described above, tight incomes and heavy housing costs make that credit union presence a meaningful alternative to the banks around it.
Brendan Boyle.p3: As of 2023, health care and social assistance dominated the job base, employing 31.3 percent of workers, a share far beyond the national norm. Utilities and public administration also carried far more weight than typical staffing levels elsewhere. Total employment approached 283,400 jobs, concentrated in institutions that serve people directly rather than in sectors that make or ship goods.

Brett Guthrie.p1: Housing here costs far less relative to income than in most congressional districts: the median home is valued at 3.4 times median household income, and rent runs to just 16.9 percent of that income. Median household income sits below most peer districts. Homeownership is unusually high at 70.5 percent, and both the poverty rate and the unemployment rate run higher than the typical district.
Brett Guthrie.p2: Credit union staffing and credit union office presence pull in different directions in this district, and that split is worth noting before anything else: offices run specialized against the national norm while jobs barely clear it, so branches on the ground outnumber what local payrolls would predict. Abound, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Liberty are the names doing that work. Credit unions hold 18.2 percent of retail offices here, a thinner slice than most comparable districts carry, against Independence Bank of Kentucky, booked as the top name by deposits under federal reporting rules.
Brett Guthrie.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing dominated employment here, holding 18.5 percent of jobs at more than twice the national norm, a concentration nothing else measured came close to. Utilities and transportation and warehousing were also specialized, though smaller in scale. Total employment ran to roughly 259,200 jobs, in a district built around making and moving goods. Finance and insurance employment, by contrast, ran below the national norm.

Brian Babin.p1: Unemployment sets this district apart right away: at 7.5 percent, it stands among the highest of any congressional seat in the country, with poverty running high alongside it. Median household income, 76,372 dollars, trails most other districts. Still, homeownership is strong at 69.9 percent, and housing costs sit in line with typical burdens elsewhere. This is also a spread-out district, built around construction rather than dense job clusters.
Brian Babin.p2: Credit unions hold 34.0 percent of retail offices here, a much larger slice than most districts can claim, well ahead of the area's bank branch network. Rave Financial, Navy Federal Credit Union, and JSC anchor that presence. Credit union offices are planted more thickly here than the national norm, while credit union employment runs close to typical levels, so branches carry more weight per job than usual. For a workforce under the income and job pressures described above, that kind of dense, accessible network matters.
Brian Babin.p3: As measured in 2023, construction stood out sharply, employing 12.0 percent of local jobs and running more than twice the national norm. Mining and oil and gas extraction, though a small slice of employment, ran even further above the norm. Transportation and warehousing also ran ahead of typical levels. Overall finance and insurance employment ran well under the national norm, leaving this a district defined less by finance than by what it builds, moves, and extracts.

Brian Fitzpatrick.p1: Poverty here sits at 5.7 percent, among the lowest of any district in the country, and it frames everything else about the place. Households earn a median of 112,090 dollars, well above other districts, while most residents own their homes. Rent and home prices stay modest next to what people here earn. People are also packed onto the land more tightly than in most comparable seats.
Brian Fitzpatrick.p2: Credit union employment runs close to the national norm even though the credit union office footprint sits well under it, and that gap is worth naming first. Police & Fire, American Heritage, and Navy Federal Credit Union carry the sector's local weight, holding only 17.6 percent of retail offices between them. TD Bank, National Association books the largest deposit share among the many bank branches operating here, though that figure reflects reporting rules more than local market weight. For a credit union, this is a district of steady earners and homeowners, served by fewer branches than the workforce behind them would imply.
Brian Fitzpatrick.p3: Manufacturing anchored the working economy as of 2023, holding 12.5 percent of jobs at well above the national norm. Wholesale trade ran even more concentrated here than manufacturing did. Health care and social assistance drew a bigger share of the workforce than any other sector measured. This is a district defined less by finance than by making and moving goods.

Brian Jack.p1: Homeownership here runs well above most comparable districts, at 75.2 percent, and that sets this place apart from its neighbors. The median household earns $83,442 in a district of 799,818 residents, where the typical age lands at 40.0. Density stays thin, and poverty sits low. Owning rather than renting defines how people here live, and there is room to spare.
Brian Jack.p2: Credit unions hold only 14.8 percent of retail offices here, a share far below what most comparable districts show, so banks handle the bulk of branch business. Delta Community, Navy Federal Credit Union, and The Southern are the names working this ground. Credit union employment also trails the national norm, though jobs outpace office presence, meaning fewer branches are doing comparatively more work. That leaves a homeowning, middle-income population for credit unions to serve without matching banks branch for branch.
Brian Jack.p3: Manufacturing was the standout industry in 2023, claiming 16.1 percent of the workforce at well above the expected national rate for that sector. Retail trade and accommodation and food services followed close behind as areas of modest specialization. Broader finance employment lagged the national norm even as finance and insurance growth outpaced it. Home purchases dominated mortgage activity, fitting a district where ownership is the default.

Brian Mast.p1: Housing here costs more relative to income than in almost any comparable district, with home values running 5.4 times the median household income. Ownership dominates the housing stock, and fewer households fall below the poverty line than in most other districts. Residents run a touch older than the national picture, centered around 48.6 years. Joblessness holds steady at a level that puts this district squarely among the average, neither crowded nor empty by population density.
Brian Mast.p2: Retail banking here runs mostly through banks rather than credit unions, which account for only 10.1 percent of offices, a smaller footprint than nearly every other district carries. Ithink Financial, MidFlorida, and Velocity Community are the institutions holding that ground. Credit union employment lines up closely with the national norm, but at a level well under typical intensity elsewhere. What results is a limited credit union presence next to a banking sector where Seacoast National Bank leads on deposits among a wide field of local competitors.
Brian Mast.p3: The district's employment in 2023 clustered around utilities and around arts, entertainment, and recreation, both far above the national norm, alongside a specialized construction trade tied to steady homebuilding demand. Health care and retail trade carried the largest share of jobs, though only slightly above typical concentration for those fields. Overall finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm, even as that combined sector expanded at a faster clip than the nation's over the ten years measured.

Brian Schatz.p1: Hawaii carries a household income of $100,745, among the highest in the country, but housing absorbs that advantage fast. A median home value of $875,900 runs 8.7 times income, and rent leaves little room on top of that. Homeownership lags behind most of the country, even though unemployment and poverty both sit well under typical levels. The state is also more crowded than most, a place where land and housing stay under constant pressure.
Brian Schatz.p2: Navy Federal, HawaiiUSA, and Hawaii State anchor a credit union presence that fits this expensive, tightly held market. Credit unions hold 43.8 percent of retail offices here, a share matched in few other states, while Bank of Hawaii leads the field measured by deposits booked locally. Credit union employment runs at 1.83 times the national norm and office presence at 2.11 times, offices built out well ahead of staffing. That is a footprint sized for the high earners and high costs described above, not for a small or casual operation.
Brian Schatz.p3: As of 2023, accommodation and food service work defined the state's economy, employing workers at nearly twice the national norm. Utilities also stood out as a specialized source of work, well above what the mainland typically carries. Healthcare and retail trade rounded out the largest categories of work without any unusual concentration. Overall finance and insurance employment stayed below the national norm even as credit unions themselves stood apart within it, a hospitality economy first, a banking one second.

Brittany Pettersen.p1: Median household income in the 7th congressional seat of Colorado runs well above most other districts, at $104,378 a year, and that affluence shapes everything else here. Home values reach $651,600, more than six times that income, while typical rent runs well into the four figures a month. Homeownership is high and poverty runs low, at 7.7 percent. The district is thinly populated for its size, closer to open land than to a dense urban seat.
Brittany Pettersen.p2: Credit union employment runs well ahead of office presence here, at 1.84 times the national norm against an office count that sits close to typical. Bellco, Ent, and Credit Union of Colorado carry that presence, and together credit unions hold 28.1 percent of retail offices, a strong share against FirstBank and the district's many other banks. That mismatch points to institutions doing more with less real estate, staffing up rather than building branches. In a district this wealthy and this owner-heavy, that is a workforce built for mortgage and savings business rather than a thin storefront presence.
Brittany Pettersen.p3: As of 2023, the district's economy centered on professional, scientific, and technical services, its top sector by both size and specialization. Public administration also ran well above the national norm, reflecting the government work concentrated here. Overall finance and insurance employment lagged the national norm, and growth in that combined sector was modest over the prior decade. Total employment stood near 300,600 jobs, built on technical and public-sector work rather than on banking itself.

Bruce Westerman.p1: Fewer than 33 people live on each square mile of this district, a sparseness that separates it from nearly every comparable seat. Its 744,382 residents earn a median household income near the bottom of all districts, and home values sit low as well. Owning a house is far more common here than renting one, even as poverty stays high. The home is often paid off, but the paycheck behind it runs thin.
Bruce Westerman.p2: Credit unions hold just 13.7 percent of retail banking offices in this district, well below what is typical elsewhere. Arkansas Federal, Red River Employees, and Mil-Way carry that work locally. Credit union employment trails the national norm by a wide margin, while their office count, though still light, comes closer to matching it, a sign these institutions run leaner staffs relative to their footprint. Simmons Bank shows the largest deposit figures here under federal booking rules, which reflects accounting geography more than an actual branch advantage on the ground.
Bruce Westerman.p3: Manufacturing anchored the local economy in 2023, employing 20.7 percent of jobs, over twice what the national picture would predict. Agriculture and utilities were also unusually concentrated here, pointing to an economy rooted in growing and making things rather than in services. Health care and retail rounded out the largest sources of work, near typical levels elsewhere. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases over refinancing.

Bryan Steil.p1: Housing here costs less relative to income than the typical district sees: home values run 3.6 times the median household income of 79,452 dollars, and rent takes under a fifth of that income. Poverty and joblessness sit lower than most places measure. Set against a population of 739,693, the arithmetic works out kinder for a household budget than the national housing conversation might imply.
Bryan Steil.p2: Credit unions hold 32.0 percent of retail offices here, a share that stands well above most comparable districts, next to a crowded field of competing banks with no single dominant player. Educators, Landmark, and Blackhawk Community are the names behind that share. Credit union employment runs above the national norm, and office presence further still, spread wider than staffing would predict. That is a deep bench for a district where household budgets already carry lighter housing costs than most.
Bryan Steil.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing anchored the job base here, employing 20.7 percent of workers, a specialization well beyond the national norm and a leading sector in the district. Transportation and warehousing, and wholesale trade, followed as the next most specialized industries. Finance and insurance employment lagged the national norm by a wide margin, pointing to a local economy weighted toward producing and shipping goods rather than handling money. Total employment across the district stood near 291,100 jobs that year.

Burgess Owens.p1: Poverty here is rare, just 5.4 percent, and few people are out of work. Households earn a median of $109,469, comfortably ahead of most other districts, and the population skews young. Homeownership is common even though homes carry a median price of $558,900, well beyond what income alone would predict. What renters pay eats up little of the typical paycheck, and housing costs overall sit easier here than in most places like it.
Burgess Owens.p2: Credit unions hold 63.2 percent of retail offices here, a share among the highest anywhere measured. Mountain America, America First, and Utah Community anchor that presence. Federal rules credit Synchrony Bank with the most deposits in the district, simply because of where accounts happen to be booked rather than any sign of local reach, and plenty of other banks compete for business on the ground. Jobs and offices in the credit union sector both dwarf the national norm, with office growth outrunning hiring.
Burgess Owens.p3: Construction stands out as this district's most distinctive sector, employing 10.3 percent of workers and running well above the national norm. Retail trade employs the most people of any sector. Finance and insurance jobs ran ahead of the norm too, and that broader sector grew quickly over the decade measured. Home purchases made up 51.9 percent of all mortgage originations, in a district still very much building out its housing stock.

Byron Donalds.p1: Homeownership defines this district more than anything else measured here, reaching 76.4 percent, a level few congressional districts approach. Pay runs comfortably above what most districts report, yet home prices have outrun it further still, with the median home value now 5.2 times median household income. Both poverty, at 10.6 percent, and joblessness, at 3.3 percent, stay well under typical levels. The result is a settled, built-up district, denser than most peers, where owning rather than renting is the norm.
Byron Donalds.p2: Credit unions hold just 12.9 percent of retail offices here, a thin slice compared with most districts, leaving banks to run the bulk of the branch network under many separate names. Suncoast, Lake Michigan, and Achieva Credit Union are the largest credit unions serving the area. Both credit union staffing and branch presence trail the national norm, and offices outpace jobs, pointing to lean operations relative to footprint. The opportunity here is a well-off, high-equity homeowner base that banks currently serve from a much larger physical base.
Byron Donalds.p3: Construction dominated local employment as of 2023, running far above the national norm and accounting for 12.8 percent of jobs. Health care and social assistance was the single biggest source of jobs in the district. Arts, entertainment, and recreation also ran well ahead of national levels, rounding out an economy built on construction and leisure. Home purchases accounted for the large majority of mortgage activity, fitting a district shaped by ownership rather than tenancy.

Carlos Gimenez.p1: Housing here costs far more than local paychecks can comfortably absorb: the median home value runs 6.7 times median household income, among the highest such gaps of any district. Median household income sits at $83,629, unremarkable next to other districts, while home values near $562,100 are not. Unemployment runs low here, though the poverty rate stands well above what most comparable districts report. Population reaches 791,591, and the typical resident is 41 years old.
Carlos Gimenez.p2: Space Coast, Dade County, and Keys credit unions serve this district, where credit unions hold just 19.0 percent of retail offices, thinner than what most similar districts show, against a bank branch network run by many separate lenders. Bank of America comes out ahead on local deposits, a result of where deposits get booked under federal rules rather than an edge in branches or customers. Credit union employment runs well below the national norm, tracking office presence closely rather than outpacing it. That leaves credit unions a small but plainly needed footing against expensive housing and everyday need.
Carlos Gimenez.p3: Tourism and agriculture defined the job base measured in 2023: accommodation and food service employment far exceeded the national norm, and agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting ran higher still, enough to mark the district as highly specialized in that one field. Retail trade also employed a large share of workers here. Overall finance-sector employment lagged the national norm, even as finance and insurance jobs together grew faster than the country as a whole.

Carol Miller.p1: Household income here is 56,624 dollars a year, among the lowest figures any district posts, and poverty runs deeper than in most parts of the country. Housing costs little by comparison: a median home value of 145,100 dollars and rent near 851 dollars a month. Homeownership is common here, well past what most districts show, in a place that is sparsely settled and aging.
Carol Miller.p2: Credit union offices outnumber what the workforce here would predict, since staffing at these institutions falls below the national norm even as their branch presence runs above it, a mismatch worth noting. Pioneer Appalachia, Star USA, and West Virginia credit unions anchor that presence, holding 21.9 percent of retail offices, against Truist Bank, the largest by deposits booked here among 282 total bank branches. For a workforce this thin on finance work generally, credit unions carry more of the branch network than their staffing alone would account for.
Carol Miller.p3: As measured in 2023, extraction of coal, oil, and gas stood out sharply here, at over eight times the national norm, alongside public administration. Health care and social assistance employed the most people, well ahead of retail trade and food service. Finance and insurance employment and growth both lagged the country as a whole. This is a district built on extraction and public-sector work, not on finance.

Catherine Cortez Masto.p1: Nevada carries a median household income of 81,134 dollars, an ordinary figure set against a housing market that is not: a typical home runs 455,500 dollars, and rent lands near 1,709 dollars a month. Homeownership here is uncommonly rare for a state this size, and joblessness runs among the highest anywhere. This is also a sparsely settled state, built around a workforce concentrated in a handful of industries.
Catherine Cortez Masto.p2: America First, Navy Federal, and Greater Nevada anchor the credit union presence here, holding 23.6 percent of retail offices against banks, a share that lands squarely in the middle compared with other states. Bank of America books the largest deposit total under federal rules, though that reflects booking practice more than branch reach, and the state runs hundreds of branches under many separate banks. Credit union employment here runs well below the national norm even as office presence holds closer to it, a leaner staffing pattern than the sector keeps elsewhere. That is the thin bench a member institution works with in a state where pay is ordinary but housing is not.
Catherine Cortez Masto.p3: As of 2023, Nevada's job base leaned hard on accommodation and food services, which alone claimed nearly a fifth of all jobs, a concentration far beyond the national norm. Mining held a small but outsized footprint, and arts and entertainment ran above typical levels too. Overall finance employment lagged the country, but the finance and insurance sector combined grew well ahead of the national pace over the decade to 2023.

Celeste Maloy.p1: This district spreads its people thin, among the lowest population densities of any congressional seat in the country, at just 22.5 people per square mile. Within that wide footprint live 880,783 residents earning a median household income of $90,523, well above the typical district. Home values run high too, and unemployment stays low. Work here skews toward people holding jobs across a large, sparsely built area.
Celeste Maloy.p2: Credit unions hold 50.5 percent of retail offices here, a share few other districts match, and Mountain America, America First, and Chartway anchor that presence. Credit union employment sits far past the national norm, tracking closely with how thick credit union offices run here too. That matters in a district this spread out, where reaching the people described above means covering real distance. Synchrony Bank shows the largest deposit figure under federal reporting rules, a single address among 135 bank branches run by many separate competitors.
Celeste Maloy.p3: As measured in 2023, transportation and warehousing stood out sharply as the district's most distinctive sector, employing a large share of workers at a rate far above the national norm. Construction and manufacturing also ran specialized, giving the local economy a strong tilt toward building and moving goods. Overall finance employment sat just under the national norm that year. Credit unions filled an outsized share of the financial footprint left over from an economy centered on freight and industry.

Charles Fleischmann.p1: Population here spreads thin, just over 200 people per square mile, a district of wide distances rather than dense neighborhoods. Residents earn a median household income of 74,530 dollars, and home values sit at 315,200 dollars, a gap between the two that comes in easier than what most comparable districts face. Rent runs 1,189 dollars a month. Both poverty and unemployment climb higher than most similar districts report, a harder edge beneath what otherwise looks like an affordable place to live.
Charles Fleischmann.p2: Credit unions hold 32.5 percent of retail offices here, a share well above most districts in the country. Tennessee Valley, ORNL, and Y-12 anchor that presence, competing against Pinnacle Bank, the top institution here by deposits booked to local addresses. Credit union offices are far more concentrated than the national picture, and employment in the industry runs well above it too, with offices growing faster than jobs. For the working households described above, a credit union is not a niche option here, it is close to a parallel banking system.
Charles Fleischmann.p3: Manufacturing set this district apart in 2023, employing close to a fifth of all workers, a concentration far beyond what the nation shows. Transportation and warehousing added further weight to that pattern. Finance and insurance jobs matched the national norm on headcount but outpaced it on hiring gains across the ten years before. Factories and freight give this district its character, and finance moves alongside them rather than out front.

Charles Schumer.p1: New York state holds nearly 19.9 million residents, and the typical age here is 40.1, spread across a population density far higher than nearly any other state manages. A typical household earns 85,820 dollars a year, more than most states report, yet housing swallows the gain: homes valued near 449,800 dollars and rent above 1,600 dollars a month put costs well past what most states see. The poverty rate and the unemployment rate each land higher than most other states record.
Charles Schumer.p2: Fourleaf, United Nations, and Broadview carry the credit union presence, while the largest deposit total on paper belongs to JPMorgan Chase, a result of how one institution's accounts get assigned to an address rather than proof of its reach on the ground. Credit unions account for just 21.5 percent of retail offices statewide, a smaller footing than most states give them. Credit union employment here sits below the national norm, modest given how large and how financially squeezed this population is.
Charles Schumer.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance employment ran well above the national norm, joined by strength in information and in real estate and leasing, a mix that marks this out as a finance-heavy economy rather than a typical one. Retail trade ran below the national norm, thin next to those other strengths, in an economy leaning more on finance and knowledge work than on shopfronts.

Chellie Pingree.p1: Unemployment here sits lower than almost any comparable district, at 2.7 percent, and poverty runs low too. Households earn a median of 90,131 dollars, comfortably ahead of most peers, and homeownership is high at 72.6 percent. Home values run high as well, at 448,800 dollars, a wide gap against income even where monthly housing costs land in the middle of the pack. Density is low, marking this as a spread-out, settled place rather than an urban one.
Chellie Pingree.p2: Credit unions hold 31.4 percent of retail offices here, a share well above most comparable districts, a genuine rival to the banks rather than a minor presence beside them. Atlantic Regional, Evergreen, and Town & Country anchor that presence. Credit union employment and office density both run above the national norm, with offices growing faster than staffing, a specialized footprint rather than a passing one. TD Bank tops the local deposit figures under federal booking rules, but many other lenders operate branches across the district too.
Chellie Pingree.p3: The district's work, measured in 2023, leaned toward management of companies, retail trade, and, distinctly for Maine, agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting, each running above the national norm. Health care, retail, and manufacturing made up the broadest employing sectors. Finance and insurance employment ran above the norm too, though its growth over the prior decade lagged slightly behind the nation's. Home purchases, rather than refinancing, dominated the mortgage market that year.

Chip Roy.p1: Household income is the number that marks the 21st district of Texas out from other Texas districts, running well above most at $100,260. Homes carry a median value of $442,300, several times that income, yet rent takes just 18.5 percent of what a household here typically earns, a lighter load than most districts carry. Homeownership runs high, and both poverty and unemployment sit low.
Chip Roy.p2: Credit union employment here runs far ahead of the national norm, out of step with the number of branches on the ground, since offices hold only 17.0 percent of the retail share and sit close to typical levels elsewhere. That gap between people employed and doors open marks this district out. Randolph-Brooks, Security Service, and Pentagon Federal carry that presence, competing against USAA Federal Savings Bank, the area's top holder of deposits under federal booking rules. The income and homeownership described above give these institutions a base of stable, high-earning borrowers to build on.
Chip Roy.p3: As of 2023, construction and mining both outpaced the national norm by wide margins, and real estate followed close behind, marking a district built on land and building rather than routine trade. Professional and technical services also ran ahead of the norm, layered atop a workforce anchored by health care and retail. This is a district that builds and finances at a pace ahead of most of the country.

Chris Pappas.p1: A poverty rate of 7.1 percent, among the lowest of any comparable district, sets this place apart. Households here earn a median of 102,258 dollars, well ahead of most peer districts, and joblessness runs to just 2.6 percent. Home values run high against that income, though rent claims a modest share of what people take home. Most residents own rather than rent, in a district of moderate density and a middle-aged population.
Chris Pappas.p2: Credit union jobs here run thicker than credit union offices do relative to the national norm, a gap worth noting before anything else. SERVICE, St. Mary's Bank, and Lighthouse anchor that presence, and together credit unions hold 26.2 percent of retail offices, a share ahead of most other districts. Citizens Bank, National Association books the largest deposit total under federal rules, but that reflects where deposits are recorded, not a lack of local rivals. For a population this affluent and this steadily employed, credit unions here carry a workforce well out of proportion to their office count.
Chris Pappas.p3: Local industry leaned specialized in retail trade and in finance and insurance, both running ahead of the national norm. Health care and social assistance employed the most people, alongside manufacturing running a bit ahead of the national norm too. Across all lenders, home purchases made up 46.1 percent of mortgage originations, with a meaningful share of lending reaching lower income neighborhoods. This is a district built on steady, well-paid work rather than any single dominant employer.

Chris Van Hollen.p1: Maryland's economy runs on government and the professional services that orbit it: public administration employs at nearly twice the national norm, and scientific and technical services show a similar tilt. People are packed in tightly here, more densely settled than nearly every other state. Median household income is among the highest in the country, a wage base that meets home values pushed up well past what most states see.
Chris Van Hollen.p2: Credit unions hold 21.3 percent of retail offices against banks here, a thinner slice than most states hold, even as Navy Federal, State Employees CU of Maryland, and Tower anchor the field. Bank of America tops the deposit figures for this state, a number that follows where accounts get booked rather than where customers actually bank, and plenty of other lenders compete for business here too. Credit union employment tracks closely with credit union office presence, both a step below the national norm. That leaves a population with comfortable income served by a credit union sector that is present but thin.
Chris Van Hollen.p3: Beyond that, 2023 figures put overall finance and insurance employment below the national norm, with growth over the prior decade running at that same slower pace. Construction employed slightly above typical levels, a modest second note next to the state's real weight in government and technical work. Poverty stayed lower than in nearly any other state. What sets Maryland apart is not one booming industry but the weight of government-adjacent and technical work layered over a dense, well-off population.

Chrissy Houlahan.p1: Median household income in the 6th congressional seat of Pennsylvania runs well above most comparable districts, at $109,810, and that gap shapes everything else here. Homes carry a median value of $448,500, and typical rent takes just 17.0 percent of income, a light load given what people earn. Ownership is common, at 72.2 percent of households, and poverty is low. Unemployment is the one figure that runs a bit harder here than in most comparable places.
Chrissy Houlahan.p2: Credit union offices here outpace credit union employment, an unusual split worth noting up front: office presence sits close to the national norm while jobs in the industry run thin against it. Citadel, Utilities Employees, and TruMark Financial anchor that office network, holding 21.3 percent of retail offices against banks. Customers Bank leads all institutions on deposits booked to addresses here, a distinction shaped by reporting rules more than by local presence. For a credit union, that combination means real office reach into a wealthy, low-cost population, without matching depth in local staff.
Chrissy Houlahan.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance and the management of companies both stood out sharply against the national pattern, marking this as a district built around corporate and financial back offices rather than storefronts. Health care and professional or technical services also carried significant weight in daily employment. Finance and insurance together grew faster than the national pace across the prior decade. Mortgage lending here leaned heavily toward home purchases.

Christian Menefee.p1: Poverty here runs at 21.0 percent, a rate few other districts approach, and unemployment sits high too. Median household income lags far behind what most comparable districts report. Housing still costs more than that: rent runs 1,391 dollars a month, and homeownership has slipped to 45.5 percent, one of the lower rates around. Packed into 3,576 people per square mile, this is a dense, largely working, largely renting district.
Christian Menefee.p2: Credit union offices here outrun credit union employment, a split unusual enough to open on: offices hold close to the national norm in number while jobs in the industry run well below it. Houston Police, Chevron, and Texas Dow Employees anchor that presence. Credit unions hold 27.4 percent of retail offices against banks, a share few comparable districts match, even with JPMorgan Chase booking the largest deposit total among many separate competing banks. That is a thin staff footprint carrying an outsized share of the storefronts people actually walk into.
Christian Menefee.p3: Employment counts from 2023 show mining and oil and gas extraction, utilities, and transportation and warehousing running far heavier here than the national picture. Professional and technical services and wholesale trade also employed heavily. Overall finance employment ran below the national norm even as finance and insurance growth outpaced it. Mortgage lending stayed heavily purchase-driven, and lower-income neighborhoods captured 54.6 percent of all originations.

Christopher Coons.p1: Delaware carries a household income of 87,534 dollars, comfortably above other states, in a state of 1,051,917 people with a median age of 42.1. Homes run expensive too, a median value of 371,600 dollars, yet homeownership here is among the highest anywhere. Poverty runs low, but unemployment runs higher than in most states, an odd pairing for a place this comfortable on paper.
Christopher Coons.p2: DEL-ONE, Dover, and Tidemark carry the credit union presence here, but together they hold only 20.6 percent of retail offices, a smaller footprint than most states manage, against a much larger field of banks led on paper by Capital One's deposit booking rather than any real branch dominance. Credit union employment runs far below the national norm, thinner even than their own office count. For a state with this much income and this much finance activity close at hand, credit unions here work a small corner of a much larger table.
Christopher Coons.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance jobs ran far above the national norm, by far the state's most specialized line of work and a good part of why the money above concentrates the way it does. Retail trade and transportation and warehousing also ran a bit above the usual national mix. Growth in finance and insurance over the decade to 2023 tracked the national pace closely, nothing unusual there. This is a state built around finance work, just not around credit unions doing much of it.

Christopher Deluzio.p1: What people earn in the 17th goes further on housing than in almost any comparable district, with home values running under three times median household income and rent taking up a modest fraction of it. Household earnings here beat most similar districts, and homeownership sits high at 73.5 percent. The population is thick on the ground for the region, at 843.6 people per square mile. Work tends toward the steady and the well paid.
Christopher Deluzio.p2: Credit unions hold a 22.7 percent share of retail offices against area banks, yet the jobs behind that presence trail the national norm even as office count runs ahead of it, an imbalance worth flagging. Clearview, West-Aircomm, and Omega hold that ground locally. TriState Capital Bank comes out largest by deposits under federal booking rules, a measure of where deposits land rather than where branches sit, and 193 bank branches from many separate banks compete for the same households whose earnings and homeownership make this a district built for lending.
Christopher Deluzio.p3: As of 2023, management of companies was the district's standout sector, employing at more than twice the national rate, alongside specialization in utilities and in professional, scientific, and technical services. Health care and retail trade employed the most people day to day. Overall finance employment ran below the national norm, and growth in that broader sector lagged the country over the prior decade.

Christopher Murphy.p1: Connecticut households earn 96,049 dollars at the median, well above most states, and that pay meets a housing market priced high too, a median home value of 396,900 dollars. Home values run at 4.1 times income, ordinary for the region rather than stretched. Homeownership trails most other states, and the population is dense, well above the norm for the country. Poverty stays low even as unemployment runs higher than most peers see.
Christopher Murphy.p2: Connecticut State Employees, American Eagle Financial, and Charter Oak carry the credit union presence here, yet together those institutions hold only 19.9 percent of retail offices, a smaller slice than almost anywhere else. Bank of America shows up as the largest holder of deposits under federal booking rules, not through local presence or customer reach, in a market where many bank rivals still compete for that business. Credit union employment runs well below the national norm even though office presence lands almost exactly on it, a footprint that outpaces its own staffing.
Christopher Murphy.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance stood out as the state's most specialized sector, well above the national norm, though its growth over the decade to 2023 lagged the country's pace. Educational services and manufacturing also ran ahead of the norm, rounding out a base built on institutional and skilled production work. Across the state's roughly 1,511,300 jobs, that lean toward finance and steady sectors set Connecticut apart from most of the country.

Christopher Smith.p1: Homeownership here sits among the highest of any congressional district, at 80.9 percent, and that fact shapes the place more than any other. Income runs high too, a median of 103,769 dollars a year, well ahead of most comparable districts, and poverty stays low. Home values run high against income, a ratio of 5.0. Owned homes and comfortable pay define this district far more than turnover or rental living do.
Christopher Smith.p2: Credit unions hold just 7.6 percent of retail offices here, one of the thinnest shares of any district. First Atlantic, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Affinity are the names present, competing against a banking sector where TD Bank books the largest deposits. Credit union employment runs far below the national norm, at 0.13 times, and office presence sits at 0.24 times, so what offices exist carry more weight than staffing alone would imply. That is a thin footprint for a district built so heavily on home equity and steady income.
Christopher Smith.p3: The district ran specialized in utilities, in arts, entertainment, and recreation, and in real estate and rental and leasing, all well ahead of the national norm. Overall finance and insurance employment sat below that norm, with growth over the prior decade also lagging. Buyers, rather than people refinancing, drove most mortgage activity here. A meaningful share of that lending reached lower-income neighborhoods.

Chuck Edwards.p1: Household income in this district lags most comparable districts, at $67,690 a year, and poverty runs a touch higher than typical too. Unemployment, though, is unusually low at 3.5 percent, and homeownership stands out sharply at 75.2 percent, a district of owners even where paychecks run thin. Home values and rent both land at typical levels for the region. Few people live packed close together here, well below the usual density for a district this populous.
Chuck Edwards.p2: Credit unions hold 32.3 percent of retail deposit-taking offices in this district, a share that stands well above most comparable places. State Employees', Champion, and Civic are the credit unions with a strong presence here, in a market where First-Citizens Bank & Trust Company leads on deposits, one name among many banks competing for business. Credit union employment runs at 1.4 times the national norm, and office presence tracks closely with it. That is a deep credit union footprint set against a district where income runs low and homeownership runs high.
Chuck Edwards.p3: As measured in 2023, this district leaned hardest on Arts, Entertainment, and Recreation, well beyond the national norm and its most specialized sector by a clear margin. Health care, retail, and manufacturing employed the most people, with manufacturing itself running somewhat above the norm. Overall finance and insurance employment came in well under the national norm, even as credit unions themselves ran specialized. Total employment approached 280,300 jobs across the district.

Chuck Grassley.p1: Just over 3.2 million people call Iowa home, with a median age of 39 and a population scattered lightly across wide-open land. Median household income trails most other states, but housing eats up far less of it: a median home value of 227,300 dollars against that income is among the lowest ratios anywhere, and rent runs 981 dollars a month. Homeownership stands far higher than most states manage. Unemployment holds low as well.
Chuck Grassley.p2: GreenState, Veridian, and Dupaco Community anchor credit union business in Iowa, though their statewide retail office share, 18.4 percent, trails most other states, well behind Principal Bank and the many competing banks it stands among. Credit union work still runs thick relative to the national picture, with offices built out faster than staffing has followed. For a household earning modest wages and paying down a home worth roughly three times that income, credit unions here compete for a steady, well-anchored customer.
Chuck Grassley.p3: Manufacturing anchored the state's economy as of 2023, employing 15.5 percent of workers, well ahead of the national norm and ahead of both health care and retail as employers. Agriculture employed a small share of workers but ran far more concentrated here than across the country overall. Finance and insurance work also ran deep in the state, though the broader finance sector's growth over the following decade lagged the nation slightly.

Cindy Hyde-Smith.p1: Mississippi's population stands just under 2.94 million; the typical resident is just past 39. Median household income runs low next to other states, at 59,127 dollars, and poverty touches a large share of residents, among the highest in the country. Even so, most residents own their homes, with 70.5 percent doing so, and home values relative to income are unremarkable. Open land dominates here, with population spread thin across the state.
Cindy Hyde-Smith.p2: Navy Federal, Keesler, and Mutual anchor the credit union presence in a state where credit unions hold just 16.4 percent of retail offices, a modest foothold measured against how much ground banks cover. Cadence Bank shows the largest deposit sum tied to addresses here, a distinction that follows federal reporting rules rather than branch counts, and plenty of other banks operate throughout the state alongside it. Credit union offices are still more common relative to the national norm than credit union jobs are, a thin-staffed but present branch network serving the modest incomes and high homeownership described above.
Cindy Hyde-Smith.p3: By 2023, Mississippi's job base was tilted toward making and growing things rather than moving money. Manufacturing, utilities, and agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting all ran well above national norms, with manufacturing alone accounting for 13.4 percent of jobs. Finance and insurance employment, by contrast, trailed the national norm by a wide margin. This was a state built on production and land, not on financial services.

Claudia Tenney.p1: Homes here cost about two and a half times what a typical household earns, and rent runs under a sixth of income, a lighter housing burden than almost anywhere else measured. Median household income sits at 72,396 dollars, trailing most other districts, though joblessness runs low at 3.3 percent. Households here lean strongly toward ownership over renting, well beyond what most districts show. Fewer than 110 people occupy each square mile, a rural and small-town footprint by Northeast standards.
Claudia Tenney.p2: ESL, Empower, and Reliant Community are the credit unions with a presence here. Between them, credit unions account for 29.3 percent of the district's retail banking offices, a bigger slice than most comparable places carry. Five Star Bank shows up as the largest by deposits under federal booking rules, a distinction that says more about accounting than about a dominant local presence. Credit union employment sits at 1.68 times the national norm, with office presence running in step, evidence that credit unions carry unusual weight in this district's financial life.
Claudia Tenney.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing anchored a good share of local employment, and farming stood out sharply against national patterns, running at more than four times the concentration seen nationally. Public administration also ran well above typical levels, pointing to a substantial government presence in the local economy. Overall finance and insurance employment sat well under national norms, leaving credit unions unusually prominent in an otherwise thin financial sector.

Clay Fuller.p1: Housing here costs far less relative to pay than in most districts: home values sit at 4.1 times the typical household income, well below most comparable places. Median household income runs $78,969, and homeownership is common. Poverty and unemployment both run low. It is a place where people work steadily and mostly own the roof over their heads.
Clay Fuller.p2: Credit union employment here runs below the national norm, even though credit union offices are closer to typical, a mismatch worth noting before anything else. Tennessee Valley, LGE Community, and Coosa Valley anchor that office network, which holds 26.3 percent of retail offices against banks. Regions Bank shows a large deposit total on the books, but that reflects which office deposits get assigned to, not where customers actually bank. For a credit union in this district, the footprint on the map is doing more work than the payroll behind it.
Clay Fuller.p3: As measured in 2023, manufacturing dominated the job base, employing 20.6 percent of workers, well above the national norm and the clear specialization here. Retail trade and educational services followed as modest secondary strengths. Overall finance employment ran light against the national norm, though the broader finance and insurance sector expanded at a faster clip than the nation across the prior decade. Mortgage originations that year tilted heavily toward home purchases, at 55.0 percent of the total.

Clay Higgins.p1: Household income in the 3rd district of Louisiana is among the lowest of any congressional district, at 59,769 dollars a year, and poverty here runs high to match. Housing costs remain modest despite that: a median home value of 208,300 dollars against local income comes to a ratio of just 3.5. Most residents own rather than rent, a figure that stands well clear of most districts, spread across a lightly populated stretch of the state.
Clay Higgins.p2: Credit union staffing and credit union office presence tell different stories here: jobs run well under the national norm while office counts sit closer to it, so a lean workforce is stretched across a wider branch footprint than the national pattern would predict. CSE, Advancial, and Meritus carry that presence, holding 16.7 percent of retail offices in a market still dominated by banks. Against a district of modest income and high homeownership, that is a thin footprint asked to cover a lot of ground.
Clay Higgins.p3: By 2023, oil and gas extraction had become the district's standout industry, specialized far beyond the national norm, with real estate and construction also running heavy. Health care, retail, and manufacturing carried the largest share of jobs overall. Finance and insurance employment sat below the national norm, though the sector had been gaining ground over the prior decade. Hancock Whitney Bank booked the most deposits in the district, one name among many competing banks here.

Cleo Fields.p1: Pay in this district lags well behind most of the country, with median household income at $50,642 a year. Homes are priced modestly too, yet the cost of housing takes a bigger bite out of local paychecks than it does in comparable districts elsewhere. Poverty and unemployment both climb well past typical levels, and homeownership trails most other districts as well. People here live spread out, and skew a touch younger than the national picture.
Cleo Fields.p2: The share of retail offices held by credit unions is the standout fact here: 30.9 percent, far more than most districts see. EFCU Financial, Neighbors, and Campus account for that presence, against JPMorgan Chase, whose deposits booked locally make it the top bank on paper without that meaning it outmatches every other institution operating on the ground. Credit union employment runs 1.25 times the national norm, and their office footprint runs even further ahead at 1.53 times it, a build-out that has outpaced hiring. That kind of reach matters where incomes are tight and borrowing needs run high.
Cleo Fields.p3: As measured in 2023, drilling and mineral extraction stood out sharply against the rest of the country, alongside real strength in public administration and construction employment. Health care and social assistance and retail trade were the two largest sources of jobs. Overall finance sector employment sat below the national norm even as credit unions themselves ran ahead of it. Lending data show home purchases dominating mortgage activity, at 64.0 percent of all originations.

Cliff Bentz.p1: This district covers ground so sparsely settled that it sits among the lowest population densities of any congressional seat in the country, just 9.8 people per square mile across 704,768 residents. Household income of 68,267 dollars comes in well under the mark set by comparable districts, and home values sit at 385,600 dollars, with ownership the norm over renting. Poverty and joblessness both press harder on this district than on most others.
Cliff Bentz.p2: Credit unions hold 32.6 percent of retail offices here, a share far out of line with what most comparable districts show. Rogue, Spokane Teachers, and First Community carry that share, set against Umpqua Bank, the leading name here by deposits booked under federal reporting rules. Credit union employment outpaces the national norm by a wide margin, and outpaces even their own strong office presence. That is a workforce with thinner incomes and more exposure to unemployment than most, exactly the base these institutions are built to serve.
Cliff Bentz.p3: As of 2023, this district's economy leaned hardest on agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting, a sector running well above the national norm. Retail trade and health care and social assistance carried significant weight too, both above the norm. Overall finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm even as credit unions themselves stayed dense, a split that marks this district's financial activity as unusually concentrated in cooperative institutions. Total employment stood near 238,700 jobs.

Cory Booker.p1: New Jersey packs work and people into one of the densest states in the country, with warehouses, wholesalers, and trucking moving goods through a corridor tied to major ports and cities beyond its borders. Households here earn among the highest incomes in the country, but home values near half a million dollars and rents well above typical push housing costs high as well. It is a place where money is plentiful but the cost of a home eats hard into it.
Cory Booker.p2: Credit unions hold just 12.4 percent of retail offices here, a thin share next to other states, leaving banks to carry most of the business including Bank of America, which books the largest deposits by address among many rivals with branches statewide. Affinity, Police & Fire, and Visions carry the credit union side instead, though credit union employment and office presence both sit well under the national norm. In a state this expensive, that small footprint still has to serve a lot of high-income households.
Cory Booker.p3: Finance and insurance employment ran a bit above the national norm as of 2023, though growth over the prior decade lagged the country somewhat. The real specialty sat in moving and distributing goods, transportation, warehousing, and wholesale trade, all well above the norm, alongside professional and technical services running slightly ahead too. Health care and retail employed the most people, ordinary in scale but essential to a state built on logistics and density.

Cory Mills.p1: Housing here runs expensive against what people earn, 4.7 on the home value to income scale, a level well above most comparable districts, with rent claiming 26.9 percent of median household income. About 813,213 people live in the district, median household income lands at 82,897 dollars, and homeownership climbs past nearly every peer district. Both poverty and joblessness read low. Density runs high too, this is a comparatively comfortable place to live, just not an inexpensive one.
Cory Mills.p2: Credit union employment outpaces the national norm here more than credit union office space does, a divergence worth flagging before anything else about the sector. FAIRWINDS, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Addition Financial anchor that presence, holding 28.5 percent of retail offices between credit unions and banks. Bank of America carries a sizable deposit total booked to addresses here, in a district with no shortage of other banks competing for business. For a credit union in this district, that combination means more staff per office than is typical elsewhere, serving a footprint of branches that has not grown to match.
Cory Mills.p3: As of 2023, construction and finance and insurance stood out as this district's most specialized sectors, each running well above the national norm. Administrative and support services ran strong as well. Finance and insurance jobs alone reached 1.58 times the national norm. Building things and financing them define this district more than any one sector carrying the load.

Craig Goldman.p1: This district is packed in tighter than most of its counterparts, a dense corner of Texas holding 852,259 people. Households here earn a median $90,319, well above the typical district. Homeownership sits at 62.4 percent, trailing most peers, and rent runs a median $1,673 against home values well above that. Neither joblessness nor hardship stands out from the pack.
Craig Goldman.p2: Credit unions hold just 15.2 percent of retail offices here, a share that runs well below most districts, leaving banks with the bulk of the branch network. EECU, Navy Federal Credit Union, and American Airlines Federal Credit Union carry that smaller share. Credit union employment runs thinner than the national norm, and offices are outpacing jobs, a light footprint for an economy where incomes and home costs both run high. That leaves a credit union here working with better-paid households than most districts see, while competing for a smaller slice of the map.
Craig Goldman.p3: Health care and social assistance, together with manufacturing, carried much of the job base by 2023, a total approaching 368,800 positions. A far smaller corner of that base, oil and gas extraction and quarrying, ran well above the national norm for concentration, a tight pocket of specialization rather than a broad one. Home purchase loans made up most mortgage originations, marking a district still adding housing stock rather than one dominated by refinancing. Manufacturing's weight only reinforced an economy already tilted toward industrial specialization.

Cynthia Lummis.p1: Wyoming holds a small population across a vast stretch of open land, one of the least crowded states in the country. The typical household earns 75,532 dollars, trailing most states, though joblessness stays low and poverty is rare. Housing costs little by national standards: a median home value of 339,500 dollars against that income and rent near 998 dollars a month leave the state among the cheapest places to live measured anywhere. Owning a home is the norm here far more than renting, a pattern less common elsewhere.
Cynthia Lummis.p2: UNIWYO, BLUE, and Meridian Trust anchor the credit union presence here, and together with others they hold 23.8 percent of retail offices statewide, a stronger share than most states manage. Credit union employment runs well ahead of the national norm, outpacing the growth in offices these institutions keep open, evidence of thin branch networks carrying an unusually large workforce. First Interstate Bank carries the largest deposit total under federal booking rules, a distinction that says nothing about how many rival banks operate across the state. The households behind those figures are the steady, homeowning kind described above.
Cynthia Lummis.p3: As measured in 2023, mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction towered over the national norm, the state's clearest specialty by far. Public administration also ran ahead of typical staffing levels. Health care, retail trade, and accommodation and food services together anchor the broader job base. Overall finance and insurance employment lagged the national norm, leaving credit unions as the sector's standout strength.

Dale Strong.p1: This district's housing stands apart on one measure above all: a home costs 3.7 times the median household income of 80,140 dollars, and rent claims just 17.7 percent of that income. Homeownership runs high, at 70.7 percent, and joblessness is low. Across 773,877 people spread thinly across the district, families here tend to own rather than rent, and keep most of what they earn after paying for shelter.
Dale Strong.p2: Credit unions hold 31.7 percent of retail offices in the district, a share well above most comparable places. Redstone, Family Security, and Alabama carry that share, competing for room against a field of bank branches led by Regions Bank. Credit union employment runs far above the national norm, outpacing even that solid office presence, which points to institutions doing more business per branch than is typical elsewhere. Given the ownership and affordability described above, credit unions here carry more weight than the broader local finance sector does on its own.
Dale Strong.p3: By 2023, manufacturing and professional, scientific, and technical services anchored the job base, both employing well beyond the national norm. Retail trade added a smaller, still above-norm, share of jobs. General finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm even so, a sign that the credit union strength described earlier sits apart from the broader finance sector. Technical and industrial work, not finance, is what sets this district's economy apart.

Dan Crenshaw.p1: Median household income in the 2nd congressional district of Texas runs well above most comparable districts, at $101,405. Home values land close to the median for districts nationwide, a ratio of 3.3 against earnings. Homeownership is common here, well ahead of most districts like it, and poverty is rare, affecting just 8.9 percent of residents. This is a settled, owner-occupied population earning noticeably more than the typical district.
Dan Crenshaw.p2: Credit unions hold just 11.9 percent of retail offices here, a smaller slice than in almost any comparable district, leaving banks to carry most of the footprint across 150 branch locations. Navy Federal Credit Union, First Service, and Smart Financial are the names holding that small share. Credit union jobs are scarce against the national norm, and branch presence lags too, though offices still outnumber what the jobs figures would predict. Between the earnings and the ownership rates seen here, this is a district credit unions have only lightly touched.
Dan Crenshaw.p3: As measured in 2023, oil and gas extraction stood out sharply, at over twelve times the national norm for its share of jobs, easily the clearest specialty in the local economy. Retail trade employed the most people, ahead of accommodation and food service and health care. Overall finance employment ran below the national norm even as finance and insurance jobs grew faster than the norm over the prior decade. Home purchase loans dominated mortgage activity, making up 77.9 percent of all lending.

Dan Newhouse.p1: Unemployment here runs higher than in almost any comparable district, at 6.5 percent, and poverty runs well above the typical seat. Median household income sits at 78,605 dollars, unremarkable next to other districts, in a population that skews young at a median age of 35.6. Home values run 5 times the median income, yet rent and homeownership both stay modest by national standards. Density is thin, a place built around open land rather than a dense job center.
Dan Newhouse.p2: Credit unions hold 35.0 percent of retail offices here, a share among the highest of any district in the country. HAPO Community, GESA, and Spokane Teachers anchor that presence. U.S. Bank National Association books the largest deposit sum under federal reporting rules, a measure of where deposits are recorded rather than where customers bank. Credit union employment runs well ahead of the national norm, and further ahead still of the district's already strong office presence, so these institutions employ far more people here than banks of similar footprint.
Dan Newhouse.p3: As measured in 2023, agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting employed 13.8 percent of workers, a concentration far above the national norm and unlike almost anywhere else. Health care and social assistance and retail trade also employed large shares, though neither ran far past what the nation sees. Overall finance and insurance employment stayed thin against the national norm, leaving credit unions to fill a role banks elsewhere might otherwise cover.

Dan Sullivan.p1: Alaska skews young, its residents typically 36.3 years old, and typical household earnings reach $95,665, a figure few states surpass. A typical home there is priced near $376,500, yet rent asks far less by comparison, close to $1,444 a month. Fewer than two people occupy each square mile of the state, and the share of workers without jobs sits above the rate found across most of the country.
Dan Sullivan.p2: Global, Credit Union 1, and Nuvision anchor a credit union presence that runs deep here: credit unions hold 40.5 percent of retail deposit offices, among the highest shares of any state, ahead of Wells Fargo Bank, National Association, the name that leads this state's books under federal booking rules. Credit union employment runs at more than triple the national norm, well out ahead of the sector's office count, which itself runs almost double that norm. For a population this scattered, with income this strong, that mix of thin branch networks and thick staffing says credit unions do real work here.
Dan Sullivan.p3: In 2016, Alaska's economy leaned hard on extraction and government. Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction ran over ten times the national norm, and public administration ran two and a half times it. Transportation and warehousing also stood out as specialized, while health care and retail trade employed more people overall but sat close to the national average. Finance and insurance employment as a whole ran below that norm, well under the weight carried by credit unions alone.

Daniel Goldman.p1: This district crowds people into less space than nearly any other in the country, close to 49,400 per square mile. Incomes run high, with median household income near $119,517, but housing sits far out of reach for most residents: home values are exceptionally high, homeownership is rare at 29.9 percent, and poverty touches this population more than it does most other districts. High earnings and real hardship sit close together, and ownership is the exception rather than the rule.
Daniel Goldman.p2: Credit unions hold only 6.5 percent of the district's retail banking offices, among the lowest shares of any district. United Nations, Municipal, and Self Reliance Financial carry that presence. Both credit union employment and their office footprint sit far below the national norm, tracking each other closely, in a market where 210 bank branches compete for business and Bank of New York Mellon books the largest deposits, by reporting rules rather than local dominance. The people this district produces, high earning, often renting, rarely owning, are exactly the customers credit unions here reach least.
Daniel Goldman.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance employed 12.9 percent of workers here, at nearly three times the national norm, alongside heavy concentrations in information and public administration. Professional and technical services employed the most people of any sector. Specialized, high value work defines the local economy more than broad-based employment does, and the finance sector added jobs over the prior decade at a pace close to the national norm.

Daniel Meuser.p1: Household income in the 9th district lags most comparable districts, at $68,016. Housing stays within reach of that: a median home value of $226,000 and rent near $973 a month keep costs low, and homeownership climbs to 73.5 percent, well ahead of comparable places. The district is thinly settled, and joblessness sits a shade above what similar districts report. Pay is modest here, but the cost of a home rarely swallows it.
Daniel Meuser.p2: Credit union offices hold a 21.7 percent share of retail branches, a middling figure among peer districts, yet credit union employment sits just under the national norm even as branch presence climbs well past it, a district with more offices open than its payrolls alone would explain. Pennsylvania State Employees, Lebanon, and Members 1st carry that branch presence. Manufacturers and Traders Trust books more deposits than other banks here, though only by federal booking rules, not by local reach. For a credit union here, the members are moderate earners with affordable homes, not high-balance borrowers.
Daniel Meuser.p3: As measured in 2023, transportation and warehousing employment ran far above the national norm, and manufacturing added another strong concentration of jobs.
