Overall finance and insurance employment sat well below typical levels even as it outgrew the nation's pace by a slim margin. Mining and utilities work also ran well above typical levels. This is a district built on moving and making things, not on managing money.

Daniel Webster.p1: Home values here run 4.8 times the median household income, a wider spread between cost and pay than nearly all peer districts show. Rent takes 25.8 percent of the median household income. Owners far outnumber renters, at a share well above most comparable districts, and poverty sits far below the norm. The strain here falls on buying in, not on households already struggling to get by.
Daniel Webster.p2: Credit union offices sit at the national norm, but credit union jobs lag well behind it, and that mismatch is the more telling fact: about as many locations as elsewhere, staffed far more thinly. Fairwinds, Suncoast, and MIDFLORIDA carry that presence. Credit unions hold 20.8 percent of retail offices, and JPMorgan Chase leads the district under federal deposit-reporting rules, which credit deposits to wherever they were booked rather than to where customers actually bank.
Daniel Webster.p3: This district's jobs, measured in 2023, tilted heavily toward hospitality and leisure: accommodation and food service alone held 20.2 percent of local jobs, and arts, entertainment, and recreation added 16.5 percent, both far above national norms for those sectors. Finance and insurance employment stayed light against the national norm but grew fast over the decade before. Retail trade added a modest further slice of employment. Purchase loans made up most mortgage originations in this district, a heavier tilt toward buying than the typical refinance-heavy mix elsewhere.

Danny Davis.p1: This district packs people in tighter than almost anywhere else in the country, a crowding that shapes everything else measured here. Household income runs comfortably ahead of typical districts at $90,223, yet homeownership is rare here and poverty runs high, at 17.1 percent. Home values run about four times the median income, and rent eats a sizeable share of what households bring in. Work is harder to find here too, with unemployment running high.
Danny Davis.p2: Credit union employment here is thin against the national norm, while credit union offices, though also below that norm, hold up better by comparison, an unusual split worth noting going in. Alliant, Verve, and Credit Union 1 anchor that presence, though credit unions hold just 18.8 percent of retail offices, a smaller slice than most comparable districts see. Banking here otherwise runs through a dense field of branches, with BMO Bank National Association booking the largest deposits on paper.
Danny Davis.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance employment ran far above the national norm, at 2.78 times, alongside heavy concentration in professional, scientific, and technical services. Health care and social assistance also accounted for a notable slice of the job base, though without the same concentration. Home purchases dominated mortgage activity here, at 70.6 percent of originations, with meaningful reach into lower income neighborhoods as well.

Darin LaHood.p1: Homes here carry a price-to-income ratio of 2.5, among the lowest of any congressional district, and that gap between what a household earns and what a house costs marks this district out. The 16th district of Illinois carries a median household income of 85,435 dollars, well above typical districts, alongside low poverty and unemployment. Homeownership runs high and density stays thin across the district. Few places in the state let a paycheck cover this much.
Darin LaHood.p2: Credit unions hold just 15.6 percent of retail offices here, a thinner presence than most comparable districts carry, leaving banks as the main source of branch banking. Citizens Equity First, Streator Onized, and Connexus carry that smaller share. On the jobs side, the credit union sector sits just slightly above the national norm here, and its office count keeps pace with that figure. For a credit union working this district, that means competing for a modest slice of a market where many separate banks, Morton Community Bank foremost by deposits booked here, hold the rest.
Darin LaHood.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing anchored the job market here, accounting for close to 15 percent of local jobs at a level well above the national norm, alongside a utilities sector that was highly specialized against the rest of the country. Overall finance and insurance employment trailed the national norm, and had grown more slowly than the country as a whole over the prior decade. This remains a district built on making and moving goods, not on finance.

Darrell Issa.p1: Poverty here is among the lowest of any congressional district, just 7.2 percent, and everything else follows that lead. Median household income reaches 114,972 dollars, well clear of most comparable districts. Housing is expensive against that income, a median home value of 794,700 dollars, yet most households own rather than rent. The district is also spread out, far less dense than most of its peers.
Darrell Issa.p2: Credit unions hold 28.6 percent of retail offices here, an unusually strong foothold, yet credit union employment runs slightly below the national norm. Navy Federal, San Diego County, and Mission carry that presence. The single largest deposit total belongs to JPMorgan Chase under federal reporting rules, which credit deposits to the office where they are booked rather than to where customers actually bank, and dozens of other bank branches compete on this same ground. A credit union here works a market with real income and real home equity behind it, against rivals who outstaff it relative to their footprint.
Darrell Issa.p3: As measured in 2023, construction was the standout sector, 13.9 percent of jobs and well above the national norm. Arts, entertainment, and recreation ran nearly as specialized, well above typical levels nationally. Health care was a large employer but not a distinctive one here, closer to the national norm than above it. Finance and insurance employment sat below the national norm overall, despite faster than average growth across finance and insurance together.

Darren Soto.p1: A home in this district runs 4.9 times what a typical household earns, a housing burden matched by few other seats nationwide. Median household income is unremarkable next to other districts, while home values near 401,100 dollars are not. Homeownership trails most comparable places, and both poverty and unemployment run higher than typical. Across 909,540 residents, the cost of shelter has pulled well away from what people bring home.
Darren Soto.p2: Credit union offices here outpace credit union employment, branches persisting even where staffing has not followed. Suncoast, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Addition Financial anchor that presence, which adds up to 21.5 percent of all retail offices, a share in the middle of the pack for districts like this one. Credit union jobs and offices both run well under typical national levels for the industry. Against Bank of America, named here only for the deposits booked to its address, and dozens of rival branches citywide, credit unions hold a real but secondary share of where people can walk in.
Darren Soto.p3: As measured in 2023, this district's job base leaned hard on tourism, logistics, and property. Transportation and warehousing, and real estate, both ran well over twice the national norm, and food service and lodging were not far behind. Finance and insurance jobs overall stayed thin, even though the sector had grown fast over the prior decade. Roughly 290,200 jobs anchored the district, built far more on moving goods and housing guests than on managing money.

Dave Min.p1: Household income in the 47th district sits among the highest of any congressional district, and the rest of the picture follows from that. Homes carry a value near 1,361,700 dollars against that income, a gap wide enough to put ownership out of easy reach, and rent runs 2,832 dollars a month. Homeownership runs low for a district this affluent. This is a dense, coastal, high-pay, high-cost economy.
Dave Min.p2: Credit unions hold just 12.4 percent of retail offices here, a thin slice next to the banks that dominate deposits, including Wells Fargo, named here only for deposits booked to addresses in the district, not for having the most branches nearby. A regional financial cooperative and two other credit unions carry the presence that does exist locally. Employment in credit unions runs close to the national norm even though office presence sits far below it, so the people working in the sector do more with a smaller footprint. A credit union here is serving households already priced past what many banks offer as standard.
Dave Min.p3: Local industry measured in 2023 leaned into real estate and rental leasing and into management of companies, both far above the national norm for their share of jobs. Professional, scientific, and technical services added real depth too, well above the norm. Finance and insurance employment overall ran strong against the national norm, at 1.6 times. This is a district shaped by high-value services and corporate management, not by sheer job count.

David Joyce.p1: What sets this district apart is how far income stretches over a house: the home value to income ratio runs 3.0, among the lowest anywhere comparable. Median household income sits at $73,552, and most households own rather than rent. Poverty and unemployment both run low next to other districts. Modest paychecks here still buy a house more often than not.
David Joyce.p2: Credit union offices keep pace with the national norm even as credit union jobs lag it, a split worth flagging before anything else about the sector. Seven Seventeen, Cardinal Credit Union and Lakeview carry that presence locally, holding 23.2 pct of retail offices against banks, a share close to what similar districts show. The Huntington National Bank is named locally as the top bank by deposits booked here, one competitor among many branches in the district. A credit union here is working with modest, steady incomes, not a wealthy customer base.
David Joyce.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing dominated the job base, employing 21.5 pct of workers and running at 2.43 times the national norm, the one clear specialty in the district. Retail trade and wholesale trade each ran a shade above the national norm too, rounding out a goods-moving economy. Overall finance employment sat far under the national norm, so this was never a banking town to begin with. Total employment approached 257,900 jobs, anchored by factory floors more than office towers.

David Kustoff.p1: A home in the 8th congressional seat of Tennessee runs about 3.7 times the annual earnings of a typical household, and rent takes only a small bite from that income, a housing cost lighter than nearly all comparable districts carry. The typical household earns 70,081 dollars, and homeownership is common here, well beyond what most comparable districts see. Unemployment is low, at 4.1 percent. Population density is thin, with the district spread wide rather than crowded.
David Kustoff.p2: Credit unions hold just 13.2 percent of retail offices here, a smaller foothold than in most comparable districts, leaving banks the dominant presence in this market. Leaders Credit Union, Orion, and First South Financial carry the credit union side locally. Credit union office presence runs slightly above the national norm, but credit union staffing lags behind it, meaning offices here outpace jobs. For a credit union serving this district, that means a modest retail position against a crowded banking field, working with households that own rather than rent and borrow on affordable terms.
David Kustoff.p3: As measured in 2023, manufacturing dominated the local economy, employing 16.5 percent of workers at nearly twice the national norm, the clearest specialization here. Health care and social assistance was nearly as large a source of jobs. Overall finance employment and its growth over the prior decade both ran a touch below the national norm. Total employment approached 301,800 jobs, built on a factory base that peer districts do not share.

David McCormick.p1: Pennsylvania holds just over 13 million people at a density that outpaces nearly every other state, packed into a Northeast footprint. Median household income sits near 77,545 dollars, a middling number nationally, while home values trail most of the country. Homeownership runs unusually high, a sign of a settled population rather than a transient one. The state's median age of 41.2 years fits that same steady, unhurried character.
David McCormick.p2: Pennsylvania State Employees, Members 1st, and Police & Fire anchor the credit union presence here, and together with smaller institutions credit unions hold 22.9 percent of retail offices statewide. Credit union offices edge above the national norm on count, even though jobs in those offices lag behind it, meaning branches here get by with leaner staffing than the country typically shows. PNC Bank is the name that leads deposits booked to state addresses, one competitor among thousands of branches operated by rival banks across the state. That crowded retail-banking field is what a credit union in Pennsylvania works against for the same household dollars described above.
David McCormick.p3: As measured in 2023, health care and social assistance carried unusual weight in the state's job base, running above the national norm. Management of companies and enterprises ran more specialized still, and manufacturing added further weight beyond what the national pattern would predict. Finance and insurance jobs overall ran slightly above norm, though growth in that sector lagged the country across the prior decade.

David Rouzer.p1: This district's clearest distinction is a jobless rate of just 3.6 percent, well below most comparable seats, across a population of 805,748 whose typical resident is 42 years old. Incomes trail most peer districts, and poverty is somewhat more common here too. Housing costs press harder than typical, with home values running about 4.6 times income, even as homeownership stays high at 73.2 percent.
David Rouzer.p2: State Employees', Corning, and Pentagon are the credit unions named here, and together with others they hold 21.7 percent of retail offices, a slice roughly on par with what similar districts show against their banks. Credit union employment and office presence track each other closely, neither running noticeably thicker than the other. Live Oak Banking Company turns up as the top name by deposits booked to addresses here, which reflects where filings land rather than a bigger branch footprint locally. A credit union working here is dealing mostly with homeowners and moderate earners rather than renters or the affluent.
David Rouzer.p3: As measured in 2023, construction and public administration stood out as specialized sectors, employing well above the national norm. Health care, retail trade, and accommodation and food services employed the most people, each running slightly above typical concentration. Finance and insurance employment overall ran well below the national norm. The district's redrawing since the last map means any comparison across the decade is a comparison of two different places, not a record of one.

David Schweikert.p1: Unemployment sits at 3.2 percent, among the lowest of any comparable district, and it frames a place that is comfortable by most measures. Median household income runs to 102,195 dollars, well clear of most other districts, while poverty stays unusually low. Housing carries a real premium, with a median home value of 696,200 dollars against income at a ratio of 6.8, and homeownership trails most other districts even so.
David Schweikert.p2: Credit unions hold just 13.1 percent of retail offices here, a thin slice next to most comparable districts, leaving banks to fill most of the storefronts even where Desert Financial, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Arizona Financial carry the credit union name. Western Alliance Bank books a leading deposit share among local institutions, though that figure reflects where deposits get recorded rather than who dominates the local market. Credit union employment tracks its office footprint closely, both running a bit below the national norm, in a district where the money on offer is unusually large for a credit union to work with.
David Schweikert.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance stood out sharply, employing 10.1 percent of the district's workers at well above the typical national share, the clearest specialty this district has. Health care and accommodation and food services employed more people overall, rounding out an economy built on offices and services rather than production. Lending here leans heavily toward home purchases rather than refinancing, a district where finance is not just present but is the thing it does best.

David Taylor.p1: Median household income in this district lands well below most comparable districts, at $67,801, well behind what supports budgets elsewhere. Home values sit low to match, at $225,700, and rent takes only a small cut from what a household brings home. Homeownership is unusually common here, while poverty runs higher than in most peer districts, alongside a jobless rate that stays low. This is a Midwest district built around modest costs rather than crowding, with people spread thin across it.
David Taylor.p2: Credit union offices here carry more weight than credit union jobs do, an unusual split worth noting up front: office presence runs above the national norm while employment trails just behind it. ATOMIC, HOMELAND, and DESCO anchor that presence locally. Even so, credit unions hold only 17.1 percent of retail offices in the district, and a wide field of bank branches, topped on paper by National Cooperative Bank, does most of the remaining business. The households described above, modest income, high ownership, are what any credit union here actually serves.
David Taylor.p3: By 2023, transportation and warehousing and manufacturing had both grown well above the national norm for jobs in those fields, marking this district's industrial core. Health care and social assistance drew a wide slice of the workforce too, alongside manufacturing and retail trade, across roughly 213,800 jobs total. Finance employment overall sat well below the national norm here. Manufacturing and logistics stand out as this district's clearest strengths.

David Valadao.p1: Median household income here sits low against other districts nationwide, at 60,072 dollars, with poverty and unemployment both running well above typical levels. Homes cost less than in most comparable places, yet the distance between what they sell for and what households earn stretches unusually wide, and homeownership itself falls well short of most districts. Work here leans heavily on agriculture, spread across a district with far fewer people per square mile than most.
David Valadao.p2: Credit unions hold 38.8 percent of retail offices here, a share topping nearly every other district measured. Valley Strong, Employees, and SAFE 1 anchor that presence, well ahead of Wells Fargo, the deposit leader among the district's 56 bank branches under federal reporting rules. Both credit union staffing and office count run comfortably above the national norm, with the office count climbing faster still. In a place where income stretches thin and homeownership lags, that physical footprint matters more than it would elsewhere.
David Valadao.p3: General finance and insurance work runs far below the national norm here, suggesting this district earns its keep elsewhere. As measured in 2023, agriculture stood out as sharply specialized work, far above typical national levels, alongside a smaller concentration in oil and gas extraction. Public administration also ran well above typical levels. Mortgage lending activity leaned heavily toward home purchases over refinancing.

Deb Fischer.p1: Nebraska is home to just over two million people spread thinly across the state, more evidence of small, scattered labor markets than one dense center. Median household income sits at 76,376 dollars, trailing most states, and home values follow the same pattern at 263,100 dollars. Housing still costs little against income here, among the lowest burdens in the country. Unemployment stays low, which points to steady work even as wages sit behind the national picture.
Deb Fischer.p2: Pentagon, Veridian, and Cobalt anchor the credit union presence here, though together credit unions hold only 12.6 percent of retail offices, a small share next to banks, and First National Bank of Omaha leads locally booked deposits on paper, without being the only bank families here use. Credit union employment runs a touch below the national norm, tracking closely with how thin their office footprint is too. For a credit union, that means fewer doors but a state full of moderate earners and low housing costs still worth reaching.
Deb Fischer.p3: As of 2023, Nebraska's economy leaned hardest on agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting, a concentration well above the national rate despite a small share of jobs. Health care and social assistance employed the largest share of workers, ahead of manufacturing and retail trade. Finance and insurance employment overall ran above the national norm, though the combined sector's growth trailed peer states across the prior decade. Farming and factory supply chains define the working core of this state, well ahead of any financial center.

Debbie Dingell.p1: People are packed more tightly into this district than in most of its counterparts, a place built up rather than spread out. Households here earn a median of $96,954, comfortably ahead of typical peer districts, and homes carry a value-to-income ratio of 3.8, a comfortable middle by national standards. Nearly 70 percent own their homes, and both poverty and unemployment run low. This is a working, settled population with room to breathe financially even at density.
Debbie Dingell.p2: Credit unions hold 33.7 percent of retail offices here, a share well above most peer districts, in a market where DFCU Financial and Michigan's state employee credit union carry the local name recognition. JPMorgan Chase books the top bank deposit figure in the district, though that reflects reporting geography more than branch muscle, and many other banks still compete for the same households. Credit union offices are far thicker on the ground here than the national norm, while credit union employment sits right at that norm. That is a lot of storefronts chasing a fairly ordinary staffing base.
Debbie Dingell.p3: In 2021, the district's economy leaned on instructional services, which held a large share of jobs and ran well ahead of the national norm. Health Care and Social Assistance employed a substantial share of workers too. Overall finance and insurance employment lagged the national norm by a wide margin, a sign this district leaned toward instruction and services rather than finance. Total employment approached 325,600 jobs that year.

Debbie Wasserman Schultz.p1: A home in the 25th district of Florida runs 6.4 times what the typical household earns, a ratio among the highest of any district measured. Median household income clears 87,097 dollars, well ahead of many comparable places, yet ownership lags behind those same districts, with just 64.6 percent of households owning their home. Poverty stays low, at 10.0 percent, even as the cost of shelter stays high.
Debbie Wasserman Schultz.p2: Credit union jobs here sit much closer to the national norm than credit union offices do, and that mismatch says more about the sector locally than either figure alone. Space Coast, Navy Federal, and BrightStar carry that presence on the ground, even though credit unions hold only 16.9 percent of retail offices in the district, thin next to the banks. Bank of America books the most deposits to addresses here, though plenty of other banks compete for branches alongside it. The credit unions active in this district run leaner on offices than their staffing would imply.
Debbie Wasserman Schultz.p3: By 2023, employment in the district leaned hardest on Real Estate and Rental and Leasing, a sector running well past twice the national norm. Health Care and Social Assistance and Retail Trade employed the most people day to day. Mortgage lending tilted heavily toward home purchases, 55.2 percent of originations, with a smaller share reaching lower-income neighborhoods. Real estate stands out as the thing this district does more of than almost anywhere else.

Deborah Ross.p1: Homeownership in the 2nd congressional seat of North Carolina sits well below most comparable districts, even with median household income reaching $93,949 and home values at $470,600. Rent runs $1,664 a month, and home values sit at five times that income, a gap that points toward renting as the more common path here. Unemployment and poverty both come in light. It is a place of steady paychecks and crowded ground where owning lags behind what people earn.
Deborah Ross.p2: Credit union jobs here run far above the national norm, outpacing the credit union share of retail offices, which lands right at that norm, a split marking this as a place where credit unions employ heavily without branching to match. State Employees', Coastal, and Navy Federal anchor that presence, and credit unions hold 27.4 percent of retail offices, a strong share against comparable districts. First-Citizens Bank & Trust Company books notable deposits here among many competing banks. Given the income described above, this is fertile ground for credit union work even where the office count alone understates it.
Deborah Ross.p3: As measured in 2023, this district's economy leaned on public administration, well beyond the national norm, alongside strength in information work and in professional, scientific, and technical services. Overall finance and insurance employment ran modestly above the norm too, and grew faster than the norm over the prior decade, a figure covering finance broadly rather than credit unions alone. This is a government and knowledge-work economy first, with finance riding along behind it.

Delia Ramirez.p1: Few places on this list match how densely this district is settled, home to 732,771 residents living the closely built life typical of Chicago-area suburbs. Households earn a median $87,098, comfortably ahead of most districts, though unemployment runs high. Rent claims a modest 19.5 percent share of that income, but only 58.4 percent of residents own their homes, a homeownership rate well behind most peers. This is a place of solid earnings paired with unusually thin homeownership.
Delia Ramirez.p2: Credit unions hold just 6.6 percent of retail offices here, a thinner claim on the branch network than in most districts this size. Alliant, GreenState, and DuPage carry the credit union name locally, working against that thin footing while banks handle the rest of the deposit business. Credit union employment tracks the sector's office presence closely, both sitting well under national levels. For a credit union, this is a district with real income to work with and little institutional ground yet claimed.
Delia Ramirez.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing anchored the local economy, employing 18.5 percent of the workforce, a concentration far beyond the national norm. Wholesale trade and transportation and warehousing were also unusually concentrated here, the signs of an economy built around factories and freight rather than offices. Overall finance employment sat well under typical levels, and growth in finance and insurance trailed the broader pace too. Money management has never been this district's strength.

Derek Schmidt.p1: Home values here run lower than nearly every comparable district, at $189,600, and that single fact shapes most of what follows. Household income trails most peer districts too, at $68,050, though rent stays modest at close to $975 a month. Homeownership sits unremarkable next to other districts, near 68 percent, and poverty runs a bit above typical levels. The land itself spreads thin, far emptier than most seats its size.
Derek Schmidt.p2: Credit unions hold a small slice of the retail offices here, just 15.7 percent, leaving banks with most of the storefronts people see. Navy Federal Credit Union, Azura, and Envista carry the local name recognition. Credit union employment tracks the national norm closely, but branch presence runs well ahead of it, more offices per worker than the country typically carries. One savings bank posts the top deposit figure under federal rules crediting the office where funds are booked, not the branches serving customers locally.
Derek Schmidt.p3: The industry base here was measured in 2023. Manufacturing carried real weight, close to twice the national norm, a much larger share of work than most places see. Public administration ran stronger still, government offices anchoring a big piece of the job count. Overall finance employment lagged the country. Lending activity leaned heavily toward home purchases, 58.0 percent of originations, a district built on government work and factory floors more than finance.

Derek Tran.p1: People are packed into this district more tightly than in almost any other, at over 7,160 per square mile, and that density shapes everything else about it. Income here reaches a median of 105,531 dollars, well above most districts, yet home values near 934,500 dollars leave the district at 8.9 times income, among the steepest ratios anywhere. Homeownership trails most districts, and poverty runs low while unemployment sits unremarkable. The strain here is about housing cost, not income or work.
Derek Tran.p2: Credit union jobs in this district run close to the national norm, while credit union offices lag well behind it, a gap wide enough that staffing clearly outpaces branch presence. A statewide-charter credit union serving educators, alongside Navy Federal Credit Union and Christian Community, hold the largest footprints among them, though credit unions hold only 16.8 percent of retail offices here, a lower share than most districts, competing against a far larger set of bank branches where JPMorgan Chase books the most deposits. For a district this dense and this costly, credit unions work with fewer doors than their staffing implies.
Derek Tran.p3: The district's work leaned toward arts, entertainment and recreation, wholesale trade, and management of companies, all well above their national weight. Health care, retail, and food service each employed large shares of workers as well. Overall finance employment ran below the national norm, with growth in finance and insurance well under typical pace. Mortgage lending here skewed heavily toward home purchases, making up 38.9 percent of originations.

Derrick Van Orden.p1: Unemployment here sits among the lowest of any district we track, at 2.9 percent, and the rest of the numbers describe a place that runs steady rather than hot. Median household income trails most peer districts at 73,367 dollars, while home values and rent are modest by comparison, with typical homes near 262,700 dollars. At 66 people per square mile, this is a sparsely settled district.
Derrick Van Orden.p2: Credit unions hold 30.2 percent of retail offices here, a figure that sets this district apart from comparable ones, and the field is anchored by ROYAL, WESTCONSIN, and ALTRA rather than the large bank names that lead on deposits. Credit union employment runs close to four times the national norm, and office presence more than double that norm, both marked highly specialized. Associated Bank, National Association shows up as the top holder of deposits booked to this district, a quirk of federal reporting tied to where accounts are recorded rather than a sign of dominance, and hundreds of bank branches operate here too.
Derrick Van Orden.p3: Working from a 2023 picture, manufacturing accounted for 16.0 percent of jobs, well above the national norm, alongside notable strength in agriculture and in transportation and warehousing. Overall finance employment ran only slightly above the national norm, so this district's financial character comes through credit unions specifically, not the sector as a whole.

Diana DeGette.p1: Just under 47.7 percent of households in the 1st district of Colorado own their homes, among the lowest shares of any comparable district. That sits alongside income well ahead of typical districts and home values that push the price of a typical home to 6.8 times typical earnings. The district is also densely built, consistent with a packed urban core. Unemployment and poverty both sit close to what most other districts report.
Diana DeGette.p2: Credit unions hold just 15.5 percent of retail offices here, a smaller footprint than in most comparable districts, leaving banks with most of the physical presence even though Bellco, Westerra, and Ent all carry real weight locally. Wells Fargo books the most deposits to addresses in this district, one name among 163 bank branches operated under separate ownership. Credit union work here is thinner on payroll and storefronts alike compared with the national norm, though jobs are holding up better than offices are, a sign of leaner branches doing more with less for the district's renters and high earners alike.
Diana DeGette.p3: The district's economy, measured in 2023, leaned heavily on professional, scientific, and technical services, employing 15.3 percent of workers at a concentration far above the national norm. Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction employed a small share of workers but stood out as the most specialized sector in the district. Across all lenders, home purchases made up 58.9 percent of mortgage originations.

Diana Harshbarger.p1: Household income in the 1st district of Tennessee sits among the lowest of any district in the country, at $60,591. Home values and rent are modest by comparison, with a median home value of $255,800, and homeownership is common at 72.4 percent. Poverty is well above typical levels here, even though unemployment stays low. It is a lightly settled district, spread across 797,902 people.
Diana Harshbarger.p2: Credit unions hold 29.5 percent of retail offices here, a share far ahead of most districts and the standout fact about them locally. Eastman, Knoxville TVA Employees, and ORNL are the names behind that presence. Credit union employment runs well beyond the national norm, and office presence sits in that same range. First Horizon Bank books more deposits here than any other name, under federal reporting rules, one among many banks competing here.
Diana Harshbarger.p3: As measured in 2023, manufacturing was the district's defining industry, employing 16.4 percent of workers at nearly twice the national norm. Accommodation and food services and arts and entertainment also ran well ahead of typical levels, rounding out a district built on making things and hosting visitors. Overall finance and insurance employment stayed well below the national norm, leaving credit unions as the disproportionate face of the financial sector here. Home purchases made up most mortgage originations across all lenders.

Dina Titus.p1: Unemployment stands out first here, at 6.6 percent, higher than almost anywhere comparable, and that fact colors everything else about the local economy. Household income trails most peer districts at 72,138 dollars, while home values have climbed to 429,100 dollars, pulling the home-value-to-income ratio to 5.9. Rents run high enough against that income to strain household budgets. This is a dense district, built around Las Vegas and the workforce that keeps it running.
Dina Titus.p2: Credit union offices here do more work than credit union staffing alone would explain: employment in the sector runs well below the national norm, while office presence holds up much closer to it, so fewer people cover a wider footprint. America First, Boulder Dam, and Silver State Credit Union anchor that presence, though credit unions hold only 20.7 percent of retail offices against a much larger network of bank branches. For a workforce already stretched by income and rent, that share of the market still matters.
Dina Titus.p3: Measured in 2023, the local job base rested heavily on accommodation and food service work, which accounted for 39.3 percent of all jobs, a rate more than four times the national norm. Retail and health care followed at far smaller shares. Finance work overall stayed thin against the national norm, even as finance and insurance jobs together grew faster than the country did between 2013 and 2023. Hospitality anchors this economy at a scale few other districts can match, with everything else secondary to it.

Don Bacon.p1: What sets this district apart is how little housing eats into pay: a home value to income ratio of 3.6, with rent claiming just 17.6 percent of the median household's earnings. Home values run modest by comparison with other seats, and most households own rather than rent. Unemployment sits low, in a district that otherwise looks like a typical middle-income Midwestern seat.
Don Bacon.p2: Credit union offices here outpace credit union employment, a gap worth leading with: office presence clears the national norm by a wide margin while jobs barely reach it. Veridian, Pentagon, and Centris anchor that footprint, holding 26.3 percent of retail offices against banks, a share above most comparable districts. First National Bank of Omaha leads locally by deposits booked here, but with 206 bank branches total, it works alongside many rivals rather than over them. A credit union in this district has more storefronts to lean on than staff to run them.
Don Bacon.p3: Corporate back offices stood out most in the 2023 employment count, the single sector where this district diverged furthest from the national pattern. Finance and insurance followed as a strong presence too, alongside sizable employment in health care. Mortgage lending that year skewed heavily toward home purchases, at 58.8 percent of originations, with a smaller share reaching lower-income neighborhoods.

Donald Beyer.p1: This district is packed far more tightly than comparable districts, one of the densest anywhere, and that crowding shapes everything else about it. Households here earn among the highest incomes measured, while few residents live in poverty and joblessness is rare. Home values run just as high, yet homeownership lags well behind, a striking gap for a place this affluent. Work is steady and well paid, even as tight housing keeps ownership out of reach for many.
Donald Beyer.p2: Credit union employment here shows up as a highly specialized concentration against the national norm, even though credit union offices hold a modest slice of retail branches, 24.2 percent. Navy Federal, Pentagon, and State Department credit unions anchor that footprint, doing more with less physical space. Truist Bank carries the largest deposit total among banks in the district, a figure driven by where accounts are booked rather than by branches on the ground. Credit unions here clearly employ far more people than their share of branches alone would explain.
Donald Beyer.p3: As of 2023, this district's mix of work concentrated in Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services, employing that sector at more than three times the national norm, alongside strong concentrations in Educational Services and Other Services. Overall finance and insurance employment sat modestly below the norm, even as credit unions themselves punched above it. This is a district built on specialized, high skilled work rather than broad-based industry.

Donald Davis.p1: Median household income in this district is $58,749, one of the lowest figures recorded for any congressional seat, and poverty here runs noticeably heavier than the typical district carries. Home values and rent are similarly modest, though these are published midpoints rather than a measure of what any one household pays. Homeownership trails most peer districts at 65.2 percent. With just over 90 people per square mile, this is a lightly settled place, and joblessness sits above what most other districts report.
Donald Davis.p2: Credit unions hold 30.8 percent of retail offices here, a share far beyond most comparable districts. State Employees', Navy Federal Credit Union, and Coastal are the names behind that presence, operating alongside 139 bank branches spread across numerous competing lenders. Credit union employment towers over the national norm, running at nearly triple the usual concentration, and outpaces even the district's already strong office presence. That is a lot of credit union capacity serving a population with tight incomes and real borrowing needs.
Donald Davis.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing dominated the job base here, accounting for 17.7 percent of employment and running twice the national norm, the clearest specialization in the district. Public administration and agriculture also ran well above typical levels, a pattern of making and growing things rather than managing money. Overall finance employment ran below the national norm even as the broader sector grew somewhat faster than typical nationally between 2013 and 2023. This remains a district built on production, not on banking it.

Donald Norcross.p1: Unemployment here runs unusually high for a district this comfortable, at 5.6 percent, the fact that separates it most from places like it. Households earn a median 94,772 dollars a year, well ahead of typical districts, and poverty stays low. Homeownership is high at 69.7 percent, and housing costs measured against income are easy compared with most peer districts. This is a dense, built-out corner of the Northeast, more crowded than most comparable seats.
Donald Norcross.p2: Credit unions hold just 12.4 percent of retail offices here, a share far smaller than most districts carry, even with a crowded field of bank branches sitting alongside them. Police & Fire, Navy Federal Credit Union, and American Heritage carry that presence locally. Jobs and offices in the credit union sector both sit well under the national norm, with the office count shrinking less than the job count did. For a district this well-off and this settled in homeownership, that is a light institutional footprint for the money involved.
Donald Norcross.p3: As of 2023, health care and social assistance was a leading and concentrated sector for the district, holding 18.8 percent of jobs, followed by retail trade and educational services. All three ran above the national norm for their size here. Overall finance and insurance employment stayed below the national norm, and its growth from 2013 to 2023 lagged slightly as well. This remained a place organized around care work and classrooms rather than finance.

Doris Matsui.p1: Unemployment here runs well above most comparable districts, at 5.6 percent, a sign of a labor market still working through slack. Median household income sits comfortably above the norm for districts like this, at 96,869 dollars, but housing eats into that advantage: home values run nearly six times median income. This is a crowded, costly place for a workforce that has not fully found its footing.
Doris Matsui.p2: Credit union employment here runs specialized, at 1.72 times the national norm, well ahead of credit union office presence, which sits only slightly above that same norm. Golden 1, SAFE, and a large statewide credit union anchor that footprint, holding 26.5 percent of retail offices against every bank competing here. U.S. Bank National Association books the most local deposits under federal reporting rules, though that reflects booking practice more than branch reach. The story for a credit union weighing this seat is an employment presence that outruns its office count, serving an income base that is solid but squeezed by housing costs.
Doris Matsui.p3: Work here concentrated heavily in public administration as of 2023, holding 24.1 percent of jobs, over five times the national norm. Utilities work also ran far heavier than the national picture, while health care and social assistance added real weight without approaching that concentration. Overall finance and insurance employment ran far below the national norm. This is a district built around government work first, with everything else well behind it.

Dusty Johnson.p1: This district covers the entire state of South Dakota, and it is empty in a way few other seats are, just over twelve people per square mile. Households earn $76,881 a year, unremarkable next to other districts, and unemployment runs low at 2.8 percent. Housing costs stand apart most: homes run cheap relative to income, with a value-to-income ratio of 3.8 and rent claiming just 15.6 percent of the median household income.
Dusty Johnson.p2: Credit union employment here sits at 1.32 times the national norm, even though credit unions hold only 20.3 percent of retail offices in the district. Black Hills, Dakotaland, and Levo carry that presence against Citibank, National Association, which leads the district by the deposit figures federal rules assign to it, not by any real branch network on the ground here. Staffing in the district's credit unions runs thicker than their share of offices alone would account for.
Dusty Johnson.p3: Farming and its supply chains define the work measured here in 2023, with agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting running far above the national norm. Wholesale trade and public administration each ran a quarter above that norm too, a mark of an economy still built around moving goods and running government offices. Manufacturing, retail, and health care rounded out the largest slices of work, each somewhat thicker here than the norm elsewhere. Lending activity in the district leaned heavily toward buying homes, with the remainder going to refinancing and other purposes.

Dwight Evans.p1: This district is packed tightly, among the most densely settled in the country, and that crowding shapes everything else about it. Pay in the typical household lands at $65,154 a year, modest for a district like this, and poverty runs high enough to stand out nationally. Rent runs $1,546 a month, and homeownership sits low at 47.7 percent, a sign that renting, not owning, is the norm here.
Dwight Evans.p2: Credit union jobs are thinner on the ground here than the national norm, even though the branch network is not: offices are outpacing jobs. Police & Fire, American Heritage, and Philadelphia anchor that network, which claims 25.2 percent of retail deposit-taking offices across the district, a share above most comparable places. Bank of America shows the largest deposit total booked here, a reflection of reporting rules more than branch strength, one name among 120 bank branches. For a workforce this dense and this income-strained, that credit union presence carries real weight against the banks around it.
Dwight Evans.p3: As of 2023, health care and social services anchored the job base, alongside a strong presence in professional and technical work. Information work stood out sharply, more than twice the national norm, making this one of the most specialized districts in the country for that field. Finance and insurance employment also ran well above the norm, though it grew only in step with the nation over the prior decade.

Earl Carter.p1: Unemployment here runs well above most comparable districts, at 6.0 percent, a signal worth sitting with before anything else. The district holds 806,580 people, a median age near 38, with household income trailing what similar districts report. Home values run four times the typical income, and rent takes a bigger bite than it does in most peer places. Poverty runs high measured against comparable districts.
Earl Carter.p2: Credit union employment here sits well under the national norm, at 0.52 times, even though credit unions hold 27.4 percent of retail offices, a figure that outpaces nearly every comparable district. Navy Federal, Georgia's Own, and Interstate anchor that presence. Ameris Bank books more deposits here than any other name, under federal reporting rules, among many banks competing in the district. For a credit union in this district, the households earning below the peer norm and stretched by rent are exactly who that thin staffing has to serve well.
Earl Carter.p3: By 2023, transportation and warehousing along with accommodation and food services stood out as this district's clearest specialties, both well above national norms. Health care employed the most people, though without any particular specialization there, alongside strong numbers in food service and retail. Overall finance employment sat well below the national norm. Home purchases dominated mortgage lending, while only a small share of loans reached lower-income neighborhoods.

Ed Case.p1: At 3.0 percent, the jobless rate in this district counts among the lowest anywhere in the country, and it sits beside a household income of 102,713 dollars, well clear of most other seats. Home values near 912,300 dollars run far out of proportion to what people earn, and just 57.2 percent of households own the roof over their heads. The district is packed tightly onto the land it has, far more densely settled than most of the country, consistent with an island economy.
Ed Case.p2: Credit unions hold 42.8 percent of retail offices here, a share that sits near the very top nationally, in a market where First Hawaiian Bank leads on deposits booked to local addresses under federal reporting rules, alongside a wide field of bank rivals. Hawaii State, Navy Federal, and HawaiiUSA anchor the credit union side. Credit union offices run at twice the national norm and employment in the industry well above it too, offices outpacing jobs, a sign of a dense branch presence built to serve the high-income, high-cost households described above.
Ed Case.p3: The 2023 employment picture leaned heavily on accommodation and food service and public administration, both well above the national norm for their size here. Overall finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm, with growth over the prior decade roughly flat against it. This is an economy built around tourism and government rather than banking, one where the credit union footprint stands out precisely because conventional finance does not dominate.

Edward Markey.p1: Massachusetts carries a population just over 7.1 million with a median household income of 104,828 dollars, among the highest of any state. Housing runs expensive to match, with a median home value of 607,400 dollars against income at a ratio of 5.8, and rent near 1,848 dollars a month. Homeownership trails most of the country here, while few residents live in poverty and joblessness stays modest.
Edward Markey.p2: First Technology, Rockland, and Metro are the names carrying credit union business across a state where those institutions hold just 20.3 percent of retail offices, thinner ground than credit unions hold in comparable states. Credit union employment sits below the national norm too, even as office presence runs slightly ahead of it, meaning branches persist where staffing has not followed. That leaves a dense, high-income population still served mostly through banks, State Street Bank and Trust chief among them by deposits booked locally, though far from alone among the state's many branches.
Edward Markey.p3: Work in 2023 concentrated in professional, scientific, and technical services and in information, both well above the national norm. Health care and social assistance made up the largest share of jobs of any sector. Finance and insurance jobs overall ran above the national norm too, though that sector's growth over the prior decade lagged the country's pace. This is a state built on service work rather than production, dense and costly, with money concentrated in institutions built for scale.

Eleanor Norton.p1: Washington packs nearly 11,500 people per square mile onto a compact grid, among the densest counts of any state. Median household income runs to 109,707 dollars, well above most states, but that prosperity sits beside a poverty rate and an unemployment rate that both sit near the top nationally. Home values near 733,400 dollars work out to 6.7 times that income, a gap wide enough to price out most local buyers.
Eleanor Norton.p2: A credit union working this market is lending against some of the priciest housing stock and thinnest homeownership in the country, and rent alone eats up better than a fifth of what the typical household brings home. Credit union employment here runs thin relative to the national norm, in a workforce built mostly of federal offices and consulting firms rather than the branch-heavy sectors that usually staff credit unions. The institution meets a population with money and a population without a mortgage in the same building.
Eleanor Norton.p3: The 2023 employment mix was dominated by government and the firms that serve it: Public Administration ran at more than four times the national norm for its size, and Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services ran at over two and a half times the norm while also employing the largest share of workers. Other Services added another layer of specialization far above typical levels. This was, and remains, an economy built to run the federal government and advise it, not to house it cheaply.

Elijah Crane.p1: People are spread thin across the 2nd congressional seat of Arizona, among the lowest densities of any congressional district in the country. The population, near 853,923, is middle-aged on the whole and earns a median household income of 70,376 dollars, well under what most districts report. Homeownership runs high, near 76 percent, but poverty and joblessness both run deeper here than in most parts of the country. Housing costs press hard too, with a home value to income ratio of 5.2.
Elijah Crane.p2: Credit union offices here outnumber credit union jobs by a wide margin, with staffing well under the national norm for the sector. ONEAZ, Desert Financial, and America First anchor the local presence, and credit unions hold 26.4 percent of retail offices, a larger slice than most districts carry, and they compete with a crowded bank branch network topped on paper by JPMorgan Chase, whose deposit figure reflects booking rules rather than actual branch strength. That is a wide field for credit unions to work, serving people who own homes at high rates but carry real income pressure.
Elijah Crane.p3: As of 2023, the district's economy leaned on public administration and mining extraction, both far more concentrated here than nationally, alongside a notable arts and entertainment presence. Health care and food service employed the most people, with food service especially overrepresented. Finance and insurance employment stayed thin against the norm, even as the broader sector grew a bit faster than the country did between 2013 and 2023.

Elise Stefanik.p1: Home values in the 21st district sit among the lowest of any congressional district, at $196,800, and that gap shapes everything else here. Households earn less than most places, yet owning a home is the norm, and typical housing costs stay light relative to what people earn. The district is spread thin across the land, far emptier than most seats in the region, and its boundaries shifted at the last redistricting.
Elise Stefanik.p2: Credit unions hold 30.8 percent of retail offices here, a share that stands out from nearly every other district and is the most notable fact about financial services locally. AMERICU, Navy Federal Credit Union, and SEA Comm carry that presence, set against a field of 196 bank branches run by many separate banks, among which Arrow Bank National Association books sizeable deposits under federal reporting rules rather than local branch weight. Credit union employment runs close to twice the national norm, tracking a similarly elevated office presence. For a district of modest incomes and inexpensive housing, that is an unusually deep bench of cooperative finance.
Elise Stefanik.p3: As of 2023, the job base leaned heavily on public administration, more than twice the national norm, alongside farming and fishing work at a similar multiple. Overall finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm, a sign that much of the district's financial activity runs through credit unions rather than banks. This was an economy built on government and land, not on finance.

Elissa Slotkin.p1: Michigan is home to just over 10.1 million people, and the typical resident is 40.4 years old, in a state packed more densely than most. Median household income runs 72,389 dollars, trailing most of the country, and homes carry a value of 254,200 dollars, cheap relative to what households earn. Homeownership stands among the highest in the nation at 73.5 percent, even as the poverty rate runs higher than most states see.
Elissa Slotkin.p2: Credit unions here carry familiar names: Lake Michigan, DFCU Financial, and Genisys anchor a sector that holds 39.0 percent of retail offices, a bigger slice than nearly any other state claims, well ahead of JPMorgan Chase, the top bank by deposits booked in the state, in a market with plenty of competing banks. Credit union payrolls are unusually thick here relative to the rest of the country, and the office network thicker still, branches having multiplied faster than staff. For the homeowners and modest earners described above, that is a sector that has built out its physical presence more than its payroll.
Elissa Slotkin.p3: In 2021, manufacturing defined the state's specialty, employing a well above average share of workers relative to the rest of the country. Health care and social assistance employed a slightly larger slice still, with retail trade close behind. Overall finance employment ran a touch below the national norm that year, even as finance and insurance growth outpaced the country's. Michigan's 2021 economy leaned on making things and caring for people more than on moving money.

Elizabeth Warren.p1: Massachusetts packs work and people tightly together, among the densest states in the country. Jobs cluster around health care, technical services, and a strong knowledge sector, the kind of economy that pays well: median household income runs $104,828, among the highest anywhere. That income meets a housing market to match, with homes at a middle value of $607,400 against a home-value-to-income ratio of 5.8, and rent claiming a real slice of the typical household's income. Homeownership lags well behind most other states, even as unemployment stays low.
Elizabeth Warren.p2: Credit unions hold 20.3 percent of retail offices here, a smaller share than in most states. Their office presence still runs slightly above the national norm even though credit union staffing runs below it, so offices here outpace jobs rather than the other way round. First Technology, Rockland, and Metro anchor that footprint. Against a market of 1,887 bank branches, credit unions work a state of high earners and high housing costs from a narrow base.
Elizabeth Warren.p3: As measured in 2023, finance and insurance jobs overall ran above the national norm, even as growth in that combined sector lagged over the prior decade. The state's sharper edge sat in professional, scientific, and technical services, well above the norm, alongside a strong information sector. Across roughly 3,323,800 jobs, this was an economy built on expertise rather than sheer volume.

Emanuel Cleaver.p1: Household income in the 5th congressional seat of Missouri sits at $67,960, a good deal lower than most districts see, while the poverty rate of 15.1 percent climbs well above most. Unemployment, at just 3.3 percent, tells a different story, one of a labor market with little slack. Rent runs $1,239 a month, and housing costs overall land on the high side even where home values themselves stay modest. Density here runs higher than in most seats.
Emanuel Cleaver.p2: Credit union employment runs below the national norm here, even though credit union offices run slightly above it, a gap worth noting: these institutions hold more storefronts than staff would imply. ComunityAmerica, Mazuma, and Public Safety anchor that branch presence, which adds up to 24.3 percent of all retail bank and credit union offices in the district. UMB Bank, National Association shows a large deposit total booked to an address here, a reporting quirk more than a portrait of who residents actually bank with, since dozens of other banks operate branches across the district too.
Emanuel Cleaver.p3: As of 2023, professional and technical services employers stood out most against the national norm, and finance and insurance followed close behind, both well ahead of typical staffing levels for those sectors elsewhere. Health care still commanded a wide share of the workforce. Home purchases made up most mortgage originations, and a substantial share of lending reached lower-income neighborhoods, a sign of credit reaching beyond the district's wealthier corners.

Emilia Sykes.p1: Housing here is unusually cheap set against what people earn: the median home runs 3.2 times median household income, and rent takes just 17.2 percent of a typical paycheck. Median household income lags behind comparable districts, while poverty runs higher than most. Unemployment, by contrast, is low, at 3.8 percent.
Emilia Sykes.p2: Credit union offices here are far more common than credit union jobs, and that gap is the place to start: the workforce is thinner than the national norm at 0.54 times, while offices come close to matching it at 0.93. Canton Employees, Seven Seventeen, and Towpath carry that presence, holding 24.1 percent of retail offices against banks. Huntington National Bank books the most deposits locally, though it shares the district with a broad field of other banks. For a place with modest incomes and cheaper than average housing, that office footprint matters more than the payroll behind it.
Emilia Sykes.p3: Manufacturing, wholesale trade, and management of companies and enterprises stood out most in the 2023 industry count, with management running well above the national norm. Health care and social assistance employed more people than any other sector, ahead of manufacturing and retail trade. Finance and insurance employment sat near the national norm, and hiring there climbed at a faster clip than the nation's over the prior decade.

Emily Randall.p1: People here are spread far apart, a fraction of the density found in comparable seats. The typical household brings in $94,385, well ahead of most districts, and most residents settle into ownership rather than renting. Home values track high alongside that income, and poverty is uncommon at 10.2 percent. Unemployment sits unremarkable, suggesting a stable if unevenly spread economic base.
Emily Randall.p2: Retail offices here belong to credit unions at a rate of 30.3 percent, well above almost anywhere else. Navy Federal Credit Union, Boeing Employees, and Kitsap anchor that presence, serving a base of homeowners whose mortgages run 5.7 times the median income, a debt load these credit unions absorb into their daily business. Credit union employment runs 1.79 times the national norm, and offices 1.59 times, with jobs growing faster than office count. Bank of America books more deposits by address than any other bank operating here, though it competes against numerous local rivals.
Emily Randall.p3: As of 2023, this district's economy leaned hardest into Arts, Entertainment, and Recreation, far beyond what national patterns would predict, alongside a strong Public Administration presence. Health Care and Social Assistance, Retail Trade, and Accommodation and Food Services together accounted for a sizable share of workers. Overall finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm even as the sector grew roughly in step with the country. Loans for buying homes made up most mortgage activity, underscoring a market still built around purchase rather than refinancing.

Eric Burlison.p1: Household income in the 7th district of Missouri runs well below most comparable districts, at 66,064 dollars a year. Home values are modest too, and the gap between what homes cost and what people earn is not wide by national standards. Unemployment, at 3.5 percent, runs low. Population is thin across the land here, roughly 803,037 people scattered over a largely rural footprint.
Eric Burlison.p2: Credit unions hold just 12.9 percent of retail offices in this district, a thin share, and that is the fact that most marks the sector here. Assemblies of God, BluCurrent, and Multipli carry that share between them. Credit union employment and office presence both trail the national norm, with branches here outnumbering the jobs behind them relative to other places. Great Southern Bank accounts for more deposits booked to this district than any other single bank, under federal reporting rules, among many banks present here.
Eric Burlison.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing anchored the local economy, employing 12.1 percent of jobs, well ahead of what the national norm would predict. Transportation and warehousing showed the same pattern, also concentrated well beyond the national mark. All finance and insurance jobs together sat below the national norm here. This is a district shaped by moving and making things, not by financial services.

Eric Crawford.p1: This district spreads its people thinly, among the lowest counts of any district in the country, a stretch of small towns and farmland rather than dense suburbs. Across its 754,656 residents, median household income runs low at $52,325, and home values sit at $171,700. Housing costs, measured against income, come in lower than most other districts. Poverty and unemployment both run high here, a sign of an economy that has not fully recovered its footing.
Eric Crawford.p2: Credit unions hold just 3.9 percent of retail offices here, a share few other districts fall below, leaving banks to carry nearly all of it. Arkansas Federal, Success, and Baxter are the names carrying that small footprint. Centennial Bank books the largest local deposits, one name among many separate competitors here. Credit union employment and office presence both run far below the national norm, tracking each other closely, a modest presence that matches the thin branch share above.
Eric Crawford.p3: Arkansas's 1st was measured in 2023 with about 246,600 jobs, anchored by manufacturing, which holds 18.1 percent of jobs and runs more than twice the national norm. Agriculture, forestry, fishing, and hunting is even more disproportionately concentrated here relative to the rest of the country, despite its smaller share of jobs. Finance and insurance employment overall runs well under national norms. Manufacturing and agriculture are what set this economy apart from the rest of the country.

Eric Schmitt.p1: Missouri runs about 6.2 million people, spread thin across the state. Median household income sits at $71,589, trailing most of the country, and poverty runs somewhat higher than typical. Unemployment stays low, and homes carry a modest value-to-income ratio of 3.6, with most households owning rather than renting.
Eric Schmitt.p2: First Community, CommunityAmerica, and Multipli carry the credit union presence in a state where credit unions hold just 14.1 percent of retail offices, among the lowest shares anywhere. Credit union employment here falls short of the national norm, and thinner still than the office count itself, so branches outnumber staffing relative to peers. UMB Bank, National Association books a sizable deposit share, one name among many competing banks statewide. For the modest incomes and ownership-heavy households described above, that leaves credit unions working a small, thinly staffed corner of a bank-dominated map.
Eric Schmitt.p3: As measured in 2023, Missouri's economy leaned on manufacturing, running a bit above the national norm, and on management of companies and enterprises, smaller in headcount but more concentrated still. Health care and social assistance employed a bigger share of workers than any other line of work, out of the state's roughly 2,664,800 jobs. Finance and insurance jobs overall also ran a touch above the national norm, in an economy still built foremost on making things and running them.

Eric Sorensen.p1: Median household income in the 17th congressional seat of Illinois sits at $60,530, among the lowest of any district measured nationwide, and that fact runs under everything else here. Home values and rent stay low too, and housing eats a smaller slice of pay than most districts see. Homeownership falls short of most peers, while poverty climbs far past the typical rate. People here live spread thin across the land rather than packed into one place.
Eric Sorensen.p2: Credit union employment runs far ahead of the national norm, outpacing even the strong presence of credit union offices, a sign that the credit unions here run lean, heavily staffed operations relative to how many branches they keep open. State Farm, Citizens Equity First, and I. H. Mississippi Valley anchor that presence. Credit unions hold 26.0 percent of retail offices in the district, a strong share held against many competing banks, among them PNC Bank, which leads on deposits credited to addresses here, though far from the only bank at work locally. For a district with modest incomes, that is a substantial footprint for member-owned finance.
Eric Sorensen.p3: As measured in 2023, manufacturing drove much of local employment, claiming 16.1 percent of jobs at a rate well beyond the national norm. Finance and insurance ran specialized too, and management of companies added a further concentrated slice of employment. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, 64.2 percent of all originations, with a substantial portion of lending reaching lower-income neighborhoods.

Erin Houchin.p1: Housing in the 9th district costs little against what people earn: the median home runs 3.5 times median household income, and rent takes just 17.7 percent of it. Income itself falls below most districts, and poverty runs higher than most, but unemployment stays low. Owning a home here is the norm far more than renting, more so than in a typical district.
Erin Houchin.p2: Credit union offices here outweigh credit union jobs, a specialized presence in the office count against a workforce that sits almost exactly at the national norm, an imbalance worth flagging up front. Credit unions carrying local names hold 20.9 percent of retail offices against banks, putting this district roughly in line with its peers on that measure. A regional bank books sizable deposits under federal reporting rules, though it shares the district with many other banks and branches. Against a population earning modest incomes and owning homes at a high rate, these institutions work with a customer base long on homeowners and short on high earners.
Erin Houchin.p3: Manufacturing defines the work here, employing a share of the district's jobs that far exceeds the national norm and topping every other sector measured. Transportation and warehousing and educational services also employ more than their national share would predict, though by a smaller margin. Mortgage lending skewed heavily toward home purchases among all originations, in a district still anchored by factory work.

Eugene Vindman.p1: Household income in the 7th district of Virginia sets it apart from most other districts, at $113,690, paired with poverty and unemployment rates that both run low. Homeownership is high too, at 74.4 percent, across a population near 825,445 whose midpoint age lands at 37.2. Home values sit at roughly four times what the typical household earns, while rent takes about a fifth of median income.
Eugene Vindman.p2: Credit unions here hold 22.4 percent of retail offices, a middling share, but credit union employment runs thinner than that office presence, well under the national norm even though office presence itself sits close to it. Navy Federal, Pentagon, and Apple credit unions anchor the field. Atlantic Union Bank books more local deposits than any other bank here, though federal reporting rules credit deposits to the office where they are booked, not to where the branches or customers actually are. This is a well-off, heavily homeowning district for a credit union to work with, carrying less weight in institutional employment than its office count implies.
Eugene Vindman.p3: The job mix in 2023 leaned hard into retail trade and educational services, each well above the national norm, alongside a smaller but still elevated concentration in other services. Finance and insurance employment overall ran below the national norm, and its pace of change since 2013 fell short of the national mark as well. Mortgage originations tilted toward home purchases rather than refinancing, with a portion of that lending reaching lower-income neighborhoods.

Frank Lucas.p1: People here are spread out, just 24.4 per square mile, a figure few other seats can match on the low side. Median household income comes to 59,917 dollars, well under what most districts report, and home values land in similar territory. Housing costs relatively little against income in this district, though homeownership still trails most other seats. Poverty runs high and so does joblessness, both well above what is typical nationally.
Frank Lucas.p2: Credit unions hold just 11.0 percent of retail offices here, a share smaller than nearly every comparable district reports, leaving banks to dominate the retail branches that remain. TINKER, COMMUNICATION, and WEOKIE carry the credit union presence that exists. MidFirst Bank books the largest deposits under federal rules, though 312 bank branches from many separate banks operate across the district. Credit union employment runs close to the national norm even where offices are scarce, so the offices that exist tend to be fuller than usual.
Frank Lucas.p3: Oil and gas extraction, along with utilities, drove much of what set this district's job base apart in 2023, with mining, quarrying, and extraction work running more than nine times the national norm. Retail trade and health care employed large numbers of people day to day, though health care ran below the national norm and finance overall sat under national levels too. Mortgage lending here tilted heavily toward home purchases, at 66.3 percent of originations, and a fair portion of that credit reached lower income neighborhoods.

Frank Mrvan.p1: The 1st congressional district of Indiana is settled far more densely than comparable districts elsewhere, a legacy of the industrial towns strung along the state's northern edge. Its 760,512 residents skew middle-aged, and median household income of $75,199 trails most other districts. Housing costs stay modest by comparison: a median home value of $263,800 against that income, and most households here own rather than rent.
Frank Mrvan.p2: Credit union offices are heavily overrepresented here even though credit union employment falls short of the national norm, and that mismatch shapes what these institutions look like on the ground. EVERWISE, TECH, and U S credit unions anchor that branch presence, holding 25.2 percent of retail offices, a share above most comparable districts. Centier Bank comes out ahead of the district's other institutions on deposits booked to local addresses, a figure driven by federal reporting quirks as much as by where customers actually bank. Many separate banks still compete alongside it for the same households and small businesses.
Frank Mrvan.p3: Manufacturing anchored the economy as measured in 2023, employing a large slice of the workforce at a rate well above the national norm, alongside a specialized utilities sector. Health care and social assistance and retail trade rounded out the other sizable sources of work. Finance and insurance employment overall stayed below the norm even as its growth kept pace with the country. Mortgage lending that year leaned heavily toward home purchases over refinancing.

Frank Pallone.p1: Unemployment here runs higher than in almost any comparable district, at 6.5 percent, even though household income sits well above other districts at $104,316. Home values run five times the median income, and rent claims 21.7 percent of it, a heavier cost burden than most places carry. Homeownership trails typical levels, and nearly 787,000 people are crowded into a district far denser than most.
Frank Pallone.p2: Credit unions hold just 12.7 percent of retail offices here, a share that runs well below most peer districts, in a market with a couple hundred competing bank branches. Affinity, Navy Federal Credit Union, and United Teletech Financial carry that thin share between them. Credit union employment runs far behind the national norm, weaker still than the office count on its own, meaning existing branches operate leaner on staff than elsewhere. For a credit union working this ground, the income and density described above mean a deep pool of potential members reached through a small local footprint.
Frank Pallone.p3: Transportation and warehousing drove this district's job base as of 2023, holding 10.2 percent of employment at a concentration well beyond the ordinary national share. Administrative and support services and wholesale trade sat above their usual weight too. Health care and educational services employed more people day to day but without that same distinctiveness. Finance employment overall lagged the national norm, even as home purchases made up the bulk of lending activity across all lenders.

Frederica Wilson.p1: This corner of Florida is one of the most densely settled districts in the country, an urban stretch where space itself is the scarce commodity. The median household earns $72,293, trailing most comparable districts, while the median home is valued at $463,000, among the highest housing costs measured anywhere. Rent runs a median of $1,946 a month, and ownership here is the exception rather than the rule. Poverty and unemployment both run well above what most other districts report.
Frederica Wilson.p2: Credit unions hold just 13.0 percent of retail offices here, a small slice of a market with 136 bank branches on top of it. Navy Federal Credit Union and American Airlines are among the names that show up in this market. Credit union jobs sit far below the national norm, and the office count tells the same story. In a district this dense and this costly, credit unions work with a population stretched thin on housing and often shut out of ownership.
Frederica Wilson.p3: Accommodation and food services employment ran well above the national norm as of 2023, alongside real estate and rental services, marks of a place tilted toward hospitality and property. Overall finance sector employment sat below the national average, while finance growth roughly matched it. Mortgage lending here leaned heavily toward home purchases, 59.1 percent of originations.
