This is a district built on service work and shaped by housing costs that outrun what most residents can comfortably carry.

French Hill.p1: The 2nd congressional district of Arkansas posts a median household income of 67,021 dollars, well below most congressional districts, and that number sets the tone for the district. Home values run cheap at 234,600 dollars, and rent claims just 19.1 percent of income. Homeownership still trails most peer districts, even with poverty running higher than typical. Unemployment, at 3.6 percent, stays low, a district where work is easier to find than money is to stretch.
French Hill.p2: Credit union employment here runs below the national norm even though credit union offices sit slightly ahead of it, an unusual split for a place this size. Arkansas Federal, TELCOE, and Barksdale carry the local presence, holding just 17.0 percent of retail offices against area banks, a smaller cut than most districts see. Bank OZK is named the top bank here under federal reporting rules that credit a single office with deposits gathered far more broadly, though many banks compete for business in the district. For members earning near the district median, that thin office share matters more than which name sits on top.
French Hill.p3: As of 2023, health care and social assistance anchored the economy, employing 20.5 percent of the district's jobs and specialized well above the national norm. Retail trade and food service rounded out where people worked, without either running especially strong. Utilities showed the sharpest specialization of any sector measured here. Mortgage lending that year leaned heavily toward home purchases.

Gabe Amo.p1: Homeownership here sits well below most comparable districts, a minority holding on home turf in a district otherwise defined by renting. Home values run far above income, six times the median household income of 77,683 dollars, while rent runs to 1,408 dollars a month. Poverty and housing costs both run higher than in most peer districts, and density is high too, at 2,074.6 people per square mile. This is a tightly packed, largely rental Northeast district.
Gabe Amo.p2: Credit union offices here outrun credit union jobs, staffing below the national norm even as office presence sits slightly above it. Navigant, Coastal1, and Navy Federal Credit Union anchor that presence, holding 28.1 percent of retail offices against banks, a stronger showing than in most comparable districts. Citizens Bank, National Association books more deposits than any other name here, one bank among many competing for business in the district. For a district built on renters and modest incomes, that office footprint matters more than the payroll behind it.
Gabe Amo.p3: As measured in 2023, health care and social assistance carried the most jobs, at 16.8 percent of employment, with educational services close behind. Management of companies and enterprises stood out as a specialized sector, running well above the national norm. Overall finance employment ran above the national norm even as finance and insurance growth lagged the country over the prior decade. This is a district built on institutional employers rather than one dominant industry.

Gabe Evans.p1: Household income in this district clears $100,033 a year, well above most comparable districts, and that sets the tone for everything else here. Home values and rents run high to match, homeownership sits at 71.1 percent, and poverty stays low. People here are packed in more tightly than in most districts, a place filling in rather than spreading out. Unemployment sits at an ordinary level, nothing that stands out against the rest of what's measured here.
Gabe Evans.p2: Credit union employment here runs well below the national norm, at 0.47 times, even though credit union offices come closer to typical, and that split is the first thing to understand about the sector locally. Bellco, Ent, and Canvas anchor that presence, holding 20.9 percent of retail offices against area banks. Wells Fargo books the top deposit total under federal reporting rules, but it shares the district with 128 bank branches run by other institutions. A credit union here is working with income and homeownership levels that beat most of the country.
Gabe Evans.p3: As measured in 2023, construction carried heavy weight in the local economy, at 11.8 percent of jobs and more than twice the national norm. Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction ran highly specialized too, alongside strong transportation and warehousing employment. Finance and insurance employment overall stayed light against the national norm, and growth in that sector over the prior decade lagged typical as well. This is a district built on building and moving things, not on finance.

Gabe Vasquez.p1: This district spreads its 710,491 people across a vast, empty stretch of land, thinner on the ground than almost any other congressional seat. Households earn a median $60,933, near the bottom nationally, while unemployment runs high. Home values sit far under the typical district's, yet homeownership is common, a rate few places exceed. Housing costs here fall right around the national middle.
Gabe Vasquez.p2: Credit union jobs run well ahead of credit union offices in this district, at 1.44 times the national norm for employment against 1.22 for office presence, meaning the work here is thicker on the ground than the branch tally alone would show. NUSENDA, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Sunward anchor that presence, holding 29.3 percent of retail offices against banks. Wells Fargo carries the largest deposit total booked to addresses here under federal reporting rules, one name among many banks operating locally. For a population spread this thin and stretched this tight on income, that office share gives credit unions unusual weight.
Gabe Vasquez.p3: As measured in 2023, mining and oil and gas extraction stood out sharply, running well over ten times the national norm, with agriculture also highly specialized. Health care and retail trade employed the most people locally. Overall finance and insurance employment stayed thin, leaving credit unions to carry disproportionate weight in that sector. Total employment stood near 194,100 jobs, built on extraction and services rather than finance.

Gary Palmer.p1: Unemployment here is scarce, just 3.1 percent, and the rest of the picture matches. Median household income runs high at 86,712 dollars, while home values stay modest by comparison at 297,800 dollars. Homeownership is common at 75.9 percent, well ahead of typical districts, and poverty stays low. This is a place of steady work and owned homes rather than a tight rental market.
Gary Palmer.p2: Credit unions hold 29.8 percent of retail offices here, a share that far outpaces most districts. America's First, Southern Energy, and MAX carry that presence, working alongside ServisFirst Bank, which shows up with a large deposit sum booked to this district by federal reporting convention, not by branch presence or local customers. Credit union offices here run close to twice the national norm, a stronger showing than credit union employment, which points to a dense branch footprint layered onto the income and ownership patterns above.
Gary Palmer.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance was the sector where this district specialized most, employing well beyond the national norm. Retail trade and health care together accounted for a large share of jobs, with food service close behind. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, and only a small share of that lending reached lower income neighborhoods. Finance sits close to the center of what this district does, not at its edges.

Gary Peters.p1: Michigan runs on making things, with factory jobs still built into the state's bones and workers spread more densely across the land than most states. The median household brings in $72,389 a year, and the typical home is valued at $254,200, both on the low side nationally. Homeownership stands out at 73.5 percent, among the highest anywhere, even as poverty runs higher than most states report. Work is steady but unremarkable, with unemployment landing right around the national average.
Gary Peters.p2: Credit unions hold 39.0 percent of retail offices here, a share few states match, in a market where banks still compete hard for the rest, JPMorgan Chase among them on deposits booked to the state. Lake Michigan, DFCU Financial, and Genisys carry that credit union presence. Employment in the sector runs well above the national norm, and offices further still, growing faster than the jobs behind them. For a state of modest paychecks and high homeownership, that is a deep credit union footprint to work alongside.
Gary Peters.p3: In 2021, Michigan's economy still leaned on manufacturing, its clearest specialty and a big share of all jobs. Health care employed even more workers, just ahead of manufacturing's share, with retail trade close behind. Across roughly 3.8 million jobs, Michigan's 2021 economy was an industrial state that had built out health care without losing its manufacturing core.

George Latimer.p1: Few places in this country pack people in as closely as this district does, and that crowding runs through everything else here. Households earn a median $102,025, well above most other districts, but housing runs expensive too, with a median house price of $671,100 against that income marking a ratio of 6.6. Homeownership sits at just 54.2 percent, a mark of a place built more around renters than owners. Unemployment runs a touch higher than in peer seats, even as poverty stays lower.
George Latimer.p2: Credit unions hold just 13.0 percent of retail locations here, a thin slice next to nearly every comparable district, leaving deposit business concentrated among banks. Quorum, USAlliance, and Municipal carry that thin share locally. Morgan Stanley Private Bank leads the district on the deposit measure, a figure shaped by which office a bank books its deposits to rather than by how many branches it runs nearby, and it sits alongside many competing banks in the area. Credit union staffing and location footprint both run well under the countrywide baseline here, tracking each other closely.
George Latimer.p3: In 2023, the seat's job mix relied hardest on real estate and rental and leasing, its most specialized sector by a wide margin against the countrywide baseline. Management of companies and other services added further specialization on top of that. Health care, retail, and related sectors employed the most people day to day. Mortgage lending here skewed heavily toward home purchases, 65.4 percent of originations, with only a small share reaching lower-income neighborhoods.

George Whitesides.p1: Unemployment sits among the highest of any district in the country at 7.0 percent, an odd fit alongside the money visible elsewhere. Median household income runs high at 103,643 dollars, and home values, at 663,100 dollars, top most other districts. Renters put a sizable cut of that income toward a typical month's rent, and homeownership runs high at 72.4 percent too. This is a place where households look comfortable on paper while the labor market is not cooperating.
George Whitesides.p2: Credit union employment here runs below the national norm while credit union offices run even further below it, an unusual gap where jobs outpace the office footprint that would normally justify them. LOGIX, Financial Credit Union, and Los Angeles Police Credit Union anchor the local presence, and credit unions hold 25.0 percent of retail offices, a share that clears most comparable districts even against 64 bank branches led on deposits by JPMorgan Chase. For an institution working this district, that means real reach carried on a lean physical footprint.
George Whitesides.p3: The district's work leaned toward manufacturing and retail trade, both running above the national norm, with health care taking a sizable slice of employment too. Finance and insurance work overall stayed thin against the national norm, even though that sector's growth has kept closer pace with the nation. Mortgage originations skewed toward home purchases over refinancing, with a modest share of lending reaching lower income neighborhoods. This is a district built on making things and selling things, not on finance.

Gilbert Cisneros.p1: Home values in this district are among the highest of any congressional seat in the country, at a median of 756,100 dollars against a household income of 90,291 dollars, stretching the home price to income ratio to 8.4. Rent runs well past what most households nearby could carry on that income. Homeownership is uncommon here, and the population lives packed together far beyond typical density.
Gilbert Cisneros.p2: Credit union jobs here run thicker on the ground than credit union offices do, a gap between the two worth flagging before the figures: jobs sit at 0.67 times the national norm, offices lower still at 0.43 times. America's Christian, Christian Community, and Navy Federal supply that local presence, inside a market where credit unions hold 22.1 percent of retail offices. East West Bank tops all lenders on deposits tied to addresses in the district, one competitor among a crowded field of banks serving these same expensive streets.
Gilbert Cisneros.p3: Work in this district, measured in 2023, leaned hard on wholesale trade, well above the national norm, alongside utilities and manufacturing, both concentrated past typical levels. Health care, manufacturing, and retail trade were common sources of work by share. Finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm, and growth in that sector over the decade lagged the rest of the country.

Glenn Grothman.p1: This district's home values sit at 3.5 times median household income, among the lowest such ratios in the country, meaning a paycheck here covers more house than in most places its size. That paycheck itself runs modest, a median of 76,182 dollars, and most households hold the deed rather than pay rent, a pattern less common elsewhere. Unemployment sits at 2.9 percent, low by any comparison. The district runs to small cities and farmland rather than a single dense core.
Glenn Grothman.p2: Retail banking offices here are unusually likely to belong to a credit union, 33.1 percent of them, a concentration well beyond what most districts show, and Bank First, N.A. leads local deposit bookings against a wide set of competing bank branches. Community First, Landmark, and Kohler carry the credit union presence locally. Credit union employment runs well above the national norm, and the office network has expanded even faster than staffing, a dense branch footprint built to reach the homeowners and working households described above.
Glenn Grothman.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing dominated the district's economy, employing 27.2 percent of workers, more than three times the national norm and the most specialized sector measured here. Agriculture and corporate management functions also ran ahead of national patterns, though on a smaller scale. Broader finance and insurance employment sat close to the national norm, growing at a similar pace to the country overall. This remains a manufacturing district first, with finance and farming as its notable seconds.

Glenn Ivey.p1: Few districts in the country hold people as close together as this one, a density well above most peers, and that crowding sets the tone for the rest of it. Households earn 87,647 dollars, a solid figure by national standards, but the local home value climbs to 414,200 dollars against that income, a heavy load, and only 56.0 percent hold a mortgage outright rather than lease. Unemployment runs high at 5.6 percent. Renters and commuters outnumber owners with easy margins here.
Glenn Ivey.p2: Credit union jobs here run far thicker than the national norm, 2.25 times over, while office presence barely edges past it, a gap peer districts do not show. Navy Federal, Tower, and NASA anchor that presence. Credit unions hold 25.2 percent of retail offices, competing against banks led by Bank of America on deposits booked locally. For an income base this size and a rental population this large, that is a wide footprint to work with.
Glenn Ivey.p3: As of 2023, the job mix leaned hard on Public Administration, over three times the national norm, alongside Construction and Transportation and Warehousing, both above typical levels. Finance work stayed thin against the national norm, at less than half. Government and logistics anchor the economy, with finance a minor thread running under it rather than through it.

Glenn Thompson.p1: Housing here costs little against what people earn: a home's median value sits at just 2.8 times median household income, among the lowest such ratios of any district. Median household income runs to $65,193, and homes trade at a median $184,100. Homeownership runs high, and unemployment stays low. The district is thinly populated and skews a bit older in age.
Glenn Thompson.p2: Credit union offices here run ahead of credit union employment, a district where the branch network outpaces the jobs behind it. Pennsylvania State Employees, Penn State, and Service 1st carry the local credit union business, competing against 249 bank branches, the most deposits among them booked to Northwest Bank. Credit unions hold 19.5 percent of retail offices here, a smaller share than most districts carry, leaving banks the dominant face of everyday banking. That gap looks like room for a credit union to grow against a population whose income and housing costs make it fertile ground for member lending.
Glenn Thompson.p3: Manufacturing anchored the economy as measured in 2023, work that ran well above the national norm and sat alongside health care and educational services in this district's mix of jobs. Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction stood out most sharply, a small slice of jobs but running far above the national norm, the district's most distinctive line of work. Total employment approached 244,600 jobs, built on an old industrial base that still sets this district apart.

Grace Meng.p1: Few congressional districts anywhere squeeze in as many people per square mile as this one, with 726,418 residents packed across a small footprint of the city. Household earnings land near the national average at $82,145, though home values and rents sit well above the norm for districts like it. Owning a home here is unusual, and poverty touches a bigger slice of the population than in most places. Joblessness, by contrast, is nothing out of the ordinary.
Grace Meng.p2: Credit unions hold one of the thinnest footholds in retail banking of any place measured this way, just 5.1 percent of offices here. FOURLEAF, MUNICIPAL, and AMERICAN AIRLINES are the credit unions with the largest presence. JPMorgan Chase books the most deposits of any institution in the district, though that reflects reporting rules more than local branch strength, and it competes with many other banks. Credit union employment runs well below the national norm, though jobs still outpace office presence, pointing to leaner branches doing relatively more with less.
Grace Meng.p3: As of 2023, this district's economy leaned hard on one sector: Health Care and Social Assistance accounted for 40.8 percent of its jobs, nearly three times the national norm. Educational services added further weight behind it. Finance and insurance employment sat below the national norm and grew more slowly than the country overall between 2013 and 2023. Mortgage lending here favored home purchases heavily over refinancing.

Greg Casar.p1: Housing prices and earnings do not align well here. A typical home costs 4.4 times annual household earnings, while the middle household brings in 73,298 dollars, less than many peer seats. Owner occupancy is uncommon and poverty is widespread. The district holds 873,155 residents at a relatively high density, making it a tightly settled place where housing pressure reaches a large population.
Greg Casar.p2: Credit unions command 33.6 percent of retail offices, giving cooperatives a substantial role beside banks. Randolph-Brooks, Security Service, and Credit Human anchor that network. USAA Federal Savings Bank appears ahead in federal deposit records because of address attribution, not branch strength. Credit union staffing reaches 1.72 times the national norm, a stronger concentration than physical locations show. For households working through the housing pressures above, that produces a sizable credit union alternative to conventional banks.
Greg Casar.p3: The 2023 job picture was most distinctive in utilities, which ran well past the national norm, alongside transportation and warehousing and wholesale trade. Finance and insurance employment was below its national baseline, while local growth in that broader sector outpaced the country during the preceding decade. Purchase mortgages dominated originations, with many loans going to lower-income neighborhoods. The district's strength sits in moving and storing goods, not in finance itself.

Greg Landsman.p1: Housing here costs far less than income alone would predict: the home value to income ratio sits at 4.1 and median rent takes about 17.5 percent of a typical household's earnings, both well below what most districts show. Median household income runs near 82,099 dollars, a fairly ordinary figure for a congressional seat. Homeownership lags behind most comparable districts, and poverty runs somewhat higher than most too. This is also a dense district, packed well above the typical seat in people per square mile.
Greg Landsman.p2: Credit union offices here sit close to the national norm while credit union jobs run well under it, at 0.57 times that norm, a gap wide enough to notice. GENERAL ELECTRIC, KEMBA, and WRIGHT-PATT CREDIT UNION carry that presence, against U.S. Bank National Association, the largest bank by deposits booked in the district. Credit unions hold just 16.2 percent of retail offices, a thinner footprint than most peer districts manage. That leaves more storefronts than staff behind the counter, serving the income and housing picture described above.
Greg Landsman.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance employment ran well above the national norm, and growth in that combined sector since 2013 stayed only slightly ahead of typical. The standout was management of companies and enterprises, running at more than three times the national norm. Health care and social assistance carried a substantial share of the district's roughly 481,600 jobs. Manufacturing held a modest, steady share alongside professional and technical services.

Greg Stanton.p1: Population here is packed in tight, well ahead of typical congressional districts, and that crowding sets the tone for 793,264 residents whose median age comes to 36.2. Household income lands near the national middle, but housing costs break from that pattern: a median home value of $449,900 outstrips what that income would ordinarily buy. Only 55.6 percent of homes are owner occupied, a low rate for a district this size.
Greg Stanton.p2: Credit unions have built an unusually strong foothold here, holding 32.8 percent of retail offices, a share running well above most other districts. Desert Financial, Navy Federal Credit Union, and TruWest anchor that presence, competing against a broader banking market where Wells Fargo books the most deposits without necessarily running the most branches. Credit union employment sits below the national norm, tracking closely with a similarly light office presence. For a district with costly housing and a thin ownership rate, that presence gives renters and modest earners an alternative to the bigger banks.
Greg Stanton.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance jobs ran well above the national norm, a specialized slice of a workforce anchored more heavily still in utilities. Health care, retail trade, and educational services carried the most jobs without any particular concentration relative to the rest of the country. Lending skewed toward home purchases, 47.8 percent of originations, with a smaller share reaching lower income neighborhoods.

Gregory Meeks.p1: This district packs people together tightly, among the densest in the country, and the crowding shapes everything else here. Households earn $82,463 a year, near the middle for districts like this, but housing costs run high: a median home value of $687,800 against that income, and rent near $1,683 a month. Homeownership is uncommon here compared with most other districts, and unemployment sits among the highest anywhere.
Gregory Meeks.p2: Employment at credit unions here runs thin against the national norm, yet it still holds up better than their office count, worth noting before the numbers. Municipal, Fourleaf, and American Airlines carry that presence. Credit unions hold just 17.6 percent of retail offices, thinner ground than in most comparable districts, which leaves JPMorgan Chase, the top bank by deposits booked here, competing against a wide field of other branches in a market where money is tight and housing swallows income fast.
Gregory Meeks.p3: As of 2023, the district's job base leaned hard on moving goods and people: Transportation and Warehousing accounted for 20.5 percent of jobs, a concentration more than four times the national norm. Health Care and Social Assistance ran close behind in both share and specialization, and Public Administration and Educational Services rounded out the district's strengths. Finance and insurance jobs overall stayed well below the national norm, underscoring how much this economy runs on logistics and public-facing services rather than banking.

Gregory Murphy.p1: Median household income in the 3rd congressional seat of North Carolina sits at $65,164, well below most comparable districts, and poverty runs high as well. Home values, at a median $261,300, trail most peers, while typical rent of $1,112 a month works out to four times that income once set against the median home value. Unemployment runs higher than most districts see. Homeownership sits close to average, in a district whose population is scattered over a large stretch of land rather than packed into it.
Gregory Murphy.p2: Credit union employment here runs slightly ahead of the national norm while the number of credit union offices sits almost exactly at it, a gap worth naming given the incomes above. State Employees', Navy Federal Credit Union, and Marine anchor that presence. Credit unions hold 26.3 percent of retail offices, a bigger footprint than most districts carry, competing against banks such as First-Citizens Bank & Trust, whose deposits booked in this geography lead the field though it is not the only bank serving it.
Gregory Murphy.p3: As measured in 2023, health care, retail trade, and food service and accommodation employed the most people here, with total jobs near 246,600. Agriculture stood apart on specialization, well beyond the national norm even though it accounts for a small share of jobs. Overall finance-sector employment ran well under the national norm. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, and only a modest share of that lending reached lower-income neighborhoods.

Gregory Steube.p1: A home here is valued at 5.1 times what a household actually earns, a ratio among the highest of any district measured, with rent adding further pressure on top. Median household income sits at 79,214 dollars, unremarkable next to other districts. Homeownership is unusually widespread, and unemployment runs low. This is also a denser district than most, with a population older than the national pattern.
Gregory Steube.p2: Credit unions hold just 14.4 percent of retail offices here, a share that trails most comparable districts, against a market of 192 bank branches. Suncoast, Achieva Credit Union, and Lake Michigan carry what presence exists. Credit union employment sits well under the national norm, lighter still than their own modest office footprint would predict. Against homeowners already stretched by some of the steepest housing costs measured anywhere, that leaves a narrow base for a credit union to build from.
Gregory Steube.p3: As of 2023, construction accounted for 11.0 percent of jobs, close to twice the national norm, and administrative and waste management services also ran well above it. Health care and retail trade were the largest sources of work, though neither stood out as unusually concentrated here. Arts, entertainment, and recreation likewise ran above the norm, rounding out a district built on building things and hosting people. Finance overall was thin, a reminder that money here moves mostly through banks and builders rather than the sector this brief serves.

Gus Bilirakis.p1: Housing eats a bigger bite of income here than comparable districts see, even though the dollar figures themselves run below the norm. A home's median value sits at 4.7 times median household income, and rent claims 27.8 percent of it. Ownership dominates the district, at a rate among the highest anywhere measured. The population, just over 871,000, works in an economy with unemployment and poverty rates that are unremarkable against similar places.
Gus Bilirakis.p2: Credit union employment here runs thin, well below the national norm, even as credit union offices sit nearer typical levels, a gap that puts local staffing under more strain per branch than elsewhere. Suncoast, GTE, and Achieva Credit Union carry the local presence, but credit unions hold only 19.4 percent of retail offices, a smaller share than most districts post. Truist Bank shows the largest deposits booked here, though that outcome owes more to reporting rules than to local reach. Given the costly housing and heavy homeownership described above, thin staffing on the credit union side carries real weight in this district.
Gus Bilirakis.p3: The district's workplace economy leaned toward retail trade and construction, both well above the national norm, alongside utilities, all sectors that point to a place building and supplying rather than just serving itself. Retail trade alone accounted for 15.5 percent of jobs. Total employment approached 184,300 jobs. Mortgage lending skewed heavily toward home purchases, with most of it going to purchases rather than refinancing.

Guy Reschenthaler.p1: A home here is priced at about 2.9 times the going median income, a ratio among the lowest anywhere in the country, and what tenants pay each month barely dents typical pay. Household income lags most other districts. Homeownership is unusually common, and unemployment runs low even as poverty sits on the high side. Housing costs have stayed contained here even as earnings trail the national picture.
Guy Reschenthaler.p2: Credit union employment here runs well under the national norm even though credit unions hold a larger share of retail offices, 25.3 percent, than in most districts, a mismatch between footprint and staffing. Pennsylvania State Employees, Clearview, and Frick Financial carry that presence. PNC Bank holds the top spot on deposits booked locally, though that figure follows accounting rules more than customer relationships or presence on the ground. For a population working with modest incomes and cheap housing, these credit unions run a wide office network on a lean staff.
Guy Reschenthaler.p3: By 2023, the district leaned hard on extraction: mining, quarrying, and oil and gas ran far above the national norm, unusual concentration for the Northeast. Manufacturing added further weight to the job base. Health care and retail trade employed the most people day to day. Overall finance employment stayed well under national levels, underscoring how much this district's working economy still runs on production and extraction rather than financial services.

Gwen Moore.p1: This district is packed tightly by Wisconsin standards, among the densest in the state at over 5,160 people per square mile. Within that footprint, household income sits low against peer seats, at 62,083 dollars, and homeownership sits similarly near the bottom at 47.4 percent. Rent eats 21.5 percent of the median household's earnings even though housing is comparatively cheap to buy against income. Poverty and unemployment are both well above what most similar districts see.
Gwen Moore.p2: Credit union staffing here runs below the countrywide baseline even as credit union offices run above it, an unusual split for a place this size. Landmark, Educators, and UW Credit Union anchor that location footprint, which holds 22.5 percent of the retail branch market. U.S. Bank National Association books the leading deposit position in federal records, one name among many banks competing here. That footprint of branches is what the renters and lower-income households described above actually have to work with.
Gwen Moore.p3: In 2023, the seat's job mix depended most on management of companies and enterprises, more than two and a half times the countrywide baseline. Health care and social assistance employed the most people outright, nearly a fifth of all jobs, well ahead of manufacturing and other large employers. Finance and insurance jobs ran far beyond the countrywide baseline too, a real cluster in a district otherwise built on services. Mortgage lending leaned toward home purchases over refinancing, with lower-income neighborhoods capturing a real share of that activity.

Hakeem Jeffries.p1: This district is one of the most densely settled places in the country, and that crowding is the fact that separates it from almost anywhere else. Median household income sits far under what most comparable districts report, at 63,052 dollars, while the median home value runs much higher than typical, at 781,700 dollars. Very few households here own their home. Poverty runs well above what most districts report.
Hakeem Jeffries.p2: Credit unions hold a thin slice of the retail banking market here, just 12.0 percent of offices, among the lowest such shares of any district. Municipal, Consumers, and People's Alliance are the names doing business in that small space. Deposits booked to addresses in this geography lean most heavily toward JPMorgan Chase, though many other banks compete for local customers here. Credit union employment tracks the office footprint closely, and both sit far below the national norm.
Hakeem Jeffries.p3: As of 2023, health care and social assistance towered over every other sector, employing 38.4 percent of all workers here, more than two and a half times the national norm. Educational services and public administration followed as the next most specialized lines of work. Overall finance employment ran well below typical levels even as finance and insurance jobs nationally grew faster than most sectors over the prior decade. Mortgage lending here leaned heavily toward home purchases, which made up 60.7 percent of all originations.

Haley Stevens.p1: Housing here costs far less than incomes would predict, even though home values sit at 345,700 dollars, a figure that sits squarely in the middle among comparable districts. Household income of 92,977 dollars runs high next to that. Homeownership is unusually strong, and poverty runs low. Density is high too, marking this as a built-up, largely owned, comfortably-earning district.
Haley Stevens.p2: Credit unions hold 35.7 pct of retail offices here, among the highest share of any district measured. Genisys, Michigan Government and Community Credit Union, and DFCU Financial are the names behind that presence. Credit union employment and office presence both run well above the national norm and track each other closely, so the specialization runs deep rather than resting on one institution. That gives a credit union here a base of higher-income, high-ownership households to work with, not a thin or marginal one.
Haley Stevens.p3: The working economy measured in 2021 leaned on professional, scientific, and technical services, which employed 14.7 pct of roughly 454,900 jobs and stood out as a strength alongside management of companies and finance and insurance, itself running well above the national norm. Manufacturing and health care rounded out the job base that year. Mortgage lending was dominated by home purchase loans, 51.8 pct of originations, with a meaningful share reaching lower-income neighborhoods. That mix of finance, management, and technical work gives this district an economy unusually tilted toward office and knowledge-based employment.

Harold Rogers.p1: Low household earnings define Kentucky's 5th: the median is $46,664, while its $121,100 middle home remains inexpensive beside that pay. Poverty is widespread, and unemployment is also elevated. Ownership is still common, so the low cost of housing supports buying even where incomes are limited. Only 62.7 people occupy each square mile, giving the seat a distinctly rural settlement pattern.
Harold Rogers.p2: Credit unions account for 9.4 percent of retail deposit-taking offices, leaving them with an unusually small position beside banks. Y-12, L & N, and Members Choice provide the principal credit union names. Their employment intensity and office density both fall far short of the national norm, with neither materially ahead of the other. Community Trust Bank has the leading deposit total attached to local addresses, but federal booking practices make that label different from customer reach, and many banks operate here.
Harold Rogers.p3: Measured in 2023, the job mix depended heavily on health care and social assistance, the largest field, plus retail trade. Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction held the sharpest concentration versus the nation, although its share of employment was small. Utilities also had a heavier local presence than elsewhere. Finance and insurance remained comparatively thin. Extraction and care work therefore give the local economy its strongest distinction, while financial activity occupies a supporting position.

Harriet Hageman.p1: With just 6.1 people per square mile, open land outweighs people here more than in any comparable seat, and that scarcity runs through every other number. Household income lags most other districts at $75,532, while poverty and joblessness both sit well under typical levels. Homeownership is high, and housing costs are among the lowest of any district, a home value of $339,500 against rent near $998. Owning, working, and paying little for shelter are simply the norm here.
Harriet Hageman.p2: Credit union employment here runs well ahead of credit union office presence, a gap worth noting up front: staffing is specialized against the national norm while office counts barely exceed it. UNIWYO, BLUE, and Meridian Trust anchor that presence, holding 23.8 percent of retail offices, against a field nominally led by First Interstate Bank. Given the income and homeownership patterns above, the credit unions here are built more around people than storefronts.
Harriet Hageman.p3: Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction dominated the 2023 job count, running more than sixteen times the national norm. Public administration and utilities were also concentrated well beyond typical levels. The larger employers were more ordinary day to day: health care, retail trade, and accommodation and food services. Extraction and government work carry unusual weight here, alongside a credit union sector that punches above its office count in people employed.

Henry Cuellar.p1: Poverty in the 28th congressional seat of Texas runs among the highest of any comparable district, at 18.9 percent, alongside elevated unemployment. Median household income, 64,511 dollars, trails well behind most other districts. Rent claims 22.2 percent of the typical household's earnings even though homes are comparatively cheap against income. This is thinly settled ground, home to 825,116 people.
Henry Cuellar.p2: Credit union jobs here run slightly ahead of the national norm while credit union offices lag behind it, a sign that the credit unions present, Randolph-Brooks, Security Service, and Pentagon among them, operate leaner branch networks but staff them more heavily than typical. Credit unions hold just 20.6 percent of retail offices, a smaller share than most districts carry, against a wider field of bank branches. USAA Federal Savings Bank books the top deposit total here under federal reporting rules, a quirk of addressing rather than local dominance, and it has plenty of company on the ground. For a credit union here, the work is fewer doors serving a lower-income population than the norm.
Henry Cuellar.p3: As measured in 2023, this district's economy leaned hard on transportation and warehousing and on mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction, both well beyond their typical weight in the workforce. Educational services also formed a notable part of the job base here. Overall finance and insurance employment sat well under the national norm by comparison. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, drawing on all lenders active in the district.

Henry Johnson.p1: Housing here costs far more than typical local pay would cover: home values run five times the median household income of $71,524, a gap wider than nearly anywhere else in the country. Homeownership trails most peer districts, sitting at 54.4 percent of households. The district is also dense, packing 2,819.9 people per square mile into a small footprint. This is a crowded, expensive corner of the South.
Henry Johnson.p2: Navy Federal Credit Union, Georgia United, and Delta Community anchor credit union presence here, though credit unions hold just 17.5 percent of the district's retail banking offices, a smaller cut than most comparable places see. Bank of America comes out largest locally by deposits, but that reflects where deposits get booked under federal rules, not where branches or customers actually sit. Credit union employment sits at 0.57 times the national norm, with office counts moving in step. Against the costly housing described above, the credit unions here are working a market where banks still occupy most of the ground.
Henry Johnson.p3: As of 2023, wholesale trade was the standout, employing 8.8 percent of the workforce at a rate well above what the nation sees. Administrative and support services and corporate management employment climbed higher than typical too. Finance and insurance jobs overall exceeded the national norm as well. The district leans on distribution and back-office work, not on housing anyone here would call cheap.

Herbert Conaway.p1: Few congressional districts anywhere post a household income like this one's $116,950. The typical home is valued at $445,200, a little over three and a half times that figure, while rent absorbs 19.3 percent of the median household's earnings. Ownership is the norm here, and poverty touches far fewer households than in most places. Unemployment, though, runs a bit higher than in most peer districts, at 5.3 percent.
Herbert Conaway.p2: Credit union offices hold a smaller slice of retail banking here than in most districts, 16.0 percent, and credit union employment runs thinner still against the national norm, well behind even that modest office presence. Pentagon, Andrews Federal Credit Union, and Police & Fire are the names carrying that work locally. TD Bank, National Association books the largest deposits of any bank tied to an address here, out of a much wider field of competitors doing business in the district. A credit union working this ground serves high-earning, heavily mortgaged homeowners, with few institutions of its own kind sharing that load.
Herbert Conaway.p3: The district's economy in 2023 leaned hardest on transportation and warehousing, finance and insurance, and professional and technical services, all well above what the country sees generally. Health care and retail trade employed the most people day to day, but neither stood out by the same measure. What set this district apart was its strength in moving goods and managing money, not in the sectors that simply employed the most people.

Hillary Scholten.p1: This district packs people in more tightly than most comparable districts, a denser settlement pattern than the typical seat. Across its 791,175 residents, household income sits at $77,215, an unremarkable figure next to other districts. Home values, at $309,200, trail most peer districts, while rent and homeownership both land close to typical. Work looks ordinary too, with unemployment and poverty both unremarkable against other districts.
Hillary Scholten.p2: Credit unions hold an outsized place in this district's retail banking, claiming 45.5 percent of retail offices, a share among the highest of any congressional district in the country. Lake Michigan, Consumers, and DFCU Financial anchor that presence. Credit union employment here runs well above the national norm, and office presence runs higher still, so offices are more plentiful than staffing alone would predict. Northpointe Bank stood ahead of every other bank on deposits tied to addresses here, a reporting quirk rather than proof of a bigger branch network among this district's 162 bank branches.
Hillary Scholten.p3: In 2021, manufacturing anchored this district's economy, employing 17.7 percent of workers at nearly twice the national concentration. Administrative, support, and waste services followed as a second specialty. Health care employed more people in raw terms but did not distinguish the district the way manufacturing did. Finance and insurance employment sat near the national norm that year, even as the sector had been growing faster than typical nationally.

Ilhan Omar.p1: This district crowds people together more than nearly any comparable seat, with 705,006 residents settled on tight ground rather than spread out. Median household income sits at $80,274, fairly typical next to other districts, though renting is far more common here since just 53.0 percent own their homes. Hardship shows up too: poverty and joblessness both climb higher than in most similar districts. The overall shape is a place built for close quarters and a workforce carrying more strain than its peers.
Ilhan Omar.p2: Credit union employment here runs thin against the national norm, trailing well behind the sector's office footprint, and that divergence sets the local picture apart from the start. TruStone Financial, Ent, and Blaze anchor that footprint, holding 23.1 percent of retail offices, a middling share next to other districts, against a banking field led on paper by U.S. Bank, a figure that reflects deposit booking rules more than actual branch reach. Credit unions here run leaner staffing per location than the national pattern shows elsewhere.
Ilhan Omar.p3: As measured in 2023, this district's economy leaned heavily on corporate management functions, nearly four times the national norm, alongside strong footholds in finance and insurance and in professional and technical services. Health care and social assistance employed the most people of any sector. Lending data show a sizable share of mortgage originations reaching lower income neighborhoods. This is a district built on headquarters and expertise work, not on any single sprawling employer.

Jack Bergman.p1: This district spreads its people thinly across the land, fewer to the square mile than almost any comparable seat. Income here settles at a median of 64,299 dollars, on the low side for a district, and home values sit modestly as well. Homeownership is unusually widespread at 81.1 percent, even as the poverty rate runs somewhat higher than typical. Joblessness, by contrast, stays low.
Jack Bergman.p2: Credit unions hold 39.6 percent of retail offices here, among the highest shares measured anywhere. Alpena-Alcona Area, 4Front, and Northland Area are the names behind that footprint, while on the banking side Huntington National books the largest deposits, one name among several competing for business in the district. Credit union employment runs more than three times the national norm and office presence nearly triple it, both rated highly specialized, with jobs growing faster than office counts, a sign of institutions built for exactly this kind of sparse, modest-income ground.
Jack Bergman.p3: Back in 2021, health care and social assistance accounted for the largest slice of jobs, followed by retail trade and manufacturing, with the latter two both running above the national norm for their size. Public administration stood out as especially concentrated work, well above what its share elsewhere would predict, alongside smaller but notable footholds in mining and agriculture. General finance employment ran below the national norm even as credit unions themselves ran far above it, a district where broad banking is thin but credit union work is not.

Jack Reed.p1: Rhode Island packs about 1.1 million people into some of the densest square mileage in the country, earning a median household income of 83,504 dollars, well up on the typical state figure. Housing costs bite too: a median home value of 455,700 dollars runs 5.5 times that income, and fewer households here own their home than is typical elsewhere. Getting by is harder on two other counts, with poverty and joblessness both running higher than the national picture.
Jack Reed.p2: Navigant, Coastal1, and Greenwood carry the credit union presence here, and together with the rest of the sector they hold 26.5 percent of retail offices, a share that stands out nationally. That is real weight against Citizens Bank, National Association, which leads all institutions on deposits credited to addresses within the state, though far from the only one competing for the same customers. Credit union offices run slightly ahead of the national norm while credit union jobs run just under it, an unusual split: the physical presence outruns the staffing behind it.
Jack Reed.p3: As of 2023, Rhode Island's economy leaned into finance and insurance, alongside management of companies and other services. Health care and social assistance made up a sizeable slice of jobs statewide. Retail trade was unremarkable by comparison. Finance's growth from 2013 to 2023 lagged the national pace even as its footprint stayed above the norm, a state whose money sector runs dense but not fast-growing.

Jacky Rosen.p1: Nevada's economy runs on hospitality: nearly a fifth of jobs sit in accommodation and food services, a concentration far beyond the national norm. The state's population sits at a low density, and the typical resident is 39.5 years old. Housing runs well above most states, home values sit far past income at a 5.6 ratio, and unemployment sits noticeably higher than in most of the country.
Jacky Rosen.p2: Credit unions hold 23.6 percent of retail offices here, a share that lands in the middle range next to other states, working alongside 404 bank branches split among many competitors, with Bank of America booking the largest deposit sum under federal reporting rules. America First, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Greater Nevada do business in a place where costly housing and an unsteady job market give lending real weight. Credit union staffing comes in thin against the national norm, even as office presence holds closer to the typical mark, leaving fewer workers spread across a comparable number of branches.
Jacky Rosen.p3: As measured in 2023, finance and insurance jobs overall sat below the national norm, though the sector had expanded at a faster clip than the nation across the prior ten years. The working economy leaned hardest on tourism and gaming-adjacent hospitality, a specialization far beyond what any other sector here approaches. Mining also stood out as a smaller but genuine strength. Nevada's distinct advantage remains hospitality at a scale almost no other state matches.

Jahana Hayes.p1: People are packed more tightly into this district than in most comparable ones, a Northeast seat where that crowding sets the tone for everything else. Households here earn 92,097 dollars, above most peer districts, and poverty runs lower than most as well. Home values run 4.2 times income, while the typical rent claims a comparatively modest slice of what households bring home. Most residents own their homes rather than rent.
Jahana Hayes.p2: Credit union employment here runs well below the national norm, at 0.43 times expected, even as credit union offices sit closer to that norm at 0.78, and this district is where that split shows up first. Connecticut State Employees, American Eagle Financial, and Waterbury Connecticut Teachers anchor the local branch presence, which holds 16.9 percent of retail offices, well under the share credit unions typically claim against banks elsewhere. Webster Bank, National Association leads the district by deposits booked to its addresses, one name among many banks operating here.
Jahana Hayes.p3: As of 2023, Health Care and Social Assistance was a leading and especially concentrated sector in this district, holding 20.2 percent of jobs. Educational Services followed as a second concentration, and Management of Companies and Enterprises added a smaller specialty beyond the two. Overall finance employment sat just under the national norm, and finance sector growth over the prior decade trailed that norm too.

Jake Auchincloss.p1: Household income in the 4th congressional seat of Massachusetts stands out immediately, at $115,485, higher than nearly every other district in the country. Housing runs expensive in absolute terms, a median home value of $641,000, but that cost weighs on residents less heavily than it does elsewhere, since local pay outpaces it by an unusual margin. Poverty is low and unemployment lower still. The district is also denser than the typical seat, a place of close-set towns rather than open land.
Jake Auchincloss.p2: Credit union employment here tracks the national norm closely, yet the sector's office footprint runs noticeably heavier than that norm, an imbalance that marks how credit unions operate in this district. St. Anne's, Rockland, and Sharon & Crescent United anchor that presence, though credit unions still hold only 20.0 percent of retail offices, thinner ground than most similar districts give them. Deposits booked locally credit Bank of America as the largest holder under federal reporting rules, which tracks where accounts are recorded on paper rather than which bank residents actually use.
Jake Auchincloss.p3: Employment counts from 2023 showed finance jobs running below the national norm here, and the finance and insurance category as a whole had not kept pace with national hiring trends across the ten years before. Retail trade, wholesale trade, and arts and entertainment were the standout specialties by comparison with typical patterns nationwide. Purchase loans made up 48.3 percent of mortgage originations, and only a modest fraction of that lending reached lower-income neighborhoods.

Jake Ellzey.p1: This district spreads its 848,575 people thinly across the land, sparser than most comparable districts, which shapes how far people commute and how a branch network has to reach them. Household income sits in the middle of the pack, and home values run modest for a district this size even as rent and overall housing costs land on the high side. Poverty is low, though unemployment runs a touch higher than in most comparable seats.
Jake Ellzey.p2: Credit union employment here is thin against the national norm, at 0.37, while credit union office presence, though it holds only a 20.0 percent share of retail offices against banks, fares much better by that same measure, at 0.58. Navy Federal Credit Union, Texas Trust, and EECU anchor that presence against 141 bank branches, led on deposits by JPMorgan Chase, though many other banks compete for the same customers. Offices have kept a foothold here even where staffing has not.
Jake Ellzey.p3: Manufacturing anchors the local economy, accounting for 14.1 percent of employment, well ahead of the national norm, alongside wholesale trade and transportation and warehousing, both similarly concentrated here. Retail trade and administrative and support services add further weight to a workforce oriented toward moving and making goods rather than managing money. Finance and insurance employment overall stayed close to the national norm. This is a district defined by logistics and production, not financial services.

James Baird.p1: Housing here costs far less than the typical district relative to what people earn, with home values running about 3.6 times the median household income of $78,399. Rents sit near $1,146 a month, a modest slice of that income, and most residents own rather than rent. The district carries low poverty and unemployment as low as 3.5 percent, spread across a sizable population.
James Baird.p2: Credit unions here hold just 15.8 percent of retail offices, well below most comparable districts, leaving most of the ground to banks. Purdue, Everwise, and Indiana Members credit unions carry the local presence, set against a wider field of separate banks, among them JPMorgan Chase Bank, which books a large share of deposits here under federal reporting rules rather than by local presence. Credit union employment runs below the national norm even as office presence runs slightly above it, so these offices do more with leaner staff. That is the environment for a credit union working among homeowners with modest housing costs and steady incomes.
James Baird.p3: The economy here leans hard on moving and making things: transportation and warehousing employment ran nearly three times the national norm, and manufacturing ran close to twice it, in an economy of roughly 309,000 jobs. Agriculture also outpaced the national norm, rounding out a district built on goods rather than services. Overall finance employment ran well under the national average, underscoring how physical this economy is.

James Clyburn.p1: Household income in the 6th district of South Carolina sits among the lowest nationwide, at 58,458 dollars a year, while poverty stands at 18.0 percent, a steep rate by comparison. Home values run modest against that backdrop, but rent still eats deeply into what households take home. Ownership lags well behind the pattern seen in most other districts. The district itself is thinly settled, roughly 110 people per square mile spread across 762,934 residents.
James Clyburn.p2: Navy Federal Credit Union, Boeing Employees, and Palmetto Citizens are the names on record here, and together credit unions hold 25.2 percent of retail deposit-taking offices, a share well ahead of most comparable districts. That is a notable footprint in a place where incomes run this tight and lending to lower-income neighborhoods makes up a meaningful slice of mortgage originations. Credit union jobs cluster here at well above the national rate, and office presence tracks closely with that pattern. Bank of America shows up with the largest deposit sum under federal booking rules, though that reflects where deposits get recorded, not a lack of local competition.
James Clyburn.p3: As measured in 2023, public administration stood out as the district's most specialized sector, employing at nearly twice the national norm. Manufacturing also ran a little ahead of the norm and figured among the district's larger employers by job share. Home purchases dominated mortgage activity, making up 63.4 percent of all originations recorded, in a district still stretching to house the people who live and work there.

James Comer.p1: Household income in Kentucky's 1st congressional district sits near the bottom nationally, at $57,974. Home values follow the same pattern, with a median of $188,700 keeping housing costs low, even as poverty remains high. Homeownership is common here, and people are spread out, with just 66 residents per square mile. Joblessness stays low despite the income picture.
James Comer.p2: Credit unions hold only 12.1 percent of retail banking offices in this district, one of the thinner shares among comparable places. Navy Federal, Commonwealth, and Signet carry that presence. Community Financial Services Bank posts the largest deposit figure under federal reporting rules, yet many separately owned banks operate branches throughout the district, so that number says more about where deposits land on paper than about who actually banks residents. Credit union employment and office counts both run modestly above the national norm and track each other closely, a real if limited presence given how far incomes here stretch.
James Comer.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing anchored the local economy, employing 18.4 percent of workers and far outpacing the national norm, the clearest concentration found here. Public administration and mining also employed more workers, proportionally, than is typical elsewhere in the country. Finance jobs overall lagged well behind the national norm, even though finance and insurance combined grew at a pace matching the rest of the country. Manufacturing, not money management, defines what this district does.

James Gallagher.p1: Few congressional districts anywhere hold as few people per square mile as this one, and small towns take the place of any real city. The typical household earns 69,829 dollars a year, less than most districts see, and the poverty rate climbs well past what most places report. A typical home price runs 5.6 times the typical paycheck, and monthly rent claims a bigger bite of it than most comparable places see. Just 62.4 percent of households own their home.
James Gallagher.p2: Credit union offices here outrun credit union employment, an imbalance that sets this district apart from similar ones. The Golden 1, Sierra Central, and Rogue anchor that presence, though credit unions hold only 19.9 percent of retail offices against a much larger run of bank branches, with Tri Counties Bank leading on deposits. That office share sits below most peer districts. Given the income and cost pressures already bearing on households here, credit unions cover a thinner slice of local banking than residents likely need.
James Gallagher.p3: As of 2023, the job mix leaned hard into agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting, more than seven and a half times the national norm, alongside public administration at twice that norm. Health care and social assistance and educational services both ran well above typical national levels too. Overall finance employment ran far below the national norm. Most of the mortgage lending measured here went toward buying homes outright, and a smaller portion reached lower income neighborhoods.

James Himes.p1: Household income in the 4th congressional district of Connecticut is among the highest of any congressional district in the country, at $122,642. Home values, at $704,000, run far above typical levels, yet the cost of housing relative to income stays lighter than that price tag implies. The district is dense and largely built out, with unemployment running a bit higher than usual even as poverty stays uncommonly low. It is a place of comfortable averages with some slack in the labor market.
James Himes.p2: Credit unions hold only 13.6 percent of retail offices here, a thin slice next to what banks control elsewhere. Sikorsky Financial, Affinity, and Mutual Security carry the credit union name in a market where banks, led on deposits by Webster Bank, National Association, otherwise set the terms. Credit union employment runs at 0.28 times the national norm, and office presence at 0.64 times, both well short of what banks have built here. For a credit union, this is a district of high incomes and high prices where the competition has the upper hand.
James Himes.p3: Finance and insurance employment ran at 2.22 times the national norm as of 2023, the clearest specialization in the district, alongside strength in information work and in arts, entertainment, and recreation. Health care and retail employed more people overall but without that same concentration. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, the majority of all originations. This is a district where finance and knowledge work sit on top of an affluent, expensive base.

James Justice.p1: West Virginia's population skews well past middle age, and its hills and hollows hold people spread thin across the land. Median household income sits at $60,798, near the bottom nationally, and poverty runs high at 16.7 percent. Homeownership, though, is among the highest anywhere at 75.5 percent, and the typical home costs only 2.8 years of what a typical household brings home. Unemployment runs higher here than in most states, at 4.6 percent.
James Justice.p2: Fairmont, First Choice America Community, and West Virginia Central credit unions anchor a system holding 23.2 percent of the state's retail banking offices, an ordinary share next to other states. Such offices turn up more often than the national norm would predict, even though credit union payrolls run leaner than typical nationally, a sign of lean staffing rather than thin presence. Federal reporting rules credit United Bank with the largest deposits booked in the state, a single name set against hundreds of branches run by many other banks. For a state this poor and this owned by its residents, that office footprint matters more than deposit totals ever could.
James Justice.p3: Working from counts taken in 2023, the state's economy leaned hardest on mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction, running far above the national norm despite employing a small share of workers directly. Health care and social assistance carried real weight too, well above the typical concentration nationally. Overall finance employment lagged well behind national levels, leaving extraction and health care to define the state's distinctive work.

James Lankford.p1: Oklahoma spreads its 4,095,393 people thinly across the state, and the job market leans hard on what comes out of the ground: oil and gas extraction runs close to five times the national norm. Health care and retail carry the bulk of actual employment. Median household income sits at $66,148, well below most states, while home values sit on the low end nationally. Poverty runs high at 14.9 percent, alongside unemployment above the typical state.
James Lankford.p2: Credit unions hold just 17.5 percent of retail offices here, a thin share next to banks, with BOKF, National Association credited with the largest deposit sum under federal booking rules even as many other banks compete for business locally. TINKER, TTCU, and COMMUNICATION lead the credit union side. Credit union jobs run at 1.15 times the national norm, slightly specialized and growing faster than office counts, which sit almost exactly at norm. In a state with tight incomes and modest home values, that means fewer branches doing comparatively more work per worker.
James Lankford.p3: As of 2023, total employment approached 1,546,200 jobs, with finance and insurance work running below the national norm and its growth trailing the broader economy elsewhere. What stood out was extraction, running highly specialized alongside utilities and arts and entertainment employment, both above typical levels. Oklahoma's economy still turns on resources pulled from the ground.

James McGovern.p1: Household income here runs to $97,024, the single fact that puts this district ahead of most others like it. Home values sit five times that figure, yet rent claims only a modest slice of it, and the overall cost of housing stays lighter than in comparable districts elsewhere. Few residents fall below the poverty line, and joblessness holds at 4.1 percent. Earners in this district are not being squeezed at the door.
James McGovern.p2: Office presence and payroll pull in different directions here, and that split matters more than either number alone. Institutions such as First Technology, Central One, and Webster First operate alongside a field of 196 bank branches, including one that leads only because Bank of America deposits get booked to a single address under federal reporting rules. Credit unions hold 24.7 percent of retail offices, a share above most other districts, even as their job count barely clears the national norm. Branches have multiplied faster than the staff behind them, against the income and housing picture already described.
James McGovern.p3: As of 2023, health care and social assistance and instructional services together carried an outsized share of the district's jobs, both running well past the national norm for their fields. Utilities employment also ran high relative to the norm, despite being a small slice of all jobs. Overall finance-sector employment sat below the national norm. Roughly 322,300 jobs anchor this economy, built on hospitals and classrooms rather than finance itself.

James Risch.p1: Idaho's two million residents earn a median household income of $81,166, higher than most states manage, spread thin across a state at just 24.2 people per square mile. Home prices run 5.5 times the median income, a stretch, yet the typical rent check stays a manageable slice of what a household brings in. Owning runs well ahead of renting in Idaho, a pattern stronger here than in nearly every other state, and joblessness stays low.
James Risch.p2: Idaho Central, Mountain America, and Potlatch No. 1 Financial anchor a credit union footprint that takes in 39.8 percent of retail offices statewide, among the highest shares of any state, ahead of U.S. Bank National Association, the top deposit holder among a crowded field of local branches. Credit union employment runs well above the national norm, a specialization that outpaces the state's already strong presence in office count. For homeowners carrying steep mortgages and renters watching every dollar, that is a dense bench of local institutions to draw on.
James Risch.p3: As measured in 2023, Idaho's job base leaned hardest into agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting, well above the norm for that line of work nationally, alongside a construction sector raising the homes behind those steep prices. Health care and social assistance, retail trade, and manufacturing were among the larger sources of jobs. Overall finance and insurance employment sat below the national norm, but grew faster than the country over the prior decade, a state whose weight still leans toward building, growing, and making things.

James Walkinshaw.p1: Household income in the 11th district of Virginia sits among the highest of any congressional district in the country, at 158,109 dollars. Home values run high too, but the ratio of home value to income stays moderate, and rent claims a smaller share of income than in most places. Poverty and joblessness are both rare here. Density is high, consistent with a compact, close-in place where people tend to work near home.
James Walkinshaw.p2: Credit union employment here runs far above the national norm, at 3.73 times the typical level, even though credit union office presence sits slightly below it, at 0.75. That gap marks this district: jobs outpace offices. Navy Federal Credit Union, Apple, and Northwest hold the largest presence among credit unions, which together account for 29.1 percent of retail deposit-taking offices. Capital One, National Association leads all banks by deposits booked here, one name among many local branches.
James Walkinshaw.p3: The district's 2023 employment mix leaned hard on professional, scientific, and technical services, which made up 32.7 percent of jobs, more than four times the national norm. Management of companies and information services were also unusually concentrated here. Health care and administrative work rounded out the larger employers, though neither concentrated the way professional services did. Finance and insurance jobs ran slightly above the national norm too, with growth in that combined sector outpacing the country over the prior decade.

Jamie Raskin.p1: Household income in the 8th district of Maryland reaches $146,362, a figure few other districts nationwide can match, and few residents here fall below the poverty line. Home values run well ahead of national norms, yet the ratio of value to income is a modest 4.9, and monthly rent absorbs a modest slice of what a typical household brings home. Homeownership lags somewhat behind other districts. The district is also considerably denser than most.
Jamie Raskin.p2: Credit unions here include Navy Federal, Lafayette, and National Institutes of Health, names tied closely to the district's federal and research workforce. Together, they hold just 18.0 percent of retail offices, well under what credit unions typically claim elsewhere, competing against a field of banks that includes EagleBank, ahead of others on deposits booked under federal reporting rules. Credit union employment sits below the national norm, and office presence tracks it closely rather than pulling ahead. That leaves a credit union sector serving a wealthy, federally anchored population without much physical footprint to work with.
Jamie Raskin.p3: By 2023, work in this district clustered around Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services, well over twice the national norm, and Public Administration, nearly three times the norm. Health Care and Social Assistance rounded out the largest sectors at a level close to typical nationally. Finance and insurance employment came in just short of the national baseline. Government and research work define this district far more than banking or manufacturing ever could.

Janelle Bynum.p1: Home values in the 5th district of Oregon sit at $587,400, and that gap is what defines the place. Median household income runs high too, at $96,200, but a household would need six years of it, undiscounted, to match the home price alone. Rent runs $1,755 a month, and poverty stays low. The district has 717,312 people spread thinly, far less crowded than most districts of its kind.
Janelle Bynum.p2: Credit unions hold 31.8 percent of retail offices here, a share well above most districts, a solid position against a crowded field of bank branches. OnPoint Community, SELCO Community, and Mid Oregon hold that ground, set against U.S. Bank National Association, which leads only on deposits booked to local addresses, not on local reach or relationships. Credit union employment runs at 1.47 times the national norm, well past what the office count alone would account for. For a district with high home values and steady incomes, that is a credit union sector doing more work per office than most.
Janelle Bynum.p3: Farming, forestry, fishing, and hunting stood out furthest against the national picture in 2023, and construction ran well above typical levels too. Health care, retail, and manufacturing employed the most people but without that same distinctiveness. Finance and insurance jobs overall sat below the national norm, though the wider sector added jobs at a pace slightly ahead of the nation's. Land and building trades carry this economy more than banking or finance do.

Janice Schakowsky.p1: This district crowds far more people into each square mile than almost any other in the country, a dense corner of Illinois carrying 740,435 residents. Median household income reaches $90,111, well past what most districts report, and home values run high relative to what residents actually earn. Renters pay a median of $1,525 a month, while just 61 percent of households own rather than rent. Joblessness sits slightly above the norm despite the strong earnings.
Janice Schakowsky.p2: Credit unions hold just 10.4 percent of retail offices here, among the lowest shares measured anywhere. Alliant, Baxter, and a Michigan-based credit union are the names on record locally, set against a market of bank branches where JPMorgan Chase books a leading share of deposits. Credit union employment runs well below the national norm, and office presence falls short too, with offices outpacing jobs rather than the reverse. Given the density and income at work here, credit unions still claim only a narrow slice of the business.
Janice Schakowsky.p3: As of 2023, health care and social assistance anchored the economy, employing 21.1 percent of jobs, a concentration well above the national norm. Educational services and arts, entertainment, and recreation also ran ahead of typical levels, marking a district built on institutions rather than industry. Finance and insurance employment ran modestly ahead of the national norm as well, with growth outpacing the country between 2013 and 2023.

Jared Golden.p1: This district is one of the most sparsely settled in the country, with just 25.3 people per square mile across a population of 697,280. Typical household income lands at $67,291, on the low side for a district, though home values and rent stay affordable by comparison. Homeownership runs high at 74.1 percent, and unemployment stays low.
Jared Golden.p2: Credit unions hold 37.1 percent of retail offices here, among the highest such share found anywhere. Maine Savings, The County, and Acadia carry that presence, alongside Bangor Savings Bank, the largest holder of deposits booked to addresses here in a market of many separate banks. Both credit union employment and office presence far exceed what shows up nationally, with offices outpacing jobs, a pattern that fits a network built for a spread-out population rather than a dense one. That scale gives credit unions real weight against the income and housing costs described above.
Jared Golden.p3: The working economy, last measured in 2023, leaned hardest on agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting, well above the national norm, alongside specialized footholds in company management and retail trade. Health care and social assistance was the largest source of work, followed closely by retail. Lending data show most mortgage activity went to home purchases rather than refinancing, with a meaningful share reaching lower-income neighborhoods. Finance and insurance employment overall trailed the national norm, leaving credit unions as this district's clear financial specialty.

Jared Huffman.p1: Home values here sit among the highest of any district in the state, at $860,700, well beyond what a typical household income of $97,004 would comfortably support. That gap, a ratio of 8.9 between home price and income, is the sharpest fact about this district. Rent runs $1,896 a month, and homeownership sits at 64.0 percent, lower than in comparable districts. The district is also thinly populated, spread out in a way most peer districts are not.
Jared Huffman.p2: Credit union jobs here sit a touch above the national norm even though credit union offices fall below it, an unusual split between where the work happens and where the branches sit. Redwood, Coast Central, and Community First carry that presence, holding 22.1 percent of retail offices against Wells Fargo Bank, National Association and a much larger field of bank branches citywide. That combination points to work built around servicing and lending relationships rather than counter transactions. It is a credit union sector doing more with less physical footprint than its peers typically manage.
Jared Huffman.p3: As of 2023, the district leaned hardest on agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting, a sector running far above the national norm here. Public administration and the arts and recreation trades also stood out as unusually concentrated.
