Overall finance sector employment ran well below the national norm, even as growth in that broader sector approached the national pace. Mortgage lending here split evenly between home purchases and other originations, with a meaningful share reaching lower-income neighborhoods.

Jared Moskowitz.p1: Space is at a premium in this district, among the densest congressional seats anywhere, with 802,266 residents settled close together rather than spread out. The typical household brings in $90,649, a level that beats most comparable districts, though that income meets a housing market that is genuinely expensive, with home values near $580,100 against a price-to-income ratio of 6.4. Poverty runs low at 10.2 percent and unemployment lower still at 3.6 percent. This is a well-paid, crowded district where steady work meets a costly place to own a home.
Jared Moskowitz.p2: Credit unions claim only a sliver of the retail branch network here, among the lowest shares recorded anywhere. Space Coast, BrightStar, and We Florida Financial carry that footprint, working against a market where Bank of America books the largest deposit share, a figure that reflects where deposits are recorded rather than local branch strength. Credit union employment runs well below the national norm, yet jobs still outpace the office count, a sign these institutions do more with a lighter physical presence. That is a small foothold for serving the high earners and costly homes described above.
Jared Moskowitz.p3: Industry data from 2023 marked real estate and rental leasing as the most specialized sector in the district, well ahead of the national norm, with administrative services and arts and entertainment also concentrated here. Health care, retail trade, and accommodation and food services together carried a large share of jobs. Mortgage lending that year leaned heavily toward home purchases.

Jasmine Crockett.p1: Housing here costs more relative to income than comparable districts typically see, even though home values themselves are modest and the median household earns $77,231 a year. A home runs 3.8 times that income, and rent alone claims a heavy share of it. Residents who own where they live are a minority, a homeownership rate well below most districts, and this district crowds more people into each square mile than most peers. Joblessness sits at a level few comparable districts reach.
Jasmine Crockett.p2: Credit union employment here runs thin against the national norm, at 0.39, while credit union offices hold up somewhat better at 0.6, a gap pointing to leaner staffing per branch rather than fewer branches outright. Navy Federal, Pentagon, and Credit Union of Texas anchor that presence, though credit unions still hold only 19.7 percent of retail offices, a smaller share than most comparable districts, against a deep roster of bank branches led on deposits by Bank of America. For the renters and stretched incomes described above, that thinner footprint matters more than it would elsewhere.
Jasmine Crockett.p3: By 2023, jobs here clustered in professional and technical services, real estate, and transportation and warehousing, each well above the national norm for its size. Overall finance employment ran strong too, at 1.26 times the norm. Home purchases dominated mortgage originations, and lending reached well into lower-income neighborhoods, a district doing real business despite its housing strain.

Jason Crow.p1: Household income in the 6th district sets it apart from any comparable place, running $103,252, well above most congressional districts. Home values follow the same pattern, at $587,200, several times that income figure, while rent runs $1,959 a month against those published middles rather than any single household's bill. Poverty is rare here, and joblessness bites somewhat harder than the typical district experiences. Density is high for a congressional seat, and homeownership lags what most similar places report.
Jason Crow.p2: Credit union employment here runs noticeably thin against the national norm, even though credit union offices are staffed close to that norm, a split worth noting up front. Bellco, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Ent hold 25.5 percent of retail offices, a share few districts match, against a field led on deposits by Wells Fargo, which books its figures there under federal reporting rules rather than through any dominant local presence. That gap between thin staffing and a solid office footprint means these institutions cover ground efficiently, in a district where high incomes give them plenty of business to build on.
Jason Crow.p3: The district's economy leans hardest on Information work, employment well beyond the national norm, alongside Finance and Insurance and Wholesale Trade. Health Care and Social Assistance employs the most people, ahead of Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services. Total employment approached 403,400 as of 2023. It is a district built on information work and finance more than on manufacturing or retail.

Jason Smith.p1: Few places hold as few people per square mile as this district does, at 42.4, a measure that separates it from almost every comparable seat. Median household income sits at $59,897, on the low end for a district of this kind, and housing costs less to match. Homeownership runs high, at 73.8 percent, even as poverty runs high too. Unemployment stays low, a labor market that clears even where pay remains modest.
Jason Smith.p2: Credit unions here hold just 8.6 percent of retail offices, a thin footing against the banks that otherwise dominate. First Community, Ozark, and Infuze carry what credit union presence exists, working a market crowded with bank branches instead. Southern Bank carries the largest deposit figure of any institution here, though federal reporting rules assign deposits to a booking address rather than to wherever customers actually bank. Credit union employment runs well below the national norm, tracking closely with the district's thin office presence rather than one outpacing the other.
Jason Smith.p3: Manufacturing, retail trade, and health care and social assistance anchor employment, with health care alone accounting for 19.8 percent of the roughly 237,000 jobs measured in 2023. The district also carries real specialization in mining and quarrying, utilities, and agriculture, sectors that punch well above the national norm despite employing comparatively few people. Overall finance-sector employment runs below the national norm as well. Home purchase activity drove most mortgage originations recorded.

Jay Obernolte.p1: This district spreads its 758,179 people thinly across the land, among the lowest counts of any congressional district in the country. Income sits near the middle nationally at a median $77,137, but home values run far higher than most districts at $436,600, and the gap between home prices and income stands out even more sharply. Poverty and unemployment both run higher than most peer districts.
Jay Obernolte.p2: Credit unions here include Navy Federal, Global, and a large statewide institution built around public employees, and together credit unions hold 26.3 percent of retail office share, a large slice for a congressional district. That is a strong footprint set against Bank of America, the largest bank by deposits booked locally, though it competes with many other banks operating in the district. Credit union employment and credit union office presence both sit well below the national norm and track each other closely. Against the sparse population and steep housing costs described above, that is the base a credit union here actually works with.
Jay Obernolte.p3: As of 2023, the working economy leaned heavily on health care and social assistance, which alone accounted for 26.2 percent of jobs, well above the national norm. The standout was arts, entertainment, and recreation, specialized at more than three times the national norm, a distinct mark for this district. Overall finance employment ran far below the national norm, leaving finance a minor share of the working mix. Retail trade also figured among the larger sectors of local work.

Jeanne Shaheen.p1: New Hampshire carries a household income of $99,782, comfortably higher than most states, and a population of 1,409,032 with a middle age of 43.6. Home values sit at $458,800, though typical housing costs remain modest by national standards. Close to 73 percent of residents own their homes outright rather than renting, among the highest shares anywhere. Steady work and settled homeownership define the place more than a young or transient workforce.
Jeanne Shaheen.p2: SERVICE, St. Mary's Bank, and First Technology anchor the credit union presence here, and together with other institutions they hold 24.2 percent of retail offices, a share topping most states. Credit union employment sits well past the national norm too, at roughly the same level as their office count locally. TD Bank shows the largest deposit book by federal booking rules, though that reflects addressing more than any real edge over the state's other lenders. For a credit union here, the customer base is exactly the homeowning, employed population just described.
Jeanne Shaheen.p3: As measured in 2023, retail trade and manufacturing stood out as the state's specialized sectors, both employing well above the national norm. Wholesale trade followed close behind them. Overall finance employment ran slightly below the national norm, and growth in finance and insurance over the prior decade lagged as well. New Hampshire's edge showed up less in finance broadly and more in the goods and trade moving through it.

Jeff Crank.p1: Poverty here runs well below most comparable districts, a rate of 8.5 percent, even as unemployment climbs higher than most peers see. Household income reaches 91,125 dollars. Home values near 486,500 dollars price well above what income alone would support, and homeownership trails most comparable districts. This is a place where people earn well but the cost of owning has pulled ahead of what earnings alone would predict.
Jeff Crank.p2: Credit union employment here runs far thicker than the national norm, while the credit union office count barely clears that norm at all, a gap between people and branches worth noting. ENT, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Security Service anchor that workforce. Credit unions hold 26.5 percent of retail offices, competing against a market of bank branches where Wells Fargo Bank, National Association books the top deposit sum under federal reporting rules rather than local branch weight. A credit union here works with an income base and a housing market both running ahead of the norm elsewhere.
Jeff Crank.p3: As measured in 2023, Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services made up 12.4 percent of jobs, a clear specialty for the district against the national norm. Health Care and Social Assistance and Accommodation and Food Services rounded out the sectors employing the most people locally. Total employment ran near 267,500 jobs. Mortgage lending that year leaned heavily toward home purchases as the dominant type of loan, across all lenders active in the district.

Jeff Hurd.p1: Few districts anywhere spread their population as thin as this one does. Across its 742,698 residents, median household income sits at $71,165, on the low side of what other districts report. Homeownership stands out, though: 72.4 percent own their homes rather than renting, well above what most districts show. Unemployment holds steady in ordinary territory.
Jeff Hurd.p2: Credit unions here include ENT, Bellco, and Canvas, and together they hold 20.8 percent of retail offices, a share that lands in the middle range for a district like this. Alpine Bank tops the local deposit figures, though that number follows accounting rules about where deposits get recorded, not branch counts or customer loyalty, and plenty of other banks compete for business here regardless. Credit union employment runs below the national norm, and office presence tracks closely with it. Given the income and homeownership patterns above, that is a modest footprint for a place where retail banking relationships matter.
Jeff Hurd.p3: As measured in 2023, this district's economy leaned on a few distinctive sectors: mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction ran well above the national norm, and arts, entertainment, and recreation showed similar strength. Health care and retail trade carried much of the job base. Overall finance-sector employment sat below the national norm, and its growth over the prior decade lagged too. Mortgage lending skewed heavily toward home purchases over refinancing, at 53.9 percent of originations.

Jeff Merkley.p1: Oregon's 4.27 million residents earn a median household income of $85,220, above most states, but housing swallows that advantage fast. A home costs 5.8 times what a household typically brings in, and homeownership has fallen to 63.1 percent as renting becomes the norm. Joblessness runs higher here than in most states, and people are spread thin, with far more open land than crowd.
Jeff Merkley.p2: Onpoint Community, First Technology, and Oregon Community lead a credit union presence claiming 35.0 percent of retail offices statewide, a share few states match. That sits alongside U.S. Bank National Association, the deposit leader on paper in a field crowded with rival banks. Credit union employment runs at 1.78 times the national norm, well ahead of the sector's own office footprint, meaning these institutions run leaner branches staffed more heavily than the country's norm. For the renters and middle earners described above, that translates into real capacity on the ground.
Jeff Merkley.p3: As measured in 2023, overall finance and insurance employment trailed the national norm, growing more slowly than the country as a whole too. Oregon's real edge lay elsewhere: agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting ran highly specialized against that same norm, and construction and corporate management posted their own strength. Health care and retail carried the most jobs day to day, but the state built its distinction on growing and building things, not managing money.

Jefferson Shreve.p1: Unemployment here sits at 3.1 percent, among the lowest of any comparable district, and it colors everything else about the local economy. The typical household earns 77,374 dollars a year, and home values of 250,900 dollars sit far below what most districts report, with rent claiming a modest share of income. Ownership is the norm rather than the exception. Poverty also runs lower than in most places this size.
Jefferson Shreve.p2: Credit unions here employ thinner than the national norm, even though they hold a larger than typical share of office space, a mismatch worth noting to anyone in this business. FORUM, CENTRA, and Indiana Members anchor that presence. Together, credit unions account for 23.9 percent of retail offices, against 164 bank branches led on deposits by PNC, though that figure reflects booking rules more than local rivalry. Given the income and housing patterns above, this is a market where credit unions occupy real space but employ leanly relative to it.
Jefferson Shreve.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing and health care were two major sources of jobs in a district employing roughly 269,900 people. Transportation and warehousing stood out against the national norm, marking this as a logistics-heavy district alongside its manufacturing base. Overall finance and insurance employment ran thin here. Home purchases dominated mortgage activity, and only a small slice of that lending reached lower-income neighborhoods.

Jefferson Van Drew.p1: Unemployment here runs well above most comparable districts, at 6.0 percent, even though poverty stays low. Households earn $84,183 at the median, and homeownership stands high, at 76.1 percent. Home values run at 4.3 times income, unremarkable next to other districts. This is a place of settled homeowners, not a tight labor market.
Jefferson Van Drew.p2: Credit unions hold just 13.6 percent of retail offices here, a share far smaller than in most districts, leaving most of the field to banks. TD Bank, National Association books the most deposits locally, though it is one rival among many branches here. Jersey Shore, First Harvest, and Deepwater Industries carry the credit union side, with office presence and employment tracking each other closely, both thin against the national norm. For a credit union here, this is a market of homeowners and moderate incomes that credit unions have barely touched.
Jefferson Van Drew.p3: As of 2023, the district's economy leaned on hospitality: Accommodation and Food Services employed 15.6 percent of workers and ran well above the national norm for its size. Utilities stood out further still on that same measure, despite employing far fewer people. Health care and retail trade filled out the rest of the picture. Overall finance employment ran thin against the national norm, underscoring how much this district's identity rests on feeding, housing, and powering people rather than banking them.

Jennifer Kiggans.p1: Unemployment sits at 3.1 percent here, among the lowest anywhere, with poverty low as well. Median household income runs to 93,827 dollars, well clear of the typical district, and home values of 397,800 dollars sit high too. Ownership holds near 68.5 percent, in line with the national pattern, marking a population that is stable and steadily employed.
Jennifer Kiggans.p2: Credit unions hold 33.1 percent of retail offices here, a share far above what most districts see, and that is the fact that matters most about credit union banking in this place. Navy Federal Credit Union, NASA, and Langley all have a real local presence, next to TowneBank, which books the most deposits by address within the district. Credit union employment runs about half again above the national norm, tracking closely with how common their offices are here too. Given the income and ownership levels above, this is a district where credit union relationships have room to run deep.
Jennifer Kiggans.p3: The 2023 employment picture favored accommodation and food services and educational services, both well above the national norm, with real estate and leasing also running ahead of typical levels. Overall finance and insurance employment came in below the national norm, and the pace of hiring across finance and insurance lagged the country's over the ten years before. Credit unions stand apart from that broader finance picture, holding a specialization in this district that the rest of the finance sector does not share.

Jennifer McClellan.p1: Local earnings do not keep pace with shelter prices. The median home equals 4.4 times median household income, and rent consumes 24.8 percent of middle earnings. The middle household brings in 69,839 dollars. Owner occupancy falls short of peer patterns, while poverty is more widespread. Residents are dispersed across the district rather than packed into a single urban footprint.
Jennifer McClellan.p2: Virginia Credit Union, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Henrico Credit Union lead a cooperative network that operates 27.2 percent of retail offices, more than the usual peer share. Federal address records place Bank of America first on the local deposit measure, but many banking companies compete here. Credit union staffing is just below the national norm and closely matches its office concentration. That physical reach gives households managing the conditions above a practical local alternative to the larger bank field.
Jennifer McClellan.p3: The 2023 employment mix had unusual weight in management of companies, public administration, and transportation and warehousing. Each field was more concentrated than its national counterpart. Finance and insurance employment also sat slightly beyond its countrywide baseline. Purchase loans accounted for 56.6 percent of mortgage originations. Institutional and logistics work, rather than one dominant line of business, gives the economy its shape.

Jerrold Nadler.p1: Few places in the country pack people together as tightly as this district, with roughly 78,589 residents per square mile. That density sits alongside a household income near $153,117, well above most comparable districts, and a population of about 752,016. Home values run far higher than what typical earnings would support, and only 32.2 percent of residents own the home they live in. Poverty runs low here even as rent claims a heavy portion of what households bring in.
Jerrold Nadler.p2: Retail banking in this district belongs almost entirely to banks, with credit unions holding just 5.0 percent of offices, a thinner slice than nearly anywhere else. United Nations, Pentagon, and Fourleaf are the credit unions present here, competing against 329 bank branches, the largest by deposits booked to JPMorgan Chase. Credit union jobs and credit union offices both fall well short of the national norm, moving in step with each other rather than one leading. Given how dense and well-off this district is, credit unions touch only a small corner of that economy.
Jerrold Nadler.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance specialization here ran at more than three times the national norm, alongside strong concentrations in information and in real estate, rental and leasing. Professional, scientific, and technical services accounted for the largest slice of local employment. Home purchases dominated mortgage activity in this district, while lending reached few lower income neighborhoods.

Jerry Moran.p1: Kansas holds just under three million people spread thin across wide-open land, in a state where the typical household earns 75,514 dollars a year, somewhat below what most states report. Housing runs the other direction: a median home value of 238,700 dollars against that income lands among the lowest cost burdens in the country, and rent stays a modest slice of pay. Unemployment and poverty rates both run better than most states manage.
Jerry Moran.p2: Navy Federal Credit Union, Credit Union of America, and Meritrust anchor the credit union presence here, though credit unions hold only 15.7 percent of retail offices statewide, a smaller slice than most states show, against a banking sector where Bank of America books a large deposit share without necessarily running the most branches. Credit union payrolls carry a touch more weight here than the national norm. That is a population with room in its budget and a banking sector credit unions have not come to dominate.
Jerry Moran.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing stood out, employing 12.8 percent of the workforce at 1.44 times the national norm, with agriculture also running specialized despite its small share of jobs. Public administration showed slight specialization too, reflecting the state's government workforce. Health care and social assistance drew a sizable share of jobs, though not an unusual concentration. Finance and insurance employment overall matched the national norm closely, with hiring there having lagged the broader pace since 2013.

Jesús García.p1: This district is one of the most densely settled in the nation, 712,078 people packed into a compact stretch of land. Household income lands squarely in the middle range for districts like it, at $80,103, while home values and rent both run modest by comparison. Homeownership and job security both trail what most comparable districts see. Poverty runs higher here too.
Jesús García.p2: Credit unions hold a thin footing in this district, just 10.5 percent of retail offices, one of the smallest shares of any comparable seat. Alliant, Self-Help, and Chicago Firefighter's carry that presence. Credit union jobs and credit union offices both come in at roughly a third to two-fifths of the national norm and move in step with each other, while JPMorgan Chase leads a field of 150 bank branches on deposits booked locally. For a credit union working this ground, banks, not other credit unions, are the competition for everyday deposits.
Jesús García.p3: The working economy here, measured in 2023, turned on the movement of goods. Transportation and Warehousing stood out as highly specialized, employing 11.2 percent of workers, and Manufacturing led all sectors at 13.6 percent. Wholesale trade and administrative and support work rounded out an economy built on logistics and distribution, each employing far more of the workforce than is typical elsewhere. Overall finance employment ran below the national norm, and mortgage lending here leaned heavily toward home purchases.

Jill Tokuda.p1: Home values here sit among the highest of any congressional district, at 838,900 dollars, far outrunning even the area's strong household incomes. Median household income runs to 97,135 dollars, comfortably ahead of most other districts, and rent lands at 1,982 dollars a month. Unemployment stays low. This is a place of well-paid workers priced into expensive housing rather than a renter's district.
Jill Tokuda.p2: Credit unions hold 44.9 percent of retail offices here, a share that puts them well ahead of banks on that measure. HFS, GATHER, and Hawaii Community Federal Credit Union anchor that presence, while Bank of Hawaii books the largest deposits among the district's many bank branches. Credit union employment runs nearly twice the national norm, and office presence has grown even faster than staffing. For the high earners and stretched housing budgets described above, that gives a credit union here real reach.
Jill Tokuda.p3: The 2023 job mix leaned hard on tourism: accommodation and food services alone ran to 23.1 percent of jobs, far above the national norm for that industry. Agriculture and the arts also showed unusual concentration, pointing to an economy built around visitors and the land rather than offices. Overall finance employment, by contrast, ran well below the national norm even as credit unions stood apart within it. Mortgage lending leaned toward home purchases over refinancing as the dominant type of loan issued.

Jim Banks.p1: Indiana is home to 6,924,275 people, earning a median household income of 71,959 dollars, well below most other states. Housing costs less too: a home value to income ratio of 3.4, and homeownership near 71 percent, well above the norm elsewhere. Poverty runs a bit higher than typical, even as unemployment stays lower. This is a place that owns more, houses more people per square mile, and earns less than most of the country.
Jim Banks.p2: EVERWISE, Indiana Members, and Elements Financial anchor the credit union presence here, and together they help explain a retail office share of 27.1 percent, a bigger slice than most other states give their credit unions. Credit union employment runs modestly ahead of the national norm, but the office network has grown even further out in front, more branches than the staffing behind them. Banking overall still runs on a mix of national and local names, with thousands of branches spread across many competing institutions statewide.
Jim Banks.p3: Manufacturing set Indiana apart across the decade ending in 2023, employing 17.8 percent of workers and running far above the national norm for the sector. Transportation, warehousing, and wholesale trade filled out smaller layers of that same freight and factory economy. Health care and retail employed plenty of people too, without marking the state as unusual. Overall finance employment stayed below the national norm, leaving manufacturing as the clearest signal of what this economy does differently.

Jim Costa.p1: Poverty here runs higher than in almost any other congressional district, at 21.5 percent, and unemployment climbs nearly as far. Median household income, at 66,399 dollars, trails far behind most comparable districts. Housing still costs more than that income can comfortably absorb, with rents and home values pushing well above what peer districts see. Homeownership, meanwhile, has slipped well behind the levels found in most other districts.
Jim Costa.p2: Credit unions have a bigger footprint here in offices than in jobs, holding 26.7 percent of retail offices against banks, a share above most peer districts, while credit union employment itself sits just under the national norm. Employees Credit Union, The Golden 1, and Noble anchor that branch presence. Bank of America leads the district under federal deposit-booking rules, one name among many competing banks locally. For a district with income this constrained, that many storefronts per household points to credit unions doing more counter work than back-office work.
Jim Costa.p3: The employment base, measured in 2023, leans hard on agriculture, which runs more than eleven times the national norm and marks this district as unusually specialized in that line of work. Public administration and transportation and warehousing also run well above typical levels. Health care employs the most people day to day, running somewhat above the national norm as well. Overall finance and insurance employment runs far below national levels, even as the sector has grown slightly faster than the country as a whole.

Jim Jordan.p1: This district's homes carry a light price tag relative to what people earn: the median value runs 3.2 times median household income, and rent takes just 15.0 percent of that income, lighter than almost every other district measured. Home ownership runs high at 73.8 percent, and unemployment stays low. Household income sits near the middle of the national pack, across a district spread thin on the land.
Jim Jordan.p2: Credit union offices here outrun credit union jobs, a gap unusual enough to note: office presence runs specialized against the national norm while staffing levels stay only slightly above it. Superior Credit Union, KEMBA Financial, and Wright-Patt Credit Union anchor that office network, which holds 23.9 percent of retail bank and credit union locations combined, a share about even with comparable districts. Deposits booked to JPMorgan Chase lead the field under federal reporting rules, though 214 bank branches from many separate banks compete here on the ground.
Jim Jordan.p3: As measured in 2023, manufacturing dominated the job base, holding 21.5 percent of employment and running at nearly two and a half times the national norm. Management of companies and enterprises ran even more concentrated relative to the country as a whole, a sign of corporate offices layered on top of factory work. General finance and insurance jobs were thin on the ground, well under the national norm even as the sector grew roughly in step with the country over the prior decade.

Jimmy Gomez.p1: Population sits at 754,617 across a footprint so compact that density here outranks nearly every other congressional seat measured. Typical household earnings come to 63,879 dollars, well below most districts, and that stretches against a median home price of 824,200 dollars, far beyond what such income could support. Few residents own their home, and rent takes a heavy bite out of typical pay. Work centers heavily on public administration, alongside health care and technical services.
Jimmy Gomez.p2: Credit union employment here runs much closer to the national norm than the number of branches would, meaning these institutions employ more locally than their storefront count implies. Water and Power Community, California Credit Union, and Credit Union of Southern CA anchor that presence, holding 17.7 percent of retail offices, while City National Bank tops 117 area bank branches on deposits booked locally. For households already stretched by housing costs, that thin branch footprint against a fuller payroll matters. Finance and insurance work overall ran above the national norm here.
Jimmy Gomez.p3: The local economy, in its 2023 snapshot, leaned hard into government work and utilities, both far more concentrated here than nationally. Public administration alone accounted for a fifth of all jobs, dwarfing every other sector measured. Mortgage lending skewed toward home purchases, with a substantial share going to lower-income neighborhoods. That concentration in government work, layered onto the density that opens this brief, is what sets the district apart.

Jimmy Panetta.p1: Household income in the 19th congressional seat of California is among the highest of any congressional district, at 124,559 dollars. Home values run high too, and the ratio of home value to income, at 9.1, shows owning far outpacing what local pay alone would cover. Homeownership trails most comparable districts, and rent claims 23.4 percent of the typical household's income. Poverty stays low, well under what most districts see.
Jimmy Panetta.p2: Credit unions here carry more weight in employment than their office presence would imply, a case of jobs outpacing offices. Star One, Bay, and The Golden 1 anchor that presence against Wells Fargo Bank, National Association, the name that leads the district under federal deposit-reporting rules. Credit unions hold 23.1 percent of retail offices, and their employment sits close to the national norm even as their office footprint runs well under it. The district's high earners and costly housing give these institutions a rich customer base without a matching number of doors.
Jimmy Panetta.p3: As of 2023, work in the district leaned heavily toward agriculture and utilities, both far more concentrated here than the national norm, alongside a strong pull toward accommodation and food service. Health care and social assistance and retail trade rounded out the largest slices of work, with retail tracking the nation closely. Finance and insurance employment overall ran well under the national norm. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, with 48.3 percent of originations tied to buying rather than refinancing.

Jimmy Patronis.p1: Housing here costs more against income than in nearly every comparable district, with home values running 4.4 times the typical household income. That sits against a median household income of 77,014 dollars, fairly ordinary for a congressional district. Homeownership runs higher than most peers at 70.8 percent. The district is spread thin, with population near 817,541 and little density pressure.
Jimmy Patronis.p2: Credit unions hold 32.9 percent of retail offices here, a share well above most districts nationally, even with 150 bank branches on the ground under many separate charters. Navy Federal Credit Union, Eglin, and PenAir carry that presence locally. Credit union employment runs far above the national norm too, a specialization in staffing that outpaces the specialization in office count. For the homeowners and renters described above, that makes this a place where credit unions do a disproportionate share of the work.
Jimmy Patronis.p3: The industry base measured in 2023 leaned on accommodation and food service, construction, and real estate, all specialized well beyond the national norm. Retail trade and tourism-related jobs made up a sizeable share of employment among the district's total job count. Finance and insurance employment also grew faster than the country as a whole over the prior decade. This is a district built on tourism, building, and property, not on any single dominant employer.

Joaquin Castro.p1: In the 20th congressional district of Texas, the fact that stands out most against comparable places is household income, low at 62,044 dollars a year. Home values run modest alongside it, yet rent still claims a large slice of a typical paycheck, and fewer households here own their homes than in most districts. The area is also crowded, with population packed far more tightly per square mile than the country typically sees, and poverty reaches levels most districts do not approach.
Joaquin Castro.p2: Credit unions claim 37.3 percent of retail office locations in this district, an unusually large slice for the industry to hold anywhere. Randolph-Brooks, Security Service, and Credit Human anchor that presence locally. Credit union employment runs far thicker than the national norm, well out of proportion even to a healthy office count. That combination points to a workforce built to serve the income-strapped, renter-heavy households described above.
Joaquin Castro.p3: Back in 2023, finance and insurance employed 13.5 percent of this district's 328,800 jobs, a concentration triple the national norm and the heaviest specialty the district had. Health care employed a substantial share of workers as well. USAA Federal Savings Bank was named the top bank by deposits booked to addresses here, though many competing banks also operate in the district. Mortgage lending skewed heavily toward home purchases over refinancing.

Jodey Arrington.p1: This is wide-open country, just 26.1 people per square mile, thinner than nearly every other district in the country. Across its 787,118 residents, the median age is 34.0 and household income sits at 64,889 dollars, low next to most districts of its kind. Home values sit low too, and homeownership, at 63.7 percent, trails most comparable places. Poverty runs high here even as unemployment stays modest, a mismatch worth noting.
Jodey Arrington.p2: Abilene Teachers, Alliance, and Texas Tech carry the credit union presence here, holding 21.6 percent of retail offices, a middling share against comparable districts. First Financial Bank posts the largest deposit figure of any name in the district, a quirk of how deposits get booked rather than a sign of dominance on the ground, since many other banks operate here too. Credit union employment runs slightly above the national norm, matched closely by how many offices they keep open, giving these institutions a real foothold in a place where income runs thin and cash matters.
Jodey Arrington.p3: Extraction and land defined this economy: Mining, Quarrying, and Oil and Gas Extraction ran at more than eight times the national norm, and Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Hunting nearly four times it, marking out genuinely distinctive ground. Overall finance-sector employment ran below the national norm even as credit unions held their own. Almost all mortgage activity here was tied to purchasing property outright, with little coming from homeowners refinancing what they already had.

Joe Courtney.p1: Household income in the 2nd district of Connecticut runs well above most comparable districts, at 98,155 dollars a year. Homes carry a middle-of-the-road price for the region relative to that income, and housing costs overall stay lower than in most other districts, with owners making up 73.8 percent of households. Poverty and unemployment both stay lower than in most other districts too. Steady work and high homeownership define daily life here more than anything else measured.
Joe Courtney.p2: Credit union offices here outpace credit union jobs, offices run specialized against the national norm while jobs stay only slightly ahead of it, so the sector's local footprint leans more toward storefronts than headcount. Charter Oak, CorePlus, and Navy Federal Credit Union anchor that presence. Credit unions hold 21.3 percent of retail offices, roughly matching what similar districts show, competing with 170 bank branches, the top one by deposits booked to Manufacturers and Traders Trust Company. That is a substantial branch network for credit unions to compete against in a district with this much income to work with.
Joe Courtney.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing was a leading sector here and ran well above the national norm, with educational services close behind on both counts. Accommodation and food services also ran heavier than the norm. Overall finance and insurance employment stayed below the national norm, a sign this economy leans on making things and teaching people rather than financial services. Home purchase loans made up 49.1 percent of all mortgage originations, well ahead of refinancing.

Joe Neguse.p1: People spread thin across this district, just 63.6 per square mile, a sparseness that sets it apart from most comparable places and shapes how people here live and work. Residents earn a median household income well ahead of other districts, while unemployment stays low. Housing runs expensive by contrast, with a median home value of $721,500 against that income, a ratio of 7.2, and homeownership trails most peers even with earnings this strong.
Joe Neguse.p2: Credit union employment here runs thinner than credit union office presence, well behind the national norm even as offices come closer to it, an unusual split worth noting up front. Elevations, Ent, and First Technology anchor the credit union presence, though they hold just 18.4 percent of retail offices, below most peer districts. FirstBank leads on deposits booked locally, one name among 202 bank branches competing for this same spread-out, high-income population.
Joe Neguse.p3: The district's economy leaned hard into Arts, Entertainment, and Recreation, a specialty far beyond the national norm, alongside real strength in Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services and Information. Overall finance employment ran well below the national norm, and finance and insurance growth trailed too, even as the broader economy found its footing in tourism and technical work rather than banking. Home purchase loans made up 56.4 percent of all mortgage originations, a district shaped by distance and destination rather than density.

Joe Wilson.p1: Homeownership runs high in the 2nd district of South Carolina, well above most comparable districts, and most households here own rather than rent. Median household income sits at 77,683 dollars, an unremarkable figure against other districts, while the typical home is valued at 273,300 dollars, a number that trails most peers. Unemployment, at 5.1 percent, climbs higher than most districts of this kind, a note of friction in an otherwise comfortable picture.
Joe Wilson.p2: Credit unions hold 32.5 percent of retail offices in this district, a figure that separates it from most others in the country. Navy Federal, SRP, and AllSouth carry that presence, set against Wells Fargo, whose deposits lead the district on paper though many banks compete for business here. Credit union employment runs about half again the national norm, and their office count outpaces even that strength, meaning offices have grown faster than staffing.
Joe Wilson.p3: The district's 2023 economy drew its identity from administrative and support services, finance and insurance, and retail trade, each employing people well beyond what the national mix would predict. Retail trade and health care between them accounted for a good chunk of area jobs, with accommodation and food service not far behind. Lending activity across all lenders skewed heavily toward home purchases, which made up 61.3 percent of originations.

John Barrasso.p1: Wyoming spreads about six people across each square mile, among the thinnest settlement in the country, and the working economy sits on top of that emptiness. Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction employs a small share of workers but at a rate over sixteen times the national norm, alongside a public sector that also runs heavy. Median household income sits at $75,532, lower than most states report, though unemployment at 3.4 percent runs well under typical. Most people here own their homes rather than rent them.
John Barrasso.p2: Credit unions hold 23.8 percent of retail offices in Wyoming, a larger cut of the market than most states show, and the names behind that figure include UNIWYO, BLUE, and Meridian Trust, set against First Interstate Bank, whose deposit total leads only because federal rules book it there. Credit union employment runs at 1.72 times the national norm, well ahead of the office count itself. That gap means these institutions staff up more heavily than their branch footprint alone would explain. They are built to serve homeowners and wage earners scattered thin across the state.
John Barrasso.p3: Beyond mining and government work, Wyoming's 2023 job count of roughly 254,500 leaned on health care, retail trade, and accommodation and food services, none of them especially specialized here. All finance and insurance jobs together ran below the national norm, at 0.65, with growth over the prior decade tracking close to typical. The state's real distinction was extraction and public administration carrying an otherwise ordinary, service-heavy job base.

John Boozman.p1: Arkansas counts just over 3.09 million residents, and the median age runs to 39.1 years. Median household income sits at 62,106 dollars, among the lowest of any state, and housing stays cheap alongside it, with rent near 982 dollars a month. Unemployment is low, but poverty runs unusually high. People are spread thin across the land here, well below the crowding found almost anywhere else.
John Boozman.p2: Arkansas Federal, CommunityAmerica, and United are the credit union names on record here, operating in a state where credit unions hold just 10.7 percent of retail banking offices. Bank OZK books the largest deposits in the state, though its many bank branches statewide, run by separate institutions, show how crowded the field around it is. Credit union employment runs well below the national norm, thinner even than the office count would imply. For a state with modest incomes and cheap housing, that is a light footprint to build member relationships on.
John Boozman.p3: As of 2023, the state's economy leaned on manufacturing, which held 13.8 percent of jobs, well above the national norm, alongside health care and social assistance and retail trade as the other big employers. Management of companies and utilities stood out too, concentrated well beyond what the state's size would predict. Overall finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm, even as the sector grew roughly in line with the country. The base runs on manufacturing and management more than most states do.

John Carter.p1: Poverty in the 31st congressional seat of Texas sits well below most comparable districts, at 8.6 percent, alongside low unemployment. Income here clears $96,045 at the median, in a district of 901,458 people. The typical home is valued at $402,000, well above what that income would comfortably support, while rent runs $1,608 a month. Population density is thin for a district this size, pointing to a workforce spread across suburban and outlying communities rather than packed into a dense core.
John Carter.p2: Credit union offices here hold a slightly larger footprint than the national norm, but credit union employment runs lighter than that norm would predict, an unusual split where offices outpace jobs. Pentagon, Navy Federal, and Randolph-Brooks anchor that office presence, though credit unions still hold only 17.2 percent of retail offices overall. JPMorgan Chase books sizable local deposits, one name among many banks with branches here. For a credit union, that means a lean workforce relative to a comparatively thick office network to compete against.
John Carter.p3: As measured in 2023, construction, utilities, and mining each employed workers well above the national norm, giving this district a build-and-extract edge among its jobs. Health care and retail employed sizable shares of workers by headcount. Finance and insurance jobs overall ran below the national norm even as the sector grew fast over the prior decade. Mortgage lending skewed strongly toward buyers purchasing homes rather than homeowners refinancing.

John Cornyn.p1: Texas is home to just over 31 million people, and at a median age of 35.9 it skews younger than most states. Median household income sits at 79,721 dollars, roughly in the middle nationally. Housing costs run well above what most states see, and homeownership trails most of the country too. Unemployment and poverty both sit above most states as well.
John Cornyn.p2: Navy Federal, Randolph-Brooks, and Pentagon give Texas some of the biggest credit union names in the country, and together with the rest of the sector they hold 22.7 percent of retail offices statewide, a share that lands in the middle against other states. JPMorgan Chase is credited with more bank deposits booked here than any other institution, one name among many competing banks across the state. Credit union employment runs just slightly below the national norm, tracking closely with how thin the office footprint is here too. For a state with this much income and this much housing pressure, credit unions hold a real but unremarkable piece of the field.
John Cornyn.p3: As of 2023, Texas employment leaned hardest into mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction, running at four times the national norm and marking a clear strength for the state. Health care, retail, and educational services accounted for sizable slices of the workforce, without running especially far ahead of the national pace. Finance and insurance employment overall ran above the national norm, and grew faster than the country as a whole over the prior decade.

John Curtis.p1: Utah is young and comparatively well off, with a median household income of $96,658 and a median age of just 32.5. A typical home costs 5.6 times what a household earns in a year, even as rent claims a smaller portion of that same paycheck. Homeownership is common and poverty is rare here compared with most of the country. The population spreads thin across wide, largely open country.
John Curtis.p2: America First, Mountain America, and Utah Community anchor a credit union presence that stands out nationally: credit unions hold 51.9 percent of retail offices statewide, a share few other states can match. Credit union jobs run at 2.46 times the national norm, and offices at 2.08 times, both rated highly specialized, with hiring in the sector pulling ahead of its own branch growth. One out-of-state bank leads the state's booked deposits simply because of accounting rules on where funds are recorded, not because it beats the many other banks operating branches here. For a state this young and this middle-income, a credit union is close to the default financial relationship.
John Curtis.p3: Construction, mining and quarrying, and arts and entertainment all employ Utah workers at rates well above the national norm for their size. Health care, retail, and manufacturing employed the most workers without being specialties. Finance and insurance overall grew faster here than nationally between 2013 and 2023, a backdrop that matches the credit union sector's outsized footprint.

John Fetterman.p1: Pennsylvania packs 292.3 people per square mile, a density well above most states, with hospitals and health systems anchoring the job base at 18.2 percent of employment. Manufacturing still holds a solid share of jobs, and corporate management offices cluster here more than in most states, a sign of institutions doing the heavy lifting rather than one boomtown. Households bring in 77,545 dollars at the midpoint, and homeownership runs high at 69.3 percent, even as home values trail what most states report. Unemployment sits at 4.3 percent, unremarkable and stable.
John Fetterman.p2: Credit unions account for 22.9 percent of retail offices in the state, unexceptional next to other states, working alongside PNC Bank, the deposit leader in a field crowded with local competitors. Pennsylvania State Employees, Members 1st, and Police & Fire Credit Union carry the name here, serving the salaried, homeowning population described above. Credit union offices sit slightly ahead of the national norm while credit union employment runs a bit thin against it, an imbalance between branch presence and staffing.
John Fetterman.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance jobs overall ran ahead of the national norm, even as hiring across that combined sector cooled compared with the national pace over the decade before. What set this state apart was health care, manufacturing, and transportation and warehousing together, each employing more heavily than the national norm, with corporate management functions the most specialized work measured here. That points to an economy organized around caring for, moving, and administering things, not any one industry alone.

John Garamendi.p1: In the 8th district of California, a typical home carries a price tag near seven times the going household paycheck, one of the widest such gaps found anywhere in the state's districts. Households here bring in 95,876 dollars a year, comfortably more than in most other districts, yet homeownership lags well behind at 59.2 percent, a sign of how far prices have outrun earnings. Rent runs 2,185 dollars a month. Unemployment sits high at 8.4 percent, and people are packed more tightly onto the land here than in most comparable places.
John Garamendi.p2: Credit union jobs here run noticeably thicker than the national norm, well ahead of how much office space credit unions actually hold, a gap worth noting before anything else. Travis, The Golden 1, and 1st Northern California anchor that presence, in a district where credit unions hold 28.1 percent of retail offices, a share topping most comparable districts. Wells Fargo books the most deposits to addresses here, though many competing banks operate branches in the district as well. Credit unions, by contrast, carry far more staff than their small office footprint would imply.
John Garamendi.p3: Public administration, construction, and health care carried unusual weight in the district's 2023 job mix, all specialized well above the national norm, with health care alone accounting for a fifth of local employment. Retail trade and manufacturing followed close behind, both a bit above the national norm. Mortgage lending stayed dominated by home purchases, and a sizable slice of that lending flowed into lower income neighborhoods.

John Hickenlooper.p1: Colorado's median household earns 97,113 dollars a year, well above most states, and housing costs match that reach: the typical home runs 574,600 dollars, high by national standards, against rent near 1,822 dollars a month. Renting is more common here than ownership tends to be elsewhere, even as poverty stays low. The population sits far below the national average in density, scattered across wide open land.
John Hickenlooper.p2: ENT, Bellco and Canvas anchor the credit union presence here, and the sector holds 22.3 percent of retail offices statewide. Credit union jobs hold nearly steady against the national norm even as the office count falls short of it, so each branch carries more work than that pattern would predict. Wells Fargo books the largest deposit share of any institution, one name among many banks competing across the state. That is the terrain a credit union works in here, well-paid households carrying expensive homes, served by a comparatively lean branch footprint.
John Hickenlooper.p3: As of 2023, Colorado's economy leaned hardest into mining and oil and gas extraction, a concentration well above the national norm, alongside real strength in professional and technical services and in arts and entertainment. Health care employed a large share of workers, though without the same concentration. Total employment stood near 2.62 million jobs, built on a state economy unusually good at resource extraction and technical expertise at once.

John Hoeven.p1: North Dakota's population skews young, a median age of 36.7, earning $77,871 at the midpoint, about average next to other states. Buying a home there typically costs $266,100, well under what most states report, and rent runs $980 a month, leaving housing costs among the lowest anywhere. Unemployment stays remarkably low. Homeownership trails what most other states report.
John Hoeven.p2: First Community, Capital, and Town and Country are the credit unions on record here, in a state where credit unions hold 23.4 percent of retail offices, roughly in line with other states of its kind. Credit union branches are unusually plentiful relative to the national norm, having multiplied faster than credit union payrolls have, a sign that footprint has outpaced staffing. Bell Bank posts the largest deposit figures under federal booking rules, but plenty of other banks compete for business on the ground. For a state this thin on population, that branch presence gives credit unions real reach into how people here manage money.
John Hoeven.p3: North Dakota's 2023 job base tilted toward extraction: mining, quarrying, and oil and gas work ran more than eleven times the national norm, easily the state's most distinctive line of work. Agriculture and utilities also stood above typical levels for the country. Health care and retail carried the broadest employment base, each only modestly above what other states see. Total employment across the state ran near 382,600 jobs.

John James.p1: People are packed tightly into this district, more densely settled than almost anywhere else on the map of Michigan's congressional seats. Income here lands at a median of 74,512 dollars, lower than most other districts manage, while the typical home carries a value of 254,200 dollars, also on the modest end. Ownership is the norm rather than renting, with 70.7 percent of households owning, a rate that outpaces most comparable places. Joblessness runs at 4.8 percent, a shade above the usual mark.
John James.p2: Credit unions hold 35.2 percent of retail offices here, a share that sits among the highest of any place this size. Genisys and Christian Financial anchor that presence, alongside JPMorgan Chase, the name that comes out on top locally under federal deposit reporting rules. Credit union offices are unusually concentrated relative to the national norm, more so than credit union employment, which runs only slightly above typical. That is a dense branch presence serving a population that is closely settled and earning below the national middle.
John James.p3: In 2021, manufacturing dominated this district's job base, employing nearly a fifth of workers and running more than twice the national concentration. Professional, scientific, and technical services and corporate management roles were also disproportionately represented that year, layering more specialized work atop the industrial base. Overall finance and insurance employment ran well below the national norm that year. Manufacturing stood as the clear signature of the local economy in that period.

John Joyce.p1: The gap between what homes cost and what households earn is unusually narrow here: the median home value sits at roughly three times median household income, among the lowest ratios of any district nationwide, and rent claims only a modest share of that income. Earnings themselves trail many peer districts, though most households in this district own rather than rent. Joblessness stays low, across a population of 769,505 spread thinly over the land.
John Joyce.p2: Credit union offices here outpace credit union jobs, an unusual split: staffing in the industry sits just under the national norm, while office presence runs half again above it, specialized even where payrolls are not. Patriot, Pennsylvania State Employees, and Members 1st anchor that office network, though credit unions still hold only 19.8 percent of retail offices, a smaller footprint than in comparable districts, against 244 bank branches led on deposits by First National Bank of Pennsylvania. For an income base already stretched, that thinner office share matters more than it would elsewhere.
John Joyce.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing accounted for a substantial slice of the district's roughly 248,000 jobs, well above the national norm, alongside strength in transportation and warehousing and, more strikingly, agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting, the most specialized sector of all. Health care and social assistance and retail trade also carried real weight in the job count. Overall finance employment sat well under the national norm, and mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, accounting for 45.4 percent of all originations.

John Kennedy.p1: Louisiana's job base leans on what the ground provides, oil and gas extraction runs at four times the national norm, and construction is not far behind it. Wages lag behind that activity, median household income sits at $60,986, one of the lowest figures among the states, and unemployment runs well above typical levels. Housing costs less too, but rent still claims 20.9 percent of that median income, a load the state carries at a moderate, unconcentrated density.
John Kennedy.p2: Credit unions hold 25.1 percent of retail offices here, a share above most states, in a place where oil-and-gas cycles and tighter household budgets make a member-owned option matter. Barksdale, Keesler, and Neighbors carry that share, and JPMorgan Chase shows up as the top bank by deposits booked here, a figure that says more about reporting rules than about branches on the ground. Credit union offices are built out at 1.44 times the national norm, well ahead of the 1.02 reading for credit union employment. The office network, in other words, has grown faster than the staff behind it.
John Kennedy.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance jobs statewide ran below the national norm, at 0.72, and the ten years before that showed the same sector falling behind most other states. The state's real specialization sat elsewhere, in extraction and building trades, work tied to commodity cycles rather than steady office employment. That leaves credit unions serving a workforce whose paychecks trace the state's wells and job sites more than its bank towers.

John Larson.p1: This district is settled more tightly than most of its peers, a place of dense towns rather than open land. Across its roughly 735,000 residents, median household income runs to 85,466 dollars, well ahead of most other districts. Home values sit at a middling point against that income, while homeownership here trails what most districts see. Joblessness runs somewhat elevated compared with most other districts too.
John Larson.p2: Credit union offices here outpace credit union employment, an unusual split: office presence runs slightly above the national norm while the jobs behind those offices run well under it. Credit unions still hold 24.6 percent of retail deposit-taking offices, a share topping most other districts, held up by names like American Eagle Financial, Connecticut State Employees, and Nutmeg State Financial. Bank of America shows a sizeable deposit total on paper, a figure driven by where deposits get booked rather than by how many branches a bank actually runs among the district's many local banking options.
John Larson.p3: The employment picture for 2023 showed finance and insurance highly specialized here, running more than twice the national norm, alongside real depth in manufacturing and in transportation and warehousing. Health care and social assistance accounted for a substantial share of jobs among the sectors measured too. Finance and insurance jobs overall lagged the national trend across the decade before that. Home buying dominated that year's lending activity, with refinancing well behind and only a small slice of loans reaching lower income neighborhoods.

John Mannion.p1: This district's defining trait is cheap shelter relative to pay: a home value to income ratio of only 2.9, with rent claiming well under a fifth of the typical household's earnings. Median household income comes to 75,553 dollars, a modest figure set against other districts, and 13.7 percent of residents live in poverty, a share that runs high by comparison. Homeownership and joblessness both land at ordinary levels here, and people are spread across the district at a density that stands out neither way.
John Mannion.p2: Credit unions hold 35.0 percent of retail offices here, a share among the highest of any congressional district measured. EMPOWER, AMERICU, and FIRST SOURCE anchor that presence, competing for deposits against Manufacturers and Traders Trust Company, which leads locally on booked deposits alone and faces plenty of other banks on the ground. Credit union employment runs well above the national norm, and office presence further still, expanding faster than the jobs behind it, a footprint suited to a population that earns modestly and feels poverty more sharply than rent.
John Mannion.p3: Employment counts from 2023 show this district weighted toward Educational Services, which employs a well-above-average share of workers, alongside strong employment in Health Care and Social Assistance. Public Administration adds a slighter specialization on top of those two. Overall finance and insurance employment sat just under the national norm, and its growth from 2013 to 2023, measured for finance and insurance together, trailed the country as a whole.

John McGuire.p1: Unemployment sits at 3.1 percent here, among the lowest of any congressional district, a marker that separates this seat from most of its peers. Median household income runs 73,090 dollars, trailing much of the country's district map, and home values near 315,600 dollars sit in similar territory. Homeownership is high at 70.8 percent, and with only 85.1 people per square mile, this is a spread-out, low-density place. Poverty runs somewhat elevated even as work is easy to find, a combination worth sitting with.
John McGuire.p2: Credit union offices here make up 16.4 percent of retail branches, a thinner slice than most other districts carry, and that share actually outruns credit union employment, which sits well under the national norm while offices track closer to it. A credit union bearing the state's name, along with Beacon Credit Union, carries the local presence amid a broad crowd of bank branches, with Truist Bank booking the most deposits under federal rules that reflect address, not necessarily local footprint. A thin staffing base serving a comparatively light office presence is the credit union story in this district.
John McGuire.p3: In the most recent year measured, 2023, finance and insurance stood out as specialized local work, alongside instructional services and utilities, all employing at higher rates than the country overall. Finance and insurance alone ran well above the national norm and grew at a similarly elevated pace over the prior decade. Mortgage lending here leaned heavily toward home purchases, a pattern that dominated all originations recorded.

John Moolenaar.p1: Housing here costs little against what people earn, among the lowest burdens of any congressional district, with a home value pegged at 3.4 times median household income and rent near 16.3 percent of that income. The household income underneath those figures is modest, $66,726 at the median, well down the national list. Owning a home is the default here, not the exception. This is also open country, sparsely settled, a Midwest district built around owned homes on spread-out land.
John Moolenaar.p2: Credit unions hold 34.5 percent of retail offices here, a share far above the typical split with banks elsewhere. Lake Michigan, Members First, and PFCU carry that presence, set against a banking side where Huntington National Bank books the largest local deposits, amid a crowded field of other banks doing business here. Credit union employment runs well above the national norm, and their office presence runs higher still, built out ahead of the jobs behind it. For a district of modest incomes and widespread homeownership, that is a heavy footprint for credit unions to hold.
John Moolenaar.p3: In 2021, manufacturing anchored the district's economy, employing about a fifth of all workers at more than twice the national norm. Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting ran even more concentrated against the national norm, though it employed far fewer people. Overall finance employment sat only slightly above the national norm, with little growth in finance and insurance across the following decade.

John Rose.p1: The 6th congressional seat of Tennessee posts an unemployment rate of 3.4 percent, well below most comparable districts and the sharpest thing about its labor market. Household income has not kept pace, at 72,083 dollars, and poverty runs above what most peer districts see. Housing carries its own weight too, with rent taking 21.5 percent of median income. The district counts 803,181 residents, scattered across a mostly rural footprint.
John Rose.p2: Credit unions hold just 15.0 percent of retail offices here, well behind the banks that dominate this market. ASCEND, OLD HICKORY, and TEN carry that share, competing against a deep roster of bank branches under separate ownership, Pinnacle Bank among them. Credit union jobs sit thin against the national norm even though office counts have held up somewhat better, a presence spread thinner on staff than on storefronts. Given the incomes and rents above, that is a light institutional base for residents to lean on.
John Rose.p3: As measured in 2023, manufacturing held 12.0 percent of jobs and ran well above the national norm, and transportation and warehousing and administrative support services were specialized in the same way. Retail trade employed a comparable share of workers. Home purchases dominated the district's lending activity, and a solid portion of loans went to lower income neighborhoods. The district's economy turns on moving and making things, not on finance.

John Rutherford.p1: Unemployment in the 5th congressional seat of Florida sits at 3.1 percent, among the lowest of any comparable district, and it points to a labor market with little slack. Households here earn a median of 90,333 dollars, comfortably ahead of typical districts, while poverty runs low at 7.4 percent. Home values, at a median of 457,100 dollars, run far beyond what those incomes would comfortably support. Homeownership here trails most comparable places even so.
John Rutherford.p2: Credit union employment in this district runs well ahead of what the sector's office footprint alone would predict, even though credit unions already hold a strong 28.0 percent of retail offices. VyStar, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Community First Credit Union of Florida anchor that presence. Bank of America is named the top deposit holder under federal booking rules, one name among many banks competing for the district's retail business. For a credit union here, that combination points to a workforce built for growth even where branch counts alone would understate it.
John Rutherford.p3: Finance and insurance stood out as this district's defining sector, employing 11.3 percent of its workforce at more than twice the national norm. Administrative and support services and construction followed as secondary specialties, both moderately concentrated here. Health care and retail trade rounded out the district's other main sources of jobs, reflecting a broad services base beneath the finance specialty. Mortgage data show purchase loans driving most originations, evidence of a housing market still central to how the district's money moves.

John Thune.p1: South Dakota spreads its 924,669 people thin across wide open land, among the lowest densities of any state. A typical household earns 76,881 dollars, neither high nor low against the other states, but housing asks little of that income: a home value of 289,600 dollars sits at 3.8 times earnings, and rent stays cheap. Owning a home is common here, and few residents fall into poverty or go without work.
John Thune.p2: Black Hills, Dakotaland, and Levo carry the credit union name across a state where such institutions hold just 20.3 percent of retail offices, a smaller footprint than most peer states manage, with Citibank chief among the banks by deposits booked rather than doors opened. Credit union employment runs 1.32 times the national norm, well ahead of the more modest reading on office presence. For the moderate earners and mortgage-light households described above, that is a workforce staffed more heavily than its office presence alone would imply.
John Thune.p3: As measured in 2023, finance and insurance jobs ran well above the national norm here, though the same combined sector had not been adding ground over the prior decade. Farming, forestry, fishing and hunting stood out furthest from typical state patterns nationwide. Health care, retail, and manufacturing carried the bulk of the workforce, each a shade heavier than the country's usual mix. This is a state whose distinctive strength is land-based production, not its office towers.

Johnny Olszewski.p1: Poverty here sits well below most districts, at 8.4 percent, and that scarcity of hardship shapes everything else about the seat. Median household income runs to 94,537 dollars, comfortably ahead of peer districts, while unemployment also undercuts the norm elsewhere. Rent takes 21.1 percent of what a typical household brings home, unremarkable next to comparable seats. This is also a dense district, packed with people who are, on the whole, working and getting by.
Johnny Olszewski.p2: Credit unions here include First Financial of Maryland, State Employees CU of Maryland, and Point Breeze, and together the sector holds 17.6 percent of retail offices, a thinner slice than in most comparable districts. Bank of America leads locally by deposits credited to this district under federal reporting rules, one name among several competing for the same business. Credit union employment tracks office presence closely, both running below the national norm. That leaves these institutions serving a population that is comparatively well off and fully employed, working hard for a limited slice of the local banking market.
Johnny Olszewski.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance stood as this district's most specialized sector, well above the national norm, with real estate and construction also elevated. Health care, retail, and educational services employed the most people, each modestly ahead of the norm too. Mortgage lending data shows just 14.4 percent of loans going to lower income neighborhoods. This is a district built around finance and property, with money and paperwork as its trade.

Jon Husted.p1: Ohio's economy still runs on making things: manufacturing accounts for a big share of jobs, well ahead of the national pace, and management of companies clusters here at an even higher rate. Health care employs a large slice of workers, with retail trade close behind. People are packed into this state far more tightly than most. Incomes trail most other states, and unemployment runs low at 4.0 percent.
Jon Husted.p2: Credit unions hold 20.0 percent of retail offices here, a slimmer cut than most states manage, even though credit union offices themselves run slightly above the national norm relative to population. Credit union payrolls, by contrast, run below that norm, so each office covers more ground than the typical office elsewhere. Wright-Patt Credit Union, General Electric, and Kemba Financial anchor that presence. Against thousands of bank branches statewide, including U.S. Bank as the top deposit holder among many competitors, credit unions serve the same manufacturing and health care workforce from a smaller footprint.
Jon Husted.p3: Finance and insurance jobs in 2023 lined up closely with the national norm. Housing remained a real advantage: the ratio of home value to income came to 3.3, low compared with other states, and rent claimed just 18.1 percent of median income. Homeownership was unremarkable next to other states. What sets Ohio apart is manufacturing depth paired with housing costs that let a working wage still stretch.

Jon Ossoff.p1: Georgia counts just over 11.18 million residents and a median age of 38, in a South Census region where the state's population sits more tightly packed than most. A typical household earns 79,991 dollars a year, an unremarkable figure next to other states, but the state's home values, at 343,300 dollars, run high against that income. Homeownership, at 66.3 percent, falls short of most states, while poverty and unemployment both climb past what most states report.
Jon Ossoff.p2: Three names carry credit union business across the state: Navy Federal Credit Union, Delta Community, and Robins Financial. Even so, credit unions hold just 20.1 percent of the state's retail offices, thinner ground than most states hold, against Truist Bank, the top holder of deposits here by booking address rather than local branches. Credit union employment across Georgia sits well under the national norm, moving in step with how few offices it keeps here rather than outrunning them.
Jon Ossoff.p3: As of 2023, Georgia's economy ran on moving goods: Transportation and Warehousing employment came in well above the national norm statewide, with Wholesale Trade and Information close behind. Health Care, Retail, and Manufacturing employed the most people in the state, without any particular pull toward or away from the national picture. Finance and insurance employment sat near that same national norm, though it grew faster across Georgia than the country as a whole between 2013 and 2023.

Jonathan Jackson.p1: Unemployment stands at 8.3 percent here, among the highest of any district in the country, and it colors everything else in this profile. Household income lags comparable districts at 69,490 dollars, and poverty runs well ahead of what most peer districts report. Home values trail similar districts too, at 291,700 dollars, against a median rent of 1,166 dollars. This is a dense, largely built-out part of the Midwest.
Jonathan Jackson.p2: Credit union employment here runs thin, well under the national norm, even though credit union offices are comparatively more common, a gap that shows offices outpacing jobs. Alliant, Covantage, and Numark carry the credit union presence. Even so, credit unions hold just 18.9 percent of retail offices, leaving JPMorgan Chase as the name booking the most deposits here, in a market with many separate banks competing for branches. For a credit union, this is a district of stretched household finances and a modest institutional footprint to build from.
Jonathan Jackson.p3: Health care and social assistance employed a large share of workers, alongside educational services and transportation and warehousing, all sectors well above the national norm in concentration. Overall finance employment ran under norm too. Home purchases made up most mortgage activity, and a meaningful share reached lower-income neighborhoods. This is a district built on institutions, care, instruction, and logistics, more than on finance.

Joni Ernst.p1: Iowa's economy still runs on making and growing things: manufacturing holds a bigger share of jobs than almost any state, and agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting is similarly concentrated even though it employs a small slice directly. People are spread thin across the land, well below the density found in most states. Unemployment sits low and homeownership runs high, so the state's workers mostly own the modest houses they live in.
Joni Ernst.p2: Credit unions hold 18.4 percent of retail offices here, a share well below most states, even though the sector runs thick: credit union employment sits above the national norm and office presence runs even higher against it, meaning offices have outpaced staffing.
