GreenState, Veridian, and Dupaco Community carry the state's credit union identity, set against Principal Bank, which leads locally on deposits booked to its addresses among 1,419 bank branches statewide. That imbalance, thin office share but dense specialization, is what a credit union here works within, serving homeowners and manufacturing workers on modest, steady incomes.
Joni Ernst.p3: Finance and insurance jobs ran well above the national norm as of 2023, though the sector's growth from 2013 to 2023 lagged the national pace slightly. Manufacturing led all sectors in size, with health care and social assistance and retail trade close behind, in an economy of about 1,435,900 jobs. Iowa's distinct strength was specialization itself, in making goods, growing food, and financing both, rather than in any single dominant employer.

Joseph Morelle.p1: Unemployment here runs low, a rate other districts rarely touch, and it anchors a district of 768,525 people with a middle-aged population. Household income sits at an unremarkable level, but home values run cheap by comparison, and rent stays modest against what people earn. Poverty climbs higher here than the typical district manages. This is a crowded corner of the Northeast, dense with people, not a struggling one.
Joseph Morelle.p2: Credit unions hold 35.1 percent of retail offices here, a share among the highest of any comparable district, putting them on close to equal footing with banks rather than in a supporting role. ESL, The Summit, and Kinecta anchor that presence, while Manufacturers and Traders Trust comes out ahead on the deposit figures credited to its addresses here, just one bank among many with a presence in the district. Both credit union jobs and credit union offices cluster well past the national norm, with office growth outpacing hiring. That footprint lines up with the moderate incomes and rents described above.
Joseph Morelle.p3: Educational services stood out most in the district's 2023 job mix, well above the national norm, alongside a smaller specialization in managing companies. Health care made up a large slice of jobs too, a specialization in its own right. Overall finance employment ran below the national norm, and growth in finance and insurance combined tracked just under the national pace. Total employment approached 372,400 jobs, built on institutions and instruction rather than on finance itself.

Josh Brecheen.p1: Fewer than 38 people occupy each square mile here, a sparseness matched by almost no comparable district in the country. Household income falls low against other seats, and the share of residents in poverty climbs higher than nearly every peer reports. Housing costs little by comparison: a median home value near 176,700 dollars against income puts the value-to-income ratio at 3.2, and owning a home is the norm more often than in most districts.
Josh Brecheen.p2: Credit unions hold just 10.5 percent of retail offices here, a share few other districts fall beneath, so banks fill nearly every other storefront. TTCU, Truity, and First Family carry the credit union presence that exists. First United Bank and Trust Company books the largest deposits under federal rules, a distinction tied to where deposits are recorded rather than to how many rival banks operate branches nearby. Credit union employment sits close to the national norm even where office counts fall short of it, so the sector's workforce here does more per storefront than the national pattern would predict.
Josh Brecheen.p3: As measured in 2023, this district's economy leaned hard on extraction, utilities, and government work, each employing far beyond its national share. Health care, retail, and manufacturing employed the most people day to day. Overall finance employment sat well below the national norm, at 0.58, in a place whose real specialty was pulling resources and public payrolls, not banking.

Josh Gottheimer.p1: Household income in the 5th congressional seat of New Jersey sits near the top of every congressional district, at 130,387 dollars. A home here runs 628,800 dollars at the midpoint, yet what people pay in rent and housing costs stays modest against what they earn. Homeownership is common, near 72 percent, in a district of 794,119 people with little poverty and low unemployment. This is dense country for the Northeast, built around steady work rather than people getting by.
Josh Gottheimer.p2: Credit unions hold just 5.7 percent of retail offices here, a share few other districts fall below. VISIONS, AFFINITY, and GREATER ALLIANCE are the names carrying that small share, competing against a field dominated by bank storefronts. Credit union employment barely registers against the national norm, thinner even than the office footprint itself. The income and home values described above are largely banking territory, not credit union territory, in this district.
Josh Gottheimer.p3: As measured in 2023, health care and social assistance held 20.3 percent of the district's jobs, well ahead of the national norm for that sector. Wholesale trade and management of companies also ran strong against national norms, rounding out a district built on managing and moving things as much as treating patients. Overall finance employment lagged the national norm, a reminder that banking and credit union work here is a smaller piece of a larger, steadier economy. Health care, wholesale trade, and corporate management are what this place does best.

Josh Harder.p1: Unemployment in the district sits among the highest of any comparable seat, at 8.0 percent, a sign the local labor market has not fully steadied. Household income runs comfortably higher than most peer districts, at $92,036, yet home values have climbed far past what that income would normally support. Renters pay $1,771 a month on median, and homeownership lags behind most comparable districts. The population here is large and closely packed.
Josh Harder.p2: Credit union employment runs thin against the national norm, while credit union offices hold up better, at 0.72, pointing to leaner staffing per branch rather than a thin footprint. The Golden 1, Valley Strong, and UNCLE anchor that presence, though credit unions hold only 20.6 percent of retail offices, trailing most comparable districts, against a bank branch network led on deposits by Wells Fargo. That leaves banks dominant on paper, even as the income and housing pressures above are exactly what a credit union member here is contending with.
Josh Harder.p3: As measured in 2023, the district's work leaned hard on moving goods: Transportation and Warehousing was both a major source of jobs and the most specialized sector, running well beyond the national norm. Health care and retail filled out much of the rest of the local job mix, ordinary in scale next to that logistics base. Mortgage lending skewed toward home purchases, making up most originations. This is a logistics corridor first, with health care and retail rounding it out.

Josh Hawley.p1: Missouri's economy runs on health care, manufacturing, and retail trade, the sectors that employ the most people, with corporate management offices adding an unusual concentration on top. The state is settled at a density that sits in the middle of the national range, spread across small and mid-sized centers rather than one dominant metro. Households earn a median of 71,589 dollars, well below most states, and unemployment stays low at 3.2 percent. Homeownership here beats most of the country.
Josh Hawley.p2: Credit unions hold 14.1 percent of retail offices, one of the thinnest shares of any state, leaving banks to carry most of the branch business, UMB Bank chief among them by deposits booked, though its network is just one of many rivals across the state. First Community, CommunityAmerica, and Multipli carry the credit union side instead. Credit union employment runs well under the national norm even as the office count holds closer to it, so the offices that exist run leaner on staff than the national picture would call for. That is a modest footprint set against a household economy of tight incomes and high ownership.
Josh Hawley.p3: Beyond finance, the 2023 employment count showed manufacturing and management of companies both running above the national norm, marking Missouri as a place that makes things and runs back-office operations for firms based elsewhere. Poverty ran higher than in most states, a sign that the strength in production and management has not lifted every household equally.

Josh Riley.p1: This district spreads its people thin, fewer than a hundred to the square mile, a sparser settlement pattern than almost any comparable district. Households here earn less than most, with median income at 73,323 dollars, and home values sit low too, at 249,500 dollars. That keeps the value-to-income ratio modest at 3.4 and rent manageable against typical earnings. Poverty runs harder than in most peer districts.
Josh Riley.p2: Credit union employment here runs far ahead of what the office count alone would explain, at 2.35 times the national norm against 1.74 for offices, so these institutions staff up more heavily than their branch footprint alone would account for. VISIONS, Hudson Valley, and Broadview anchor that presence. Credit unions hold 29.0 percent of retail offices, a share above most peer districts, even as NBT Bank leads on deposits booked locally among a field of bank branches run by many separate banks.
Josh Riley.p3: As measured in 2023, jobs here concentrated heavily in public administration and in the sector that trains and teaches, both well beyond typical national weight. Overall finance and insurance employment, by contrast, ran below the national norm, a reminder that credit unions carry local weight that finance as a whole does not. Mortgage lending leaned toward home purchases over refinancing, a district built more on institutions and payrolls than on trading floors.

Joyce Beatty.p1: Population density sets this district apart before anything else, with residents packed far more tightly together than in comparable districts across the country. Close to 787,191 people live here, working urban and inner-suburban jobs rather than spreading across open land. Median household income sits low against other districts at 72,896 dollars, and homeownership trails well behind most peers. Rents and other housing costs bear down harder on residents here than in most comparable places.
Joyce Beatty.p2: Credit union employment runs thinner than office presence would imply, a gap worth noting first: offices are outpacing jobs on the ground. Wright-Patt Credit Union, Kemba Financial, and Telhio anchor the local presence, yet credit unions hold only 19.7 percent of retail offices, a share below most comparable districts, leaving Bank of America and the district's other 184 bank branches to hold the bulk of deposits. For a population living this densely, that leaves fewer credit union doors per resident than similar districts typically offer.
Joyce Beatty.p3: As measured in 2023, this district's economy leaned hard on institutional and knowledge work: management of companies and enterprises ran far above the national norm, and educational services employed a well-above-typical share of workers. Finance and insurance jobs also ran well above the national norm, marking this as a genuine finance employment center even as credit unions stayed thin on the ground. Mortgage lending to lower-income neighborhoods accounted for 31.6 percent of all originations.

Juan Ciscomani.p1: This district spreads its population thin, well under most comparable seats, people scattered across the land rather than clustered together. Around 833,838 people live here, with household income unremarkable at $80,251 next to other districts. Homeownership runs unusually high at 71.6 percent, and few residents here fall into poverty or go without work compared with elsewhere. Home values against income work out to an ordinary ratio, one that says nothing about what any one household actually pays.
Juan Ciscomani.p2: Credit unions hold 30.6 percent of retail offices here, a figure few comparable districts come close to, putting them squarely in competition with the banks rather than at the margins. Vantage West, Hughes, and Pima anchor that presence. JPMorgan Chase books the largest bank deposits in the district under federal reporting rules, one name among many local rivals. Credit union employment runs at 1.27 times the national norm, tracking closely with how thick their office presence runs across the district.
Juan Ciscomani.p3: Measured in 2023, mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction stood out most in this district's job mix, a small slice of employment but disproportionately concentrated compared with the rest of the country. Manufacturing also carried unusual weight. Health care and social assistance employed the most people, followed by retail trade. Overall finance and insurance employment lagged the national norm even as credit unions themselves carved out unusual scale.

Juan Vargas.p1: Space runs tight in this district, one of the most densely populated anywhere, holding roughly 756,396 people within its borders. Household income runs above most comparable districts, but housing costs have outrun it: home values and rent both sit near the top nationally, and rent alone eats close to 29 percent of what a typical household brings home. Homeownership runs low, and unemployment climbs well past the level seen across comparable districts.
Juan Vargas.p2: Credit unions hold an unusually large slice of this district's retail banking presence, with 38.8 percent of retail offices, a share few comparable districts match. Navy Federal Credit Union, Mission, and San Diego County Credit Union anchor that presence, competing against 57 bank branches overall, of which JPMorgan Chase books the largest deposit sum under federal reporting rules. Credit union employment here runs slightly above the national norm even though the office count itself runs a bit below it, meaning these institutions employ steadily on a leaner branch footprint, well suited to the income-strained households described above.
Juan Vargas.p3: The job mix leans hard into retail trade, with a concentration well above the national norm, alongside health care and social assistance as a major source of work. Overall finance-sector employment runs well under the national norm, so the credit union presence stands apart from a thin surrounding finance sector. Lending data covering all lenders shows purchase loans making up 44.1 percent of originations, with 39.3 percent reaching lower-income neighborhoods, a meaningful channel given the housing cost pressures here.

Judy Chu.p1: Home values in this district sit among the highest anywhere, a median of $1,044,100, roughly 9.4 times the median household income. Households earn far more than most districts too, a median of $111,299, yet rent still runs $2,219 a month against that income. Homeownership trails well behind comparable districts, even as poverty stays low. Money moves freely here, but owning the roof over your head is another matter.
Judy Chu.p2: Credit unions hold just 15.2 percent of retail offices in this district, a slim slice compared with similar geographies, and JPMorgan Chase is the largest bank by deposits booked locally among many competing banks. Caltech Employees, F&A, and a large institution serving public employees are the credit unions with a presence here. Credit union employment runs below the national norm, and the office footprint runs even thinner, meaning the jobs that remain outpace the branches themselves. Set against the income and home values above, credit unions here work a wealthier market with a lighter physical footprint than most.
Judy Chu.p3: As measured in 2023, the job mix leaned heavily on health care, food service, and finance and insurance, the last well above the national norm. That finance specialization lines up with the high earners and expensive homes noted earlier. Utilities also stood out as a local strength. Mortgage lending that year skewed toward home purchases, at 43.8 percent of originations, with little of that lending reaching lower-income neighborhoods.

Julia Brownley.p1: Household income in the 26th congressional seat of California sits at $120,711, a figure that stands out sharply against comparable districts, and poverty runs low too. Housing costs match that altitude: a median home value of $886,000 runs 7.3 times the median income, and rent takes a real bite out of a typical paycheck. Unemployment, by contrast, sits uncomfortably high given how well-off the district otherwise looks. This is a district with money in the household budget but real strain in getting hired and housed.
Julia Brownley.p2: Credit unions here include LOGIX, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Ventura County, and together credit unions hold 24.8 percent of retail offices, a bigger slice of the market than most districts see. JPMorgan Chase leads on deposits, a figure driven by federal booking rules rather than local branch presence, among many banks competing for business in the district. Credit union employment tracks the national norm closely. Against the district's high incomes and expensive housing, these institutions work a market where members carry real earnings but also real borrowing needs.
Julia Brownley.p3: As measured in 2023, the district's economy leaned hardest on agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting, a highly specialized sector far above the national norm, alongside finance and insurance, also specialized. Health care, manufacturing, and retail trade employed the most people without unusual concentration. Mortgage lending here ran 44.6 percent toward home purchases. The pairing of strong finance employment with heavy agricultural specialization is unusual, and it is what sets this district's economy apart.

Julia Letlow.p1: Median household income here runs low next to other congressional districts, at $59,583, and poverty runs high in the same comparison. Home values stay modest too, so the gap sits between what people earn and what a house costs rather than between rent and income. Homeownership is common here, 70.3 percent, a rate that beats most peer districts. This is also a spread-out, rural seat, thin on people per square mile, which shapes how far anyone drives for a branch.
Julia Letlow.p2: Credit union offices here outpace credit union employment: offices run at 1.61 times the national norm, wider than the 1.31 posted on jobs. Neighbors, EFCU Financial, and Ouachita Valley anchor that presence, together holding 23.4 percent of retail offices, in line with comparable districts. Chase leads the district by the deposit figures federal rules assign to booking offices rather than to branches, and plenty of other banks operate branches here besides. For an income base this modest, credit unions do a disproportionate share of the district's financial work.
Julia Letlow.p3: Total employment stood near 287,900 in 2023, with finance and insurance jobs running slightly below the national norm and flat in growth over the prior decade. Construction stood out most, well above the national norm, alongside utilities and retail trade. Health care and social assistance employed the largest share of workers, with retail trade close behind. This is a district built on building things and moving goods, not on finance.

Julie Fedorchak.p1: North Dakota's single district holds only 11.5 people per square mile, one of the thinnest populations any seat in the country has to represent. Its 796,568 residents earn a median household income of $77,871, fairly ordinary by national standards. Home values sit well below most districts relative to income, and rent runs low too, among the smallest housing burdens anywhere in the country. Unemployment is about as low as it gets anywhere.
Julie Fedorchak.p2: Credit union offices here far outnumber what the workforce alone would explain, since jobs in the sector barely exceed the national norm while office presence runs well above it. First Community, Capital, and Town and Country carry that footprint, together holding 23.4 percent of retail offices against banks, an ordinary share nationally but built on unusually dense branch coverage relative to staffing. Bell Bank tops the deposit figures tied to addresses here, though plenty of other banks compete for the same customers those credit unions serve.
Julie Fedorchak.p3: Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction was, in 2023, the sector that set this economy apart, running far above the national norm and dwarfing every other line of work measured here. Beyond that, the biggest sources of jobs were health care and retail, both somewhat above national levels. Overall finance employment also ran slightly above average, though the sector's growth over the prior decade lagged the nation's. Home purchases dominated mortgage activity, 63.4 percent of all originations, a market built around buying rather than refinancing.

Julie Johnson.p1: Few congressional districts hold people as close together as this one does. Population runs to 765,626, with a fairly young median age, 33.1. Household income lags behind most comparable places at $72,478, and homeownership sits low at just 38.2 percent. Housing costs press harder here than in most districts, even as the typical home price stays roughly average for a seat this size.
Julie Johnson.p2: Credit unions hold on to a narrow corner of the branch business here, 12.1 percent of offices, among the lowest shares of any district measured. Navy Federal, Texans, and Pentagon supply what presence exists, competing against a field of banks where JPMorgan Chase claims the top spot for deposits on paper. Credit union staffing sits well below what the national pattern would predict, and branch presence trails similarly, thin on both fronts. That leaves little capacity to serve the renters and lower-income households described above.
Julie Johnson.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance stood out as this district's leading sector, more than twice the national norm. Professional and technical services and real estate leasing also ran well ahead of typical levels. Total employment reached roughly 515,800 jobs, built on a decade of finance-sector growth that outpaced the nation. This is a district shaped by finance work, even where credit unions themselves hold only a small piece of it.

Kat Cammack.p1: The 3rd congressional seat of Florida carries a poverty rate among the highest across the nation's districts, a fact that shapes everything else here. Middle household income lands at $63,348, and home values sit at $279,900, both toward the low end for a district this size. Rent still eats deep into the middle household earnings, and roughly 845,635 people call this district home, sparsely settled across the land.
Kat Cammack.p2: Credit unions hold 29.5 percent of retail locations here, a share that stands well above peer seats and marks these institutions as central to how people actually bank. CAMPUS USA, Florida Credit Union, and VyStar carry that presence, set against Wells Fargo, named here only because federal rules book its deposits to this district, not because it out-competes rivals on the ground. Credit union staffing runs at 1.82 times the countrywide baseline, outpacing even their strong office share, a sign these institutions put down deeper local roots in staffing than their branch presence alone would show.
Kat Cammack.p3: Finance and insurance jobs overall run far short of the countrywide baseline, trailing what the credit union numbers alone would imply. Health care and social assistance make up a large slice of employment, while agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting stands out as the most specialized sector relative to the rest of the country. In 2023, this was an economy anchored in public-sector and service work rather than finance, totaling roughly 288,800 jobs.

Katherine Clark.p1: This district in Massachusetts posts a household income among the highest of any seat in the country, $136,612, with home values just as elevated. Renting takes up a moderate share of that income compared with other districts. Homeownership lags behind most places, set inside a district far more densely populated than typical. Poverty and unemployment both sit well under the levels seen elsewhere.
Katherine Clark.p2: Credit unions hold just 15.3 percent of retail offices here, a slim slice by comparison with other districts and the fact that stands out most about them in this market. First Technology, MIT Federal, and USAlliance carry that presence, working against a banking sector where Bank of America claims the top spot for deposits among many rival banks. Credit union jobs and offices each sit slightly above the national norm and move in step with one another. That is a modest footprint for an institution type competing in a wealthy, high-cost market built for larger lenders.
Katherine Clark.p3: By 2023 the mix of jobs here tilted heavily toward Management of Companies and Enterprises and toward Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services, both far more concentrated than the national norm allows. Information also ran well ahead of typical levels. Finance and insurance work overall stayed below the national norm and grew slowly across the prior decade. This is a district built on corporate headquarters and technical expertise, not on finance itself.

Kathy Castor.p1: A home in the 14th district of Florida costs 5.5 times the typical household's income, a ratio among the highest of any congressional seat in the country, and rent alone runs 27.2 percent of median earnings. Household income sits at $81,076, unremarkable next to that housing math. Homeownership lags most other districts, and the population is packed in tight, well above the density found in comparable seats. Poverty here runs higher than most peer districts too.
Kathy Castor.p2: Credit union employment runs at 1.63 times the national norm, far out of proportion to the office footprint, which sits just below that norm. Suncoast, Grow Financial, and Navy Federal Credit Union anchor that presence, and together credit unions hold 29.0 percent of retail offices, a strong share even with many bank branches still competing for the same customers, Raymond James Bank chief among them by deposits booked locally. That combination points to substantial credit union staffing built on a comparatively modest branch network. The households paying those steep housing costs are exactly who these institutions serve.
Kathy Castor.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance was this district's most specialized sector by a wide margin, running well above the national norm. Professional, scientific, and technical services followed as the next most concentrated field. Finance and insurance jobs overall grew faster than the national pace over the prior decade. Mortgage lending here leaned heavily toward home purchases, 58.1 percent of all originations, with a meaningful share reaching lower-income neighborhoods as well.

Katie Britt.p1: Alabama's median household income runs $66,659, thin next to most other states, and its median age sits at 39.6. Home values follow the same modest pattern at $233,300, while rent claims a small share of that income by comparison. Most households own rather than rent, and poverty runs well above what is typical elsewhere.
Katie Britt.p2: Redstone, All In, and America's First anchor a credit union presence that runs deep here, with credit unions holding 30.1 percent of retail offices statewide, a share well above most other states, against a banking field led on deposits by Regions Bank but populated by many rivals. Credit union jobs run 1.47 times the national norm and offices run 1.83 times, so branch capacity has grown faster than staffing has. For an income base this modest, that is a substantial amount of local financial infrastructure to work with.
Katie Britt.p3: As of 2023, Alabama's economy leaned on manufacturing, which held a share of jobs well above the national norm, alongside utilities work running close to double that norm. Retail trade added further weight of its own, and health care and social assistance made up a sizeable slice of the job base without being unusual by national standards. Overall finance and insurance employment came in under the norm even as credit unions ran thick, a state that manufactures and moves goods more than it banks.

Keith Self.p1: Median household income in the 3rd congressional seat of Texas reaches 124,853 dollars, among the highest figures any congressional district posts, and it sets the tone for everything else here. Homes here cost far more than the typical district's stock, yet a home-value-to-income ratio of 4.0 shows that price tag stays in reach of what residents actually earn. Ownership is the norm rather than the exception, and hardship is uncommon. Pay outpaces the cost of living in this district, not the reverse.
Keith Self.p2: Credit union jobs here sit closer to the national norm than credit union offices do, a gap worth leading with: offices run at 0.44 times the norm while jobs reach 0.57, so the credit unions present carry more staff than their office footprint alone would explain. Randolph-Brooks, Credit Union of Texas, and Navy Federal anchor that presence, but credit unions hold only 15.9 percent of retail offices here, a thinner slice than most comparable districts. JPMorgan Chase leads the district's largest bank by the deposits recorded to addresses here, though it shares the market with many other lenders.
Keith Self.p3: Measured in 2023, retail trade formed an outsized share of the district's employment, well beyond what its population alone would predict. Finance and insurance employment sat near the norm overall but had grown fast over the prior decade. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, accounting for 75.7 percent of all originations among lenders active in the district.

Kelly Morrison.p1: Poverty here is rarer than in almost any comparable district, at 5.9 percent, alongside unemployment that stays low too. Median household income reaches 106,557 dollars, well ahead of what most districts see, in a place of 710,658 people. Homes carry a median value of 423,800 dollars, about four times median income, while rent runs modest as a share of that income. Homeownership is common here, well above the norm, in a district denser than most.
Kelly Morrison.p2: Credit union offices here outpace credit union jobs, an unusual split worth noting up front. Offices hold 24.5 percent of retail branches, a larger share than most peer districts carry, while credit union employment sits at just 0.39 times the national norm. ENT, TrustOne Financial, and TopLine Financial anchor that branch footprint. Wells Fargo Bank, National Association books a leading deposit sum among the district's numerous bank branches, a figure that owes more to federal booking rules than to actual local reach, and credit unions here work against a well-employed, low-poverty population with more branch presence than staff behind it.
Kelly Morrison.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance jobs ran well above the national norm, and management of companies and wholesale trade specialized further still, marks of a district built around back-office and distribution work rather than storefronts. Health care and manufacturing employed large numbers alongside that finance base. Mortgage lending here leaned heavily toward home purchases, across all lenders active in the district.

Ken Calvert.p1: Household income in this district clears $101,842, well above most comparable districts, and that gap shapes everything that follows. Home values, at $653,500, and rent, at $2,122 a month, sit well above what most peer districts show, though homeownership runs unusually high at 74.5 percent and poverty stays uncommonly low. Joblessness edges past most similar districts, in a place more crowded than most.
Ken Calvert.p2: Credit unions here include Navy Federal Credit Union and Altura, holding 17.9 percent of retail offices between them, a thinner slice than most comparable districts show against their banks. Branch banks still outnumber them by a wide margin, and JPMorgan Chase books more deposits here than any other bank, a figure driven by where deposits get recorded rather than where branches actually stand. Credit union employment runs below the national norm, moving in step with how many offices they keep rather than pulling ahead or falling behind. Given the income and housing costs above, that leaves member-owned lenders a modest footprint to work with.
Ken Calvert.p3: As of 2023, work here leaned heavily on construction, running well beyond typical levels elsewhere, alongside arts, entertainment, and recreation and accommodation and food services. Health care and social assistance accounted for a sizable slice of jobs too, close to the national norm. Overall finance and insurance employment ran well below the national norm, and its growth over the prior decade lagged the country as a whole.

Kevin Cramer.p1: North Dakota spreads barely anyone across its land, one of the emptiest settlement patterns of any state, and unemployment sits at a mere 1.9 percent. Household income lands in ordinary territory next to other states, but housing has not caught up: a home value of $266,100 against typical earnings works out to a ratio of 3.4, cheap by comparison with most of the country. Homeownership is still lower than nearly everywhere else, an odd pairing with such affordable housing.
Kevin Cramer.p2: Credit unions hold 23.4 percent of retail offices here, unremarkable next to other states, but their office presence still runs at 1.64 times the national norm, well into specialized territory, while the jobs they support sit only slightly above that same norm. First Community, Capital, and Town and Country carry that presence locally, competing for deposits against Bell Bank, the largest institution here by that measure among a deep field of bank branches statewide. Offices have multiplied here faster than staff has. In a labor market this tight, a steady workforce is worth something.
Kevin Cramer.p3: The job base leaned hardest on extraction: Mining, Quarrying, and Oil and Gas Extraction ran at over eleven times the national norm, the most distinctive sector in the state. Agriculture and utilities also punched above their weight, both drawing more workers than the nation typically assigns them. Health care and retail carried the largest share of employment day to day. This was, in 2023, an economy still built on what comes out of the ground.

Kevin Hern.p1: This district packs more people into each square mile than most comparable seats, a settlement pattern that sets it apart more than any other single fact here. Around 827,396 people live here, with a median age of 37.1. Household income sits at $71,143, trailing most peer districts, and home values lag national peers as well. Poverty runs higher here than in most districts measured.
Kevin Hern.p2: Credit unions here carry more weight in branch presence than in payroll: offices run at 1.29 times the national norm, while credit union employment sits only slightly above norm at 1.16. TTCU, WESTREET, and Oklahoma Central anchor that presence, holding 26.3 percent of retail offices, a share above most peer districts. BOKF, National Association books the most deposits by address here, one bank among a crowded field of others with branches across the district. That imbalance leaves a dense branch network serving a payroll base that has grown more slowly.
Kevin Hern.p3: Oklahoma's 1st district ran on jobs measured in 2023, built on a base that leaned unusually hard into oil and gas extraction, running at more than twice the national norm. Manufacturing also ran well above the norm, forming a solid share of the job base alongside health care and retail trade. Overall finance employment sat slightly below the national norm, and growth in finance and insurance together trailed the country across the prior decade. Home purchases dominated the district's mortgage originations.

Kevin Kiley.p1: This district spreads its people thinly, among the lowest counts of any comparable district in the country. Households here earn well into six figures, a median of 107,122 dollars, and homeownership runs high at 74.2 percent. Housing costs a great deal by comparison, with a home value to income ratio of 6.2. Poverty runs low, even as unemployment sits somewhat elevated.
Kevin Kiley.p2: Credit union jobs here run ahead of credit union office presence, a divergence worth noting: employment in the sector sits close to the national norm, while office presence trails further behind. SAFE, The Golden 1, and a credit union serving public employees anchor that side of the market against a wide field of bank branches, including the bank with the most deposits booked locally, though far from the only one competing here. Credit unions hold 21.2 percent of retail offices, a share that puts them on comparable footing with peer districts.
Kevin Kiley.p3: This district's economy leans hard into arts, entertainment, and recreation, running well above the national norm in concentration. Construction and real estate also cluster more heavily here than is typical elsewhere. Health care, retail, and accommodation and food services employ the most people, each running a bit above national norms. Overall finance sector employment trails the national norm, a gap that has persisted through the years measured.

Kevin Mullin.p1: Few places in the country pack as many people into a square mile as this one does. That crowding shapes everything else here: households bring home some of the highest incomes measured anywhere, and only a small share live in poverty. Home values and rent climb just as high, though, and homeownership trails most other districts. Unemployment sits at an ordinary level. Dense living here comes with a steep price attached.
Kevin Mullin.p2: Credit unions here include Monterra, Provident, and Patelco, and together with the rest they hold 22.0 percent of retail offices, a middling share against comparable districts. Credit union employment runs below the national norm, and the thinness of their office footprint matches it closely. Against 133 bank branches, including Bank of America's locally booked deposits, credit unions work a modest slice of a market otherwise crowded with bank competitors, serving the same high-earning, high-cost households described above.
Kevin Mullin.p3: As of 2023, Information and Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services stood far above the national norm and anchored what people here did for work. Transportation and Warehousing showed a similar, smaller lean beyond the national pattern. Health Care and Social Assistance made up a large slice of employment on its own, without being unusually concentrated. Finance and insurance jobs sat modestly below the national norm but expanded faster than the country as a whole over the following decade. Specialized, high-skill work defines this district far more than broad or routine employment does.

Kim Schrier.p1: This district clears $130,695 in median household income, among the highest of any congressional seat in the country. Home values run high too, at $726,100, though owning is far more common than renting, with 79.2 percent of households holding title. Poverty and unemployment both sit low, the latter at 4.1 percent. Fewer than a hundred people live on each square mile, marking a district of settled, spread-out prosperity rather than a dense urban core.
Kim Schrier.p2: Boeing Employees, First Technology, and Washington State Employees are the credit unions with a foothold here, though credit unions altogether hold only 20.7 percent of retail offices, a slimmer cut than most comparable districts see. Credit union employment runs a bit under the national norm, tracking closely with that thin office presence. Under federal reporting rules, Bank of America's booked deposits here outweigh any other bank's, though that reflects where deposits are recorded more than local branch strength. High earners and homeowners like these are exactly the customer base a credit union wants more of.
Kim Schrier.p3: As measured in 2023, the district's roughly 169,500 jobs concentrated hardest in agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting, and in management of companies and enterprises, both far above the national norm. Health care, retail, and educational services employed the most people, without any unusual concentration. Overall finance employment ran below the national norm even so. Finance and insurance jobs together, however, grew faster here than nationally over the prior decade.

Kirsten Gillibrand.p1: New York packs 19.9 million people into a state that runs far denser than most, with work concentrated in finance, information, and health care rather than spread evenly across the map. Median household income sits above most states at 85,820 dollars, but that cushion meets a housing market to match: home values run to 449,800 dollars against income at a ratio well above the norm. Homeownership and poverty both sit at levels that set New York apart from most of the country.
Kirsten Gillibrand.p2: Credit unions hold just 21.5 percent of retail offices here, a modest share next to the reach banks maintain across the state. Fourleaf, United Nations, and Broadview carry the credit union presence into a market where JPMorgan Chase leads on deposits booked locally, though that figure reflects reporting rules more than local customers or actual presence. Credit union employment runs below the national norm here, a state where the income and housing costs described above give any credit union a demanding field to work in.
Kirsten Gillibrand.p3: Beyond banking, the 2023 employment picture showed a state built on finance and insurance, information, and real estate at rates well above national norms, alongside outsized health care and educational services sectors that anchor most of the job base. Finance and insurance alone accounted for 6.1 percent of the state's 8,557,100 jobs, underscoring an economy tilted toward high-value, specialized work rather than volume employment.

Kristen McDonald Rivet.p1: Home values in this district sit near the bottom of the national range, a median of $187,100, and that low ceiling colors the rest of the picture. Household income runs well under what most comparable districts see, yet 73.6 percent of households still own their homes, a rate that outpaces most peers. Rent stays modest against that income. Both poverty and joblessness climb well past what most other districts report, a strain that sits under the cheap housing rather than beside it.
Kristen McDonald Rivet.p2: Credit unions hold 55.5 percent of retail offices here, a share far ahead of banks on pure presence and higher than nearly anywhere else measured, even though Huntington National Bank, drawing on deposits booked to this geography under federal rules, still shows the largest deposit figure on paper. DOW, ELGA, and Financial Plus anchor the credit union side locally. Credit union employment runs at 3.62 times the national norm, offices at 3.36 times, both rated highly specialized, a workforce built for the modest-income, high-ownership households described above.
Kristen McDonald Rivet.p3: The industry mix, as measured in 2021, leaned on health care and social assistance, manufacturing, and retail trade, each employing well above the national norm for its sector. Total employment stood near 253,000 jobs. General finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm even as credit union work ran far above it, a split that marks this district's financial sector as unusually credit union heavy. Home purchase lending accounted for most mortgage originations that year.

Kweisi Mfume.p1: People are packed into this district more tightly than in nearly any other in the country, a crowded corner of Maryland where household income lands at $66,738, thin compared with most congressional districts. Housing runs cheaper than typical, with a median home value of $254,400, yet cost still bites: rent and home prices sit heavier against local pay than in most places. Homeownership trails most districts of this kind, and the poverty rate climbs well past the norm.
Kweisi Mfume.p2: Credit union employment here runs thinner than the office network would imply, at 0.56 times the national norm against an office presence at 0.67, meaning these institutions keep more branches open per worker than is typical elsewhere. Municipal Employees Credit Union of Baltimore, Johns Hopkins, and State Employees Credit Union of Maryland anchor that presence, though credit unions hold only 18.9 percent of retail offices, a thinner claim on the market than most comparable districts post against their local banks. With income and homeownership already stretched thin, that smaller footprint leaves fewer local alternatives to the banks that otherwise fill the gap.
Kweisi Mfume.p3: The job mix that 2023 data captured leaned heavily on government work, with Public Administration employing at 2.75 times the national norm, this district's most specialized sector by far. Transportation and Warehousing and Utilities also ran well above typical concentration. Overall finance-sector employment ran below the norm, and its growth over the prior decade lagged the nation as well.

LaMonica McIver.p1: This district holds one of the tightest concentrations of people found in any congressional seat, and that density sets the terms for nearly everything below. Roughly 800,200 residents live here with a median household income of $76,594, about average next to other districts. Housing costs run well above most peers, with homes valued far beyond what that income would comfortably support. Few residents own the place they live in, and joblessness and poverty both climb higher than in most comparable districts.
LaMonica McIver.p2: Credit union employment here runs thin against the national norm, even as credit union offices, still a minority presence, hold up better against that same measure, an imbalance worth flagging first. AMERICAN AIRLINES, THE ATLANTIC, and NORTH JERSEY credit unions anchor that presence against a field of bank branches, with Wells Fargo booking the largest deposit sum under federal reporting rules, not necessarily the deepest local footprint. Credit unions hold just 19.0 percent of retail offices, leaving banks the dominant channel for the renters and lower-income borrowers who fill this district.
LaMonica McIver.p3: The district's economy leaned hard on Transportation and Warehousing, employing workers at 2.78 times the national norm, its clearest specialty. Educational Services and Public Administration followed as secondary strengths, rounding out a base built on moving goods, teaching, and government work. Mortgage lending skewed toward home purchases, and lower-income neighborhoods drew a strong share of all originations.

Lance Gooden.p1: Housing here costs more relative to income than almost anywhere comparable, even though the dollar figures underneath are modest. A home runs about 3.9 times the typical household income, and rent claims a sizable slice of the paycheck too. Most residents own rather than rent, at a rate few other districts match. Median household income sits at $75,301, and joblessness sits somewhat above the wider pattern.
Lance Gooden.p2: Credit union employment here runs thinner than the office network alone would explain, an unusual split worth noting before anything else. Navy Federal, Randolph-Brooks, and Neighborhood credit union carry the local presence, holding 18.5 percent of retail offices, a thinner cut of the market than in most peer districts, against a bank sector led on deposits by The American National Bank of Texas. That name reflects deposits booked to an address here, not an absence of local competitors. Either way, these institutions work with the same stretched housing math and moderate incomes described above.
Lance Gooden.p3: As of 2023, retail trade anchored the job base, employing 16.4 percent of workers, well above the national pattern. Construction and utilities were the other strong points, filling out an economy weighted toward building and selling rather than offices. Total employment stood near 172,000. Home purchases dominated local lending, accounting for 75.0 percent of originations, while only a modest slice reached lower income neighborhoods.

Lateefah Simon.p1: This district packs people in tightly, among the densest of any congressional seat, and the numbers around it fit that pattern. Households earn a median $111,408, comfortably ahead of most districts, but housing costs run even further ahead, with a typical home valued at $992,700 against rent near $2,129 a month. Homeownership is uncommon here compared with most districts, and unemployment runs noticeably higher than most peers.
Lateefah Simon.p2: Credit unions hold just 14.7 percent of retail offices here, well below most comparable districts, leaving Wells Fargo Bank as the largest deposit holder among 118 bank branches citywide, alongside credit union names like Patelco, 1st United, and The Golden 1. Credit union employment runs below the national norm, tracking office presence closely rather than outpacing it. For a district with high earners and higher costs, that thin footprint means credit unions compete for a smaller slice of a market banks currently dominate.
Lateefah Simon.p3: As of 2023, the district's work leaned hard into utilities, a highly specialized sector here, alongside strong footholds in professional and technical services and in transportation and warehousing. Health care and professional services carried an outsized share of the job mix, each running above the national norm for its field. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, with roughly a third going to lower-income neighborhoods.

Laura Friedman.p1: Housing here sells for 13.1 times what a typical household earns, a multiple that puts this district near the top of anything measured nationwide, and that single fact shapes everything else about the place. Median household income, at $89,846, runs comfortably ahead of most peer districts, yet homeownership stays rare, well below what most other districts see. Rent alone eats close to three tenths of a typical income. The area is densely built, and finding work takes longer here than it does across most of the country.
Laura Friedman.p2: Credit union jobs here sit closer to the national norm than credit union offices do, a gap worth noting since the two usually move together: employment in the sector holds up even where physical presence thins out. First Entertainment and Partners anchor that presence locally. Together, credit unions hold 27.5 percent of retail offices measured against banks, a bigger foothold than most comparable districts show. A major national bank leads locally on deposits booked here, though that mainly reflects where deposits get recorded rather than any absence of local competition.
Laura Friedman.p3: Work here concentrated hard in Information, which held 28.3 percent of jobs, a level of specialization far beyond almost anywhere else measured. Health care followed as the next largest source of work, well above the national norm in its own right. Overall finance employment ran below what the national mix would predict. Home purchases made up 45.0 percent of all mortgage lending, with a much smaller share of loans reaching lower-income neighborhoods.

Laura Gillen.p1: People here live stacked close together, among the most densely settled districts anywhere, and that crowding coexists with real affluence. Households earn a median $137,724 a year, near the top of all districts, and very few live in poverty. Home values reach $663,600, but the ratio of that value to income and rent's share of income both sit below what most districts see, and homeownership runs unusually high. Unemployment is unremarkable.
Laura Gillen.p2: Credit union jobs here run close to the national norm even though credit union offices are thinner on the ground, a gap that points to leaner branch networks doing more per worker. Fourleaf, Jovia Financial, and Teachers carry the credit union name locally. Credit unions hold 21.1 percent of retail offices, a middling share, against a much larger stock of bank branches, the most deposit-heavy of them booked to JPMorgan Chase. For a district this affluent and this densely peopled, that leaner footprint means covering a lot of household wealth with fewer doors.
Laura Gillen.p3: The job market in 2023 leaned heavily on public administration and other services, both well above the national norm. Retail trade carried unusual weight too. Finance and insurance jobs sat slightly below the national norm, and their pace of hiring over the prior decade fell short of the country's. Home buying rather than refinancing dominated mortgage activity, making up 52.6 percent of originations, and a much smaller slice of loans went to neighborhoods with lower incomes.

Laurel Lee.p1: A home in the 15th district of Florida runs roughly five times what a household there typically brings in, and rent alone claims close to three tenths of that pay, a housing burden among the highest of any congressional seat. Median household income sits at 72,384 dollars, trailing most comparable districts. Most households still own rather than rent, though at a rate lower than typical. The district is also more crowded, on a per-mile basis, than most of its peers.
Laurel Lee.p2: Credit unions here hold 34.6 percent of the retail branch market, a share far beyond what most districts see, with Suncoast, Navy Federal Credit Union, and MidFlorida all present in that mix. Bank of America comes out ahead on deposits, but federal rules book deposits to a single address rather than counting branches or local customers. Credit union employment runs at 1.6 times the national norm, well ahead of what office counts alone carry. That is a workforce doing more per address, in a district where income is tight and housing eats deep into it.
Laurel Lee.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance jobs ran at 1.89 times the national norm here, and management of companies ran even higher, at 2.04 times, the most specialized sector the district has. Transportation and warehousing added a third point of strength. Lending data from all lenders show home purchases made up 65.5 percent of mortgage activity that year.

Lauren Boebert.p1: Fewer than 25 people share each square mile of the 4th congressional district of Colorado, land so open it has few equals among comparable seats. The people who live here bring home a median $120,070, well clear of the typical district, and most sit in houses they own rather than rent. Homes carry a steep median price, $629,100, though what people pay monthly for housing stays modest by comparison, and joblessness and poverty are each rare here.
Lauren Boebert.p2: Credit union jobs here run well above what the national norm would predict, yet credit union offices sit slightly under that same norm, and the distance between those two figures says something this district's own numbers do not usually show. ENT, Bellco and Canvas anchor that presence, competing for deposits against 188 bank branches credited on paper to Wells Fargo, a name that tops the list only because of federal rules on where a bank's deposits get recorded. Credit unions hold 23.5 percent of retail offices here, an ordinary share for a district with well-off, spread-out borrowers to serve.
Lauren Boebert.p3: By 2023, farming, forestry, fishing and hunting had grown into the district's most disproportionate sector, nearly three times the national norm, alongside specialized construction and mining work. Finance and insurance jobs overall ran well above the national norm too. Total employment stood near 241,300, built on a mix of resource work and open land that few comparable districts share.

Lauren Underwood.p1: Housing is inexpensive relative to local pay: the median home equals about 3.1 times median household income, placing that ratio near the low end for districts. Households bring in a median of 98,492 dollars a year, comfortably ahead of the ordinary district, and owner occupancy is widespread. Poverty is low, while joblessness is slightly elevated beside peers. The settlement pattern is open rather than densely urban.
Lauren Underwood.p2: Credit unions operate just 15.2 percent of retail offices here, leaving a modest position beside banks. Financial Plus, Earthmover, and GreenState provide the main credit union names. Old National Bank has the leading locally assigned deposits, but numerous banks compete across the district. Credit union staffing is far less concentrated than the national norm, while office concentration sits somewhat closer to that baseline. The network therefore carries more physical reach than staffing weight for households with relatively high incomes and common homeownership.
Lauren Underwood.p3: The district's economy leans hard on transportation and warehousing, more than twice the national norm and its most specialized sector by far. Overall finance employment runs well under the national norm too. Across all lenders, home purchase loans made up 58.9 percent of mortgage activity. This is a logistics and distribution economy first, built around moving goods rather than moving money.

Linda Sánchez.p1: Home values in this district sit at $822,000, among the highest anywhere in the state, and that gap between price and paycheck defines the place. Median household income of $101,415 clears most other districts by a wide margin, yet the home value to income ratio of 8.1 shows how far local pay still trails local property costs. Rent runs $2,112 a month, a heavy load even against this area's strong incomes. Density here is high, describing a workforce that is comfortable but priced tightly into its own market.
Linda Sánchez.p2: Credit union employment here is thin against the national norm, yet office presence is thinner still, so the credit unions on the ground carry more staff than their branch footprint would imply. One large cooperative anchors that presence, alongside F & A and Credit Union of Southern CA, though credit unions hold only 16.2 percent of retail offices, a smaller cut of the market than in comparable places, against a market led on deposits by Bank of America. For a credit union working this seat, that means fewer doors but relatively fuller ones, serving high earners carrying some of the steepest housing ratios around.
Linda Sánchez.p3: As of 2023, the district's job mix leaned heavily on wholesale trade, which ran at nearly three times the national norm, alongside strength in transportation and warehousing and in administrative and support services. Overall finance employment stayed well below the national norm here. This is a district built on moving and distributing goods rather than on finance itself.

Lindsey Graham.p1: South Carolina holds 5,478,831 people, with a median age of 40.7 and a population density that outpaces most states. Median household income comes in at 72,350 dollars, below most of the country, while homeownership runs high at 72.3 percent. Poverty, though, is more common here than in most other states, so a place where owning a home is the norm still leaves less cushion underneath renters and lower earners.
Lindsey Graham.p2: Navy Federal, Founders, and South Carolina credit unions anchor a sector that holds 24.5 percent of retail offices statewide, a bigger footprint than most states give their credit unions against banks. Bank of America carries the top deposit total on paper, a figure tied to where deposits get booked rather than where branches actually sit among the state's many local rivals. Credit union employment and office presence both run above the national norm, with offices out front, a network built for reach into the income and housing patterns just described.
Lindsey Graham.p3: As measured in 2023, manufacturing stood out, employing well above the national norm and outpacing every other sector for concentration, with utilities also running specialized. Health care employed the most people overall, though at a lighter concentration than manufacturing carried. Overall finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm even as the sector's job growth outpaced it. This was a state built on making things, with credit unions filling a retail banking role wider than their workforce alone.

Lisa Blunt Rochester.p1: Delaware's economy sits unusually close to finance, with health care and retail trade rounding out the biggest sectors of work. Households here earn more than in most states, at a median $87,534, and homeownership is high at 73.8 percent. Housing carries a premium to match, with a median home value of $371,600. At 539.8 people per square mile, this is a densely settled state, not a rural one.
Lisa Blunt Rochester.p2: Credit unions hold just 20.6 percent of retail offices here, a smaller share than in most states, leaving banks the dominant channel even in a state this tied to finance work. DEL-ONE, Dover, and Tidemark carry the credit union side against a field led on paper by Capital One, National Association, whose deposit figures reflect booking rules more than branch presence among the state's 247 bank branches. Credit union employment runs well below the national norm even though offices run closer to it, so each office here carries a lighter staff than the office count alone implies.
Lisa Blunt Rochester.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance stood out as the state's most specialized sector by a wide margin, with retail trade and transportation and warehousing also running slightly ahead of the country. Finance and insurance growth, taken together with insurance, kept roughly level with the national rate over the decade to 2023. What sets Delaware apart is not scale but concentration: a small, densely populated state where financial work carries far more weight than its size would imply.

Lisa McClain.p1: Home values in this district run to about 3.4 times the median household income of 87,017 dollars, among the lowest ratios measured anywhere. Rent averages roughly 1,076 dollars a month, a modest draw on typical earnings. Owning outpaces renting by a wide margin here, and neither poverty nor joblessness troubles many residents. The land itself sits sparsely settled, far less crowded than most districts on the map.
Lisa McClain.p2: Credit union employment runs only a little above the national norm, but credit union offices are specialized well beyond it, a branch presence built wider than its staffing. Genisys, Frankenmuth, and Advia anchor that network, holding 26.7 percent of retail offices against banks, a share topping most comparable districts, even as Huntington National Bank claims the largest deposit total in a market it shares with many other lenders. For a credit union working here, the footprint is already broad; the opportunity is the people and the modest housing costs described above.
Lisa McClain.p3: Manufacturing carried the job base in 2021, accounting for 19.7 percent of workers and running well above the national norm, by far the most concentrated sector in the district. Retail trade followed some distance behind, itself well above the national norm. Finance and insurance jobs overall ran below the national norm that year, even as credit unions bucked the trend. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, making up 47.9 percent of originations across all lenders.

Lisa Murkowski.p1: Alaska spreads about 740,000 people across barely more than one person per square mile, about as sparsely settled as any state gets. Median household income runs high, at 95,665 dollars, and typical housing costs stay easy on that income, with homes valued well below what such earnings would demand elsewhere. Unemployment sits among the highest of any state, a sign the labor market does not clear as easily as the income numbers imply. Homeownership trails the national picture, even with prices this manageable.
Lisa Murkowski.p2: Credit unions hold 40.5 percent of retail offices in the state, a level most states never approach, in a market where many banks compete for the rest rather than one name owning it. Global, Credit Union 1, and Nuvision anchor that presence. Credit union employment runs at 3.33 times the national norm, well ahead of the growth in office count, meaning these institutions operate leaner branches staffed more heavily than the norm elsewhere. That is an unusually deep credit union bench for a state this thinly populated.
Lisa Murkowski.p3: In 2016, public administration weighed heavily in the mix, alongside oil and gas extraction and the transportation and warehousing work needed to move it. Health care was the largest single source of jobs that year. Finance and insurance employment lagged the rest of the country by a wide margin even then, so credit unions did more of the work that banks might otherwise carry.

Lizzie Fletcher.p1: This district packs people in tightly, denser underfoot than almost any other congressional seat measured, with 770,214 residents living close together rather than spread across open land. Income runs modest at a median of $75,245, while home values climb far higher, a gap that shows up when you set one against the other: 5.3 times median earnings. Homeownership is rare here, and poverty runs deeper than comparable districts tend to see.
Lizzie Fletcher.p2: Credit union offices here actually outpace credit union jobs, an unusual split: employment in the sector sits at 0.65 times the national norm while office presence, though still thinner than most comparable districts, runs higher at 0.79 times that norm. Texas Dow Employees, First Community, and First Service anchor the local credit union presence, holding 18.6 percent of retail offices, while JPMorgan Chase books the largest deposit sum among many local bank branches here. For an economy with this much low-income and rental housing, that thin staffing means credit unions are stretched to serve a base that needs them.
Lizzie Fletcher.p3: Oil and gas extraction dominated the job base measured in 2023, running over five times the national norm, alongside a sizeable cluster of work in professional and technical services. Finance and insurance jobs also gathered here well beyond typical levels, growing at roughly the national pace. Home purchases drove most mortgage activity, and only a slim portion of that lending reached poorer neighborhoods.

Lloyd Doggett.p1: Homeownership in the 37th district is among the lowest of any congressional district, even though this is not a poor place. Median household income runs to 93,776 dollars, and unemployment sits at 3.7 percent, both stronger than most comparable districts. The median home, though, is valued at 630,300 dollars, 6.7 times that income. This is a crowded, well-paid district where owning a home is the exception rather than the rule.
Lloyd Doggett.p2: Credit union employment here runs slightly above the national norm while credit union offices sit below it, a split worth noting before anything else about the sector. Randolph-Brooks and A+ are among the names doing that work, holding 27.9 percent of retail offices, a strong share for a district where branches otherwise lag behind staffing. One large bank books a sizable deposit share among many local competitors under federal reporting rules that do not reflect branch presence. Credit unions here carry more of the local workforce than their office count alone would show an outsider.
Lloyd Doggett.p3: This district's economy ran on Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services, employing 15.9 percent of its jobs, alongside a highly specialized Information sector. Finance and insurance jobs overall stood above the national norm, with the sector growing faster than the country's from 2013 to 2023. Home purchase loans made up most mortgage originations recorded here. This is a district built on skilled, specialized work, not on cheap housing.

Lloyd Smucker.p1: A poverty rate of 7.6 percent sets this district apart from comparable ones, and it comes with low unemployment. Median household income runs to 85,402 dollars, well above most peers, and housing costs sit lower relative to income than in most districts. Homeownership is high here. People in this district tend to work steadily and own the roof over their heads.
Lloyd Smucker.p2: Credit union offices claim more ground than credit union jobs do, and that gap belongs at the front of the story: employment in the industry runs to just 0.39 times the national norm, even as office presence holds close to typical levels. Members 1st, Pennsylvania State Employees, and Citadel anchor that office presence, which accounts for 22.0 percent of retail offices against banks. Fulton Bank, National Association leads all institutions on deposits booked to addresses here, though the district holds many separate competitors among its bank branches. Given the income and homeownership described above, credit unions in this district carry more real estate than payroll.
Lloyd Smucker.p3: Manufacturing anchors the local economy, employing 16.2 percent of workers at 1.84 times the national norm, a genuine specialization. Construction and agriculture also run well above national norms, rounding out an economy built on making and building things. Health care and retail trade employ the most people day to day. As of 2023, this was a district defined less by finance than by production.

Lois Frankel.p1: Housing here costs far more than local paychecks can comfortably cover, with home values running 5.7 times median household income, a burden matched by few other districts nationwide. Rent alone claims 30.2 percent of what a typical household brings home. Homeownership still runs strong, at 71.1 percent, in a place packed tightly together at over 3,200 people per square mile. Joblessness runs above the mark set by most peer districts.
Lois Frankel.p2: Credit unions hold just 6.4 percent of retail offices here, one of the smallest shares of any district. Navy Federal Credit Union, Dort Financial, and iTHINK Financial are the names doing that work, up against JPMorgan Chase, the largest bank by the deposits attributed to it here. Credit union staffing matches that thin office presence closely, both well below the national norm. For a district this expensive, credit unions operate from a narrow footing against a much bigger banking presence.
Lois Frankel.p3: In 2023, jobs in arts, entertainment, and recreation, in public administration, and in agriculture each claimed a far larger share here than the national pattern would predict. Health care and hospitality carried much of the remaining job base, with accommodation and food service work well above the national norm given the area's draw for visitors. Finance-sector employment overall stayed below norm even as finance and insurance jobs, taken together, grew faster than the national pace over the prior decade. Mortgage lending skewed heavily toward home purchases, at 57.3 percent of originations.

Lori Trahan.p1: No single number tells you more about the 3rd district than household income, at $98,501, running well above the norm for comparable districts. Home values are high as well, while homeownership trails most similar places, with just 61.8 percent of households owning rather than renting. The district is dense for its region, and unemployment runs a bit elevated even as poverty stays low. This is a place with real income but fewer owners than the paycheck would imply.
Lori Trahan.p2: Credit unions hold 34.2 percent of retail office share here, a figure that stands well above most comparable districts. First Technology, Workers, and Jeanne D'Arc carry that presence, competing against 137 bank branches held by many separate banks. Credit union jobs and office counts each edge past the national norm, though branch growth has outpaced hiring. For a lender here, credit unions already hold real ground at the retail counter.
Lori Trahan.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing led the specialized economy, employing 15.4 percent of workers, a concentration well beyond the typical national rate and unusual for this region. Health care and social assistance employed a substantial share of workers too. Overall finance and insurance employment ran well below the national norm, a smaller footprint than the credit union figures alone would imply. Mortgage lending across all lenders leaned toward home purchases over refinancing.

Lucy McBath.p1: People are packed into this district more tightly than in most congressional seats, a dense corner of Georgia built around working households rather than open land. The typical household earns 90,929 dollars, comfortably ahead of most districts, and median age sits at 36.4. A home here typically costs 4.2 times the median income, and rent runs 1,784 dollars a month, a cost burden above most peers even as homeownership trails behind most districts.
Lucy McBath.p2: Credit unions in this district employ people at a rate nearer the national norm than their office count would predict, worth flagging up front. Navy Federal, Delta Community, and LGE Community anchor that presence, though credit unions hold just 16.0 percent of retail offices, against 151 bank branches competing for the same customers. Truist books the largest bank deposits in the district, a function of where deposits land on paper rather than branch dominance. For a credit union, that means a dense, well-paid population still mostly banking elsewhere.
Lucy McBath.p3: As of 2023, the district leaned on Information and Transportation and Warehousing, both running well above national norms alongside Management of Companies and Enterprises. Transportation and Warehousing also carried real weight in overall employment, next to Health Care and Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services. Finance and insurance jobs overall ran above the national norm and had grown faster than the country over the prior decade. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, a majority of all originations.

Luis Correa.p1: This district packs people in tightly, among the most densely settled seats in the country, and that crowding shapes everything else here. Households earn a median of $90,685, well ahead of typical districts, but housing eats hard into that: a median home value of $806,700 runs 8.9 times the typical income, and rent claims 29.5 percent of it. Homeownership here is rare, well below what most comparable districts see.
Luis Correa.p2: Credit union employment here runs close to the national norm even as their physical footprint stays well below it, a gap worth noticing before anything else about the sector. Among the largest names locally are one serving educators, one tied to Orange County, and Partners, together holding 27.6 percent of retail offices against area banks, a share above most peer districts despite the thin branch presence. A single trust bank leads locally by the deposit figures federal reporting assigns to this district, one name among 74 bank branches run by many separate competitors. For the renters described above, that mix of high office share but leaner staffing marks where a credit union's reach actually sits.
Luis Correa.p3: As of 2023, the district's work leaned hard into administrative, support, and waste management services, far above the national norm, alongside public administration and accommodation and food services, both well above typical levels. Health care and social assistance employed the largest share of workers but at a level slightly below the national norm. Mortgage lending here leaned toward home purchases, and most originations reached lower-income neighborhoods.

Luz Rivas.p1: Few congressional seats hold people as close together as this one does, a density among the highest of any district in the country. Households earn $76,888 a year, yet housing runs among the most expensive anywhere, with a home value to income ratio of 10.0 and rent near $1,904 a month. Homeownership here sits at an unusually low share. Work leans toward health care, construction, and real estate, the trades that keep a crowded place running.
Luz Rivas.p2: Credit unions in this district carry more weight in jobs than in storefronts: employment runs thin against the national norm, but office presence runs thinner still, leaving jobs ahead of the branch share. LOGIX, Los Angeles Police, and GAIN hold that ground, together claiming 22.1 percent of retail offices, while JPMorgan Chase is named the largest bank here among many local rivals. For a district full of renters and workers stretched thin by housing costs, that gives credit unions a real but modest hand in local finance.
Luz Rivas.p3: Finance overall is a small slice of this economy, well below the national norm, though finance and insurance together grew faster here than nationally. As measured in 2023, the district's strength lay in health care and social assistance, which ran far above typical levels, alongside a construction sector well above the norm too. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, 42.9 percent of originations. This is a place built on caregiving and building, not finance.

Madeleine Dean.p1: Only 6.6 percent of residents in this district live below the poverty line, a level among the lowest of any district in the country, and it comes paired with strong incomes, low unemployment, and homeownership at 73.0 percent. Median household income reaches $108,414. Housing carries a premium, with home values well above income by the usual measure, though rent takes a modest bite out of that income by comparison. This is a dense, comfortably established corner of the Northeast.
Madeleine Dean.p2: Credit union employment here runs far below the national norm even though credit union offices are slightly more common than typical, a gap worth noting up front. Credit unions hold only 19.7 percent of retail offices here, leaving the deposit lead to Wells Fargo, whose booked deposits outpace a broad field of competing bank branches across the district. Citadel, TruMark Financial, and American Heritage carry the credit union side locally. Given the earnings and housing stability described above, that's a modest base for member relationships to grow from.
Madeleine Dean.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance stood out as this district's most specialized sector, employing well above the national norm, alongside management of companies and professional and technical services. Health care and social assistance was a leading employer, followed closely by professional services and manufacturing. Mortgage lending skewed heavily toward home purchases, with a much smaller share going to lower-income neighborhoods. This is a district built on finance and professional work, not on light industry or hourly retail.

Maggie Goodlander.p1: Unemployment here sits at just 3.0 percent, among the lowest recorded anywhere, a tightness in the labor market that runs through every other figure below. Households earn a median of 97,020 dollars a year, poverty is rare, and homeownership is common at 73.2 percent. A typical home is valued at 430,000 dollars, yet that price stays modest measured against what people here actually earn.
