People are steadily employed and comfortably housed, scattered thinly across mostly open, low-density territory.
Maggie Goodlander.p2: Credit union offices here outrun credit union jobs: office presence runs specialized against the national norm while staffing stays only slightly above it, a branch network that looks thicker than its payroll. SERVICE, First Technology, and St. Mary's Bank anchor that presence, holding 22.4 percent of retail offices between them, set against many separate banks chasing the same deposits, TD Bank chief among them by booked deposits alone. That is the base of income and housing wealth described above, the raw material any credit union here works with.
Maggie Goodlander.p3: As measured in 2023, manufacturing and retail trade both stood out as specialized sectors, and public administration reflected the pull of state government. Health care employed the most people of any single sector, while finance and insurance jobs overall stayed thin against the national norm. Mortgage lending that year leaned heavily toward home purchases, which accounted for 48.0 percent of all originations. This remains an economy built on making, selling, and caring for people rather than on finance itself.

Marc Veasey.p1: Housing costs press hard against what people here actually earn. The median household brings in $66,107 a year, thin by district standards, while rent runs high enough against income to sit among the heaviest such burdens found anywhere in the comparison set. Few households here own their homes, and hardship runs well past what most districts see, in a fast-growing, densely packed corner of Texas.
Marc Veasey.p2: Credit union offices here outpace credit union jobs, and that gap deserves the first word: local credit union employment sits far below the national norm, at 0.47 times, even though offices come closer to normal at 0.7 times. American Airlines, Pentagon, and EECU are the names carrying that presence. Credit unions hold just 19.8 percent of retail offices here, and JPMorgan Chase, the top bank by deposits booked locally, sits among many other bank branches active in the district.
Marc Veasey.p3: The working economy here, measured in 2023, ran on moving and storing goods. Wholesale trade was highly specialized at 2.53 times the national norm, and transportation and warehousing followed close behind. Manufacturing and administrative support services rounded out the strongest sectors, across a large local job base. Mortgage lending that year skewed heavily toward home purchases, and most of it went to lower-income neighborhoods, territory any credit union here should recognize as its own.

Marcy Kaptur.p1: A home in this district is valued at just 2.9 times the median household income, one of the lowest ratios anywhere in the country. Income itself runs modest, a median of $66,802, and the poverty rate climbs above what most other districts show. Homeownership sits at an unremarkable 68.6 percent. Pay is limited, but shelter has stayed cheap enough to match it.
Marcy Kaptur.p2: Credit union employment here sits close to the national norm, yet credit union offices run at nearly double it, and that gap is worth opening on: office presence has outpaced the workforce behind it. Directions, Sun, and Fremont hold that ground, together accounting for 27.3 percent of retail deposit-taking offices, more than in most districts of this kind. Huntington National Bank books the largest deposit total under federal rules, a figure that follows where deposits get recorded rather than where branches actually sit. For a credit union, that combination means a dense network of offices built to serve incomes and housing costs well below the national picture.
Marcy Kaptur.p3: Manufacturing anchors this economy at 19.0 percent of jobs, the clearest signature of the district as measured in 2023. Health care and social assistance follows behind it as a smaller, still notable share of employment. Overall finance and insurance work is thin on the ground here, running well under the national norm. Factory work, not finance, defines what this district does for a living.

Margaret Hassan.p1: New Hampshire's jobs cluster in retail trade and manufacturing, both running well past the national pattern, inside a state settled thinly at 157 people per square mile. Households earn far more than typical, $99,782 at the median, and joblessness is scarce. Owning a home is the norm rather than renting, and home values carry a sticker price of $458,800. Yet that price runs modest against income, and rent takes a small share of what a household earns.
Margaret Hassan.p2: Credit unions hold 24.2 percent of this state's retail banking offices, a share above most states, in a market where TD Bank books the largest deposits of any single institution while competing against hundreds of branches run by other banks. SERVICE, St. Mary's Bank, and First Technology carry the credit union name here. Credit union employment runs well past the national norm, specialized work in a state where broader finance jobs sit slightly below it. Retail-minded, homeowning households with real income to bank are what gives that presence its footing.
Margaret Hassan.p3: Employment data from 2023 put total jobs at about 631,100, with retail trade employing 13.4 percent of workers and manufacturing close behind. Both sectors carried more weight here than they do nationally. Finance and insurance as a whole grew slower than the national pace over the decade before. What stands out is a small, aging population running a retail and manufacturing economy well past its weight class, paired with some of the lowest poverty and joblessness rates anywhere.

Maria Cantwell.p1: Washington's median household income, 99,389 dollars, sits well above most states, and the poverty rate stays low by comparison. That comfort meets expensive ground: a median home value of 602,200 dollars comes to six times what a typical household earns, and renters give up 22 percent of median income each month. Homeownership lags behind most of the country, a state where owning a place to live has become the harder path.
Maria Cantwell.p2: Boeing Employees, Navy Federal, and GESA anchor a credit union presence that claims 32.9 percent of retail offices statewide, a share few other states can match. A single national bank holds the deposit lead on paper, a quirk of where big institutions book their accounts rather than a sign of local dominance. Credit union employment runs at 1.64 times the national norm, well ahead of the office footprint itself. Against incomes this high and homeownership this strained, credit unions here carry unusually deep staffing to work with.
Maria Cantwell.p3: As of 2023, overall finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm, while the broader category's pace of hiring held roughly steady. The state's real distinction lay elsewhere: agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting ran nearly three times the national norm, and information jobs ran well over twice it, both far ahead of what the rest of the country shows. Washington's economy rested on a few unusually deep sectors rather than broad strength spread evenly across the board.

Maria Salazar.p1: People sit close together across this district, more so than in nearly any other congressional seat, and that crowding shapes everything that follows. Households earn $82,215 a year, a figure close to the middle of comparable districts, but home values reach $670,900, far enough above income to leave ownership under half. Rent runs $2,123 a month, and joblessness is rare at 3.0 percent even while housing costs climb. The labor market here holds firm even where housing does not.
Maria Salazar.p2: Credit unions hold just 9.5 percent of retail offices here, one of the smaller shares found anywhere, leaving banks to carry most of the district's deposit business. Space Coast and Dade County are among the names holding that small footprint, set against City National Bank of Florida, the largest name by deposits booked locally, though far from the only bank at work here. Credit union payrolls stay thin against the national norm, and office presence sits at that same modest level. For a district this dense, credit unions remain a small piece of a much larger financial picture.
Maria Salazar.p3: As of 2023, government and expertise anchored the job base: Public Administration employed at more than twice the national norm, followed closely by Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services. Health Care and Social Assistance employed the most people outright. Finance and insurance work overall ran well above the national norm too, a strength distinct from the credit unions operating within it.

Mariannette Miller-Meeks.p1: What sets this district apart is how far income stretches over housing: homes run about 3.2 times median household income, and rent takes only a modest slice of pay, a burden lighter than almost anywhere comparable. Household income and home values both trail most other districts, yet homeownership is widespread. Unemployment runs low. The district is thinly settled, and most residents work within a manufacturing-driven Midwest economy.
Mariannette Miller-Meeks.p2: Credit unions here include GreenState, I.H. Mississippi Valley, and DuTrac Community, names that anchor a sector holding 18.8 percent of retail offices, a smaller share than in comparable districts even as Hills Bank and Trust Company leads locally booked deposits among many rival branches. Credit union employment sits well above the national norm, at 1.43 times, tracking office presence closely rather than outpacing it. Given the income levels and light housing costs described above, credit unions carry real weight in how people here bank.
Mariannette Miller-Meeks.p3: Manufacturing anchors employment in this district, measured in 2023 at 18.3 percent of jobs, more than twice the national concentration and the clearest specialty this place has. Retail trade showed a milder version of that same pull toward the national figure. Finance and insurance work, by contrast, was thin on the ground here. Home purchase loans, rather than refinancing, accounted for the bulk of mortgage activity that year.

Marie Gluesenkamp Perez.p1: Poverty here runs low, just 8.0 percent, a rate far below the norm for districts like it. Median household income reaches $92,354, and homeownership sits at 69.6 percent, both well ahead of peers. Home values, at $506,700, come to roughly five and a half years of what a typical household brings home. Population density stays sparse across this stretch of the West.
Marie Gluesenkamp Perez.p2: Retail offices split 49.0 percent to credit unions here, a share among the highest of any such district, rather than to banks. Columbia Community, IQ, and GESA anchor that presence locally. Payrolls in the credit union business run well past the national norm, outpacing even that office count, so these institutions staff more heavily relative to their footprint than is typical elsewhere. That combination gives a credit union here real weight against its banking competition.
Marie Gluesenkamp Perez.p3: As measured in 2023, construction stood out as a strong local employer, well above the national norm, alongside utilities and agriculture. Health care, manufacturing, and retail trade employed the most people, each somewhat above typical concentration nationally. Overall finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm even as the broader sector grew faster than that norm over the prior decade. Mortgage lending that year skewed toward home purchases over refinancing.

Marilyn Strickland.p1: Only 9.0 percent of residents live in poverty, a distinction that frames the rest of this district. Median household income reaches 95,458 dollars, while home values produce a 5.6 ratio against those earnings. Monthly rent is 1,887 dollars, and owner occupancy is less common than across many peer seats. Settlement is dense, with residents packed more tightly than in most congressional areas of similar size.
Marilyn Strickland.p2: Credit unions operate 41.2 percent of retail offices, placing them among the strongest cooperative footprints in comparable districts. Boeing Employees, Washington State Employees, and Navy Federal Credit Union anchor that network. Credit union staffing exceeds three times the national norm and is even more concentrated than the office network. Those institutions bring substantial financial capacity to a population with strong earnings, while numerous bank branches remain active competitors.
Marilyn Strickland.p3: As of 2023, public administration dominated the job base here, making up 13.1 percent of jobs, a mark of the district's role as a government seat. Construction and transportation and warehousing followed as the next most specialized sectors. Overall finance employment ran below the national norm even as the broader sector grew modestly over the prior decade. Mortgage lending stayed active across the district, with home purchases making up the larger share of originations over refinancing.

Mario Diaz-Balart.p1: A home here costs about seven times the typical household's income, a gap that stands among the widest anywhere, and rent alone eats 32.1 percent of that income. Median household earnings land at $75,619, modest for a district facing costs like these. Homeownership sits at 56.2 percent, thinner than in most comparable places. Poverty runs higher than typical too, at 13.9 percent, even with unemployment low.
Mario Diaz-Balart.p2: Credit unions hold just 15.0 percent of retail offices here, a share well below most comparable districts, leaving banks with most of the branch counters. Suncoast, Lake Michigan, and Space Coast are the credit unions with the largest presence in the district. Credit union employment tracks the national norm closely with office presence, both running thin next to the national picture. For households already stretched by housing costs, that leaves a smaller credit union presence than in many other places doing the same math.
Mario Diaz-Balart.p3: Transportation and warehousing employment is highly specialized here, running nearly three times the national norm and anchoring the district's job base. Wholesale trade follows close behind at a similarly elevated level, and together the two mark this as a logistics corridor rather than a typical service economy. Overall finance employment ran below the national norm, even as the wider finance and insurance sector grew slightly faster than the broader economy did.

Mark Alford.p1: Population here settles at just under 55 people per square mile, marking a rural, small-town stretch of the Midwest rather than anything urban. Median household income comes to 68,144 dollars a year, modest by comparison with other districts. Rent runs low too, near 998 dollars a month. Homeownership sits high at 71.0 percent, paired with a low unemployment rate.
Mark Alford.p2: Credit unions hold just 7.7 percent of retail offices here, among the lowest shares measured anywhere. One regional bank leads on deposits booked locally, in a market with many other banks competing for business, while Navy Federal, Infuze, and CommunityAmerica are the credit union names present. Credit union employment sits well under the national norm, and office presence tracks that same reduced level. For households earning modest incomes and paying modest rent, credit unions remain a small part of how this district banks.
Mark Alford.p3: This district's working economy, as measured in 2023, leaned on manufacturing, which employed 13.6 percent of workers, well above the national norm for that sector. Agriculture and utilities showed similar concentration, pointing to a base built on making and growing things. Retail trade and health care each accounted for a large share of jobs, filling out an employment mix tilted toward goods produced close to home. Overall finance employment ran below the national norm, leaving banking a smaller presence than manufacturing in daily working life here.

Mark Amodei.p1: People here are spread remarkably thin on the ground, just over twelve per square mile, sparser than nearly any other congressional district measured. Within that expanse, households earn a median $86,806, ahead of most districts nationwide, though joblessness runs high alongside that income. Home values sit at $491,000 against that income, a ratio of 5.7, and rent claims 22.2 percent of the median household's earnings. Most residents own rather than rent, though that ownership share still trails most other districts.
Mark Amodei.p2: Credit union employment here runs thin against the national norm, even though credit union offices nearly match it and claim a strong share of retail offices, well above most comparable districts. That gap between office presence and staffing is worth sitting with: branches outpace the jobs behind them. Greater Nevada, United, and Navy Federal Credit Union anchor that branch network, competing against Wells Fargo, the largest bank here by deposits booked locally, in a district with a great many bank branches run by separate lenders. For a footprint spread this wide, physical reach evidently matters more than staffing.
Mark Amodei.p3: As measured in 2023, the job base leaned hardest on mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction, highly specialized against the national norm, alongside transportation and warehousing. Accommodation and food services employed the most people, followed by health care and manufacturing. Home purchases made up 58.1 percent of mortgage originations across all lenders, with a smaller share of lending reaching lower-income neighborhoods.

Mark DeSaulnier.p1: Household income in the 10th congressional seat of California is among the highest of any district, at $151,546. Home values sit near $1,039,300, and homeownership is common, well above what most comparable districts see. Poverty is rare here. Set against all that, unemployment runs unusually high for a district this well off.
Mark DeSaulnier.p2: Credit unions here include Patelco, Travis, and Chevron, holding 23.5 percent of retail offices, a share that sits between the extremes seen in other districts. Wells Fargo Bank comes out ahead on deposits under federal booking rules, which reward wherever an institution files rather than where its branches sit, and plenty of other banks operate here too. Credit union employment here runs below the national norm, and office presence follows the same pattern. Given the earnings and homeownership above, a credit union here is working with a borrower base most branches would envy.
Mark DeSaulnier.p3: This district's economy leaned toward management of companies, finance and insurance, and construction in 2023, all well above national levels, with finance particularly strong. Health care and retail trade also employed a disproportionate slice of workers locally. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases rather than refinancing, and a meaningful share reached lower-income neighborhoods. This is a district shaped by corporate, financial, and technical work rather than by sheer volume of employment.

Mark Harris.p1: Homeownership defines this district more than any other measure, reaching 76.3 percent, among the highest of comparable seats. Housing costs run light against local pay, with a median home value of 373,300 dollars against household income of 81,435 dollars. Poverty sits low and joblessness stays modest here. At roughly 212 people per square mile, this is a spread-out place of owners rather than renters.
Mark Harris.p2: Credit union payrolls here trail what the sector's office footprint would lead you to expect, a mismatch worth flagging up front. State Employees', Navy Federal, and Truliant anchor that footprint, holding 24.4 percent of retail offices against Truist Bank, the largest bank by deposits booked locally. That office share lands squarely in the middle among comparable districts. A largely homeowning population is served by a credit union presence bigger on doors than on staff.
Mark Harris.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing and construction both ran well above the national norm for employment concentration. Manufacturing was the top employing sector locally, with retail trade close behind. Finance and insurance employment overall ran light against the national norm, even as the broader sector grew faster than the country between 2013 and 2023. Mortgage lending here leaned heavily toward home purchases, consistent with a district built around owning rather than renting.

Mark Kelly.p1: Arizona's population, over 7,582,384 strong, is spread thin across the state, fewer than 67 people per square mile. Median household income runs to 81,486 dollars, well ahead of most other states, but housing eats into that fast: a median home value of 426,000 dollars against that income prices out to a ratio among the highest in the country. Unemployment also runs higher here than in most states, a harder edge under an otherwise solid income picture.
Mark Kelly.p2: Credit unions carry real weight here, led by Desert Financial, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Arizona Financial. They hold 25.7 percent of retail offices statewide, a stronger share than most states manage, competing against a bank sector where JPMorgan Chase books more deposits than any other name, under federal reporting rules rather than through local branch presence. Credit union employment tracks credit union office presence closely, both near the national norm. That office share gives residents a meaningful place to bank outside the big national names.
Mark Kelly.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance was Arizona's most specialized sector, employing 5.8 percent of the workforce well above the national norm, alongside strength in construction, a natural fit for a state that keeps building. Health care, retail, and hospitality together accounted for a large share of employment without any of them counting as a specialty. Finance grew faster than the national pace over the decade leading up to that measurement.

Mark Messmer.p1: Home values here sit near the bottom of any congressional district, at $198,800, well below what households elsewhere pay for a comparable house. Median household income runs $65,297, modest by national standards, yet a home costs only about three times that figure. Homeownership is the norm rather than the exception, and the district itself is spread thin, with a population scattered well below typical density.
Mark Messmer.p2: Credit unions named Liberty, Crane, and Heritage give this district a retail banking footprint that stands out, holding 28.5 percent of retail offices against banks, a share above most comparable places. Credit union employment here runs well ahead of the national norm and tracks closely with how many offices they operate on the ground. Old National Bank leads locally by deposits booked to addresses here, one name among 218 bank branches operated by many separate institutions. For a population earning modest incomes but owning homes at a high rate, credit unions are a mainstream banking choice, not a fallback.
Mark Messmer.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing anchored the local economy, employing 20.5 percent of the district's roughly 300,300 jobs and running more than twice the national norm. Mining and quarrying, though a small slice of employment, was even more concentrated relative to the rest of the country. Overall finance and insurance employment lagged well behind the national norm, underscoring how much manufacturing dominates the workplace here.

Mark Pocan.p1: Unemployment here sits at just 2.2 percent, among the lowest across the nation's districts, a labor market running close to full strength. Households earn a median of 88,518 dollars, comfortably ahead of most districts, while home values near 405,200 dollars still leave housing costs light against income by comparison. Homeownership, at 59.3 percent, trails more districts than not. This is a Midwestern district spread thin, more suburban and small-town than urban.
Mark Pocan.p2: Credit unions hold 30.1 percent of retail locations here, a share few districts can match, putting them in real competition with banks rather than at the margins. SUMMIT, CONNEXUS, and a third large credit union carry that presence. Credit union staffing stands far above the countrywide baseline, with staffing concentration exceeding office concentration rather than institutions simply adding storefronts. That thickness matters against a population earning well, exactly the customer base a credit union here actually works with.
Mark Pocan.p3: In 2023, this district leaned on Information jobs at close to twice the countrywide baseline, alongside Public Administration and Finance and Insurance, both specialized beyond the typical district. Health care and social services carried a large share of jobs, with manufacturing not far behind. Purchase loans accounted for most mortgage lending activity, a market defined more by people buying homes than refinancing them.

Mark Takano.p1: Housing here runs far out of reach of local pay: the typical home costs 6.5 times what the typical household earns, among the highest ratios of any district measured. Median household income stands at $91,174, healthy by national standards, yet rent still averages $2,072 a month. Owning a home is less common here than in most other districts. The area is also one of the more densely settled parts of the West.
Mark Takano.p2: Credit unions here include a large statewide credit union, Altura, and Navy Federal Credit Union, holding 22.6 percent of retail offices against banks locally, a share similar to comparable districts. Wells Fargo books the largest bank deposits under federal reporting rules, a measure of where deposits are recorded rather than of branch presence or local customers. Credit union employment runs well below the national norm here, tracking closely with how thin their office presence is too. Against steep home costs and rent that consumes 27.3 percent of income, these institutions serve a population squeezed by cost rather than by weak earnings.
Mark Takano.p3: Work here concentrated heavily in transportation and warehousing, which held 17.6 percent of jobs at nearly four times the national norm, by far the district's defining specialty. Public administration followed as the next most distinctive sector. Health care and social assistance employed a large share too, though close to typical levels elsewhere. Overall finance employment ran far below the national norm, leaving logistics, not banking, as the trade this district does best.

Mark Warner.p1: Virginia is a dense, prosperous state, with a median household income of $92,090 and a population packed in well above the density of most other states. Housing costs run high too: a median home value of $403,500 and rent near $1,646 a month. Poverty runs lower than in most other states, and homeownership, at 67.1 percent, still trails most states elsewhere in the country.
Mark Warner.p2: Navy Federal Credit Union, Virginia Credit Union, and Langley Federal Credit Union anchor a credit union presence that punches above its weight here. Credit unions hold 23.7 percent of retail offices statewide, a share above most other states, even though Capital One, National Association shows up with an outsized deposit figure simply because of where its accounts get booked, not branch strength on the ground. Credit union employment runs at nearly twice the national norm and has grown faster than the office count itself, meaning these institutions are staffing up well beyond what their physical footprint would imply.
Mark Warner.p3: As of 2023, Virginia's economy leaned hard into professional, scientific, and technical services, employing workers at 1.69 times the national norm and forming its most concentrated sector. Management of companies and enterprises came in well above the norm too. Health care employed more people than any other sector, though without the same concentration nationally. Overall finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm, even as broader growth in that sector matched it over the decade to 2023.

Marlin Stutzman.p1: This district stands out on affordability: a home here typically costs about 3.2 times what a household earns, and rent claims a modest slice of income. Median household income runs on the lean side. Homeownership is common, at 75.1 percent. The district is sparsely settled, made up more of small cities and open country than dense urban blocks.
Marlin Stutzman.p2: Credit unions hold 38.4 percent of retail offices here, a share among the highest of any comparable district. Three Rivers, Midwest America, and ProFed anchor that presence. Credit union employment runs well above the national norm, and office presence runs even further ahead, meaning offices have grown faster than staff levels. That footprint sits atop a district where owning a home is the norm and housing costs stay light against income, a favorable base for institutions built around member deposits and home lending.
Marlin Stutzman.p3: The district's working economy, measured in 2023, ran heavily on manufacturing, which accounted for 24.9 percent of jobs, far above the national norm and its clearest specialty. Overall finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm. Lake City Bank was named for deposits booked in the district, though 200 bank branches operated here under many separate owners. Mortgage lending skewed toward home purchases over other loan types.

Marsha Blackburn.p1: Tennessee's jobs cluster in factories, trucks, and warehouses: transportation and warehousing and manufacturing both post well above the national norm, with manufacturing alone accounting for a eighth of all jobs. The state's 7,227,750 people are settled more densely than most states manage. Median household income sits well below most states at 71,997 dollars, while rent claims 21.4 percent of that income. Home values sit near the national middle, a contrast with the income beneath them.
Marsha Blackburn.p2: Credit unions hold 22.4 percent of retail offices statewide, an unremarkable share once set against other states, though that office presence runs ahead of the national norm even as credit union employment trails it slightly. Eastman, Knoxville TVA Employees, and Ascend anchor that presence, working alongside Pinnacle Bank, a name that leads on deposits credited to addresses here among many local rivals. That combination of manufacturing payrolls and warehousing wages is the raw material credit unions here are built to serve, workers whose income lags most of the country even as housing costs run higher.
Marsha Blackburn.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance jobs statewide sat just under the national norm, though the sector outpaced the country's own job growth across the ten years before. Manufacturing and logistics carried the state's real distinctiveness, work tied to moving goods and building them rather than to finance. Poverty ran high, at 13.5 percent. Tennessee's economic identity was, and remains, industrial rather than financial, a place that makes and ships more than it banks.

Martin Heinrich.p1: New Mexico spreads just under seventeen and a half people per square mile, one of the emptiest settlement patterns in the country, and its economy leans on public administration and oil and gas extraction rather than dense service clusters. Median household income sits at 67,816 dollars, well below most states, while unemployment runs high at 5.3 percent. Homeownership is unusually strong at 71.1 percent, even as poverty stays higher than in nearly every other state.
Martin Heinrich.p2: Credit unions hold 31.6 percent of retail offices statewide, a bigger slice than in most states and a real counterweight to the many competing banks with branches here. Nusenda, Sunward, and Sandia Area anchor that presence, serving a population where homeownership runs high but incomes lag. Credit union employment runs far thicker than the national norm, and branch presence outpaces it too, with jobs growing faster than offices. In a low-density state with high mortgage-holding, that workforce reach matters more than address counts.
Martin Heinrich.p3: As of 2023, overall finance employment stayed thin, well under the national norm, even as mining and oil extraction stood out as by far the state's most concentrated industry. Public administration also ran comfortably above the typical state's level. Wells Fargo led the state in booked deposits, a function of reporting rules rather than local branch strength. New Mexico's economy is built on extraction and government work, not banking.

Mary Miller.p1: This district spreads its 739,197 people thinly, a population density that lands near the bottom of every congressional seat in the state. Household income trails most comparable districts at $74,855, yet home values stay modest too, a median of $164,200 against that income, and monthly rent sits at $862, a light load against local pay. Homeownership runs unusually high, and joblessness stays low. Open land and settled households define this seat far more than any commuter rush.
Mary Miller.p2: Credit unions hold just 10.3 percent of retail offices here, a thinner share than almost anywhere else measured. Citizens Equity First, Land of Lincoln, and Scott carry that slice between them. First Mid Bank & Trust shows the largest deposit booking among local branches, though that reflects reporting rules more than actual local reach. Credit union jobs run a touch below the national norm here, while their office count tracks closer to it, so offices carry more weight per worker than the norm.
Mary Miller.p3: The industry picture, measured in 2023, shows manufacturing anchoring the district at 13.9 percent of jobs, well above the national norm. Health care and social assistance employed the most people, with retail trade close behind. Agriculture, though a small slice of jobs, stood out as sharply specialized. Land and factories, not finance, still set the terms of work here.

Mary Scanlon.p1: People here live closer together than in almost any comparable district, and that crowding sets the tone for everything else. Households earn a median $85,873, well above most comparable districts, while home values sit near $362,600 against monthly rent close to $1,502. Ownership outweighs renting by a wide margin. Unemployment runs higher here than it does across most peer districts, worth watching against otherwise solid income.
Mary Scanlon.p2: Credit union employment falls below the national norm even as credit union offices outnumber what that norm would predict, a split worth flagging before anything else about this market. Police & Fire, Franklin Mint, and Citadel carry the credit union name locally, competing for space among a wider field of bank branches where TD Bank, National Association books the most deposits under federal reporting rules. Credit unions hold 19.8 percent of retail offices here, a thinner slice than in most comparable districts. That leaves a dense, higher-earning population still largely banked through branches rather than credit union doors.
Mary Scanlon.p3: As of 2023, the job base leaned hard into corporate back-office and logistics work, with Management of Companies and Enterprises running far ahead of the national norm. Transportation and Warehousing and administrative support services also ran well ahead of it. Health Care and Social Assistance employed a larger share of workers than any other sector, trailed by retail and educational services. Mortgage lending skewed heavily toward home purchases that year, well above other loan types combined.

Matt Van Epps.p1: Unemployment here runs well below most comparable districts, at 3.5 percent, the clearest sign of how tight this labor market is. The 816,216 people living here earn a median household income that is unremarkable next to other districts, and are spread thinly across the land. Housing costs run harder than that income alone would cover: home values sit at 4.6 times median income, and rent takes 22.6 percent of it, both pressures landing above what most districts face.
Matt Van Epps.p2: Credit unions hold just 14.5 percent of retail offices in this district, a smaller share than nearly anywhere comparable, leaving most storefronts to banks. Navy Federal Credit Union, Ascend, and Fortera carry that smaller footprint. Bank of America books the most deposits of any bank here, a figure driven by where deposits get recorded rather than by branches on the ground, and plenty of other banks compete for business in the same district. Credit union employment sits well under the national norm, thinner even than their office share implies.
Matt Van Epps.p3: As of 2023, the job base leaned hardest on public administration, at 1.81 times the national norm, with a real concentration in information work as well. Health care was a leading source of jobs in the district too. Finance and insurance employment sat close to the national norm overall, though that combined sector had grown faster than the country over the prior decade.

Max Miller.p1: Unemployment here sits at 2.8 percent, among the lowest of any congressional district, and it fits a place that otherwise looks comfortably settled. Median household income runs to 84,749 dollars, well ahead of typical districts, while poverty stays low at 7.5 percent. Rent takes a modest bite out of that income, and homeownership is common. Density runs high too, pointing to a built-up district rather than a spread-out rural one.
Max Miller.p2: Credit union employment here runs far below the national norm even though office presence, while also below it, does not fall nearly as far, leaving offices doing more work than staffing levels alone would explain. Navy Federal Credit Union, Century, and PSE Credit Union carry that presence, holding 16.9 percent of retail offices against banks, a share smaller than most comparable districts see. Huntington National Bank books more deposits here than any other bank under federal reporting rules, one name among many competing in the district. For a credit union in this district, that means serving well-paid, steadily employed households with a thinner staff base than the office count implies.
Max Miller.p3: Manufacturing anchored the job base as measured in 2023, holding 14.4 percent of jobs and running well above the national norm for that kind of work. Management of companies and wholesale trade ran even more concentrated, pointing to corporate and distribution functions layered on top of factory floors. Mortgage lending that year leaned heavily toward home purchases, 47.0 percent of originations, with a much smaller slice reaching lower income neighborhoods.

Maxine Dexter.p1: Of everything measured in this district, household income marks it most clearly against comparable places, at 94,110 dollars a year. Housing costs track that: a median home value of 552,500 dollars runs 5.9 times income, and rent claims 21.5 percent of it, both on the high side. Homeownership lags most comparable districts, at just under 59.4 percent. Unemployment sits a bit elevated too, a quieter sign of the same story.
Maxine Dexter.p2: Credit unions hold 38.6 percent of retail offices here, a share among the highest recorded for any congressional district. ONPOINT COMMUNITY, RIVERMARK COMMUNITY, and UNITUS COMMUNITY carry that presence locally. U.S. Bank National Association books more deposits here than any other single institution, though a wide field of competing banks operates branches across the district too. Credit union employment here runs noticeably thicker than the national norm even as office counts sit right at that norm, meaning these institutions staff fuller branches rather than run more of them.
Maxine Dexter.p3: As measured in 2023, Transportation and Warehousing stood out sharply, employing workers at a rate well above the national norm. Health Care and Social Assistance carried a broad share of jobs in its own right. Overall finance employment stayed thin against the national norm, well behind the strength seen in moving goods. Lending that year leaned toward home purchases over refinancing, with a meaningful share of loans reaching lower income neighborhoods.

Maxine Waters.p1: This is one of the most tightly packed districts in the country, with nearly 10,000 people per square mile, and that crowding runs through every number that follows. Median household income comes in at 75,336 dollars, lagging most other districts, against a median home value of 716,000 dollars, a gap that puts the value to income ratio at 9.5. Rent runs a median 1,807 dollars a month. The work itself centers on moving goods, a thread the next paragraph picks up.
Maxine Waters.p2: Credit unions hold 31.1 percent of retail offices here, a share well above most of the country. A large national institution and a major regional one give this district its credit union presence, set against a field of banks topped on deposits by JPMorgan Chase, a figure driven by where deposits get booked rather than by branches on the ground. Credit union jobs trail the national norm even though offices are scarcer still, meaning each branch does more work than the typical one elsewhere. For households already squeezed by home values far outpacing income, that presence carries real weight.
Maxine Waters.p3: Transportation and warehousing defined the job mix as of 2023, employing at more than four times the national norm and making this one of the most specialized freight economies anywhere. Manufacturing came in as a smaller second specialty. Health care, despite being a large employer, fell short of its typical national footprint here. Mortgage lending that year favored home purchases, with a strong share of loans reaching lower income neighborhoods.

Maxwell Frost.p1: Housing here costs far more than incomes support: a house price near 5.4 times the middle household's earnings, and rent alone would take close to 29.6 percent of the median income. Renting is more common than owning, and few districts have a lower homeownership share. Poverty is more common here than in many peer seats, in a place that is dense and heavily urban.
Maxwell Frost.p2: Credit union staffing here is thin against the countrywide baseline, well below it, even though credit union offices are only mildly light by that same measure, an odd mismatch that puts more branches on the ground than staffing would warrant. FAIRWINDS, NAVY FEDERAL CREDIT UNION, and ADDITION FINANCIAL anchor that presence, holding 24.0 percent of retail locations against banks, a middling share of the market. Truist Bank leads all institutions by deposits booked here, though that reflects reporting rules more than local reach, and it competes with 150 bank locations run by many other banks. Renters and lower earners stretched by the housing math above have, in credit unions, a smaller-footprint alternative to the banks that dominate deposits.
Maxwell Frost.p3: In 2023, arts, entertainment, and recreation was especially concentrated, a sector far above the countrywide baseline. Administrative and support services and real estate also stood out as areas of concentrated strength. Finance and insurance employment ran slightly above the countrywide baseline and outpaced nationwide growth during the preceding decade.

Mazie Hirono.p1: Hospitality anchors Hawaii's economy: accommodation and food service jobs sit at nearly twice the national norm, the clearest specialty here, alongside a heavier-than-usual concentration in utilities. Settlement is denser than in most states, residents skew a bit older at a midpoint of 41.5 years, and unemployment is low enough to be a real outlier nationally. Housing sets this place apart, too, with home values and rents among the highest anywhere, a gap of 8.7 between home values and income, and fewer households owning than renting compared with the national pattern.
Mazie Hirono.p2: Credit unions hold 43.8 percent of retail offices, a bigger slice than almost any other state carries, against 217 bank branches spread across many competitors. Navy Federal, HawaiiUSA, and Hawaii State anchor that presence. Credit union payrolls are considerably thicker than the national norm, and the office footprint thicker still, offices outpacing jobs, a sign of a dense branch network built to serve a workforce concentrated in tourism and service work rather than high-paying finance.
Mazie Hirono.p3: Finance and insurance employment overall sits well below the national norm, at 0.61, with growth from 2013 to 2023 trailing slightly too. That leaves the credit union sector doing comparatively more work locally than finance does as a whole. Retail and health care employ plenty of people without carrying the same weight nationally that hospitality does. What Hawaii does unusually well is feed and house visitors and residents alike, an economy built around service rather than capital.

Melanie Stansbury.p1: This district spreads its population thinly across the land, a settlement pattern few other seats in the country come close to matching. Some 711,081 people call it home, earning a median household income of $77,246, unremarkable when set against other districts. Housing costs less against income here than the typical district manages, while poverty and unemployment both climb above what most places report. Distances are long here, and the wages people bring home are middling.
Melanie Stansbury.p2: Credit unions hold 37.4 percent of retail offices here, a share topped by almost no other district in the country. SUNWARD, NUSENDA, and Sandia Area lead that presence, ahead of Bank of America, National Association, which posts the largest deposit total under federal booking rules. Credit union employment runs at 2.67 times the national norm, even further out ahead than their office presence, meaning these institutions are real employers here, not just branch counts. That is a workforce built to serve the income base and housing costs described above.
Melanie Stansbury.p3: As of 2023, health care and social services occupied the largest slice of the job market, and Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services stood out as the most specialized sector, running well above the national norm. Public Administration also ran ahead of typical levels. Overall finance and insurance employment sat close to the national norm, but grew faster than that norm over the decade before.

Michael Baumgartner.p1: Washington's 5th covers a broad area, with 801,690 residents living at one of the House's lower settlement densities. Median household income is $80,002, close to ordinary district earnings, while the middle home is worth $423,300. That produces a 5.3 ratio between value and income. Owner occupancy is common, although unemployment sits somewhat above the level seen elsewhere.
Michael Baumgartner.p2: Credit unions operate 46.2 percent of retail deposit-taking offices, placing cooperatives near the top of the district range. Spokane Teachers, Boeing Employees, and Numerica anchor the network. Umpqua Bank appears first on the federally assigned deposit measure within a field of numerous banks. Credit union staffing exceeds three times the national norm, while office concentration is above twice the baseline. Employment therefore carries even greater weight than the already extensive physical network.
Michael Baumgartner.p3: In 2023, agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting provided the most distinctive employment concentration. Health care and social assistance supplied the largest number of positions within roughly 303,200 jobs. Overall finance employment stayed close to its national baseline, even while credit unions held an unusually prominent position inside that sector. That contrast places a strong cooperative network inside an otherwise ordinary finance labor market. A thinly settled, land-based economy with strong cooperative finance is the combination that separates this district from its peers.

Michael Bennet.p1: Colorado's economy sits on professional and technical work, oil and gas extraction, and outdoor recreation and the arts, all three unusually concentrated here. Settlement stays sparse across the state, with a working-age median around 38. Income runs high, a household median of $97,113, well above most states, but a home value near six times that figure keeps ownership out of reach for many, and the homeownership rate itself lags behind other states even at 65.9 percent.
Michael Bennet.p2: Credit unions hold 22.3 percent of retail offices statewide, a share about even with comparable states, against Wells Fargo Bank, National Association, which leads locally booked deposits among a large field of bank branches statewide. ENT, Bellco, and Canvas are the names that carry that share. Credit union offices run a bit light against the national norm for their footprint, but jobs within them hold closer to typical levels, so these institutions employ more thickly than their office count alone would imply. That fits an economy where pay and housing costs both climb well past the norm.
Michael Bennet.p3: Total employment reached roughly 2,623,700 jobs as of 2023. Professional, scientific, and technical services carried outsized weight for the state's identity, at 11.1 percent of jobs and nearly one and a half times the national norm. Health care and retail trade rounded out sizable shares of that total, both close to typical national levels. Finance and insurance jobs overall sat almost exactly at the national norm, growing slightly faster than the country over the prior decade.

Michael Cloud.p1: This district spreads its population thinly, just 76.1 people per square mile, among the sparsest settlement patterns of any comparable seat. Almost 794,000 people call it home, the typical resident is 38.7 years old, and household earnings run behind most other districts. Housing costs less than usual to buy, a home value that sits at 3.5 times income, even as homeownership trails most peers. Unemployment stays low, at 3.8 percent.
Michael Cloud.p2: Credit unions hold 30.3 percent of retail offices in this district, a share well above most comparable seats and a sign of real weight in local banking. Rally, Randolph-Brooks, and Texas Dow Employees are the names carrying that share. Credit union employment runs far thicker than the national norm, and outpaces even the strong office presence, meaning these institutions staff up more heavily than office count alone would explain. Prosperity Bank books more deposits here than any other under federal reporting rules, a measure of where deposits land rather than where customers actually bank.
Michael Cloud.p3: The wider economy, as measured in 2023, carried a lighter finance sector than the country overall, leaving room for credit unions to matter more than elsewhere. Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction stood out as a highly specialized sector here. Utilities and construction also ran well ahead of national patterns, with construction alone employing a tenth of all workers. Health care and retail trade rounded out sizable sources of jobs in a district built more around energy and building than finance.

Michael Guest.p1: Home values in the 3rd district are among the lowest of any congressional district, at $185,400, and household income of $66,380 trails badly too. Rent runs $1,070 a month, modest against that income, and homeownership is common at 73.4 percent. Poverty runs high here even though unemployment stays low. This is a sparsely settled place where people are more likely to own their home than chase one on a mortgage.
Michael Guest.p2: Credit unions hold just 14.1 percent of retail offices here, a thin share that puts banks firmly in charge of the market. Navy Federal, Keesler, and Magnolia are the names carrying that smaller footprint. Credit union employment runs well under the national norm, while their office count holds up somewhat better than staffing does. Trustmark National Bank leads the district on deposits, though it competes there with many other banks running branches of their own.
Michael Guest.p3: As measured in 2023, health care and social assistance employed a large share of workers, with a slight specialization relative to the country. Retail trade and educational services followed as the other big employers. Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting employed a small slice of workers but stood out as the most distinctly specialized sector against national norms. Total employment ran to roughly 293,700 jobs, spread across an economy with no single dominant industry.

Michael Lawler.p1: Household income in the 17th congressional seat of New York sits among the highest of any comparable district, at 123,436 dollars. Homes carry a median value of 635,500 dollars, but that value and the rent people pay both sit lighter against income than in most other districts. Homeownership is unusually common here, a sign of a settled, established population. The district is also denser than most, at just under 950 people per square mile.
Michael Lawler.p2: Credit unions hold just 10.4 percent of retail offices against banks, a slice few other districts fall below, in a market where 186 bank branches belong to many competing owners. Hudson Valley, Affinity, and Palisades carry that small share between them. Credit union employment and office presence both fall well short of the national norm, tracking each other closely rather than one outpacing the other. That leaves credit unions working a wealthy, high-value housing market largely on the banks' terms.
Michael Lawler.p3: As measured in 2023, health care and social assistance stood out well past its usual national weight, the district's clearest concentration, followed by educational services. Overall finance employment also lagged the national norm, even as finance and insurance jobs grew faster locally than across the country between 2013 and 2023. This is a district shaped more by institutions and care work than by finance or trading floors.

Michael McCaul.p1: Residents occupy this district at a relatively low density. The median household earns $89,284, a strong figure beside peer seats, and the middle home is worth $398,000. Housing remains comparatively inexpensive against those earnings despite the high price level. Poverty is slightly elevated, while owner occupancy sits near the ordinary district rate. The result is a prosperous but geographically dispersed household base.
Michael McCaul.p2: Credit unions operate only 13.7 percent of retail offices, giving them a small place beside banks. A+, Brazos Valley, and another large credit union provide the principal cooperative names. Federal reports put Prosperity Bank ahead on deposits assigned locally, a result of booking addresses rather than branch reach. Credit union staffing and office concentration both fall below the national norm and remain close to each other. Households therefore encounter a financial market led primarily by conventional banks.
Michael McCaul.p3: The 2023 job count was near 288,700. Educational services accounted for 19.4 percent of workers and had an unusually strong concentration. Mining and oil and gas extraction also carried much more local weight than their national share, despite employing fewer people. Finance employment was below its countrywide baseline, although the broader finance and insurance sector expanded faster locally over the preceding decade.

Michael Rulli.p1: Household income in the 6th congressional seat of Ohio sits at $60,716, a figure few districts anywhere fall beneath, and poverty runs well past the typical mark. Housing costs far less than that income picture: a median home value of $173,200 against local income works out to a ratio of 2.9, and rent takes a modest slice of what households earn. Homeownership is common here, well ahead of the usual pace elsewhere.
Michael Rulli.p2: Credit union offices here carry more weight locally than credit union jobs do, which is the place to start on this sector: office presence runs slightly above the national norm even as employment in the industry lags well behind it. Dover-Phila, Seven Seventeen, and Ohio Valley Community anchor that presence. Credit unions hold 18.9 percent of retail offices, a smaller share than most districts carry, leaving Huntington National Bank, the largest holder of deposits booked in the district, to work the same ground alongside a wide field of other banks.
Michael Rulli.p3: As measured in 2023, this district's economy leaned on extraction and manufacturing: mining and quarrying activity ran well beyond the national norm, and manufacturing employed 15.3 percent of workers, also far above the typical share. Overall finance employment trailed the country by a wide margin. This is a district built on producing things, not on managing money.

Michael Simpson.p1: This district spreads its people thin, among the lowest population densities of any congressional district in the country. Nearly a million residents live across that space, with a median household income of 79,009 dollars, about the middle of the pack nationally. Home values run high at 416,900 dollars, though rent stays moderate and homeownership holds near 69 percent. Unemployment sits low.
Michael Simpson.p2: Credit unions here hold 37.1 percent of retail offices, an unusually large share for a single district. Idaho Central, Mountain America, and Westmark anchor that presence, set against a banking sector where Wells Fargo books the largest deposits under federal reporting rules, alongside many other banks present here. Credit union employment runs far above the national norm, well ahead of their office presence, so these institutions carry more payroll than their footprint alone implies. That is a lot of financial cooperative, working a population scattered across a lot of land.
Michael Simpson.p3: As of 2023, agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting stood out most, far above the national norm, alongside construction and public administration. Health care and social assistance employed the most people, ahead of retail trade and manufacturing, out of roughly 458,400 total jobs. Overall finance and insurance employment lagged the national norm even as the broader sector grew faster than most places over the prior decade. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases that year, more than any other loan purpose.

Michael Turner.p1: Home values set this district apart before anything else: at $218,600, they run well below most comparable districts, alongside income that lags peers too. Rent comes to $1,103 a month, low enough to keep monthly costs manageable against typical earnings. Poverty and unemployment both run higher than in most districts, even in an area that is crowded and offers little open land left to develop. Homeownership sits at 64.1 percent, unremarkable next to the affordability underneath it.
Michael Turner.p2: Credit unions hold 32.6 percent of retail offices here, well beyond what most districts show, putting them in genuine competition with the local banks. Wright-Patt Credit Union, Day Air, and River Valley carry that presence locally, while Fifth Third Bank books the most deposits among the area's banks. Credit union employment runs at 1.89 times the national norm, well ahead of the office count itself, meaning these institutions employ more thickly than their branch presence alone would explain. That is a sector built around the ordinary incomes and modest homes described above.
Michael Turner.p3: Health care and social assistance is the clear specialty of the local economy, holding 19.1 percent of jobs and running well ahead of the national norm. Manufacturing adds a secondary layer of strength, employment here leaning more industrial than the typical district. Overall finance employment lagged the national norm, a separate fact from the credit union sector's own weight in the local economy. Lending across the market leaned heavily toward home purchases rather than refinancing.

Michelle Fischbach.p1: People here live spread far apart, with a population density that sits near the bottom among comparable districts nationwide, just 23.3 people per square mile. The typical household brings in $74,454 a year, and the typical home is valued at $255,000, both modest figures next to other districts. Homeownership runs high, at 76.2 percent, while poverty and unemployment both stay low. Housing costs are gentle by comparison, a combination of ownership, affordability, and steady work that sets this place apart.
Michelle Fischbach.p2: Credit unions hold just 13.8 percent of retail offices here, a thin footprint given how much everyday banking this population needs. Magnifi Financial, Affinity Plus, and Mid Minnesota carry the local name recognition, working against Old National Bank, which books the largest sum of deposits to an address here. Credit union employment falls well short of the national norm, and office presence trails it too, with offices outpacing jobs, a sign of thin staffing rather than a shrinking presence. That gap matters here specifically, in a district full of homeowners and modest earners who need a banking relationship, not a booking address.
Michelle Fischbach.p3: Manufacturing anchors this district's economy, employing 18.1 percent of workers at a rate far above the national norm, the clearest mark of specialization here. Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting runs highly specialized too. As measured in 2023, health care and social assistance employed the largest share of workers in the district. This is a place built on making and growing things, not on financial services.

Mike Bost.p1: Housing here costs little against what people earn: a home's median value sits at just 2.2 times median household income, and rent takes only 14.5 percent of it, among the lowest housing cost burdens of any congressional district. Homeownership runs high at 76.3 percent, a district of people who mostly own rather than rent. Median household income lands at 70,903 dollars, not much to work with even where housing is cheap. Poverty and unemployment register as unremarkable, neither high nor low against other districts.
Mike Bost.p2: Credit unions hold just 9.4 percent of retail offices in this district, the lowest such share among comparable places, well behind what banks control. SCOTT, SIU, and FIRST COMMUNITY are the names carrying that share. Banterra Bank books the largest deposit total under federal reporting rules, a figure that follows where deposits are booked rather than where branches sit. Credit union jobs run well under the national norm, thinner still than the office count alone.
Mike Bost.p3: The working economy, measured in 2023, leaned heavily on manufacturing and health care. Mining and agriculture stood out as highly specialized, each employing a small share of workers at rates well above the national norm. Overall finance employment also ran below the national norm. Across all lenders, 61.0 percent of originations were home purchases, a district still built around buying rather than refinancing.

Mike Carey.p1: Unemployment here sits well below most comparable districts, at 3.4 percent, a marker of a labor market that is working. The typical household earns 80,864 dollars, an unremarkable figure for a district of 823,011 people. Home values and homeownership both trail most comparable districts, even as rent stays in ordinary range. This is a Midwest district, built around working households rather than extremes.
Mike Carey.p2: Credit unions hold just 14.5 percent of retail offices here, a thin share next to most comparable districts, and banks fill nearly all the rest of the storefronts a household would walk into. Wright-Patt Credit Union, Kemba Financial, and BMI carry the credit union name locally, while Huntington National Bank shows the most deposits on paper, a reflection of where deposits get booked rather than of branches on the ground. Jobs and offices in the credit union sector both fall short of the national norm, a light footprint given the solid household income described above. It is a market credit unions have not claimed much of yet.
Mike Carey.p3: This district's economy, as measured in 2023, leaned hard on moving goods: Transportation and Warehousing employed 10.6 percent of its jobs, well above the national norm and its most specialized sector by far. Wholesale Trade and corporate management added further weight uncommon in most districts. Home purchase loans made up 54.0 percent of mortgage originations, with a fifth of lending reaching lower income neighborhoods.

Mike Collins.p1: The 10th district of Georgia spreads its 835,755 residents thinly across the land, well below most comparable districts in population per square mile. Median household income lands at $79,167, roughly typical for a district, alongside a median home value of $347,100. Housing costs take up less of income here than in most places, and homeownership runs high at 71.9 percent. Open ground and light settlement define the district more than any dense center.
Mike Collins.p2: Credit unions hold just 12.6 percent of retail offices here, a stake far smaller than what most other districts grant them. Robins Financial, Delta Community, and Peach State are the credit unions with a presence in the district, up against local banking where Synovus Bank books more deposits than any other single name. Credit union employment runs far below the national norm, and office presence trails its own norm too, but less steeply, so offices outpace jobs here. It is a district where a credit union works a narrow share of a market banks still hold.
Mike Collins.p3: Specialized sectors carried real weight in the district's employment as measured in 2023, led by transportation and warehousing and wholesale trade running well above the national norm. Overall finance and insurance employment sat below the national norm, though the sector had added jobs faster than the country did over the prior decade. Home purchase loans made up 57.2 percent of all mortgage originations. Lending to lower-income neighborhoods held a modest share of that activity.

Mike Crapo.p1: Idaho holds a population above two million spread across ground so thinly settled that people per square mile stays in the low twenties, so its economy runs on land-based, hands-on work rather than density. Agriculture and construction both employ well above the national norm. Households earn a median $81,166, and the state's home values center near $446,400, over five times that income. Ownership runs high across the state.
Mike Crapo.p2: Credit unions hold 39.8 percent of retail offices in Idaho, among the highest shares of any state, in a market still populated by hundreds of bank branches, including a large U.S. Bank presence booked mainly for deposit reporting rather than local footprint. Idaho Central, Mountain America, and Potlatch No. 1 Financial anchor the credit union side. Credit union jobs run well over twice the national norm, and that employment has climbed faster than the number of offices has. Landowners and builders here want financing close to home, and credit unions have staffed up to meet it.
Mike Crapo.p3: As of 2023, Idaho's jobs concentrated most heavily in health care, retail trade, and manufacturing, though finance and insurance work overall stayed thinner on the ground than the national picture. That combined sector nonetheless added jobs at a pace ahead of the country's between 2013 and 2023. Construction and agriculture gave the state its sharpest edge, an economy anchored in what gets grown and built rather than in offices or distribution hubs.

Mike Ezell.p1: Median household income in the 4th congressional seat of Mississippi sits well below most other districts, at $62,159 a year, and poverty here climbs past what most similar districts report. Housing stays cheap by comparison: a $213,200 median home value against that income lands at 3.4 times earnings, and typical rent runs $1,088 a month. Homeownership is common, well ahead of what most districts show. Population is spread thin across the district, and unemployment edges above what most places see.
Mike Ezell.p2: Credit union jobs here run close to twice the national norm, but credit union offices have grown even faster, a sign that branch counts have outpaced the staff behind the counter. Keesler, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Singing River anchor that presence, holding 25.9 percent of retail offices, a bigger slice than most comparable districts see. Hancock Whitney Bank leads on deposits booked to addresses here, one name among the many banks competing for this district's modest incomes.
Mike Ezell.p3: As measured in 2023, the economy leaned on Accommodation and Food Services and Manufacturing, both running well above the national norm for their sectors, while finance-sector jobs overall sat below it. Health care, food service, and retail trade together carried the bulk of employment. Home purchases made up 59.6 percent of mortgage originations across all lenders, evidence of a district built more on hospitality and factory floors than on finance.

Mike Flood.p1: Unemployment here sits among the lowest of any comparable district, at 3.1 percent, a marker of a tight labor market. Median household income is close to the middle of the pack at 77,659 dollars, in a district of 672,915 people. Housing is unusually affordable: a median home value of 278,400 dollars against that income points to a low ratio between the two. Homeownership trails other districts, and people here live spread thin across the land.
Mike Flood.p2: Credit unions hold just 13.0 percent of retail offices in this district, a smaller footprint than banks claim almost everywhere else in this comparison. Pentagon, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Cobalt are the names carrying that share. Union Bank and Trust Company books a large share of deposits under federal reporting rules, one of many bank branches here and not a sign of an empty field of rivals. Credit union employment tracks the national norm closely, proportionate to a district this size.
Mike Flood.p3: Transportation and warehousing, public administration, and manufacturing stood out as this district's specialized sectors as of 2023, each employing above the national norm. Health care and social assistance, manufacturing, and retail trade together carried substantial shares of the job base. Overall finance and insurance employment sat at the national norm, though its growth lagged over the prior decade. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, making up 60.7 percent of originations.

Mike Haridopolos.p1: Owner occupancy reaches 78 percent here, among the highest levels in comparable districts. The median household earns 78,386 dollars, and the middle home is valued at 378,100 dollars. Rent extends well into four figures each month and sits high beside peer places, while the median age is older than usual. This is a district defined more by stable ownership than by a population moving through rentals.
Mike Haridopolos.p2: Credit unions operate 31.9 percent of retail offices, enough to make them a substantial part of the branch market. Space Coast, Community Credit Union of Florida, and Launch Credit Union provide the leading cooperative names. Federal deposit records list Wells Fargo ahead locally, but many other banks maintain branches here. Credit union employment has unusually high national concentration and outweighs the location footprint, a pattern that aligns with the district's high owner-occupancy rate.
Mike Haridopolos.p3: Manufacturing and construction each have greater local weight than the national norm, joined by an unusual concentration in arts, entertainment, and recreation. Health care also provides many of the district's jobs. Overall finance employment remains far below its national baseline, making the credit union staffing position more distinctive than part of a broad financial cluster. Purchase loans accounted for most measured mortgage originations.

Mike Johnson.p1: In Louisiana's 4th district, typical household earnings land near the bottom of the national range, at $60,858. Home values stay low as well, and what renters pay each month claims only a small slice of local pay. Homeownership climbs to near 71 percent, even as poverty and joblessness both run well beyond what most districts show. Spread across just under 53 people per square mile, this is rural, low-density ground.
Mike Johnson.p2: Credit union employment here runs highly specialized against the national norm, well ahead of the credit union office footprint, which trails behind it, notable given how thin finance work runs across the district overall. Barksdale, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Carter hold the largest presence among them, together claiming 24.0 percent of retail offices in the district. Origin Bank books the largest local deposits under federal reporting rules, one name among many separate banks with branches here competing for the same borrowers described above.
Mike Johnson.p3: As of 2023, total employment stood near 204,200 jobs, with mining and oil and gas extraction running highly specialized, at over five times the national norm. Health care, retail trade, and food service made up a large share of work, while finance and insurance jobs overall ran thin against the national picture. This remains a district built on extraction and land, not banking.

Mike Kelly.p1: Housing here costs little against what people earn: a home value sits at only 3.1 times median household income, among the lowest such ratios of any district measured. Median household income runs modest at $67,473, well short of what many comparable districts report. Most residents own rather than rent, and the district spreads out thinly rather than packing people in. Age skews a touch older, with a median of 43.4 years.
Mike Kelly.p2: Credit unions hold 29.9 percent of retail offices here, a bigger slice than comparable districts typically show, working alongside a banking market where PNC Bank has more deposits booked to it than any other name under federal reporting rules, which need not mean the widest branch network or customer base. ERIE, ARMCO, and WIDGET are the names that show up here at scale. Offices run well ahead of the national norm while credit union jobs sit almost exactly at it, so the presence shows up more in storefronts than in payrolls. That is a lot of institutional reach for a population whose incomes and home prices sit on the modest side.
Mike Kelly.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing and health care anchored the job base, both running well ahead of typical national levels, with manufacturing alone employing 17.3 percent of workers. Retail trade also ran a little above the norm. Overall finance employment stayed below the national norm, a sign this district is built more on making and caring for things than on managing money.

Mike Kennedy.p1: Few congressional districts anywhere hold their population this loosely, a function of the sheer open land folded into its borders. The people here skew young, typical age just past thirty, and households bring in $96,440 at the midpoint, a sum that outpaces most other districts. Homes carry a steep median price of $611,400, yet the gap between what people earn and what housing costs runs narrower here than it does elsewhere. Fewer families here fall below the poverty line than in most comparable places.
Mike Kennedy.p2: Credit unions hold 45.0 percent of retail offices here, a share few other districts in the country can match. Mountain America, America First, and Utah Community anchor that presence, operating alongside 149 bank branches run by various competitors, including American Express National Bank, the top name by deposits booked here under federal rules rather than by local branches or customers. Credit union employment runs well above the national norm, and office presence further still, growing faster than the jobs inside those offices, a network built to serve the households and homebuyers described above.
Mike Kennedy.p3: As of 2023, mining and oil extraction stood out sharply here, several times the national norm, alongside an information sector more than twice as concentrated as the country overall. Health care, retail trade, and food service employed the most people, though none ran far from the national norm. Across roughly 383,000 jobs, this was a district shaped less by its largest sectors than by the unusual specialties layered on top of them.

Mike Lee.p1: Utah spreads its people thin across the land and skews young, the median resident just 32.5 years old. Construction carries unusual weight in the job base, well above the national norm, alongside steady work in mining. Households earn a median $96,658, comfortably ahead of most states, and poverty runs low while unemployment stays under 4 percent. Homeownership runs high, though a $545,200 median home value against that income points to a housing stock that has outpaced what people bring home.
Mike Lee.p2: Credit unions hold 51.9 percent of retail offices here, among the highest such share of any state, a footprint that matches a young, working, homeowning population more than it matches typical banking geography. America First, Mountain America, and Utah Community anchor that presence. Credit union employment runs at 2.46 times the national norm, heavier still than the office share alone would carry. Deposits nationwide get booked to a single Morgan Stanley Bank address here, which is why it tops the deposit figures despite having little local presence.
Mike Lee.p3: As of 2023, Utah's economy leaned on construction and manufacturing for jobs, both running above the national norm for their size. Finance and insurance jobs sat close to the norm overall but had climbed at a pace well ahead of the nation's over the ten years prior. What sets this state apart is the mix underneath: mining, building, and entertainment all punching above their weight, feeding a credit union sector that is unusually large for its size.

Mike Levin.p1: Household income in the 49th district of California outpaces nearly every other congressional seat, at 121,511 dollars. Home values sit just as high, a typical home priced at 1,133,300 dollars, nine and a third times that income. Ownership trails the wider pattern across districts, and the population is packed in tighter than most comparable seats.
Mike Levin.p2: Credit union employment here tracks the national norm closely, but credit union office presence lags well behind it, a gap wide enough that jobs are clearly outpacing branches on the ground. Navy Federal, San Diego County Credit Union, and a large statewide credit union anchor that presence, though credit unions hold only 19.3 percent of retail offices, well under what most similarly built districts carry. JPMorgan Chase holds the top deposit figure among the district's 128 bank branches, a reporting quirk more than a sign of dominance. For a credit union, this is a district of high-earning households currently served by a thin branch network relative to demand.
Mike Levin.p3: As of 2023, the local job mix leaned hard into accommodation and food service, arts and recreation, and professional and technical services, each well ahead of its typical national weight.
