Overall finance-sector employment ran far below what the country shows on average, even as finance and insurance growth over the prior decade kept pace with the country. Home purchase loans made up 45.6 percent of mortgage originations here. This is a district built on hospitality, culture, and technical expertise rather than finance or heavy industry.

Mike Quigley.p1: Homes and workplaces sit close together here, among the most densely populated districts anywhere, and the population, near 773,710, reflects that tight settlement. Incomes run high, with median household earnings of $111,545, alongside low poverty and low unemployment. Home values, at a median of $462,500, run well ahead of typical incomes, yet homeownership trails most comparable districts, a sign that renting is common even amid this affluence.
Mike Quigley.p2: Credit unions hold a thin slice of the retail banking market here, just 10.2 percent of offices, among the lowest shares measured anywhere. Alliant, Michigan State, and Polish & Slavic credit unions anchor what presence exists, operating in a market otherwise held by many bank branches, with deposits booked largest to JPMorgan Chase. Credit union employment here tracks that thin office footprint closely, both well under the national norm. For a credit union, this is a district of high earners and high housing costs, but not, so far, a district that banks with them.
Mike Quigley.p3: Measured in 2023, the local economy leaned hard on Transportation and Warehousing, employment there running at more than twice the national norm. Health Care and Social Assistance, Retail Trade, and Accommodation and Food Services together accounted for large shares of jobs. Overall finance sector employment ran below the national norm, a reminder that this district's financial weight sits more in household income than in financial jobs. Mortgage lending here leaned heavily toward home purchases, 65.6 percent of all originations that year.

Mike Rogers.p1: This district's median household income, 62,191 dollars, falls short of nearly every comparable seat, and that shortfall shows up everywhere else in the numbers. Home prices are similarly restrained, at 207,800 dollars, alongside rent that stays low as well. Owning a home is far more common than renting one, even while the poverty rate climbs well above most congressional districts. Few people live per square mile, marking this as a rural stretch of Alabama rather than a dense one.
Mike Rogers.p2: Credit unions here employ people at 1.52 times the national norm, yet their office footprint climbs further still, to 1.68 times, a gap worth flagging before anything else about the sector. America's First, AOD, and Emblem anchor that footprint. Credit unions hold 26.6 percent of retail offices, competing alongside Regions Bank, named here for deposits booked locally among a wider field of area banks. Modest earnings paired with widespread homeownership give a credit union network this size exactly the customer base it was built to serve.
Mike Rogers.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing anchored the economy, employing 17.2 percent of the district's jobs at nearly twice the national norm. Retail trade also ran above the norm. Broader finance employment sat well below that norm even as the sector's growth roughly matched the national pace over the prior decade. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, with only a modest share reaching lower income neighborhoods.

Mike Rounds.p1: South Dakota spreads its people thin, only about twelve per square mile, and the work follows that pattern: agriculture holds a specialized grip on the economy well beyond the national norm, alongside wholesale trade and public administration. Health care, retail, and manufacturing employ the most people, each running slightly above the national mix. Housing costs land among the lowest in the country, a home value of 289,600 dollars against rent near 999 dollars a month, and homeownership is common. Unemployment is about as low as it gets anywhere.
Mike Rounds.p2: Credit unions hold 20.3 percent of retail offices here, a smaller slice than most states carry, against a banking sector with many competing names. Black Hills, Dakotaland, and Levo anchor that footprint, doing more with less: credit union jobs run at 1.32 times the national norm even though offices sit at a slighter 1.16, staffing outpacing the office count itself. That gap suits a state where low density and modest housing costs favor lean, well-staffed institutions over wide branch networks. Citibank, National Association books the largest deposit share under federal rules, not by branch presence or local customers.
Mike Rounds.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance jobs overall ran at 1.22 times the national norm, though growth in that combined category lagged behind. The working economy leaned hardest on agriculture, its concentration far above the typical state, with wholesale trade and government work close behind. This is a place built for steady, land-tied work rather than density or fast churn.

Mike Thompson.p1: Unemployment here runs higher than in almost any comparable district, at 6.5 percent, and poverty climbs above most peers too. Median household income still reaches 98,067 dollars, well clear of most districts, a combination that points to real spread between households. Home values run seven times the median income, and just 62.5 percent of residents own their homes, a lower share than most places this affluent. Population density stays thin, under most peer districts, in a West Coast seat that otherwise sits among the more affluent ones.
Mike Thompson.p2: Credit union employment here runs slightly ahead of the national norm while office presence sits almost exactly at it, a gap worth noting, jobs are outpacing branches. Redwood, Travis, and The Golden 1 anchor that presence, and together credit unions hold 26.6 percent of retail offices, against 127 bank branches led on deposits by Wells Fargo. For a district with this much income spread and a homeownership rate lagging its wealth, that mismatch between thin office growth and stronger staffing shapes how these institutions can actually reach people.
Mike Thompson.p3: As of 2023, the working economy leaned hardest into agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting, well above five times the national norm, alongside educational services and arts and recreation, both running above typical levels. Finance and insurance employment overall stayed well below the national norm, though its growth over the prior decade nearly kept pace nationally. Mortgage lending leaned toward home purchases, with a modest share reaching lower-income neighborhoods.

Mitch McConnell.p1: Kentucky is home to 4,588,372 people with a median age of 39.3, and household income sits low, among the lowest of any state at $64,526. Housing costs stay modest to match, with rent near $998 a month and homeownership common across the state. Poverty runs high here, and unemployment sits a step above what most states report. Wages lag, but the cost of living stays low enough to soften that gap.
Mitch McConnell.p2: Commonwealth, L&N, and Abound carry the credit union presence across Kentucky, yet credit unions hold only 14.4 percent of retail offices statewide, a smaller footprint than most states show. Banking here still runs through branch networks where deposits are booked under national reporting rules that do not always reflect who serves customers locally. Credit union employment runs thinner than the national norm as well, meaning offices exist without matching staff behind them. For a credit union in Kentucky, the market is a moderate earner in a state where banking competition is dispersed rather than concentrated.
Mitch McConnell.p3: As measured in 2023, Kentucky's economy leaned hard on manufacturing, employing 13.9 percent of workers at well over one and a half times the national norm. Transportation and warehousing showed similar strength, another sector where the state outpaces the country. Health care and retail trade employed larger shares of workers still, though without the same concentration. Overall finance employment stayed below the national norm, in a state whose economy leaned industrial rather than financial.

Monica De La Cruz.p1: Poverty runs high in the 15th congressional seat of Texas, among the highest of any comparable district, and it colors everything else here. Median household income sits at 62,554 dollars, far short of most peers, and unemployment is elevated as well. Housing stays comparatively within reach, with a median home value of 197,300 dollars set against typical earnings, yielding a value-to-income ratio of 3.2. The district is spread out rather than dense.
Monica De La Cruz.p2: Credit union offices here outnumber, in relative terms, what credit union employment alone would predict, a gap worth flagging up front: jobs run at 0.59 times the national norm while office presence sits closer to typical at 0.86. Rally, Randolph-Brooks, and Security Service carry that office presence, though credit unions hold just 16.7 percent of retail offices, a thinner footprint than most peer districts. International Bank of Commerce holds the largest share of deposits booked among the district's many bank branches. That crowded field leaves credit unions working a smaller slice of the market described above.
Monica De La Cruz.p3: Health care and social assistance and educational services together anchor employment here, both running well above the national norm for their size in this district. The standout was mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction, small in headcount but far more concentrated than anything else measured. Overall finance-sector employment lagged the national norm. Energy and public-service work, more than banking, define the district's economic character.

Morgan Griffith.p1: Household income in the 9th district of Virginia sits at $59,156, among the lowest of any congressional district, and poverty runs high alongside it. Housing is inexpensive beside local pay: a median home value of $197,500 and rent near $888 a month, with homeownership common in the district. Unemployment is low. At 77.7 people per square mile, this is a rural, sparsely settled district where steady work does not always mean good pay.
Morgan Griffith.p2: Credit unions hold just 13.9 percent of retail offices here, a thin share next to other districts, leaving banks, led on deposits by Truist, as the dominant presence on the ground. Virginia, Eastman, and Freedom First are the credit unions with a foothold in the district. Credit union staffing and locations both fall below the national norm, with staffing lagging the offices that do exist. For a district this income-strapped, that leaves few local alternatives to bank lending.
Morgan Griffith.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing was a leading and heavily concentrated line of work in the district, holding 16.1 percent of jobs and running well ahead of the national norm for its size. Educational services followed as a second specialty, and mining, though a small slice of employment, ran far ahead of national levels too. Health care rounded out the largest sectors without running ahead of national norms. Purchase mortgages dominated originations; lending to lower-income neighborhoods formed a much smaller portion.

Morgan Luttrell.p1: Unemployment in the 8th congressional seat of Texas runs well above most comparable districts, at 5.5 percent, even though median household income clears $91,806 and poverty stays low. Homeownership runs high too, well ahead of other districts, and home values sit near 3.6 times median income. Almost 950,000 people call the district home, and the typical resident is in their late thirties.
Morgan Luttrell.p2: Credit unions hold just 12.3 percent of retail offices here, a small slice compared with other districts, leaving banks with most of the footprint. FivePoint, Texas Dow Employees, and First Community carry what credit union presence exists. JPMorgan Chase books more in local deposits than any other name, though that outcome follows from how deposits get booked rather than from any edge in branches or customers on the ground. Credit union employment runs far short of the national norm, and so does the office count, so the office network has shrunk faster than the jobs behind it.
Morgan Luttrell.p3: As of 2023, mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction stood out sharply, running well above the national norm despite a small share of jobs. Construction ran specialized as well. Finance and insurance employment overall sat under the national norm, though that sector grew faster than the country across the years since 2013. Home purchase loans made up most mortgage originations recorded.

Morgan McGarvey.p1: Unemployment stands out here first, at 6.1 percent and well above many peer seats. Households earn less than typical too, with median income at 68,989 dollars, while a larger than usual share of residents live in poverty. Home values sit low, at 249,300 dollars, and fewer households own their homes than is typical elsewhere. This is a denser district than most, a working population packed into a smaller footprint than usual.
Morgan McGarvey.p2: Credit union staffing here is thinner than the countrywide baseline even though credit union offices are somewhat more common than typical, a split worth noticing in a district this financially active. L & N, Park, and Liberty carry that location footprint, which reaches 24.9 percent of retail locations, well ahead of what many peer seats show. PNC Bank, National Association books more deposits to addresses here than any other bank, though many others operate branches across the district. Together that gives credit unions a defined role with the households described above.
Morgan McGarvey.p3: In 2023, Transportation and Warehousing dominated the district's specialization, employing workers at more than twice the countrywide baseline. Manufacturing and Finance and Insurance followed as specialized sectors, and finance overall staffing ran well ahead of the norm even as its growth lagged slightly behind. Mortgage lending leaned toward home purchases, making up 58.9 percent of originations, with 30.3 percent of loans reaching lower-income neighborhoods.

Nancy Mace.p1: Unemployment sits at just 2.6 percent, among the lowest of any congressional district in the country, and it sets the tone for the rest of the picture. Households here earn a median of 95,136 dollars, well above the typical district, while homeownership runs high at 76.6 percent. That ownership comes against a median home value of 466,400 dollars, nearly five times the median household income. This is a coastal South Carolina seat of stable work and expensive shelter.
Nancy Mace.p2: Credit union employment here runs slightly above the national norm even though credit union office presence runs slightly below it, an odd pairing worth noting on its own. Navy Federal Credit Union, South Carolina Credit Union, and Rev Federal Credit Union anchor that presence. Credit unions hold just 18.7 percent of retail offices, a smaller slice than most comparable districts carry, against a banking market where Wells Fargo books the largest deposit total among many competing banks. That leaves credit unions serving a well-paid, high-homeownership population from a comparatively thin office base.
Nancy Mace.p3: As of 2023, the district's economy leaned hardest on utilities, a sector far more concentrated here than the national norm, alongside real estate and the arts. Retail trade and accommodation and food services stood out too, both employing far more of the workforce than is typical elsewhere. Finance and insurance jobs, though a modest share overall, grew fast over the prior decade.

Nancy Pelosi.p1: Few districts anywhere pack residents together the way this one does, over 17,600 people per square mile, and that fact runs through every other number here. Households earn among the highest incomes of any district, but home values sit just as high, and homeownership is rare. Unemployment runs high here despite that income level.
Nancy Pelosi.p2: Credit unions hold one of the lowest shares of retail offices of any district, just 11.4 percent, so banks book the bulk of deposits and business here. Bank of America appears first on the locally assigned deposit measure in federal reports, within a field where numerous other banks compete. San Francisco Fire, San Francisco, and Patelco provide the principal credit union names. Credit union jobs are scarce against the national norm, and even the thin office presence still outnumbers them. That leaves a small cooperative footprint serving an unusually high-income, renter-heavy population.
Nancy Pelosi.p3: The 2023 employment mix depended heavily on professional, scientific, and technical services, which accounted for a fifth of jobs and ran well above typical concentration nationally, alongside an even more concentrated information sector. Utilities had an unusual concentration despite their small size. Purchase loans were the principal type of mortgage origination. Lower-income neighborhoods received a modest portion of lending.

Nanette Barragán.p1: This district packs people in tightly, among the most densely settled in the country, and that density shapes everything else here. Households earn a median $90,834, well ahead of typical districts, but housing costs run further still: a median home value of $746,200 puts the value-to-income ratio at 8.2, and rent claims 23.6 percent of the median household's earnings. Homeownership sits below most comparable districts. Poverty and unemployment both run higher than typical here.
Nanette Barragán.p2: Credit union employment runs closer to the national norm than credit union office presence does, an unusual split worth noting: offices are thinly staffed relative to the industry standard, yet the jobs on the ground hold up better than that would imply. Three institutions anchor the credit union presence here, holding 27.8 percent of retail offices, a share ahead of most other districts. JPMorgan Chase leads all banks by deposits booked here, one name among several competing institutions with a presence in the district.
Nanette Barragán.p3: As of 2023, the district's work leaned hard into logistics: Transportation and Warehousing accounted for 13.1 percent of jobs, nearly three times the national norm, the clearest specialization in the local economy. Administrative and support services and wholesale trade followed as secondary strengths, each running well above typical national levels. Health care and manufacturing rounded out the leading employing sectors, both close to national norms. Mortgage lending split close to national patterns, with home purchases making up a large share of all originations that year.

Nathaniel Moran.p1: People spread thin across this district, just 84.1 residents per square mile, a settlement pattern well below most comparable districts and the fact that sets it apart most. Household income sits at $66,563, a modest figure by congressional district standards, and home values follow suit at a median of $216,800. Renters give up under a fifth of income on rent, and ownership is common, close to 70 percent of households. Both poverty and joblessness sit a notch above what most districts report.
Nathaniel Moran.p2: Credit union offices here outpace credit union jobs, an unusual split worth noting before anything else: office presence runs well above the national norm while employment growth trails it. Eastman, East Texas Professional, and Altra anchor that presence, together holding 24.9 percent of retail offices, a sizeable slice compared with other districts. Southside Bank leads locally by deposits booked here, one name among 280 bank branches run by many competitors. For a district with modest incomes and a heavy homeowner base, credit unions carry more local weight in branch presence than in jobs.
Nathaniel Moran.p3: As measured in 2023, the economy leaned hard on oil and gas extraction, a highly specialized corner of the district's base. Manufacturing was thick on the ground too, employing over a tenth of workers. Health care employed a substantial share of workers as well. Overall finance employment ran below the national norm, leaving credit unions to carry a heavier share of that sector locally than jobs data alone would capture.

Neal Dunn.p1: Population sits thin on the ground in this district, far more so than comparable seats, with 819,004 residents at a median age of 39.0. Household income falls short of most other districts at $66,684, and both poverty and unemployment run higher than typical here. The typical home is valued at $286,000, modest against the wider field, while homeownership itself lags behind most peers.
Neal Dunn.p2: Credit unions hold 36.3 percent of retail offices here, a share among the highest of any comparable district. Tyndall, Addition Financial, and Innovations Financial carry that presence, alongside Centennial Bank, which leads all institutions on deposits credited to its local address under federal reporting rules, among many separate lenders that also operate branches here. Credit union employment runs well above the national norm, and office presence tracks closely with it, a mark of a place where credit unions carry unusual weight in local finance.
Neal Dunn.p3: As measured in 2023, government work anchored this district's economy, with Public Administration making up 14.5 percent of jobs, over three times the national norm. Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting also ran far above typical levels despite touching a small share of workers. Overall finance and insurance employment stayed below the national norm, even as that broader sector grew faster here than across the country over the prior decade.

Nellie Pou.p1: Few districts in the country pack residents in as tightly as this one, at 6,974.4 people per square mile. Household income runs comfortably above typical districts at 87,122 dollars, yet housing costs outpace it: a home value to income ratio of 5.9 and rent near 1,784 dollars a month. Homeownership sits low, just 49.3 percent, and unemployment runs high as well.
Nellie Pou.p2: Credit unions account for only 8.5 percent of retail banking offices here, among the lowest shares of any district. VISIONS, Polish & Slavic, and NOVA UA are the names carrying that presence, set against a deposit market led by TD Bank, National Association, which shares this crowded field with many other banks. Credit union employment runs far below what the national picture would predict, and office presence lags similarly. For a district this dense and this costly, credit unions occupy a small corner of where money moves.
Nellie Pou.p3: Measured in 2023, the job base leaned hard on wholesale trade, well above the national norm, alongside transportation and warehousing and real estate leasing, both concentrated here. Health care, retail, and manufacturing employed the most people, without matching that concentration. Finance and insurance employment overall ran well below what the nation would predict. Across all lenders, home purchases made up most mortgage originations, with a smaller share reaching lower income neighborhoods.

Nicholas Begich.p1: This district covers the entire state of Alaska, and it holds barely more than one person per square mile, among the emptiest stretches held by any seat in the country. That vastness sits alongside a median household income of $95,665, well clear of what most districts report, and homes that run at 3.9 times income. Rent takes 18.1 percent of the median household's earnings, lighter than most places manage. Unemployment runs high for a place this prosperous on paper, even as poverty stays low.
Nicholas Begich.p2: Credit unions hold 40.5 percent of retail offices here, a share among the highest anywhere in the country. Global, Credit Union 1, and Nuvision anchor that presence, while Wells Fargo books the biggest deposits credited to addresses in this district, a distinction that says more about reporting rules than about branch counts. Credit union employment runs at over triple the national norm, well ahead of the pace set by their office count alone. In a state this spread out, that office share carries more weight than it would somewhere denser.
Nicholas Begich.p3: In 2016, the working economy leaned hard on public administration and on mining and oil extraction, the latter specialized far beyond national norms despite a modest share of jobs. Transportation and warehousing also ran well above typical levels, reflecting a state built around moving people and goods across long distance. Health care employed more people than any other sector. Broader finance and insurance employment sat below national norms even as credit unions themselves stood apart.

Nicholas Langworthy.p1: Housing here costs little against what people earn: the median home value runs 2.7 times the median household income, a ratio lower than nearly any other district, and rent takes just 15.2 percent of it. Household income sits at $74,552, trailing most comparable seats. Homeownership is common, well past the typical district. People are spread thin on the land here, far more so than in most seats.
Nicholas Langworthy.p2: Credit unions hold 40.0 percent of retail offices here, a share among the highest of any district in the country. Corning, Visions, and First Heritage anchor that presence, competing against 175 bank branches run by many separate banks, the largest by deposits booked to Manufacturers and Traders Trust Company. Credit union employment runs close to the national norm on the high side, and their office presence stretches further still, a much denser branch footprint than the jobs alone would predict. That footprint sits on the modest incomes and low housing costs described above.
Nicholas Langworthy.p3: As measured in 2023, manufacturing defined the district, employing 15.3 percent of workers at well above the national norm. Educational services followed, also specialized, and public administration ran above the national norm too. Overall finance employment ran well short of the national norm, even with credit unions so thick on the ground. The district's boundaries changed at the last redrawing, so its ten year comparisons span two different maps.

Nick LaLota.p1: Household income in this district reaches $130,141, a figure few other districts in the country can match, and everything nearby follows that lead. Homes are worth $674,100 at the midpoint, a number that outpaces most of the country, and monthly rent lands near $2,332. Homeownership is common, and poverty is rare. This is also a dense stretch of the Northeast, built up rather than spread out.
Nick LaLota.p2: Credit union employment here holds close to the national norm, even as credit union offices sit well below it, so the jobs on the ground outnumber what the branch network alone would predict. Teachers, Fourleaf, and Suffolk supply that local presence. Credit unions account for just 17.8 percent of retail deposit-taking offices here, a smaller share than most comparable districts carry, with JPMorgan Chase the largest bank by deposits booked to this district. For an institution working here, that means a leaner branch footprint set against the high incomes and housing costs described above.
Nick LaLota.p3: The job base leans into administrative and support services and construction, both measured as more concentrated here than the national norm. Overall finance-sector employment runs below the national norm, and growth in finance and insurance jobs has trailed that norm too. Mortgage lending leans heavily toward home purchases, making up 51.2 percent of originations, with a smaller slice reaching lower-income neighborhoods. That mix describes a district with money concentrated at the top and comparatively little financial-sector hiring to match it.

Nicole Malliotakis.p1: Few congressional districts anywhere pack people together the way this one does, at more than 11,800 residents per square mile. The typical household clears $90,759 a year, ahead of most comparable districts, yet housing swallows that advantage: home values run 7.9 times income, and rent lands at a median $1,749 a month. Homeownership here trails well behind most peer districts, and poverty sits above the norm for places like it despite those healthy paychecks.
Nicole Malliotakis.p2: Credit unions hold just 4.4 percent of retail offices here, among the lowest shares of any district in the country, leaving banks to dominate this market. JPMorgan Chase leads by deposits booked locally, one name among many banks with a branch presence in the district. Municipal, Polish & Slavic, and Advantage Financial carry what credit union presence exists. Credit union employment runs at a tenth of the national norm, a striking gap given how dense and well paid the population around it is.
Nicole Malliotakis.p3: As of 2023, health care and social assistance alone accounted for 30.0 percent of jobs in the district, far above the national norm. Transportation and warehousing ran even further ahead of that norm in relative terms, and educational services rounded out the district's third specialty. Overall finance and insurance employment fell below the national norm even so. Mortgage lending skewed heavily toward home purchases over refinancing.

Nikema Williams.p1: Homeownership here sits among the lowest of any congressional district, a defining fact for a place this crowded. The district packs 3,427.6 people per square mile, and the typical resident is just 34.7 years old. Median household income runs 80,567 dollars, yet housing costs run high against comparable districts, while poverty and unemployment climb well past what most peer districts report. This is a dense, young, renter-heavy economy still finding its footing.
Nikema Williams.p2: Credit union employment here barely registers, running at 0.41 times the national norm, even though credit unions hold 23.8 percent of retail offices, so offices clearly outpace jobs on the ground. Delta Community, Navy Federal, and Associated Credit Union carry that presence, working the same renters and lower-income borrowers described above. Bank of America books a sizable deposit total in the district, one name among many bank branches competing here. For a district this size, credit unions are a real but thin channel, more storefronts than staff.
Nikema Williams.p3: Measured back in 2023, this economy ran hot in Information and in Management of Companies and Enterprises, well above the national norm in both, alongside a heavily specialized Transportation and Warehousing sector. Health care employed a large share of workers but without that same specialization. Lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, which made up 63.1 percent of all originations, with a substantial share reaching lower-income neighborhoods, a market still working to serve the renters who define this place.

Nikki Budzinski.p1: Home values in the 13th district are among the lowest of any congressional district, at $167,800, and that fact shapes everything else here. Household income falls short of the national picture, and poverty runs deeper than the typical district shows. Rent stays modest against income, and ownership trails what most districts report. Unemployment is unremarkable, across a population spread thinly through the Midwest.
Nikki Budzinski.p2: Credit union employment here is specialized against the national norm, at 1.7 times, but the office footprint climbs a step higher still, at 1.81 times, so branches have opened faster than the staff to fill them. Citizens Equity First, 1st MidAmerica, and First Community carry that presence, holding 22.4 percent of retail offices against Busey Bank and a crowded roster of competing banks. For a population managing modest paychecks and cheap housing, that is a real foothold for cooperative finance, even if it looks ordinary next to other districts.
Nikki Budzinski.p3: As measured in 2023, the district leaned hard on government work, where Public Administration held a large share of jobs at nearly three times the national norm. Other public-facing services also carried unusual weight in the job base. Overall finance employment ran below the national norm, leaving public-sector work, not banking, as the thing this district does best.

Norma Torres.p1: A home in the 35th district of California carries a price nearly seven times the median household income, a ratio among the highest of any congressional district measured, and rent claims 27.2 percent of that income each month. Earnings themselves, at $94,230, outpace most other districts, but ownership belongs to just 57.5 percent of households, a smaller share than most places see. Work here goes unfound at a higher rate than in most comparable places. The district is also dense, built more around apartments and commutes than yards.
Norma Torres.p2: Credit unions hold 29.4 percent of retail offices here, a share few other districts can match, and a real counterweight to the 77 bank branches also operating locally. Names carrying that share include Navy Federal Credit Union, Arrowhead, and a large statewide institution serving public employees. Employment inside credit unions and the number of credit union offices both sit below the national norm, moving together rather than one outpacing the other. Against the income and housing pressures described above, that share of offices is what this district actually leans on.
Norma Torres.p3: Work here, as measured in 2023, concentrated heavily in transportation and warehousing, which ran more than three times the national norm and made up 15.7 percent of jobs. Wholesale trade ran well above typical levels too. Health care employed large numbers locally, though at a level close to the national norm. This is a logistics and distribution economy first, with everything else built around it.

Nydia Velázquez.p1: This district is packed about as tightly as anywhere in the country, with more than 35,000 people per square mile. Households here earn a median of $92,194, well above what most districts see, but home values and rent sit among the highest anywhere measured. Just 22.1 percent of households own their homes, and poverty and joblessness both climb higher than the norm. This is a renter's district, dense and expensive at once.
Nydia Velázquez.p2: Credit unions here include United Nations, Fourleaf, and Polish & Slavic, and together they hold just 16.5 percent of retail offices, a much smaller footprint than comparable districts show. Bank branches far outnumber them, with JPMorgan Chase booking the most deposits locally, even as other banks keep their own branches on the ground here. Credit union employment stays similarly light against the national norm. For the renters and middle earners described above, credit unions sit on the margins of a market banks control.
Nydia Velázquez.p3: Public administration anchored the local economy as of 2023, accounting for close to a tenth of all jobs in the district and towering over typical concentrations found nationally. Health care and social assistance carried the single biggest slice of the workforce. Real estate and utilities also registered as specialized, an unusual pairing for a government town. Overall finance employment ran below national levels, and its growth over the prior decade lagged the national pace too.

Pablo Hernández Rivera.p1: Puerto Rico is dense and aging at once, packed at 935.4 people per square mile with a median age of 45.4. Households get by on a median income of 27,213 dollars, among the lowest of any state, and poverty there runs deep. Homeownership still sits at 69.3 percent, well above what most states manage, even as unemployment stays higher than nearly anywhere else on the mainland.
Pablo Hernández Rivera.p2: A credit union here is not lending against comfortable margins. Thin household incomes and a housing market where prices badly outrun what people earn mean underwriting has to work harder to reach the same family a mainland lender would take for granted. Credit union employment on the island runs below the national norm, a workforce stretched thin against a population that still needs somewhere local to bank.
Pablo Hernández Rivera.p3: Home values remain low in dollar terms, a median of 142,100 dollars, and rent runs just as modest at 580 dollars a month, yet both consume an outsized share of what households actually earn. What sets Puerto Rico apart is not a single strong sector but sheer scale of need packed into a small footprint, a market dense enough to reach and poor enough that reaching it takes real commitment.

Pat Fallon.p1: This district's median household income, $99,301, stands well above most comparable districts, alongside poverty and unemployment rates that both run low. Home values reach $437,300 and rent runs high too, figures that sit above typical districts without pinching household budgets given the earnings here. Homeownership, at 64.3 percent, trails many peer districts, a sign that renting holds real ground even in a high-income place. Population density stays low, leaving room between houses across the district.
Pat Fallon.p2: Credit Union of Texas, Texans, and EECU anchor the credit union presence here, holding 24.7 percent of retail offices, well ahead of what most comparable districts show. JPMorgan Chase Bank books a large sum of deposits within these boundaries, one name among 232 bank branches, the rest split across many other institutions competing here. Credit union employment tracks the national norm closely rather than running noticeably thick or thin. For a district this affluent, credit unions have carved out a genuine foothold alongside the banks.
Pat Fallon.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance anchored the district's economy, employing a share of the workforce reaching well beyond the typical national concentration. Professional, scientific, and technical services employed a large share of workers too, a strength alongside finance rather than instead of it. Management of companies added a further layer of specialization uncommon elsewhere. Lending here leaned heavily toward home purchases over refinancing, shaped by finance work and higher earners throughout.

Pat Harrigan.p1: Joblessness is the clearest demographic distinction in North Carolina's 10th, holding at 3.0 percent. Its 787,565 residents otherwise occupy mixed economic ground: median household earnings are $71,999, the middle home is worth $309,200, and poverty is elevated beside peer seats. Owner occupancy and the weight of housing costs stay near ordinary national levels. The result is a place with plentiful work but less uniform household security.
Pat Harrigan.p2: Local credit union staffing reaches 1.59 times the national concentration, while office density is much closer to ordinary. That imbalance means the institutions employ more people than their physical network alone would predict. State Employees', Allegacy, and Truliant are prominent; collectively credit unions command 27.0 percent of retail banking locations. Truist Bank carries the foremost locally booked deposit total, one participant in a competitive bank field. Credit unions therefore have meaningful local scale without dominating the storefront market.
Pat Harrigan.p3: In the 2023 employment picture, manufacturing supplied the most distinctive concentration. Management of companies and enterprises was another unusually common line of work. Health care and social assistance joined retail trade as large job fields, while finance and insurance remained near its national baseline. The combined finance sector nonetheless expanded faster locally during the preceding decade. Mortgage originations focused primarily on purchases, another practical tie between household needs and local lenders.

Patrick Ryan.p1: Household income sets this district apart before anything else, at 91,635 dollars a year, well past the mark most comparable districts reach. Home values, at 423,700 dollars, and rent, at 1,665 dollars a month, climb along with it, while homeownership holds at a middling level. Poverty stays low against comparable places, joblessness inching up somewhat by contrast. Population density here lands squarely in the middle of the pack.
Patrick Ryan.p2: Credit union jobs cluster here at 2.22 times the national norm, a level the office count itself does not match, a gap worth flagging before anything else about the sector. Those offices still claim 24.9 percent of retail branch share, with Hudson Valley, Pentagon, and Mid-Hudson Valley among the names holding that ground. A large national bank tops the local deposit figures booked to addresses here, a number shaped more by reporting rules than by branch strength, and it still contends with many competing banks nearby.
Patrick Ryan.p3: As of 2023, Educational Services marked itself as the standout sector, specialized well past what national job patterns show elsewhere. Health Care and Retail Trade carried large shares of the workforce without that same concentration. Finance-sector employment overall sat well under the national norm, even as finance and insurance jobs broadly grew almost in step with it. Mortgage activity here tilted toward home purchases rather than refinancing, spanning all lenders active in the district.

Patty Murray.p1: Washington's economy runs on information and trade rather than volume retail: tech and media jobs sit at roughly two and a half times the national norm, and agriculture runs even higher. The state spreads its 7,958,180 people thinly, under 120 per square mile. Median household income is well above most states at $99,389, and home values and rents run high enough to match it. Homeownership and poverty both run below typical levels, even as unemployment climbs higher than most states see.
Patty Murray.p2: Credit unions hold 32.9 percent of retail offices here, a large share for a state this thinly settled. Boeing Employees, Navy Federal, and GESA anchor that presence, set against a banking market where Bank of America books the largest deposits among many competing banks statewide. Credit union jobs run at 1.64 times the national norm, outpacing even that strong office share, meaning these institutions do more with each location. That fits a population earning well and paying dearly for housing, exactly the base a credit union here has to serve.
Patty Murray.p3: Finance and insurance jobs overall are thin against the national norm, growing at roughly the typical pace as of the 2023 count. Health care and retail carry the most jobs but neither runs hot by national standards. What sets this state apart is concentration at the top: information and management jobs cluster far beyond typical levels, a state built less on broad employment than on a handful of sectors it does exceptionally well.

Paul Gosar.p1: Population thins out fast across the 9th congressional seat of Arizona, settling at just 39.4 people per square mile, a rate few other districts fall below. Within that space live 915,903 residents earning a median household income that is typical nationally. Housing costs run high against that income, with a home value to income ratio of 5.1, yet homeownership is common here. Unemployment runs high too, even as poverty stays lower than in most other districts.
Paul Gosar.p2: Arizona Financial, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Desert Financial anchor the credit union presence here, holding 25.6 percent of retail offices between them, a share bigger than most districts see. Credit union employment sits below the national norm, and their office count runs just as thin. JPMorgan Chase carries the largest deposit sum on paper among institutions with addresses here, a booking quirk more than proof of dominance, since many separate banks compete for business locally. For a district spread this wide, credit unions represent an established way for people to actually reach a teller.
Paul Gosar.p3: As measured in 2023, agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting stood out sharply, running at nearly eight times the national norm for this district. Retail trade employed a large share of workers, 16.3 percent of total jobs. All finance and insurance jobs ran well below the national norm here. This is a district shaped by land-based industry and everyday consumer trades, not by finance.

Paul Tonko.p1: This district holds people more thinly spread out than most comparable seats, though still above the norm for density, a mix of small cities and open ground across 790,733 residents. Median household income sits at 85,230 dollars, well above many other districts, while home values run lower than most at 319,100 dollars. Rent runs 1,347 dollars a month. Unemployment stays thin next to comparable districts, and homeownership trails most as well.
Paul Tonko.p2: Credit unions here hold 31.6 percent of retail offices, a share well above most comparable districts. Broadview, Hudson Valley, and Sunmark anchor that presence, while KeyBank National Association leads a wider field of competing banks on deposits booked to this ground. Credit union jobs run at 2.22 times the national norm, a highly specialized concentration that outpaces the district's own office count. For an institution working this ground, that is a deep bench of local peers and a workforce built around the business.
Paul Tonko.p3: Government work carried heavy weight in this district's 2023 job count, a highly specialized share running well above the national norm. Educational services and health care followed, each a modest step above the norm. Finance and insurance jobs sat close to the national pace, and the broader finance sector added workers more slowly than the country did across the decade before. Home loans made up most mortgage activity here, and a smaller portion of that lending reached lower income neighborhoods.

Pete Aguilar.p1: This district packs people into close quarters, with more than 783,000 residents and density far beyond peer seats. Household earnings are comparatively strong, yet values and rents push housing costs higher still, while owner occupancy is relatively uncommon. Poverty and unemployment are somewhat elevated against similar places, a reminder that the income figure averages over real unevenness.
Pete Aguilar.p2: Credit union staffing is less concentrated than the credit union office network, the main split to notice. A large statewide credit union, a regional one, and Navy Federal Credit Union anchor that presence, and together credit unions hold 27.5 percent of retail offices, a share well above most peer districts. JPMorgan Chase carries the top deposit total booked locally, though that reflects reporting geography more than branch strength among the district's 56 bank branches. For a credit union here, the opening lies less in payroll and more in serving a dense, high-cost population that banks handle unevenly.
Pete Aguilar.p3: As measured in 2023, work in this district leaned heavily on transportation and warehousing, employing more than five times the national share, a specialization far beyond anything else recorded. Public administration also had unusual local weight. Overall finance employment trailed the national norm by a wide margin, and its growth over the prior decade lagged as well. Purchase mortgages dominated the lending mix. Some originations went to lower-income neighborhoods.

Pete Ricketts.p1: Nebraska's economy is spread thin across land rather than piled into cities: people barely number 26 per square mile. That sparseness sits alongside real specialization in agriculture, which runs well above the national norm, and manufacturing, which employs over a tenth of the workforce. Unemployment stays low, and housing remains cheap by national standards, with rent claiming 17.3 percent of the median household's income of 76,376 dollars.
Pete Ricketts.p2: Credit unions hold just 12.6 percent of retail offices here, among the lowest shares of any state, leaving banks like First National Bank of Omaha, named here for its deposits rather than for any count of local branches, as the largest such institution. Pentagon, Veridian, and Cobalt anchor the credit union side instead. Credit union payrolls come in right at what you would expect for a state built this way, serving the same lower-income, lower-cost population described above.
Pete Ricketts.p3: As of 2023, Nebraska's job base leaned harder into finance overall than most states, running well above the national norm, though the broader finance and insurance sector added jobs more slowly here than nationally across the prior decade. Health care and social assistance was where the most jobs sat, among roughly 920,800 statewide. But the state's real distinction was agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting, which ran far ahead of the national norm and marked Nebraska as a place still built substantially around land and livestock.

Pete Sessions.p1: This district spreads its people thin, just 76.5 per square mile, a sparseness that sets it apart from comparable seats. Across roughly 798,340 residents, the median household brings home $69,771 a year, on the lower side for districts like this. A typical home runs $273,900 against rents that stay comparatively modest, and homeownership trails many peers. Poverty runs somewhat elevated here as well.
Pete Sessions.p2: Credit union offices here outpace credit union jobs, a split worth noting: office presence runs above the national norm while employment sits a touch below it, so the physical footprint is thicker than the staffing behind it. Navy Federal Credit Union, Randolph-Brooks, and GENCO anchor that footprint, and credit unions hold 27.1 percent of retail offices, a share above most comparable districts. That is a lot of storefronts for a workforce that, nationally speaking, runs light.
Pete Sessions.p3: As measured in 2023, the district's job base leaned hardest on mining and oil and gas extraction, well beyond the national norm, alongside wholesale trade and public administration. Finance and insurance jobs overall sat a bit below norm but grew faster than the country as a whole. Wells Fargo Bank booked a sizable deposit share among the bank branches here, though plenty of rival banks compete on the ground locally. Mortgage lending skewed heavily toward home purchases, making up most originations.

Pete Stauber.p1: This district covers a lot of ground for the people on it, just 23.3 residents per square mile, thinner than almost anywhere else this office is drawn. Across that spread live 727,411 people with a median household income of $74,635, running below what most other districts report. The typical home is valued near $292,400, while ownership itself is unusually common, with 78.1 percent of households owning rather than renting. That combination, modest income paired with widespread ownership, shapes what financial life here looks like.
Pete Stauber.p2: Credit unions hold 30.2 percent of retail offices in this district, a share that runs well above most of the country. Affinity Plus, Members Cooperative, and Blaze carry that presence, working alongside a far larger set of bank branches, among which Wells Fargo comes out largest under federal deposit-reporting rules, though that reflects how deposits get booked more than any local footprint. Credit union employment here runs well past the national norm, and office growth has outpaced even that. For a district built on ownership more than income, that concentration of credit union activity fits the ground it sits on.
Pete Stauber.p3: As of 2023, the district's economy leaned hardest into mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction, far above the national norm for that line of work. Health care and social assistance and retail trade followed as the largest sources of jobs. Overall finance and insurance employment stayed below the national norm, a sign this district runs on extraction and services more than banking.

Peter Welch.p1: Vermont spreads its workforce thin, just 70.4 people per square mile, with jobs concentrated in clinics, retail counters, and small operations rather than any single dominant employer. Households earn a median $82,730, well above most states, while unemployment and poverty stay low. Homeownership is unusually high at 73.2 percent, a sign of a place built around long-term residents rather than transient job seekers. Rent claims a modest 19.1 percent of median household income.
Peter Welch.p2: Credit unions hold 27.5 percent of retail offices here, a share few states exceed. TD Bank, National Association books the largest deposits under federal rules that favor wherever accounts are booked, though EASTRISE, VERMONT, and NORTH COUNTRY are the names woven into this state's financial life alongside many competing banks. Credit union employment runs far past the national norm, and office presence follows well above it too, with jobs growing faster than office count, meaning these institutions do more with each location than most. That thickness in staffing fits a state full of homeowners and steady earners.
Peter Welch.p3: Vermont's job base in 2023 leaned on health care and retail trade, with a farm and forestry sector well above the national norm despite its small share of total jobs. Overall finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm, a reminder that banking is not what this state does. What it does well is hold people in place, with housing costs that stay manageable against income even as home values sit in the middle of the national pack.

Pramila Jayapal.p1: The district holds 811,726 residents in a dense urban footprint. Median household income is $119,340, far beyond the ordinary seat, but owner occupancy reaches only 44.5 percent. The middle home is worth $931,600, several times local earnings, and rent is also high. Joblessness exceeds the level seen across many peer districts. Strong pay therefore exists alongside an expensive, renter-heavy housing market.
Pramila Jayapal.p2: Credit union staffing is slightly more concentrated than the national norm even though the cooperative office network is comparatively thin. Boeing Employees, First Technology, and Salal anchor that presence. Bank of America appears first on deposits attributed locally, while credit unions operate 22.0 percent of retail offices. Those institutions place more weight in their workforce than in storefront reach, requiring service rather than physical scale to distinguish them beside banks.
Pramila Jayapal.p3: The 2023 economy was especially concentrated in management of companies and enterprises and information. Professional, scientific, and technical services also formed a large base, employing nearly 15 percent of workers. Overall finance employment remained below its countrywide baseline even as credit union staffing held above it. Purchase mortgages dominated originations, and a smaller portion of lending reached lower-income neighborhoods. Corporate management and technical work, not retail finance, define the local job mix.

Raja Krishnamoorthi.p1: Poverty runs lower here than in almost any peer district, at 6.8 percent, and joblessness stays scarce too. Households earn a median of 96,230 dollars, putting this district near the top of its class on income. Homeownership is high, at 71.5 percent, and the area is built dense, with population near 752,591. Housing costs land in the middle range nationally, rent taking a small bite out of that income.
Raja Krishnamoorthi.p2: Credit unions hold just 12.8 percent of retail offices here, well behind the share banks have claimed in this district. Alliant, Consumers, and Navy Federal Credit Union are the names that carry weight locally, set against JPMorgan Chase, which leads the district among several competing banks on the addresses reported to it. Credit union staffing runs light against the national norm, moving in step with how few offices they hold rather than outpacing it. Given the income and low poverty described above, credit unions occupy a smaller footprint than the deposit business usually gives them.
Raja Krishnamoorthi.p3: Industry here was measured in 2023. Wholesale trade stood out sharply, at 2.49 times the national norm, making it the district's clearest specialty. Finance and insurance ran specialized too, alongside a manufacturing base that anchors much of the job count. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases that year, with a modest share reaching lower-income neighborhoods, across all lenders combined.

Ralph Norman.p1: Homeownership here reaches 76.9 percent, among the highest of any district in the country, and that fact colors the whole local economy. Household income and home values both trail most comparable districts, even as unemployment stays low. Population density is thin, marking this as a spread-out place where owning rather than renting is simply the norm.
Ralph Norman.p2: Credit unions hold 32.1 percent of retail offices, a share that stands out sharply against other districts, putting them in real competition with the banks for everyday households. Founders, SAFE, and Family Trust are the names doing that work, set against First-Citizens Bank & Trust Company, the largest bank by deposits booked to addresses here, though hardly the only bank with a presence on the ground. Credit union employment runs at 2.71 times the national norm, even heavier than their share of offices. For a district this rooted in ownership, that is a lending relationship these institutions are built to serve.
Ralph Norman.p3: Manufacturing carries real weight in the local economy, running well above the national norm for concentration, with retail trade close behind it. Utilities stand out even more sharply on that same measure, a small sector but an unusually concentrated one here. Overall finance and insurance employment falls below the national norm, leaving credit unions to punch above their sector's weight. Mortgage lending leans heavily toward home purchases over refinancing, consistent with a district where buying a house, and staying put, is what people do.

Rand Paul.p1: Kentucky's economy still runs on making and moving things: manufacturing and transportation and warehousing both employ well above the national norm, with health care among the larger sectors too. The state is settled at an even density, neither clustered into metros nor truly rural. Households earn a median of 64,526 dollars, among the lowest in the country, and poverty runs high alongside it. Housing offsets that some: a home value of 226,000 dollars against income is a low ratio by national standards, and homeownership is common at 68.1 percent.
Rand Paul.p2: Credit unions hold just 14.4 percent of retail offices here, a thin share next to other states, leaving banks such as PNC Bank, National Association, the deposit leader under federal reporting rules, to account for most of the rest. Commonwealth, L&N, and Abound carry the credit union presence that exists. Credit union employment runs to 0.68 of the national norm, thinner than the office share itself, which sits closer to typical at 0.89. For a workforce earning modest wages and buying modestly priced homes, that gap in staffing is worth watching.
Rand Paul.p3: Beyond credit unions, finance and insurance jobs overall sit below the national norm, and grew slower than the country over the past decade. The employment picture shows a state still built on physical industry, with manufacturing alone accounting for a large share of all jobs. That is Kentucky's real distinction, an economy weighted toward making and moving goods rather than managing money.

Randy Feenstra.p1: With just 37.4 people per square mile, the 4th congressional seat of Iowa is one of the most thinly settled districts in the country, a place of small towns rather than a single city. Households earn a median $73,295, and home values sit low next to other districts at a median $203,700. That combination keeps housing cheap relative to income, and most residents own rather than rent. Unemployment runs low, at 3.2 percent.
Randy Feenstra.p2: Credit unions here hold just 12.0 percent of retail offices, among the lowest shares of any congressional district, leaving most of the storefront banking business to banks. Greater Iowa, GreenState, and Veridian carry the credit union presence that exists, set against a bank sector that includes United Bank of Iowa, though that name reflects deposit booking rules more than any dominant branch network. Credit union employment runs thin against the national norm, while office presence is closer to typical, so offices here outpace the jobs behind them.
Randy Feenstra.p3: As measured in 2023, manufacturing was the district's defining sector, employing 18.4 percent of workers, a concentration far above the national norm. Agriculture, though a smaller share of jobs, was also unusually concentrated here. Educational services added a third specialized layer to the mix. Overall finance employment stayed light against the national norm, and home purchases drove most mortgage lending activity, a picture of an economy built on steady production rather than finance.

Randy Fine.p1: Home values in this district run 4.9 times the median household income of 65,999 dollars, a wider gap than most comparable places show, and that income itself sits well below the norm. Rent runs 1,489 dollars a month against it. Owning a home is far more common here than renting, one of the highest such rates on record, in a population that leans older at a median 48.7 years. Hardship shows up too, with more households below the poverty line than in most districts.
Randy Fine.p2: Credit union offices here hold a bigger footprint than credit union staffing does, a district where offices outpace jobs on the ground. VyStar, Space Coast, and Fairwinds anchor that presence, holding 24.0 percent of retail offices against banks, a share in line with comparable districts. Truist Bank leads locally under federal deposit-booking rules, which credit deposits to the office where they are recorded, not necessarily to where a branch or customer is found. Thin staffing paired with steady office presence means these institutions cover a lot of ground with comparatively few local hires.
Randy Fine.p3: As of 2023, health care, retail trade, and accommodation and food service work employed the largest shares of the district's workforce. Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting stood out far more sharply, specialized well beyond the national norm despite employing a small slice of workers. Finance and insurance employment overall stayed below the national level even as the sector grew faster than the country as a whole over the prior decade.

Randy Weber.p1: Poverty affects 14.6 percent of residents, above the level in many peer seats, and unemployment is also elevated. The district holds 787,873 people with median household earnings of 77,652 dollars, close to the middle of the national district range. Home prices are comparatively modest, while owner occupancy is common. These measures describe ordinary earnings with more economic hardship than the housing market alone would imply.
Randy Weber.p2: Credit unions operate 43.1 percent of retail offices, placing cooperatives among the strongest district footprints. AMOCO, Texas Dow Employees, and JSC carry that network beside more than a hundred bank branches. Federal records assign JPMorgan Chase a substantial local deposit position, without making it the only meaningful bank. Credit union staffing is far more concentrated than the national norm and aligns closely with the office network. Cooperative finance therefore has unusual weight within the retail market.
Randy Weber.p3: The 2023 employment count was near 257,400. Construction supplied the clearest specialty, accounting for 12.6 percent of workers at a concentration beyond the national baseline. Educational services also provided a substantial job pool. Overall finance employment was below the countrywide norm, which leaves credit unions prominent inside a modest financial sector. Purchase loans dominated mortgage activity that year. Construction's weight is the district's clearest departure from the broader job mix.

Raphael Warnock.p1: Georgia moves goods for a living: transportation and warehousing employs well above the national norm, marking a state built around freight lanes rather than a single company town. The population, near 11.2 million, is settled more densely than most states and skews middle-aged, with median household income around 79,991 dollars landing squarely in the middle nationally. Home values run well above most states, and homeownership trails most others too.
Raphael Warnock.p2: Credit unions hold 20.1 percent of retail offices here, a smaller slice than most states carry, leaving Truist Bank and its many local rivals to hold the rest alongside credit unions like Navy Federal, Delta Community, and Robins Financial. Credit union employment runs below the national norm, tracking closely with how thin their office presence is here too. For a credit union working this ground, that means fewer branches per household in a state where housing costs already stretch budgets thin. The freight and warehouse workforce that defines Georgia's job market is as much a part of that ground as anyone else.
Raphael Warnock.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance jobs overall sat just under the national norm, though the sector was growing faster than the country as a whole. The state's real distinction was logistics: warehousing, wholesale trade, and information together marked Georgia as a hub for moving and routing rather than making. Georgia's economy in that year was defined less by what it produced than by what it moved through.

Rashida Tlaib.p1: Household income in the 12th district of Michigan sits below almost every other congressional district, at 57,324 dollars, and both poverty and joblessness climb well past what most places report. Rent, at 1,197 dollars a month, still eats deeply into that thin income base even though home values remain low by national standards. The district is dense, packing 751,709 people into a compact urban footprint. Homeownership trails most comparable places.
Rashida Tlaib.p2: Credit unions hold 35.1 percent of retail offices here, a share among the highest anywhere in the country. DFCU Financial, Community Choice, and Community Financial anchor that presence, in a market where credit union offices are more specialized against the national norm than credit union staffing is. Offices have grown faster than jobs behind the counter, a network built out ahead of its own hiring. Against a population stretched this thin by income and rent, that footprint carries real weight.
Rashida Tlaib.p3: Back in 2021, the working economy here leaned hardest into Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services, by far its most specialized line of work, with health care and manufacturing also employing large numbers of people. Finance and insurance employment sat close to the national norm that year, though the sector's growth over the prior decade lagged behind it. JPMorgan Chase led local deposits under federal booking rules, one name among many banks operating branches across the district. Roughly 310,000 jobs anchored the local economy that year.

Raul Ruiz.p1: This district spreads its people thinly across the land, a rural imprint rare on California's congressional map. Median household income sits at $69,516, and the median home value of $430,800 runs far past what that income supports. Rent claims 24.3 percent of income, and just 65.6 percent of households own their home. Unemployment and poverty rates here both run higher than most comparable districts see.
Raul Ruiz.p2: Sun Community, Altura, and Frontwave anchor credit union presence here, and together credit unions hold 26.8 percent of retail offices, a share above most comparable districts, ahead of Wells Fargo Bank, National Association, the top name by deposits booked locally among 66 bank branches overall. Credit union employment sits just under the national norm, tracking closely with how thick their office presence runs. For a district with strained incomes and stretched housing costs, that footprint carries real weight.
Raul Ruiz.p3: As of 2023, work here leaned hard on agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting, far above the national norm, alongside utilities, also running well ahead of it. Public administration added a further specialized layer on top. Health care, retail trade, and food service work rounded out the picture, the latter two both running above the national norm. Finance and insurance employment stayed thin against the norm nationally, leaving this district's economic identity rooted in land, government, and service work rather than finance.

Richard Blumenthal.p1: Connecticut packs 758.9 people per square mile, among the densest settlement patterns of any state, and its workforce clusters heavily in finance, insurance, and manufacturing. Median household income runs to $96,049, well above most states, though home values and unemployment both run higher than most peers. Homeownership, at 66.7 percent, trails most of the country, a sign that even a wealthy population here rents more than elsewhere.
Richard Blumenthal.p2: Credit unions hold just 19.9 percent of retail offices statewide, a thin slice next to what banks control here. Connecticut State Employees, American Eagle Financial, and Charter Oak carry the credit union name into that limited footprint, competing against Bank of America, whose deposit total leads under federal booking rules rather than any count of local branches. Credit union employment runs thin against the national norm even as office presence slightly exceeds it, meaning these institutions keep more doors open than staff to run them.
Richard Blumenthal.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance jobs ran 1.42 times the national norm, this state's most specialized sector, though that industry's growth over the prior decade lagged the national pace. Health care and social assistance employed a bigger share of workers than manufacturing did. Total employment approached 1,511,300 jobs, built on a base where insurance expertise and advanced manufacturing give Connecticut an identity that outweighs its small size.

Richard Durbin.p1: Illinois carries 12,710,158 people at a median age of 39.4, densely settled compared with most states. Median household income runs to $83,211, above most states, while joblessness runs higher than the country typically sees. Housing stays comparatively affordable: a median home value of $280,700 works out to a modest multiple of that income, and rent claims a modest share of the median household's earnings. Homeownership sits squarely in the middle of the pack among states.
Richard Durbin.p2: Alliant, Citizens Equity First, and State Farm anchor the credit union presence here, though credit unions hold only 15.1 percent of retail offices statewide, a small slice next to JPMorgan Chase, the deposit leader among thousands of bank branches run by many competing banks. Credit union employment tracks close to the national norm, and office presence tracks right alongside it. That leaves a modest footprint working with households whose housing costs, at least, run lighter than most of the country's.
Richard Durbin.p3: Illinois's economy ran to roughly 5,504,000 jobs as of 2023, built heavily around health care, manufacturing, and steady retail employment. The state carries a slight specialization in wholesale trade, transportation and warehousing, and finance and insurance alike. Finance and insurance employment there runs above the national norm, a sizable bench of institutional financial activity that a credit union operates alongside, not within. That mix of finance jobs, affordable housing, and a large population marks the state's economic character.

Richard Hudson.p1: Household income in the 9th congressional seat of North Carolina sits at $68,360, thin next to most districts, while poverty runs high at 13.7 percent even as unemployment stays low at 3.9 percent. Property values here cluster around $271,600, roughly four times what a household brings home, and rent claims a noticeable but not crushing piece of it. Ownership is the norm over renting here. The district holds roughly 790,294 people spread across ordinary density for the region.
Richard Hudson.p2: Credit unions staff this district thinner than the national norm even though their office count nearly matches it, an unusual split worth flagging. State Employees', Truliant, and Navy Federal carry that office presence, holding 24.2 percent of retail deposit-taking outlets against Truist Bank and a wider field of local rivals. For a workforce earning less than peer districts and stretching further on housing costs, that gap between offices and jobs matters more than it would somewhere richer.
Richard Hudson.p3: As of 2023, the district's job base leaned on retail trade and manufacturing, each running well above the national norm, alongside administrative and waste management work. Health care and social assistance employed a substantial share of workers too. Overall finance and insurance employment ran well below the national norm. This was and remains a place built on making and selling things rather than on finance, a district where factories and stores, not banks, set the pace of work.

Richard McCormick.p1: Median household income in this Georgia district sits among the very highest of any congressional seat, a fact that shapes nearly everything measured here. Home values run well above other districts, at 4.6 times what a household there typically brings in, yet overall housing costs stay light by comparison, with high homeownership throughout. Unemployment and poverty both sit unusually low. The district is also dense, comfortable, and largely owner-occupied.
Richard McCormick.p2: Credit unions hold just 15.0 percent of retail offices here, a thin share and the single fact that defines them locally. Delta Community, Navy Federal Credit Union and Georgia's Own are the names doing that work, competing against 163 bank branches, with Wells Fargo largest by deposits booked in the district, a figure that owes more to how deposits get recorded than to any real presence on the ground. Credit union employment here sits at 0.33 times the national norm, and office presence tracks closely with it. Against an economy this affluent, credit unions hold a small foothold.
Richard McCormick.p3: Information was this district's standout industry, at 2.76 times the national norm, well ahead of finance and insurance or professional and technical services, both specialized in their own right. Retail trade and health care employed large numbers too, without running especially concentrated. Lending here tilts heavily toward home purchases over other uses. Very little of that lending reaches lower income neighborhoods, a mark of how affluent this district already is.

Richard Neal.p1: Median household income in the 1st congressional district of Massachusetts sits below most comparable districts, at $75,462. Housing eases that some: rent runs near $1,169 a month, lighter than what most peers carry. Poverty climbs higher here than in most districts, even with unemployment held low. Pay is the strain in this district; housing is not what deepens it.
Richard Neal.p2: Credit union jobs are thick on the ground, at 1.26 times the national norm, and credit union offices thicker still, at 1.54 times, more branches than the payroll alone would explain. Greylock, Polish National, and Freedom carry that presence, holding 21.7 percent of retail offices against banks. TD Bank, National Association books a large deposit total under federal reporting rules, though many other banks compete for business here. A credit union in this district is lending into modest paychecks and real poverty at the same time.
Richard Neal.p3: As measured in 2023, health care and social assistance led local employment, holding 21.4 percent of all jobs. Manufacturing added further weight beneath it. Finance and insurance employment sat a touch under the national norm, and its growth lagged too. What sets this district apart is work anchored in institutions, hospitals and utilities among them, rather than in open markets.

Rick Allen.p1: Poverty here runs among the highest of any district in the country, at 17.9 percent, with joblessness elevated to match. Household income falls short of most peers, and home values sit lower still. The population is spread thin across the land, just 81.6 people per square mile, well under what most districts hold.
Rick Allen.p2: Credit unions here hold only 13.8 percent of retail offices, a small footprint compared with the banks that otherwise dominate. Pentagon, Navy Federal, and SRP carry the credit union presence locally, set against a far larger network of bank branches, with Wells Fargo posting the top deposit figures under federal booking rules rather than through any real local advantage. Both credit union jobs and offices trail the national norm, though offices have slipped less than employment has. Credit unions have yet to establish deep roots in this market.
Rick Allen.p3: As measured in 2023, health care and social assistance and manufacturing together made up a substantial slice of the district's jobs. Utilities registered as unusually concentrated, well past what districts of this size typically carry. Finance work overall stayed sparse against the national norm, a sign of how little this economy runs on banking or lending. What this place does well is look after people and build things, not manage money.

Rick Larsen.p1: Home values here run far higher than income alone would explain, a median of 656,300 dollars against a household income of 90,998 dollars. Rent lands at 1,784 dollars a month, a smaller stretch relative to income than the sale market implies. Homeownership trails many comparable districts, and poverty runs low. Population density stays thin for a district this costly, a spread-out place rather than a dense one.
Rick Larsen.p2: Whatcom, Boeing Employees, and Navy Federal give this district its credit union presence, and together with others they hold 28.2 percent of retail offices, a share above most comparable districts. A community bank books the top deposit total under federal reporting rules, though many other banks compete for business here. Credit union employment runs slightly above the national norm, a fitting footprint given the costly housing and solid incomes described above, which give these institutions plenty to work with locally.
Rick Larsen.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing defined the district's job base, employing 17.6 percent of workers at close to twice the national norm, alongside a highly specialized farming, forestry, and fishing sector. Health care and retail trade filled out the other prominent job categories, even as overall finance and insurance employment stayed below the national norm. Mortgage lending that year skewed toward home purchases as the dominant type of origination. This was a district built on making and growing things, not on moving money.

Rick Scott.p1: Florida packs 435.6 people per square mile, a density most states cannot match, and its 23.4 million residents work an economy tilted toward tourism, hospitality, and support services rather than production.
