Median household income sits at 77,735 dollars, unremarkable next to other states, but housing runs well ahead of it: a median home value of 396,900 dollars against that income is a ratio of 5.1. Poverty runs higher than in most states, even with unemployment at a middling level.
Rick Scott.p2: Credit unions hold just 21.4 percent of retail offices here, a smaller share than most states carry, leaving room for many rival banks to compete for the rest. SUNCOAST, Navy Federal Credit Union, and VyStar are the names that matter most. Credit union jobs run well above the national norm even as office presence lags behind it, work that is thin on branches but dense in staff, built to serve the dense, high-cost population described above.
Rick Scott.p3: As measured in 2023, Florida's job base leaned hardest into arts, entertainment, and recreation, real estate, and administrative and waste services, all well above the national norm. Retail trade and accommodation and food services also ran hotter than the country as a whole. Finance and insurance employment overall ran above the norm too, with growth over the prior decade outpacing the nation. This is a state built to host, serve, and house people, not to manufacture for them.

Riley Moore.p1: Settlement here is sparse, 93.6 residents per square mile, so a single branch or clinic often serves a wide radius. Yearly household earnings land at $64,861, trailing most other districts by a wide margin. Home values are modest too, at $206,500, and most people own rather than rent. Poverty is common, and joblessness runs higher than in a typical district elsewhere.
Riley Moore.p2: Credit union employment here tracks the national norm closely, yet the branch network built on top of it runs far thicker than that would imply. Fairmont, First Choice America Community, and West Virginia Central anchor that network, holding 24.5 percent of retail offices against banks. United Bank comes out ahead on deposits under federal rules that book them by address rather than local presence, though many other banks compete for business here. For members earning modest incomes in a low-cost housing market, that dense office presence is a real point of contact.
Riley Moore.p3: The district's 2023 job picture depended heavily on mining and utilities, both far more concentrated here than the national norm, alongside a health care sector that also ran above typical levels. Overall finance and insurance employment sat well below the norm. Home purchases dominated mortgage activity that year, making up 62.4 percent of originations, and lending reached lower-income neighborhoods at a rate of 23.7 percent.

Ritchie Torres.p1: This district is packed together more tightly than almost any other in the country, with people per square mile running into the tens of thousands. Median household income sits at $44,554, low next to other districts, while the typical home is valued at $581,800, pushing home values to more than thirteen times income. Rent runs to 38.6 percent of median income. Homeownership is uncommon here, and poverty is widespread.
Ritchie Torres.p2: Credit unions hold just 4.5 percent of retail offices in the district, a share among the lowest anywhere, so most deposit business runs through banks instead. USALLIANCE, MUNICIPAL, and NEW COVENANT DOMINION are the credit unions with a presence here. The single largest deposit total belongs to JPMorgan Chase, a result of where deposits happen to get booked rather than a sign of how many branches it runs, and several other banks compete alongside it. Credit union employment and office presence both sit far below the national norm and track each other closely.
Ritchie Torres.p3: As of 2023, the economy leaned heavily on institutions: Health Care and Social Assistance held 40.7 percent of jobs, Educational Services another 20.2 percent, both far above what is typical nationally. Public Administration came in third but well behind. Mortgage lending skewed heavily toward home purchases, with a large share of loans reaching lower-income neighborhoods, a rare channel of credit reaching this district's poorer corners.

Ro Khanna.p1: Household income in the 17th district sits far above what most of the country reports, at $181,913. Homes are priced to match, with a median value of $1,563,600, and rent runs $2,983 a month, though that claims a below-average share of income here. Homeownership is unusually uncommon, and the district is dense, packed into a compact footprint. Joblessness registers above what most peer districts report.
Ro Khanna.p2: Star One, Technology, and First Technology credit unions anchor the local field, holding 21.8 percent of retail offices against banks, a share that puts this district in the middle of the pack. First-Citizens Bank & Trust Company books the largest deposit total here under federal reporting rules, though 132 bank branches from many different institutions compete on the ground. Credit union employment and office presence both run below the national norm, tracking each other closely. Against the income and home values described above, this is a credit union sector working a market with unusually large sums moving through it.
Ro Khanna.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing dominated the working mix, employing close to three and a half times its national share. Information and professional, scientific, and technical services were both highly specialized alongside it, pointing to an economy built on hardware and knowledge work rather than typical services. Finance and insurance jobs overall ran well below the national norm, even though that broader sector grew faster here than nationally over the prior decade.

Robert Aderholt.p1: This district's defining trait is how cheap housing is against income, a median home value near 3.3 times earnings and rent well below a fifth of the typical paycheck, among the lightest housing burdens found anywhere. Median household income comes to 63,203 dollars, modest for a congressional seat, yet the great majority of homes here are owned outright or under mortgage rather than rented. Poverty is elevated all the same, while joblessness stays low. Alabama's fourth spreads its population thinly across a wide stretch of land.
Robert Aderholt.p2: Credit union jobs run at 1.62 times the national norm, but the office count climbs even higher above it, a sign that branch networks have grown faster than the staff inside them. Listerhill, Alabama Credit Union, and Redstone are the names driving that expansion. Together they hold 26.5 percent of retail offices, a larger footprint than similar districts tend to show, against roughly two hundred bank branches where Regions Bank leads on deposits. That is a heavy credit union presence layered onto a workforce earning modest pay and paying little for shelter.
Robert Aderholt.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing anchored the economy, running well above the national norm and making up well over a fifth of all jobs. Retail trade and utilities also exceeded national patterns, while finance employment overall lagged the country despite the credit union sector's unusual weight here. Total employment stood near 218,100 jobs, resting on a manufacturing base paired with some of the lightest housing costs around.

Robert Bresnahan.p1: Home values in the 8th district sit at $240,100, a level well below most congressional districts, and that gap shapes everything else here. Household income runs to $69,715, also on the low side next to peers, while rent stays light against income by comparison with other districts. Homeownership is strong at 70.9 percent, even as the district carries more poverty and joblessness than its counterparts typically do. Population sits at 773,187, spread across a district that is neither dense nor sparse next to others.
Robert Bresnahan.p2: Credit union offices here make up 20.8 percent of retail branches, a thinner presence than most districts show, and credit union jobs run even scarcer against the national norm, despite office numbers nearly keeping pace with it. Pentagon, Utilities Employees, and Pennsylvania State Employees anchor the credit union presence locally. PNC Bank carries a large deposit share under federal booking rules, a reflection of reporting addresses rather than local reach on its own. For the renters and owners described above, credit unions here operate with a lighter staffing footprint than their office presence implies.
Robert Bresnahan.p3: Transportation and warehousing stood out sharply against the national norm, marking a clear specialty for the district. Manufacturing followed as a second strength, with health care making up a large share of jobs as well. Total employment across the district ran into the hundreds of thousands. Lending here leaned heavily toward home purchases, making up 52.6 percent of all mortgage originations.

Robert Garcia.p1: A home here costs 9.9 times the median household income of $81,927, a ratio surpassed by almost nowhere else nationally. Homeownership is low, and poverty runs well above typical levels. The population is young and dense, packed into a small footprint. Housing costs outrun what people bring home here more than they do almost anywhere else in the country.
Robert Garcia.p2: Credit union employment runs below the national norm, at 0.67 times, yet the office footprint is thinner still, at 0.44 times, so jobs outpace offices, and that gap comes first because it says the most about this place. A trio of large regional credit unions anchors the presence here, holding 29.1 percent of retail offices, well ahead of most other districts. JPMorgan Chase leads all institutions by deposits booked here, though that reflects where deposits get recorded rather than where branches or customers actually sit, and many competing banks operate on the ground. For households already stretched by housing costs, credit unions hold a real, outsized foothold.
Robert Garcia.p3: As of 2023, wholesale trade stood out sharply here, at 2.08 times the national norm, alongside strength in transportation, warehousing, and corporate management functions. Health care, manufacturing, and retail trade employed the most people, with manufacturing itself running well above the national norm. Finance and insurance work overall, credit unions included, remained thin against the national norm. This is a district built on moving and managing goods, not on finance.

Robert Latta.p1: This district's housing runs cheap against what people take home, with values at 2.9 times median household income and rent claiming just 15.1 percent of it, a lighter load than nearly any comparable seat carries. Household income trails many comparable districts at 73,004 dollars, yet homeownership runs unusually high. The district also spreads thin, a Midwest seat without a dense urban core.
Robert Latta.p2: Credit union offices here outpace credit union employment, a gap wider than the norm: office presence sits slightly above the national norm while credit union jobs run well under it, so the sector shows up more in storefronts than payrolls. Firelands, Superior Credit Union and Lormet Community carry that presence, though credit unions hold just 18.2 percent of retail offices against a bank branch network led on deposits by Huntington. That leaves a district of modest, steady incomes and cheap housing where credit unions occupy fewer counters than their payroll would predict.
Robert Latta.p3: As measured in 2023, manufacturing dominated the job base, holding 24.0 percent of employment at 2.71 times the national norm, the district's clearest specialty by a wide margin. Agriculture and wholesale trade also ran above the norm, marking a district built around making and moving goods rather than services. Overall finance-sector employment ran well under the national norm. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, reinforcing a local economy centered on production rather than finance.

Robert Menendez.p1: This district crams more residents into each square mile than nearly any other in the country, and that crowding underlies most of what follows. The median household earns $88,096 a year, above most peer districts, yet home values near $565,100 and rents around $1,921 a month climb even higher above that norm. Ownership is rare here, one of the lowest rates anywhere, so most people rent rather than own. This is a young, dense, expensive place to call home.
Robert Menendez.p2: Credit union offices hold a steadier footing here than credit union jobs do, which sit far below the national norm, a gap that marks these branches as lean operations rather than big local employers. Affinity, Financial Resources, and Liberty Savings anchor that network, holding 17.2 percent of retail offices against banks, well under what most comparable districts see. Bank of America shows the largest deposit total under federal reporting rules, though many other banks also compete for business here. For a credit union, this is a market of renters and commuters, not one where local loyalty already runs deep.
Robert Menendez.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance defined this district's economy, employing 16.7 percent of workers at nearly four times the national norm. Transportation and warehousing followed at more than twice that norm, an unusual pairing for a district this dense. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases here, a sign that credit still flows into the ground beneath the finance towers.

Robert Onder.p1: What people pay for housing here is unusually light against what they earn, one of the widest such gaps found in any comparable district. Home values run to roughly 3.5 times median household income of $84,323, and rent stays modest by comparison. Owning a home is common, well ahead of most peer districts, and few residents live in poverty or without work. This is a spread-out district where owning outpaces renting by a wide margin.
Robert Onder.p2: Credit unions here include MULTIPLI, First Community, and Missouri Electric Cooperatives Empl, operating where credit unions hold just 16.1 percent of retail offices, a thinner slice than most similar districts carry. Banks still hold the bulk of deposits, led by The Central Trust Bank, though that figure reflects accounting geography more than actual local branches or customers. Credit union employment runs slightly above the national norm, a modest but real presence against the income and housing picture above.
Robert Onder.p3: As measured in 2023, the district's economy leaned hardest on Public Administration, employing 8.7 percent of workers at nearly twice the national norm. Educational Services combined size with specialization, while Health Care and Social Assistance and Retail Trade employed the largest shares of workers overall. Finance and insurance jobs sat right at the national norm, but that broader sector's growth from 2013 to 2023 ran well ahead of it.

Robert Scott.p1: People here are packed in far more closely than the typical congressional district. Households earn 67,625 dollars, on the low side nationally, and home values of 288,000 dollars run modest too, though rent still claims a large piece of the typical paycheck. Homeownership, at 53.2 percent, trails most peers, alongside poverty and unemployment rates that run higher than typical. The price tags alone undersell how tight money is for people living here.
Robert Scott.p2: Credit unions hold 44.5 percent of retail offices here, among the highest shares of any comparable district. Navy Federal Credit Union, Langley, and BayPort supply that presence, in a district where credit union employment runs 1.75 times the national norm and office presence more than double it, outpacing the jobs behind it. TowneBank books more deposits to local addresses than any other institution, though a wider field of banks holds branches across the same market. For an institution here, that is a market where credit unions already sit close to the incomes and housing costs described above.
Robert Scott.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing and administrative and support services both showed a heavier concentration than the national norm in their share of local jobs. Health care and social assistance was a leading employer, running close to the national norm. Across finance and insurance broadly, employment sat below the national norm, even as credit unions themselves outpaced it by a wide margin. Home purchases made up most mortgage activity, and a meaningful slice of that lending reached lower income neighborhoods.

Robert Wittman.p1: Poverty here touches just 6.7 percent of residents, among the lowest of any comparable district, alongside a median household income above $100,000. Homeownership runs unusually high, and joblessness is rare by national standards. Home values and rents both sit at ordinary levels once weighed against incomes this strong. Steady paychecks and paid-off houses describe the typical household far better than financial strain does.
Robert Wittman.p2: Credit unions here include Virginia, Navy Federal, and Langley, recognizable names against a backdrop of many bank branches citywide. Even so, credit unions hold just 19.8 percent of retail offices, well under what similar districts typically show. Credit union employment tracks the national norm closely, neither thin nor heavy by comparison. Income this high and poverty this rare mark real headroom for credit unions to grow into, serving households with steady paychecks and few of the credit troubles poverty tends to bring.
Robert Wittman.p3: Arts, entertainment, and recreation stood out furthest from the national pattern in the 2023 count, well beyond typical levels elsewhere, alongside a strong pull toward corporate management functions and retail trade. Health care and social assistance made up the single biggest slice of work. Broader finance and insurance employment sat close to the national norm, even as combined finance and insurance jobs grew more slowly here than nationwide over the preceding decade. Management, service, and retail work anchor this economy, with no single industry dominating it.

Robin Kelly.p1: Unemployment sets this district apart before anything else, at 9.6 percent, a rate that points to real slack in the local labor market. Deep poverty accompanies it, and household income sits far under the national middle. Home values are low, but housing still costs 2.8 times what a household earns, and rent runs 1,160 dollars a month. Across 732,352 people, the district stays sparsely settled.
Robin Kelly.p2: Credit unions here hold only 15.5 percent of retail offices, a light footprint compared with what banks control. Alliant, Credit Union 1, and Illiana Financial are the names that anchor what presence exists. Credit union employment sits well under the national norm for this line of work, a gap wider than the office count alone would explain. JPMorgan Chase leads all deposit-holders on paper, one name among many banks competing for the same strained households described above.
Robin Kelly.p3: Manufacturing and transportation and warehousing define the working economy here, with transportation running more than twice the national norm and manufacturing not far behind. Wholesale trade adds a third leg to that freight-and-goods identity, together giving the district a build-and-move character rather than a service one. Finance and insurance jobs remain scarce on the ground. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, and lower-income neighborhoods drew a substantial slice of that lending too.

Roger Marshall.p1: Kansas spreads just over 36 people per square mile, one of the emptiest population patterns any state shows, with factory floors and farm operations anchoring the job base more than most places see. Manufacturing alone accounts for a well above average share of jobs. Median household income sits at 75,514 dollars, trailing most states, but housing stays cheap by comparison, with rent running near 17 percent of median income. Joblessness sits low too, at 3.7 percent.
Roger Marshall.p2: Credit unions hold just 15.7 percent of retail offices here, well under what most states show. Navy Federal, Credit Union of America, and Meritrust are the names behind that share. Bank of America is booked as the largest name under federal reporting rules, one player among many competing statewide. Credit union employment runs slightly above the national norm, fitting a state where manufacturing wages and long distances between towns still need somewhere local to bank.
Roger Marshall.p3: As measured in 2023, health care and social assistance made up 15.0 percent of jobs, with manufacturing and retail trade close behind in the mix of work Kansans do. Manufacturing stood out as the clearest specialty, running well above the national norm. Agriculture added a second, smaller mark of distinction. Finance and insurance employment overall sat close to the national norm, with growth in that combined sector trailing it slightly.

Roger Wicker.p1: Mississippi spreads its people thin, with far fewer residents per square mile than most of the country, and factories and farms carry more weight here than in most places. Median household income sits at $59,127, among the lowest of any state, and poverty runs high alongside it. Home values stay low too, and ownership is the norm here, claiming 70.5 percent of households. Work here still runs through plants and fields more than offices.
Roger Wicker.p2: Credit unions hold just 16.4 percent of the retail offices statewide, a thin slice next to what banks control. Their office presence still runs a bit ahead of the national pattern, even though credit union employment falls slightly under it. Navy Federal, Keesler, and Mutual are the institutions doing that work here. Cadence Bank shows the largest deposits booked to addresses in the state under federal rules, though many other banks compete for business alongside it.
Roger Wicker.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing employed 13.4 percent of the workforce, one of three sectors, alongside utilities and agriculture, where Mississippi specialized well above the national norm. Health care and social assistance and retail trade rounded out the biggest sources of jobs. Overall finance and insurance employment sat below the national norm, and expanded at a weaker pace than the nation did across the ten years before. Mississippi's economy leans on production and cultivation far more than on financial services.

Roger Williams.p1: This district's 826,421 residents are spread thin on the ground, with settlement far sparser here than the typical congressional district shows. Households earn $80,242 typically, a figure near the middle for the country, while home values run near $326,100 against monthly rent that pushes housing cost above many peer districts. Poverty stays low here at 10.3 percent. Unemployment sits close to the national pattern.
Roger Williams.p2: Credit unions hold only 11.9 percent of retail offices here, a thin slice next to banks and among the lowest such shares of any comparable district. EECU, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Texas Trust supply what presence there is, against JPMorgan Chase, which comes out on top in the local figures mainly because of where its deposits happen to be recorded, not because of branch strength or a bigger local customer base. Credit union jobs and offices alike stay thin against the national norm and move together. For the money and households described above, credit unions here work with a modest footprint.
Roger Williams.p3: As of 2023, health care, retail trade, and educational services accounted for large shares of jobs in the district. Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction stood apart from the rest, rated highly specialized and well ahead of utilities and arts and entertainment as secondary strengths. Overall finance sector employment sat just under the national norm. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, at 69.1 percent of originations across all lenders.

Ron Estes.p1: A home in this district is priced at roughly three times what a household earns in a year, and only 16.6 percent of that income would cover the rent, a burden lighter than almost every comparable district carries. Earnings themselves trail behind what most other districts report. The population stands at 745,885, skewing a touch younger than middle age. Settlement is sparse across the district's land, the pattern of a place organized around small and mid-sized centers rather than a single dense metro.
Ron Estes.p2: Meritrust, Credit Union of America, and Mid American anchor the credit union presence here, though it remains a modest one: credit unions hold 18.9 percent of retail offices, well outnumbered by branches belonging to a wide field of competing banks. Credit union employment sits at 1.34 times the national norm, a specialized concentration in a district where finance and insurance jobs overall run thin. Given the cheap housing and thin earnings described above, a credit union here works with borrowers who owe comparatively little against what their homes are worth.
Ron Estes.p3: As measured in 2023, manufacturing drove this district's economy, holding 17.3 percent of jobs at nearly twice the national norm, the clearest specialization by far. Educational services followed at a more moderate but still above-average level. Home purchase loans made up 59.6 percent of all mortgage originations, marking a district still built more around buying homes than refinancing them.

Ron Johnson.p1: Wisconsin is home to nearly 6 million people with a median age of 40.7. Median household income sits at $77,488, neither high nor low next to other states. Housing costs run well below most, with a median home value of $294,700 against that income. Homeownership here is common, sitting at a share that matches the norm elsewhere.
Ron Johnson.p2: Landmark, Community First, and Summit anchor a credit union presence that is unusually large here: credit unions hold 30.6 percent of retail offices statewide, a share few other states match, against a banking sector where U.S. Bank National Association books the top deposit figure under federal reporting rules. Credit union employment runs close to twice the national norm, tracking the reach of their office network across the state closely. For an institution working this market, that means a customer base with steady income and modest housing costs, one that credit unions already serve at real scale.
Ron Johnson.p3: As measured in 2023, manufacturing anchored the state's economy, employing 17.5 percent of workers and running well ahead of the national norm for that sector. Management of companies and agriculture also outpaced national norms, rounding out an economy built on making and growing things rather than services alone. Health care and retail trade employed large shares of workers too, though neither stood out nationally. Overall finance employment tracked close to the national norm here.

Ron Wyden.p1: Oregon spreads just over 4.27 million people across wide, thinly settled ground, far emptier than most states. Work here skews toward land and materials: farming, forestry and fishing run highly specialized, and construction sits above the national norm. Typical household earnings lead most states at 85,220 dollars a year, but a home now costs 5.8 times what a household brings in in a year. Homeownership trails most other states, a sign that owning a house here has grown harder to reach.
Ron Wyden.p2: Credit unions hold 35.0 percent of retail offices statewide, a share well above most states, working alongside a bank branch network run by many competing banks. ONPOINT COMMUNITY, FIRST TECHNOLOGY and OREGON COMMUNITY anchor that presence. Credit union employment runs at 1.78 times the national norm, outpacing even their strong office footprint, a sign these institutions have grown to meet the income and housing strains just described, not merely to keep branches open.
Ron Wyden.p3: As of 2023, Oregon's economy ran on health care, retail trade and manufacturing, the sectors employing the most people, each just ahead of national norms. Banking and insurance work together barely registered by comparison, and hiring across that combined field crept up more slowly here than in most of the country over the decade before. The state's real edge lay elsewhere, in farming, forestry and management functions, sectors that set Oregon apart from a generic services economy far more than banking ever did.

Ronny Jackson.p1: People here live far apart, the population settled thinner than in nearly any other district nationwide, under 23 per square mile across almost 800,000 residents. Median household income is modest, at 69,873 dollars, and the poverty rate sits well above what most comparable districts see, even as unemployment stays low. Housing is cheap by national standards, a median home value of 216,100 dollars, though homeownership lags behind most other districts.
Ronny Jackson.p2: Union Square, and DATCU anchor the credit union presence here, holding 24.4 percent of retail office share against area banks, a share in line with comparable districts. The largest bank by local deposits leads here, though 238 bank branches across many separate institutions compete in this market. Credit union jobs are heavily concentrated against the national norm, and the district's credit union office presence sits at much the same level.
Ronny Jackson.p3: Extraction and farm work define what sets this economy apart: as measured in 2023, mining and oil and gas ran nearly five times the national norm, and agriculture nearly four times it, among the more specialized mixes of its kind. Overall finance employment fell below the national norm, leaving credit unions and banks to work a smaller financial sector than places their size usually have. Home purchase loans dominated mortgage activity, accounting for most of what got originated here.

Rosa DeLauro.p1: Unemployment here runs well above most comparable districts, at 6.0 percent, even as median household income stays stronger than most peers. The district is dense and packed toward middle age, with 741,529 people living close together across the seat. Homeownership trails most other districts, at 63.2 percent, and a typical home price runs several times median income. Renters give up about a fifth of their income on a typical lease.
Rosa DeLauro.p2: Credit union employment here runs thin against the national norm, at 0.52 times, even though credit union offices are slightly more common than typical, a gap worth understanding before walking in. Connecticut State Employees, Sikorsky Financial, and Connex anchor that office presence, holding 23.4 percent of retail offices against banks locally. The deposit figures attached to this district instead put Bank of America on top, a booking quirk among the many banks that actually compete for business here. That mismatch between thin staffing and steady office presence is the shape credit unions take in this district.
Rosa DeLauro.p3: Manufacturing and transportation carried more weight in this district's job base in 2023 than they typically do nationally, with manufacturing running well above the usual national share. Health care and social assistance stood alongside them as a mainstay of local employment. Overall finance and insurance employment ran under the national norm, with growth in that combined sector also lagging behind typical levels.

Ruben Gallego.p1: Arizona spreads 7.6 million people thinly across the land, a state settled around a few dense job centers rather than evenly filled in. Median household income runs high at 81,486 dollars, but housing costs climb even faster: a median home value of 426,000 dollars puts the value-to-income ratio at 5.2, among the highest in the country. Unemployment sits at 4.6 percent, higher than most states manage. This is a place where paychecks look strong but a house stretches them thin.
Ruben Gallego.p2: Credit unions hold 25.7 percent of the state's retail offices, a solid share of the market against the banks. Desert Financial, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Arizona Financial carry that presence, working the same ground as JPMorgan Chase, whose deposits booked here run large though it is hardly the only bank competing for customers. Credit union employment runs a touch below the national norm, tracking closely with how much office space the sector holds. With incomes and home prices both running high, that quarter of the market gives credit unions real weight.
Ruben Gallego.p3: As measured in 2023, finance and insurance stood out as Arizona's most specialized sector, employing well above the national norm. Administrative and support services and construction followed close behind in that same distinction. Health care, retail trade, and accommodation and food services carried sizable shares of jobs overall. Arizona's economy leans on a finance sector that outperforms its size elsewhere in the country, layered onto a broad service and construction base.

Rudy Yakym.p1: Household income in the 2nd district of Indiana lags well behind most congressional districts, at 66,934 dollars a year, and home values sit low as well, at 216,900 dollars. Homeownership, by contrast, runs unusually high, at 73.1 percent, and the poverty rate exceeds what most districts report. The district holds 751,821 people across a mostly rural footprint, low in density, still organized around making things rather than a dense urban core.
Rudy Yakym.p2: Credit unions hold 32.4 percent of retail offices here, a share that stands well above most districts in the country. Everwise, Interra, and Communitywide carry that presence against a banking sector led on deposits by 1st Source Bank, a name that reflects where deposits are booked more than where banks compete for customers. Credit union employment runs nearly twice the national norm, and their office presence runs further ahead still, a branch network built on a comparatively thin staffing base. That footprint is what meets the modest incomes and home values described above.
Rudy Yakym.p3: Manufacturing dominated the district's economy as of 2023, employing 32.0 percent of workers, well over three times the national norm and the clear center of gravity here. Overall finance employment ran well below the national norm, even as the broader finance and insurance sector grew modestly over the prior decade. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases that year, dominating the district's loan activity. Little of that lending reached lower-income neighborhoods, a sign of how concentrated the district's housing wealth remains.

Russ Fulcher.p1: Few congressional seats hold this few people per square mile, a district built on distance rather than density. Across that ground live a little over a million people, earning a median household income of 82,979 dollars, a figure that lands squarely in the middle range among districts. Home values sit far past what a typical district sees, yet owning a home is the norm here. This is an economy that has to travel to reach people, not the other way round.
Russ Fulcher.p2: Credit unions hold 43.2 percent of retail offices here, a share few other districts can match. Idaho Central, Potlatch No. 1 Financial, and Mountain America anchor that presence, competing against U.S. Bank National Association, the deposit leader among 161 bank branches under many separate owners. Credit union staffing and branch counts both sit well above what the country typically carries, with offices built out faster than headcount has caught up to. A place with this few residents per mile still supports this much financial infrastructure, reaching borrowers spread across wide distances rather than clustered close together.
Russ Fulcher.p3: Construction employs 10.5 percent of workers here, a specialization well beyond the national norm, and agriculture, though a small share of jobs, is highly specialized by the same measure. Finance and insurance jobs together grew faster than the country did, even as finance work overall stayed thinner here than the national picture. Mortgage lending here leaned heavily toward home purchases, 55.9 percent of all originations.

Russell Fry.p1: Household income in the 7th district of South Carolina sits at $61,149, lower than nearly every other seat in the state's delegation, and that gap shapes everything else here. Home values trail most peer districts, yet housing still eats an above average share of what people earn, and homeownership stands well above the norm at 75.2 percent. Poverty and unemployment both sit high against comparable seats. This is a spread-out district, not an urban one.
Russell Fry.p2: Credit union offices here hold a smaller share of the retail branch network than in most districts, at 16.9 percent, and credit union employment runs thinner still against the national norm, offices are outpacing jobs on the ground. Carolina Trust, South Carolina, and Founders carry that local presence. Wells Fargo shows up with the largest deposit total under federal reporting rules, but that is a quirk of where deposits get booked, not a sign of branch strength, and it faces plenty of competing banks across the district. For a lower income district with this much homeownership, thin credit union staffing matters.
Russell Fry.p3: The working economy here, measured in 2023, ran on Accommodation and Food Services, employing 15.1 percent of all jobs and well above the national norm. Retail Trade and Arts, Entertainment, and Recreation were also concentrated locally, marking a district built around hospitality and leisure rather than offices. Health Care and Social Assistance employed nearly as many people but without that same concentration. Overall finance employment ran below the national norm here.

Ryan Mackenzie.p1: Unemployment here runs well above most comparable districts at 5.5 percent, a labor market carrying more slack than elsewhere. Household income lands near the midpoint for districts like this one, a median 82,166 dollars, and home values fall in similar territory. Poverty stays lower than most peer districts at 10.1 percent. The district is also more densely settled than most, at 675.2 people per square mile.
Ryan Mackenzie.p2: Credit union offices here carry more weight than credit union jobs do: offices run slightly above the national norm, but credit union employment falls well short of it, wide enough a gap that offices are outpacing staffing. People First, First Commonwealth, and APCI anchor that branch presence, holding 23.5 percent of retail offices against banks. Wells Fargo books a sizable deposit total among the district's bank branches, though that reflects deposit-booking rules more than any dominant local footprint.
Ryan Mackenzie.p3: Measured in 2023, the job base leaned hard on Transportation and Warehousing, which employed 10.9 percent of workers, a concentration far beyond the national norm and the district's standout specialty. Health Care and Social Assistance and Manufacturing rounded out the picture, both running above the norm as well. Finance and insurance employment overall stayed below the national norm, and hiring growth in that combined sector trailed the nation across the decade before. Mortgage lending leaned toward home purchases over other loan types.

Ryan Zinke.p1: With just 14.4 people per square mile, this district sits at the sparse end of the national range, and that thin settlement pattern colors everything else about it. Median household income runs to $77,017 among 579,075 residents, a figure that lands squarely on the national midpoint. Home values run high against income, a ratio of 7.0, while ownership is the norm over renting. Unemployment sits among the lowest of any district, and poverty is rare by comparison.
Ryan Zinke.p2: Credit union employment here runs well ahead of what office presence alone would predict. Whitefish Credit Union Association, Clearwater, and Park Side Financial anchor that footprint, and together credit unions hold 25.7 percent of retail offices, a higher share than most comparable districts. Glacier Bank is named the top institution locally under federal deposit-reporting rules, though it shares the field with many other lenders. That gap between staffing and office count marks a district where credit unions have built deeper into the workforce than their footprint alone would show.
Ryan Zinke.p3: As of 2023, construction, agriculture, and mining stood out as unusually concentrated work here, alongside a retail and hospitality base well above the national norm. Health care employed the most people even without being locally specialized. Overall finance and insurance jobs ran under the national norm even as the sector grew faster than the country as a whole across the decade. Home purchase loans made up 54.4 percent of all mortgage originations, the clearest sign of a district still building itself out.

Salud Carbajal.p1: Home values in the 24th district sit near 916,600 dollars, among the highest of any district drawn in California, and run more than nine times the typical household income. Household income itself is high, at 98,127 dollars, yet homeownership here lags most comparable districts. Rent runs to 2,137 dollars a month at the midpoint. Density is thin for California, and unemployment sits above the level most comparable districts see.
Salud Carbajal.p2: Credit union jobs here track closer to the national norm than credit union office presence does, and that gap between the two is the first thing worth flagging. CoastHills, SESLOC, and The Golden 1 anchor that presence, but credit unions hold only 20.4 percent of retail offices here, thinner than most districts like it manage. JPMorgan Chase leads local deposit totals, though that reflects which office a bank books deposits to more than any real branch strength on the ground. The households a credit union here reaches are higher income than most, yet stretched by home costs few paychecks match.
Salud Carbajal.p3: As of 2023, farm work, fishing, and forestry stood out sharply, running close to ten times the national norm. Public administration and accommodation and food service also ran well ahead of the national mix. Finance and insurance employment overall stayed below that norm, while the broader sector's growth over the prior decade roughly matched the nation's pace. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, with a share of loans reaching lower income neighborhoods too.

Sam Graves.p1: Nearly 789,000 residents occupy a broad, sparsely populated district. Household earnings are lighter than those in many peer seats, but housing remains inexpensive, with a 3.2 ratio between home value and income. Owner occupancy is widespread and unemployment stands at a low 2.7 percent. The combination is a rural household market where modest earnings still reach relatively affordable property.
Sam Graves.p2: Credit unions operate only 8.9 percent of retail offices, one of the country's smaller cooperative footprints. CommunityAmerica, United, and Postal & Community provide the local names within a banking field led on deposits by U.S. Bank. Credit union staffing reaches 0.36 times the national norm, and office concentration likewise sits far below its baseline. Both measures show limited cooperative scale in a district where customers and locations are separated by long distances. The staffing and office measures reinforce the same picture of limited reach.
Sam Graves.p3: In 2023, manufacturing anchored the employment mix at 17.0 percent of jobs and stood well beyond its national concentration. Agriculture and utilities supplied additional specialties. Finance employment remained far below the countrywide norm, leaving it well behind the industries that make and grow goods. Purchase mortgages formed the principal lending activity. Manufacturing, agriculture, and utility work give this economy its identity rather than financial services.

Sam Liccardo.p1: Median household income here is among the highest of any district measured, at $181,659. Home values sit just as elevated, near $1,956,300, even though rent and other housing costs stay easier to carry than the price tags imply. Poverty is rare, just 6.6 percent, and the population is packed into a footprint denser than most seats in the country. This is a well-paid, tightly built place with little financial hardship.
Sam Liccardo.p2: Stanford, Star One, and Technology credit unions serve this district, where credit unions hold only 17.9 percent of retail offices, a thinner slice than in most similar districts, set against 135 bank branches including Wells Fargo, whose deposits booked here run highest of any lender. Credit union employment and office presence both run below the national norm, tracking each other closely. Against the income and home values above, credit unions occupy a small corner of a market banks otherwise control.
Sam Liccardo.p3: The district's work leans heavily into Information, employment nearly seven times the national norm, alongside Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services at close to double that norm. Health Care and Social Assistance employs the largest share of workers, at 17.2 percent, though only slightly above typical levels nationally. Finance and insurance work overall runs below the national norm, a modest slice of an economy built instead around technical and information-driven work. That picture, measured in 2023, describes a district oriented toward technology and expertise rather than banking or finance.

Sanford Bishop.p1: Household income in the 2nd congressional seat of Georgia stands at $51,802, among the lowest of any district nationally, with real strain showing up in both poverty and unemployment. Home values are modest, with a median of $171,000, yet rent still claims a heavier bite of income than in most districts. Homeownership falls short of typical levels too. The population here numbers in the hundreds of thousands but sits far more thinly on the land than most other districts.
Sanford Bishop.p2: Credit unions hold 28.9 percent of retail offices here, a concentration that outruns their share of local jobs, which sits almost exactly at the national norm. Navy Federal Credit Union, Robins Financial, and Georgia's Own carry that office presence, while Synovus Bank stands out among the district's 143 bank branches under federal deposit-reporting rules, not for local branch strength. For a district this income-strained, credit unions offer more doors than headcount, a cost-efficient way of reaching people banks often price out.
Sanford Bishop.p3: As of 2023, agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting stood out sharply against the national norm despite employing a small slice of workers. Manufacturing also carried outsized weight in the job mix, well beyond its share of workers. Health care and social assistance employed the largest share of the district's roughly 263,800 jobs. Mortgage lending that year tilted heavily toward home purchases, accounting for 56.4 percent of all originations.

Sara Jacobs.p1: Home values top out near the highest bracket in the state, at $919,900, roughly eight times what households here typically earn. Median household income runs $113,978, well above what most peers report, yet just 52.2 percent of residents own their homes, a low rate by comparison. Rent runs $2,403 a month. Add in the density of this place, and strong pay has clearly not translated into easy homeownership.
Sara Jacobs.p2: Credit unions here hold 40.2 percent of retail offices, a stake unmatched in most other districts nationally. Behind that figure sit Navy Federal Credit Union, Mission, and San Diego County Credit Union, all competing against 105 bank branches, among them JPMorgan Chase, which books the largest deposits locally. Credit union employment runs slightly above the national norm even as the office count itself runs a bit below it, meaning fewer branches carry more work apiece. That combination points to a high-earning, thinly-served customer base for any credit union operating here.
Sara Jacobs.p3: The 2023 job mix leaned hard on specialized work: utilities employment ran well above the national norm, and administrative, professional, scientific, and technical services followed the same pattern. Health care and social assistance made up a large share of jobs measured, close to the national norm rather than far above it. Across finance broadly, employment ran below the norm, a sign that this district's economic identity sits more in professional and technical services than in banking. Home purchase loans made up a large part of all mortgage originations measured.

Sarah Elfreth.p1: The 3rd congressional seat of Maryland reports a median household income of 136,641 dollars, among the highest figures any district posts. Homes carry a value near 539,800 dollars, a middle-value ratio of 4.0 against income, and rent claims just 18.0 percent of that pay on the same basis. Homeownership and density both run high here, while poverty and unemployment stay unusually low. Work leans toward offices and public agencies rather than warehouses or factories.
Sarah Elfreth.p2: Credit union offices here outpace credit union employment against the national norm, and that mismatch is the place to start. Tower, Navy Federal, and State Employees Credit Union of Maryland carry the credit union name locally, holding 23.0 percent of retail offices in the district between them. Federal records assign Bank of America the leading local deposit position, but branches from many other banks keep the field competitive. That gap between staffing and storefronts matters for a credit union weighing the same high-income, low-poverty base described above.
Sarah Elfreth.p3: In 2023, professional, scientific, and technical services employed 16.1 percent of workers and stood far beyond the national norm for that field. Public administration and wholesale trade likewise had greater local weight than usual for a place this size. Across all lenders, home purchases accounted for most mortgage originations, while a smaller slice of lending reached lower-income neighborhoods.

Sarah McBride.p1: Homeownership dominates here: 73.8 percent of households own rather than rent, a share that sets this district apart from most others in the country. Median household income runs 87,534 dollars, comfortably ahead of typical districts, and poverty stays low at 9.6 percent. The typical home carries a value of 371,600 dollars against that income, an ordinary ratio nationally, while rent claims about a fifth of the median household's earnings. Unemployment sits a touch higher than most comparable places, at 5.1 percent.
Sarah McBride.p2: Credit union employment here runs thinner against the national norm than credit union office presence does, an unusual gap worth noting before anything else. DEL-ONE, Dover, and Tidemark carry the local presence, holding just 20.6 percent of retail offices against banks, a modest share for the region. Capital One, National Association books more deposits here than any other bank, though that reflects reporting rules more than actual branch strength or customer count. For any credit union here, the opportunity is homeowners with solid income, not a crowded field of teller windows.
Sarah McBride.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance stood out sharply, employing well beyond the national norm and marking this district's clearest specialty. Health care and social assistance employed the most people, followed by retail trade, both running slightly above the national mix. Growth in finance and insurance together kept pace with the national rate over the ten years that followed. Home purchases made up most mortgage originations measured here, the dominant form of lending activity in the district.

Scott DesJarlais.p1: People are spread thin across the 4th congressional seat of Tennessee, well below most comparable districts. The 826,508 residents living there earn a median household income of $73,896, and a home costs 4.7 times that figure while rent takes a modest share of it. Homeownership reaches 69.5 percent, and both poverty and unemployment sit on the high side for a district of this kind. Pay is modest, yet most households here own the place they live in.
Scott DesJarlais.p2: Credit union employment runs slightly above the national norm even though credit union offices run below it, a gap that says something about how this district's institutions actually operate. Ascend, Redstone, and Liberty carry that presence on the ground. Together, credit unions hold just 17.3 percent of retail offices in this district, leaving Pinnacle Bank, whose deposits booked locally outsize any other name, and a wide field of competing banks to dominate the physical branch network.
Scott DesJarlais.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing anchored this district's economy, holding 20.8 percent of its jobs at a concentration well above the national norm. Transportation and warehousing and utilities also ran above that norm, reflecting a base built on factories and freight rather than offices. Retail trade and health care followed as sizable employers, though neither stood out nationally. Overall finance employment stayed well below the norm, a sign of how much this economy leans on production over money management.

Scott Fitzgerald.p1: This district stands out for how little housing eats into what people earn: home values sit at 4.2 times median household income, and rent claims just a small slice of it, among the lowest such burdens measured anywhere. Households here clear $91,909 a year, well ahead of most comparable districts. Homeownership is high, while poverty and joblessness both sit near the bottom nationally. It is a place of steady earners whose paychecks are not squeezed by what they pay to live there.
Scott Fitzgerald.p2: Landmark, Summit, and UW Credit Union anchor a market where credit unions hold 28.1 percent of retail offices, a share ahead of most districts nationally. The largest name by deposits here is a national bank, a technical result of federal booking rules rather than a picture of local branch competition, so office share is the more telling number. Credit union employment runs slightly above the national norm, tracking closely with how thick their office presence is. For a district built on high homeownership and light housing costs, that is a credit union sector positioned close to the business its members actually need.
Scott Fitzgerald.p3: The district's economy, as measured in 2023, ran on manufacturing above all else, more than twice the national concentration and its clearest specialty. Wholesale trade also ran well above the national norm, part of an economy tilted toward making and moving goods. Health care and retail trade employed plenty of people but without unusual concentration. Overall finance employment ran slightly above the national norm here.

Scott Franklin.p1: Median household income in the 18th congressional seat of Florida sits at $64,757, well below most comparable districts, a figure that colors housing, work, and everything downstream of it. Home values run modest too, at a median of $277,000, yet homeownership is unusually common at 74.1 percent. Poverty and joblessness both sit on the high side compared with peer districts. The district stretches thin across the map, holding 875,428 residents at low density rather than packing them into a city core.
Scott Franklin.p2: Credit union employment here outruns what the national pattern would predict, while the count of credit union offices lags just behind it, a gap worth pausing on: staffing in this sector has grown faster than its storefronts. MIDFLORIDA, SUNCOAST, and PENTAGON anchor that presence, holding a 23.8 percent share of retail offices against banks. SouthState Bank, National Association leads the field by deposits booked to local addresses, just one name among many banks with a footprint here. Given household earnings this constrained, a credit union sector top-heavy on payroll relative to branches still points to meaningful lending muscle.
Scott Franklin.p3: Working from figures gathered in 2023, finance employment here trailed the national norm by a wide margin. Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting stood out as highly specialized, alongside strength in public administration and transportation and warehousing. Health care, retail trade, and educational services employed the most people. Mortgage lending across all lenders leaned heavily toward home purchases, with a meaningful share reaching lower income neighborhoods.

Scott Perry.p1: Unemployment here sits well below most comparable districts, at 3.2 percent, and poverty stays low too. The typical household earns 81,071 dollars, a figure neither high nor low next to other districts, while home values trail most peers. Rent runs to 1,248 dollars a month, and this district is denser on the ground than most of its counterparts.
Scott Perry.p2: Credit unions hold 30.7 percent of retail offices here, a share few other districts match, giving them a genuine foothold against the banks operating in this district. Members 1st, Pennsylvania State Employees, and BELCO Community Credit Union anchor that presence, while PNC leads the field on deposits booked locally. Credit union employment runs far thicker than the national norm, outpacing even a strong office count, meaning these are workplaces here as much as they are branches. For the earners and homeowners described above, that makes credit unions an unusually large part of how money moves locally.
Scott Perry.p3: The district's employment in 2023 tilted toward transportation and warehousing, which held 10.2 percent of jobs, a concentration far above the national norm. Public administration and company management were also unusually prominent alongside it. Health care and social assistance employed a larger share of workers still, with manufacturing close behind. Home purchase loans made up 48.5 percent of all mortgage originations, in a district still built on moving goods and people.

Scott Peters.p1: This district's household income sits among the highest of any congressional seat, at $121,243. Housing costs match that altitude: a median home value of $1,190,200 against that income produces a price-to-income ratio of 9.8, and rent runs $2,510 a month. Homeownership is unusually rare here, and the district is far more crowded than most. Poverty runs low.
Scott Peters.p2: Credit union employment here runs slightly above the national norm even though credit unions hold a smaller share of offices than the typical district, a split worth noting before anything else. Navy Federal, San Diego County, and Mission credit unions anchor that presence, holding 22.9 percent of retail offices against a banking field led on deposits by Axos Bank, one name among many rivals booked to addresses here. Credit unions in this district run leaner on real estate than on payroll, employing close to the norm while occupying fewer storefronts than similar places. That is a lender base doing more with less real estate.
Scott Peters.p3: By 2023, professional, scientific, and technical work anchored this district's economy, employing at a rate well above the national norm. Accommodation and food services also ran well above the national norm, alongside a large health care and social assistance presence. Overall finance and insurance employment ran below the norm, and grew more slowly than the country as a whole over the prior decade. High-skill professional work here sits atop a service economy built to support it.

Sean Casten.p1: Owner occupancy is widespread, reaching 77.8 percent of households, a level few districts exceed. Median household income is a strong 96,658 dollars, poverty is low, and rent takes 18.7 percent of middle earnings. The relationship between home values and income is also modest. At 3,394.3 people per square mile, the district is built up rather than open, pairing density with a firmly homeowning population.
Sean Casten.p2: Credit unions operate only 10.8 percent of retail banking offices, one of the thinner cooperative positions among districts. Alliant, GreenState, and Healthcare Associates carry that local network. Federal address records give JPMorgan Chase the leading deposit position, a label separate from its physical reach amid many bank branches. Credit union staffing and office concentration are both far below the national norm and track one another closely. Comfortably earning homeowners therefore conduct most of their retail banking outside the credit union sector.
Sean Casten.p3: As of 2023, the district's economy leaned on transportation and warehousing, administrative and support services, and wholesale trade, sectors that stood out clearly against the national picture. Health care and retail trade employed the most people, out of roughly 385,300 jobs total. Overall finance employment sat near the national norm, though growth in that broader sector lagged over the prior decade. Purchase loans, rather than refinancing, drove most mortgage lending across the district.

Seth Magaziner.p1: Unemployment stands out here, well above most comparable districts at 5.7 percent, even against a district with real advantages. Median household income runs to 92,127 dollars, well ahead of most peers, and the population lives more densely packed than most congressional districts. Home values run close to five times median income, though rent claims a smaller slice of that income than in most places. This is a place of comfortable households and a labor market that has not quite kept pace with them.
Seth Magaziner.p2: Credit union offices here punch above their weight even though credit union jobs do not. Office presence beats the national norm, while employment trails it slightly, worth flagging to anyone weighing a branch investment against a hiring plan. Navigant, Coastal1, and Greenwood anchor that presence, holding 25.2 percent of retail offices against banks. Citizens Bank leads on deposits booked locally, but that reflects where deposits get reported more than any real edge over the district's other branches.
Seth Magaziner.p3: The industry base measured in 2023 leaned on finance and insurance, health care, and public administration, with health care a major source of jobs among the district's roughly 237,100 total. Finance and insurance jobs grew a bit faster than the nation from 2013 to 2023. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, at 43.7 percent of originations, with a smaller portion of loans reaching lower income neighborhoods.

Seth Moulton.p1: This district posts a median household income of $121,409, a figure that stands among the highest anywhere in the country, and that fact colors everything else measured here. Home values reach $705,600, far above the typical district, yet housing costs overall come in lighter than most places see. Poverty and unemployment are both unusually low. Population is dense here too, in a district aging into its middle years at a median 42.2.
Seth Moulton.p2: Credit union jobs sit below the national norm even though the number of branches edges slightly past it, an unusual split that points to smaller local staffs holding a real number of storefronts. First Technology, Metro, and BrightBridge are the names carrying that presence. Even so, credit unions hold only 19.3 percent of retail offices, a thinner slice than most comparable districts show, leaving Salem Five Cents Savings Bank as the top deposit-holder among 255 bank branches from many competing banks.
Seth Moulton.p3: As of 2023, the district's economy ran on manufacturing and on professional, scientific, and technical services, both well above national norms. Health care employed the most people outright but without the same specialization. Across roughly 369,400 jobs, overall finance employment sat below the national norm even as the sector's growth from 2013 to 2023 nearly kept pace nationally.

Sharice Davids.p1: Poverty in the 3rd district of Kansas is among the lowest of any comparable district, at 6.8 percent, alongside low unemployment. Median household income runs to $101,317, comfortably ahead of most peer districts, and home values reach $398,600. Despite that, housing costs stay unusually light for what households earn. The district holds 754,087 people, with a median age of 39.4.
Sharice Davids.p2: Credit unions here hold just 12.7 percent of retail offices, well outnumbered by the banks that fill out this market. CommunityAmerica, MainStreet, and Truity carry the credit union name locally, competing against a much larger bank branch network, one member of which shows the biggest deposit figure only because federal rules book nationwide deposits to a single local address, not because of any local branch advantage. Credit union employment tracks close to the national norm even though office presence lags well behind it, a sign that these institutions run leaner branch networks while still staffing them fully. That leaves credit unions serving a comparatively affluent, low-poverty population with a modest physical footprint.
Sharice Davids.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance employment ran well above the national norm, alongside strength in management of companies and in transportation and warehousing. Those three sectors mark this district's clearest specializations against the rest of the country. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, with a much smaller share reaching lower-income neighborhoods. This is a district shaped by steady, well-paid finance and logistics work rather than by density or rapid growth.

Sheldon Whitehouse.p1: Rhode Island crowds a lot of people into very little land, one of the tightest settlement patterns in the country, and jobs here cluster in hospitals, offices, and finance rather than farms or factories. Median household income sits at 83,504 dollars, ahead of most states, though the state also carries a poverty rate and an unemployment rate that both climb past what most states report. Housing shows a similar tension: a median home value of 455,700 dollars set against income yields a value-to-income ratio of 5.5, and homeownership trails well behind most states.
Sheldon Whitehouse.p2: Credit unions hold 26.5 percent of retail offices here, a share that stands above most other states. Navigant, Coastal1, and Greenwood carry that presence, competing against Citizens Bank, National Association, the deposit leader on paper though hardly the only bank with a real footprint. Credit union offices run slightly ahead of the national norm, while credit union jobs sit just under it, so the office network reaches further than the staffing behind it does. That is the market, dense and unevenly prosperous, that a credit union here actually serves.
Sheldon Whitehouse.p3: Finance and insurance jobs ran at 1.22 times the national norm, a slight specialization fitting a small state with a sizable banking and insurance presence. Health care and social assistance was a leading employer, well ahead of retail trade, which sat below the national norm. Rhode Island's economy leans on caring for people and managing money more than on moving goods.

Shelley Capito.p1: West Virginia is thinly settled, spread across just 73.6 people per square mile, and its economy leans on ground and clinic work: health care and social assistance alone hold 21.1 percent of jobs, well ahead of the national pattern, alongside a mining and gas sector few other states can match. Households earn a median $60,798, on the low end nationally, and a large share of residents live in poverty. Homeownership still sits well above what most states report, with a home value to income ratio of just 2.8.
Shelley Capito.p2: Credit unions hold 23.2 percent of retail offices here, putting the state roughly in the middle of the pack. Their office presence runs above the national norm even though the jobs behind those offices run below it, meaning fewer people staff more branches. Fairmont, First Choice America Community, and West Virginia Central are the names doing that work, serving households where owning outright is the norm but paychecks stay modest.
Shelley Capito.p3: As of 2023, total employment stood near 641,300, with finance and insurance jobs running below the national norm and growing more slowly than the country as a whole. Retail trade and accommodation and food service added modestly to that base. The state's real distinction is extraction and utility work, fields where most places no longer specialize at all.

Sheri Biggs.p1: Median household income in the 3rd district of South Carolina sits at 65,919 dollars, well below most congressional districts. Housing has not scaled up to match: a home valued at 255,400 dollars runs 3.9 times that income, modest by national standards. Owning a home is the norm here far more than renting. Population density stays low, a district of open land rather than crowded blocks.
Sheri Biggs.p2: Credit union offices here outpace credit union employment, an unusual split worth noting up front: offices run slightly ahead of the national norm while the jobs behind them run well under it. Founders, S.C. State, and Spero Financial anchor that network, holding 25.6 percent of retail offices against banks in the district. Truist Bank books more deposits to an address here than any other bank does, under federal reporting rules, one name among many banks with branches in the district. For a district built on modest incomes, that office presence gives credit unions real reach into daily financial life.
Sheri Biggs.p3: Manufacturing dominates the working economy, running nearly three times the national norm in its share of local jobs as of 2023. Educational services add a second specialized layer on top of that. Overall finance and insurance employment stays light here, well under the national norm, even where credit union offices have kept a firm footing. This is a place built on making things, not managing money, which is exactly the gap a credit union here is positioned to fill.

Shomari Figures.p1: Median household income here is $54,977 a year, lower than in most congressional districts, with a poverty rate to match. Home values are modest too, a median of $175,100, but housing costs still eat into budgets more than those prices imply. Homeownership runs below the level seen in other districts, and jobs can be harder to find than the national picture. Spread across 703,362 people at low density, this is a place with room to spare and incomes that do not stretch far.
Shomari Figures.p2: Credit unions hold 30.7 percent of retail offices here, a share well above most districts in the country. MAX, ALL IN, and Navy Federal Credit Union carry that presence, competing against Regions Bank, which leads locally on deposits under how federal reporting assigns them. Both credit union jobs and credit union offices cluster here at levels well past the national norm, with office growth having outpaced the jobs behind it. For an economy with the income and cost pressures described above, that is a heavier-than-usual credit union footprint to work with.
Shomari Figures.p3: As measured in 2023, public administration jobs stood out sharply, nearly twice the national norm, and manufacturing carried real weight too, at 10.2 percent of jobs. Health care and social assistance was the biggest single employer, at 16.4 percent, with retail trade close behind. Finance and insurance work overall sat a touch under the national norm, even though the wider sector added jobs at a somewhat quicker clip across the ten years before.

Shontel Brown.p1: Median household income here sits at $56,120, among the lowest of any congressional district, and it shapes everything else. Home values run low too, but rent still claims 22.3 percent of that typical income, a real burden for households already stretched. Homeownership lags well behind most comparable places. With 759,075 people packed into a dense district and unemployment above the norm for peer places, wages have not kept pace with the basics.
Shontel Brown.p2: Credit union employment here runs at 0.31 times the national norm, well below where office presence sits at 0.76, a gap that shows branches persisting even as staffing has thinned. Navy Federal Credit Union, Century, and Firefighters Community CU anchor that presence locally. Credit unions hold just 16.0 percent of retail offices against banks here, with KeyBank National Association booking the largest deposit share under federal reporting rules. For an income-strapped population like this one, that thin staffing behind the branches matters as much as the office count itself.
Shontel Brown.p3: As measured in 2023, health care and social assistance was the largest and most concentrated employer, well above the national norm for its share of local jobs. Finance and insurance also ran well above the national norm for concentration, and management of companies led all sectors on that measure. Mortgage lending here leaned heavily toward home purchases rather than refinancing, and a substantial share of that lending reached lower-income neighborhoods.

Shri Thanedar.p1: Median household income here sits near the bottom of all congressional districts, at $50,937, and poverty runs deep alongside it. Home values are similarly low, at $156,200, though rent still eats a substantial share of what households bring in. Fewer households here own their homes than in most other districts. The district is also dense, packing far more people into each square mile than the typical seat.
Shri Thanedar.p2: Credit unions hold 34.4 percent of retail offices here, a share that puts this district ahead of nearly every other in the country. DFCU Financial, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Diversified Members carry that presence, against Comerica Bank, named the largest locally because federal rules book deposits to a single address rather than spread them across a branch network. Credit union employment runs slightly above the national norm, but their office count runs further ahead of it still, a network built wider than its staffing. That is the institution meeting the low-income households described above.
Shri Thanedar.p3: In 2021, the district's economy leaned hardest on utilities, transportation and warehousing, and finance and insurance, with utilities employment running nearly three times the national norm. Health care and social assistance and manufacturing employed the most people. Finance and insurance jobs ran well above the national norm that same year. Mortgage lending across all lenders skewed toward home purchases over refinancing, with a meaningful share reaching lower income neighborhoods.

Steny Hoyer.p1: Household income in the 5th district of Maryland runs to 128,699 dollars, near the top among districts nationwide. Homes there are worth 477,500 dollars at the midpoint, a modest multiple against that income, and rent takes a below-average bite out of what households actually earn here. Homeownership is widespread and poverty is rare. This is a district of settled, well-paid households living at moderate density.
Steny Hoyer.p2: Credit union jobs here run well above the national norm, a specialization that outpaces the credit unions' own office presence, which sits only slightly above typical levels. Navy Federal, NASA, and Cedar Point Credit Union anchor that presence alongside Truist Bank, the top deposit holder locally among many competing banks. Credit unions hold 24.8 percent of retail offices in the district. That combination points to members who carry mortgages and want a lender rooted nearby rather than one working off a distant balance sheet.
Steny Hoyer.p3: Professional, scientific, and technical services dominated the district's job mix by 2023, a highly specialized line of work here, alongside a similarly outsized presence in construction. Retail trade rounded out the largest employing sectors. Overall finance and insurance work sat well under its typical national weight even as credit union jobs bucked that pattern. Home purchase loans made up 54.4 percent of all mortgage originations, a district built more on buying than refinancing.

Stephanie Bice.p1: The 5th district of Oklahoma spreads its population thin, just over 236 people per square mile, open country rather than dense neighborhoods. Median household income runs 76,260 dollars, on the lower side compared with other districts. Housing stays inexpensive by comparison, a median home value of 274,700 dollars against that income, with homeownership reaching 64.6 percent. Poverty runs somewhat higher than most districts here.
Stephanie Bice.p2: Credit union employment runs well ahead of the national norm here, at 1.32 times, while credit union offices sit only slightly above it, a sign the credit unions present, TINKER, WEOKIE, and COMMUNICATION, staff their branches heavily rather than building out more of them. Those institutions hold 21.9 percent of retail offices, unremarkable next to other districts, in a market where MidFirst Bank books sizable deposits among many local bank rivals. A thinly settled district with modest housing costs is one where a credit union's people, not its square footage, carry the relationship.
Stephanie Bice.p3: By 2023, oil and gas extraction had become this district's clearest specialty, running five times the national norm despite claiming only a small slice of total jobs. Public administration and administrative support work also ran well above typical levels, and health care and social assistance accounted for a sizable portion of the workforce. Among home loans issued that year, purchases far outnumbered refinances.

Stephen Lynch.p1: This Massachusetts district posts a median household income of $118,563 a year, a figure few other congressional districts can match. Housing prices track that wealth: a median home value of $664,600 stands well clear of typical levels, and rent runs near $2,227 a month. Homeownership still lags most districts. Poverty runs well below typical levels here.
Stephen Lynch.p2: Credit union employment runs far below the national norm, yet the office count credit unions hold does not fall nearly as far, a mismatch worth noting up front. Rockland, Sharon & Crescent United, and Liberty Bay anchor the local presence, together accounting for 16.7 percent of retail offices, a thinner slice than similar districts tend to show. State Street Bank and Trust books the largest sum of deposits to an address here, though that reflects reporting rules more than local branch strength, and plenty of other banks operate alongside it. For a credit union, this is a market of high earners and high housing costs, with room to build office presence toward parity with its workforce.
Stephen Lynch.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance drove the district's economy, employing workers at 2.63 times the national norm and anchoring a broader specialization in professional and technical services and information work. Health care and social assistance employed the most people overall. Finance, technology, and knowledge work defined this district's character far more than manufacturing or trade.

Steve Cohen.p1: Household income in the 9th district of Tennessee is 55,603 dollars, lower than nearly every other congressional district, and poverty runs unusually high alongside it.
