Housing is cheap by national standards, a median home value of 225,300 dollars, yet it still sits heavy against what people actually earn here. Homeownership lags most other districts. Nearly 750,000 people live here, packed more densely than most, in a district that skews young.
Steve Cohen.p2: Credit unions here hold 40.4 percent of retail offices, a bigger slice than almost anywhere else, in a market of 120 bank branches spread across many separate lenders. Navy Federal Credit Union, Orion, and Memphis City Employees Credit Union are the names doing that work. Credit union offices are overrepresented against the national norm, even though credit union jobs run below it, so these are lean operations covering a lot of ground. For the renters and modest earners described above, that office density is often the most accessible financial doorstep in the district.
Steve Cohen.p3: Local industry was measured in 2023, and it centered on movement of goods: Transportation and Warehousing alone held 17.1 percent of jobs, a highly specialized multiple of the national norm. Wholesale trade and administrative and support services backed that up. Overall finance employment ran well below the national norm. This is a logistics economy first, with finance a smaller piece of the job base than in most places.

Steve Daines.p1: Montana spreads just over 1.1 million people across wide, empty country, with very few residents per square mile. Median household income sits at 75,340 dollars, trailing most other states. Home values, at 425,400 dollars, run above what most states see, yet rent stays moderate and homeownership is common. Jobs are easy to find here, with unemployment near the bottom nationally.
Steve Daines.p2: Whitefish Credit Union Association, Clearwater, and Altana anchor a credit union presence that is unusually large for this population and this income. Credit unions hold 29.0 percent of retail offices, a share well above most other states, competing against Glacier Bank, the deposit leader in a market that includes many other banks. Credit union employment runs 1.39 times the national norm, a specialized footprint that grows even faster than the office count itself. For a state with modest incomes and high homeownership, that is a lot of local financial capacity built around member institutions.
Steve Daines.p3: As of 2023, Montana's job base leaned hard on extraction and land: mining and quarrying ran 3.42 times the national norm, well beyond agriculture or public administration, both also specialized here. Health care, retail trade, and accommodation and food services employed the most people day to day. Overall finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm even as credit unions themselves ran thick. This is a resource and tourism economy with an outsized credit union sector layered on top.

Steve Scalise.p1: The 1st district of Louisiana holds just 218.6 people per square mile, thinner settlement than almost any comparable district and the fact that most sets this place apart. Its 798,569 residents earn a median household income of $79,823, about on par with other districts. Homeownership runs high at 73.1 percent, and homes are affordable against income, valued at roughly 3.7 times what a household typically earns. Poverty nonetheless sits above what most peer districts report.
Steve Scalise.p2: Credit union staffing is less concentrated than the national norm, while credit union offices are more common than the norm, a gap between payroll and physical presence worth noting going in. Keesler, ONPath, and Chevron define that branch network. Credit unions hold 22.6 percent of retail offices, a share close to what similar districts show, competing against a bank field where Hancock Whitney books the most deposits locally, a measure of booking, not necessarily branches or customers. Reaching a population this scattered is a real test for any lender here.
Steve Scalise.p3: In 2023, mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction was the district's clearest specialty, well ahead of the national norm despite employing a small share of workers directly. Transportation and warehousing and wholesale trade also ran ahead of the norm. Overall finance employment sat slightly below the national norm, in a district still built around moving goods and pumping oil rather than finance itself.

Steve Womack.p1: Unemployment stands at 2.7 percent, lower than nearly every other district measured, and that scarcity of idle labor shapes everything else in this economy. The typical household earns 75,345 dollars a year, trailing most other districts, while a home runs 319,400 dollars, cheap by national comparison. Homes here cost 4.2 times the typical income. Homeownership runs high, and the district covers ground thinly rather than clustering people into dense pockets.
Steve Womack.p2: Credit unions hold just 7.9 percent of retail offices here, one of the smaller shares found anywhere, in a market where Arvest Bank comes out ahead on deposits booked under federal accounting quirks, competing against many other banks. CommunityAmerica, United, and Arkansas credit unions are the names with a presence in the district. Credit union jobs are thin on the ground compared with the national picture, and office presence lags similarly. That leaves credit unions working a pool of modest incomes and solid homeownership that banks have already claimed most of.
Steve Womack.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing held the biggest share of jobs at 14.0 percent, well above the national norm for that sector. Management of companies and enterprises stood out even more sharply, running well above the national norm despite a smaller share of jobs. Health care and retail trade followed as large employers, though neither ran ahead of national patterns. Finance and insurance had been adding jobs faster than the nation as a whole.

Steven Horsford.p1: This district spreads its people thin, just 19.9 per square mile, among the lowest counts of any congressional district in the country. Across that stretch live 833,125 residents earning a median household income well short of most other districts. Home values run high against that income, a median of 415,700 dollars, and homeownership lags most comparable places. Unemployment runs unusually steep here too.
Steven Horsford.p2: Credit union offices here have grown further ahead of local hiring at those institutions than in most places, an unusual split worth leading with. America First, Navy Federal Credit Union, and Clark County Credit Union anchor that side of the market, holding 24.7 percent of retail offices, a share few districts match. Bank of America shows the largest deposit book on paper, a booking effect of federal reporting rather than a sign of branch dominance among the district's many bank branches. For a district this spread out, that office presence gives credit unions real reach into household finance.
Steven Horsford.p3: As of 2023, transportation and warehousing stood out sharply, employing 10.7 percent of workers, the clearest specialty in the local economy. Educational services and accommodation and food services followed as the next largest sources of work. Overall finance employment stayed thin against the national norm, even as finance and insurance jobs grew faster locally than nationally over the prior decade. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, making up most originations.

Suhas Subramanyam.p1: Household income in the 10th district of Virginia sets it apart from nearly every comparable district, at $157,863. Home values run high too, at $706,600, yet the ratio of value to income, 4.5, and rent at 16.5 percent of income, keep housing costs among the lowest measured anywhere. Homeownership runs high, while poverty and unemployment both sit far under typical levels. Work here is steady, and most households own the roof over their heads outright.
Suhas Subramanyam.p2: Credit unions here hold just 13.0 percent of retail offices, a small share next to the banks that dominate the market. Navy Federal Credit Union, Northwest, and Apple carry that share locally. Truist Bank leads the district by deposits booked there, though that reflects reporting rules more than local branch presence. Credit union employment runs well under the national norm, thin next to a district built on steady incomes and paid-off homes.
Suhas Subramanyam.p3: As of 2023, construction was highly specialized here, running well ahead of the national norm, and professional, scientific, and technical services followed close behind. Arts, entertainment, and recreation also ran well above the typical mix. Retail trade rounded out the largest employing sectors near the national norm. Across all lenders, mortgage originations tilted heavily toward home purchases, with 14.8 percent reaching lower-income neighborhoods, a pattern that fits a district built on stability rather than turnover.

Summer Lee.p1: Home values in the 12th district sit well below what most congressional districts see, at 219,600 dollars against a median household income of 74,565 dollars, a ratio of 2.9. Rent runs modest by comparison, a small slice of that income on a monthly basis. Homeownership lags behind comparable districts, and both poverty and joblessness sit on the high side too. Population density here outpaces most peers, with 754,530 people calling the district home.
Summer Lee.p2: Credit union offices here hold more ground than credit union payrolls do: office presence sits close to the national norm while credit union employment runs well under it. Clearview, Century Heritage, and Allegent Community anchor that office network, which claims 25.8 percent of retail offices in the district. PNC Bank tops the deposit figures by booking rules alone, one name among 225 bank branches, each belonging to a different competing bank. For a district with income and housing costs this modest, that office footprint gives credit unions real reach into everyday lending even without a large local workforce behind it.
Summer Lee.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance employment ran more than twice the national norm, and management of companies work climbed higher still. Health care and social assistance accounted for a sizeable chunk of local jobs, well beyond its usual weight in the workforce. That year, home purchases dominated mortgage lending, though only a modest slice reached lower income neighborhoods. This is a district shaped by finance work more than most, layered onto a modest cost of living.

Susan Collins.p1: Maine spreads a modest population across a lot of open land, work scattered rather than concentrated in one hub. Retail trade takes a larger share of jobs than the country sees, and health care leads as the largest single sector. Households earn a median $76,442, and homeownership sits high at 73.3 percent, with a $341,900 home value against that income putting prices at 4.5 times earnings.
Susan Collins.p2: Credit unions hold 34.2 percent of retail offices here, a share well above most states, serving a population where homeownership runs high and incomes trail the national figure. Atlantic Regional, Maine Savings, and Evergreen carry that presence, while the deposit figures on file point to TD Bank as the top name, a booking quirk of where accounts get recorded rather than a sign of empty competition. Credit union offices and credit union jobs both cluster well past what a state this size would normally carry, offices growing out ahead of the hiring. Few states depend on credit unions this much for everyday banking.
Susan Collins.p3: Beyond retail and care work, Maine's 2023 employment mix showed real strength in farming, forestry, fishing, and hunting work, well above the national norm, alongside a management-of-companies presence that also outpaced the country. All-around finance and insurance work ran slightly below the national norm. The state's specialized industries, land-based and corporate alike, sit apart from the retail and care work that otherwise fills out its job base.

Susie Lee.p1: A typical home in this district sells for 5.4 times what a middle household brings home each year, a wider gap than many peer seats show, and rent alone claims 24.9 percent of that income. Household earnings here run 90,358 dollars a year, ahead of most peer seats, yet just 57.3 percent own their homes. Poverty stays low even so. Pay is solid, but shelter absorbs an outsized share of it.
Susie Lee.p2: Credit union offices hold 20.3 percent of retail branches in this district, a thinner presence than in most peer seats, and credit union staffing runs thinner still against the countrywide baseline. Clark County, America First, and One Nevada are the names carrying that presence locally, working alongside Wells Fargo National Bank West and many competing banks for deposits. Branches have held on here even where staffing has not. That leaves credit unions a real but secondary channel in a market where housing costs stretch every borrower's math.
Susie Lee.p3: In 2023, construction stood out sharply, at 2.2 times the countrywide baseline, alongside management of companies and real estate leasing, both similarly concentrated. Accommodation and food services also employed a large share of the district's jobs. Finance and insurance employment ran above the countrywide baseline too, and grew faster than that norm over the prior decade. Construction, corporate management, and hospitality define this district's work, far more than finance does.

Suzan DelBene.p1: This district's households bring in $131,159 at the median, a figure few other congressional districts can match. Housing carries a similar weight, with a median home value of $871,500 and rent near $2,302 a month. Fewer households here own their homes than in comparable districts, while poverty stays low. The area is also crowded, with more people packed into each square mile than most of the country sees.
Suzan DelBene.p2: Credit union employment sits near the national norm, yet credit unions here control a smaller share of retail offices than similar districts do, and the two figures pull apart rather than track together. Boeing Employees, First Technology, and Global are the credit unions with a footing in this district. They hold 20.8 percent of retail offices, while Bank of America comes out on top of the district's banking deposits in a market crowded with rival branches. Set against the household earnings above, that is a modest storefront presence for the money this district holds.
Suzan DelBene.p3: This district's economy, as measured in 2023, ran heavily on Information work, employing at nearly ten times the national norm and making up the single largest share of jobs by far. Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services added a second strong specialty. Total employment approached 409,500 jobs. Home purchase loans made up most mortgage activity, while lending into lower-income neighborhoods stayed thin. This is a district built around tech and professional services, not around finance itself.

Suzanne Bonamici.p1: Homeownership here sits well below most comparable districts, at 57.2 percent, even though the money and housing stock both run high. Median household income reaches 97,201 dollars, and the median home is valued at 603,600 dollars, putting the home value at 6.2 times income, a sign of a tight, costly market. Density is thin for an urban district, and poverty runs lower than in most peer places.
Suzanne Bonamici.p2: Credit unions hold 33.2 percent of retail offices here, a share well beyond what most comparable districts show. First Technology, OnPoint Community, and Rivermark Community anchor that presence, against Bank of America as the top bank by deposits booked locally. Credit union employment runs specialized, well beyond the national norm, outpacing the more modest specialization seen in office counts, meaning these institutions carry more staff per office than is typical elsewhere. That mix of high earners, expensive homes, and a rental market many still depend on is the customer base a credit union here actually works with.
Suzanne Bonamici.p3: By 2023, management of companies had become the district's dominant sector, a concentration far beyond the national norm and ahead of the other industries measured here. Manufacturing employed a large share of workers, ahead of health care and professional, scientific, and technical services. Overall finance employment ran just under the national norm. Total employment approached 426,900 jobs, built on a base unusually tilted toward corporate management functions.

Sydney Kamlager-Dove.p1: This district is packed tightly, among the most densely settled in the country, and the crowding shapes everything else here. Median household income sits low at $69,595, while home values run far above it at $878,300, a gap that helps explain why homeownership here is scarce, just 31.4 percent. Rent runs $1,778 a month, and the poverty rate climbs well past what most districts report. Renters here are stretched against a housing market priced for someone else's paycheck.
Sydney Kamlager-Dove.p2: Credit unions hold just 15.5 percent of retail offices here, a share well below most comparable districts, leaving banks the dominant storefront presence alongside 89 branch locations. USC and First Entertainment are among the named institutions serving this market, alongside a large statewide credit union. Credit union employment runs below the national norm, though it still outpaces the thin office footprint, meaning fewer branches doing more work per location. For an income-strapped, renter-heavy population, that thin presence matters more than it would elsewhere.
Sydney Kamlager-Dove.p3: As of 2023, the job mix here leaned hard into information work, over five times the national norm, alongside strong specialization in arts and entertainment and in professional and technical services. Health care and professional services carried the largest shares of work. All finance-sector employment ran below the national norm. Mortgage lending data show a substantial share of originations reaching lower-income neighborhoods, a sign of continued lending activity despite the affordability strain described above.

Sylvia Garcia.p1: Median household income in the 29th congressional seat of Texas sits at $54,102, near the bottom of every district nationwide. Poverty runs high and joblessness follows the same pattern. Home values are modest by comparison, but rent still claims a heavy share of that income. A young, dense population fills this district, and homeownership lags most of its peers.
Sylvia Garcia.p2: Credit union jobs sit below the national norm here, even as credit union offices hold a stronger footprint than that norm, a gap between staffing and physical presence worth noting on its own. Navy Federal Credit Union, Texas Bay, and Shell anchor that presence, and together credit unions hold 28.9 percent of retail offices in the district. JPMorgan Chase books the largest deposit sum among local banks, a distinction tied to where deposits are recorded rather than to how many doors it operates or how many customers it serves locally. Set against income this constrained, that office share carries real weight for where households here actually turn to borrow.
Sylvia Garcia.p3: The district's economy leans hard on construction and on transportation and warehousing, both far more concentrated here than the national pattern, alongside a sharp pocket of oil and gas extraction work. Manufacturing and retail trade round out a workforce of roughly 263,300 jobs. Mortgage lending skews heavily toward home purchase rather than refinancing. A majority of all lending reaches lower income neighborhoods, where credit demand in this district actually sits.

Tammy Baldwin.p1: Wisconsin's economy still runs on making things: manufacturing accounts for 17.5 percent of jobs, close to twice the national norm and ahead of every other sector. Almost 6 million people live across the state at a density that is neither packed nor sparse. Household income sits near the middle of the pack nationally, and unemployment runs low. Housing carries little strain, with rent claiming just 17.7 percent of the median household's income.
Tammy Baldwin.p2: Credit unions hold 30.6 percent of retail offices here, a share well above most states, alongside banks like U.S. Bank National Association, which leads the state on deposits booked to its addresses, though it is far from the only bank at work here. Landmark, Community First, and Summit anchor the credit union side of that split. Credit union employment runs at 1.79 times the national norm, specialized rather than incidental, tracking closely with how thick that office presence is. That is a workforce built around manufacturing wages and modest housing costs, not speculative lending.
Tammy Baldwin.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing's dominance was matched by real but smaller strength in management of companies and enterprises and in agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting, both above the national norm. Health care and retail trade employed nearly as many people but without that same concentration. The state's edge was never in finance, but in the industrial base that finance was built to serve.

Tammy Duckworth.p1: Illinois packs 229 people per square mile, a settlement pattern denser than most states, onto an economy anchored in moving and trading goods: wholesale trade and transportation and warehousing both run slightly ahead of the national norm. Median household income reaches 83,211 dollars, above most states, while a typical house is priced at 280,700 dollars, keeping the home value to income ratio to a modest 3.4. Joblessness here outpaces most of the country.
Tammy Duckworth.p2: Credit unions hold just 15.1 percent of retail offices in the state, a slimmer footing than most states offer them, against a banking sector built from many competing branches, with JPMorgan Chase booking a leading deposit total among them. Alliant, Citizens Equity First, and State Farm carry the credit union name into a market banks otherwise dominate. Credit union employment lags the national norm by a wide margin, tracking closely with an equally light office presence, so credit unions here work a narrow lane against a much wider banking footprint.
Tammy Duckworth.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance jobs ran noticeably ahead of the national norm, an unusual thickness for a state whose employment still centers on health care and manufacturing. Manufacturing carries slight specialization of its own, consistent with the logistics tilt seen in wholesale and warehousing work. Growth in finance and insurance jobs over the prior decade ran just under the national pace. Illinois looks built to move and finance goods rather than to lean on any single dominant employer.

Ted Budd.p1: North Carolina counts just over 11 million residents, and the typical person here is 39.4 years old. Median household income sits at $73,958, trailing most other states, and poverty touches more households than in most parts of the country. Unemployment stays lower than most states manage. Home values sit in the middling range nationally, but housing costs overall press harder on residents than elsewhere, and homeownership trails most peers too.
Ted Budd.p2: State Employees', Navy Federal, and Coastal anchor a credit union footprint that holds 26.1 percent of retail offices statewide, well beyond what most states can claim. Credit union employment here runs fuller relative to the national norm than office counts alone would carry, meaning these institutions staff up without necessarily adding branches. The most deposits booked to addresses here land with Bank of America, though that reflects reporting rules more than local footprint, and it shares the state with a deep field of other banks serving the same households earning under $74,000 a median year.
Ted Budd.p3: As measured in 2023, manufacturing and finance and insurance both ran modestly above the national norm for their share of the state's job base, alongside administrative and support services. Health care and social assistance and retail trade employed sizable slices of workers overall. Finance and insurance jobs ran ahead of the national norm, and the wider finance and insurance category grew well ahead of the national pace between 2013 and 2023.

Ted Cruz.p1: Texas spreads 31,290,831 people thin, at a density that is neither crowded nor empty by national standards. A typical household brings in 79,721 dollars a year, unremarkable next to other states, but housing has pulled away from that income: a median home value of 313,200 dollars against that income runs well above most of the country. Homeownership lags too, with just 62.3 percent of households owning where they live. Joblessness and poverty both run higher here than in most of the country.
Ted Cruz.p2: Credit unions hold 22.7 percent of retail offices here, an ordinary share once set against other states. Navy Federal, Randolph-Brooks, and Pentagon carry that presence, set against a banking sector where JPMorgan Chase books the most deposits of any single name in the state. Credit union payrolls track the national norm closely, neither thin nor heavy by comparison. Against a state with stretched housing and income that only keeps pace, that footing gives credit unions real, ordinary weight.
Ted Cruz.p3: As of 2023, oil and gas extraction stood far out ahead of the rest of the country, employing at four times the national rate despite accounting for a small slice of jobs. The larger workforce sat elsewhere, in health care, retail trade, and educational services, without any of that work running unusually specialized. Finance and insurance employment, and its growth over the decade before, both outpaced the national norm, a steady undercurrent beneath the state's energy identity.

Ted Lieu.p1: This district sits packed tightly, among the densest of any comparable district on record, a fact that colors everything else about the place. Households earn well above typical incomes, but home values run just as high, and homeownership is thin, so most people rent rather than own. Poverty runs lower than most comparable places, while unemployment climbs well above them.
Ted Lieu.p2: Credit union employment here tracks closer to the national norm than office presence does, at 0.67 against norm versus 0.43 for offices. The credit unions active locally, Kinecta, CommunityAmerica, and a third named for its statewide reach among them, run leaner branch networks relative to the staff behind them. Credit unions hold just 17.8 percent of retail offices, below most peer districts, while City National Bank holds the top deposit total among 181 bank branches citywide. That leaves credit unions working a smaller share of a market built around high-income, high-cost renters.
Ted Lieu.p3: Work here concentrated in Information, highly specialized at four times the national norm, alongside strength in Arts, Entertainment, and Recreation and Real Estate and Rental and Leasing. Health Care and Social Assistance and Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services each carried a large share of the job mix. Overall finance and insurance employment ran below the national norm, growing roughly in step with the country over the prior decade. Home purchase loans made up 48.0 percent of all mortgage originations, with lower-income neighborhood lending a thin 2.5 percent slice of that activity.

Teresa Leger Fernandez.p1: This district spreads its 708,684 people across just 13.5 per square mile, among the thinnest settlement patterns of any district in the country. Household income runs low, at $66,346, and poverty is a persistent problem for many families here. Housing still stays affordable relative to that income, with a home value to income ratio of 3.9, and homeownership is unusually common at 73.1 percent. Unemployment runs a touch higher than in most comparable districts.
Teresa Leger Fernandez.p2: Credit union employment here is specialized, well above the national norm, while their share of retail offices, though above most peers at 28.2 percent, has grown more slowly, so these institutions run leaner branch networks staffed more heavily. Del Norte, State Employees, and Nusenda anchor that presence. Wells Fargo Bank, National Association books the most deposits of any bank locally, a distinction tied to where deposits are recorded rather than to branches or customer loyalty. For a population this thin and this income-strapped, that credit union footprint carries real weight.
Teresa Leger Fernandez.p3: As of 2023, overall finance and insurance employment lagged well behind the national norm. The district's real strength lay underground and outdoors: mining and oil and gas extraction employment ran far above that norm, with agriculture and utilities also prominent. Health care, retail, and food service rounded out the biggest job sources, none of them unusual for the country as a whole. Home purchase loans made up most mortgage originations that year, across every lender active in the district.

Terri Sewell.p1: Household income in the 7th district comes to 54,635 dollars annually, near the bottom among congressional districts, and the poverty rate runs high at 19.3 percent. Home values are modest too, at 183,200 dollars, while rent still claims an outsized share of what households earn. Work is harder to find here than in most of the country. At just 70 people per square mile, the population of roughly 719,000 sits scattered across wide, mostly rural stretches.
Terri Sewell.p2: Credit unions hold 34.3 percent of retail deposit offices here, a share well above most other districts, putting them in direct competition with Regions Bank and a crowded field of other local branches. America's First, Southern Energy, and Alabama One anchor that presence. Credit union employment and office counts both run well above the national norm, with offices out front of staffing. Against the income and rent burdens described above, that many physical counters gives residents an unusual amount of choice for routine banking.
Terri Sewell.p3: As of 2023, utilities employment stood out sharply against the national norm, alongside a manufacturing base that employs a solid share of the district's jobs. Health care and social assistance drew the largest share of workers. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, with lending to lower-income neighborhoods trailing well behind. This is a district built on utilities and manufacturing work, not finance.

Thom Tillis.p1: North Carolina packs 227.2 people per square mile onto an economy still anchored in making things: manufacturing holds a slightly outsized share of jobs, alongside finance and insurance and a sizable administrative and support sector. Median household income sits at 73,958 dollars, trailing most other states, and against a middle home value of 333,000 dollars that works out to 4.5 times earnings, pushing housing cost above most states. Unemployment, at 4.0 percent, runs low, while the poverty rate climbs past what most states report.
Thom Tillis.p2: Credit unions hold 26.1 percent of retail offices statewide, an outsized share next to most other states, and the names that surface here are State Employees', Navy Federal Credit Union, and Coastal. Bank of America books a sizable deposit sum in the state's records, but that reflects accounting geography more than local reach, and the sheer number of competing banks across the state means no single one dominates the ground. Credit union employment runs thicker than the national norm, while the number of offices roughly matches what you would expect, a balance that lines up with the income picture above.
Thom Tillis.p3: As measured in 2023, finance and insurance jobs ran slightly above the national norm and had grown well past it over the prior decade. Manufacturing kept its own hold on the job base, steady rather than shrinking. That pairing set the state apart: durable manufacturing next to a financial sector expanding fast.

Thomas Kean.p1: Household income in the 7th district of New Jersey stands out most: 132,702 dollars, among the highest of any congressional district. Home values reach 591,400 dollars against that income, a ratio of 4.5, while rent claims just 16.6 percent of income, a light load by comparison. Homeownership runs high and poverty runs low. Money is plentiful here and housing costs have not caught up to it.
Thomas Kean.p2: Credit unions hold just 13.9 percent of retail offices in the district, well short of what banks claim between them. Wells Fargo Bank books the largest deposits of any institution here, though many other banks compete in the district too. Merck Employees, Affinity, and Financial Resources are the credit unions with a presence. Both credit union employment and office presence run below the national norm, tracking each other closely in a district where high incomes give a credit union plenty of secure households to work with and little shelf space to reach them.
Thomas Kean.p3: By 2023, management of companies and enterprises had become the district's clearest specialty, at more than twice the national norm. Professional, scientific, and technical services and information rounded out the list. Health care, professional services, and retail trade employed the most people. Mortgage lending that year skewed heavily toward home purchases over refinancing, a sign of a market still built on people buying in rather than pulling equity out.

Thomas Massie.p1: Housing here costs less relative to income than almost anywhere comparable: the typical home runs 3.4 times the typical household's earnings, and rent takes just 16.5 percent of median income of $81,874. That affordability carries through to ownership, which is unusually high for a district this size. Home values themselves sit below most peer districts. This is a place with room to spread out, at 160.2 people per square mile.
Thomas Massie.p2: Credit unions hold only 9.7 percent of retail offices here, one of the thinnest shares among comparable districts, leaving banks to handle most of the local business. General Electric, Commonwealth, and L&N are the credit unions holding what little of that ground exists. Fifth Third Bank carries the largest deposit total booked to addresses here, but that figure owes more to where a bank's deposits get recorded nationally than to any real local dominance, since many separate banks operate branches in this district too. Credit union employment runs far below the national norm, a sign this sector operates at unusually small scale here.
Thomas Massie.p3: Moving and making things defined the job base in 2023: transportation and warehousing employed at nearly two and a half times the national norm, and manufacturing followed as a specialty too. Wholesale trade added a third area of concentration. Health care employed nearly as many people as manufacturing but without the same specialization. This was a district built more on logistics and factories than finance.

Thomas Suozzi.p1: This district's household income sits among the highest of any in the country, at $138,234. Home values run high to match, at roughly 5.7 times what a typical household earns here. Ownership is the norm rather than the exception, and poverty sits near the bottom of the national range. This is a dense, affluent corner of the Northeast.
Thomas Suozzi.p2: Credit unions hold a thin slice of the retail banking market here, just 12.2 percent of offices, well below what is typical elsewhere. Fourleaf, Jovia Financial, and Navy Federal Credit Union are the names active in the district, working against a field of banks led on deposits by Webster Bank, National Association. Credit union employment runs modestly below the national norm, but not by nearly as much as the office count would imply. This is a market where credit unions serve a high-income, high-homeownership population without much physical footprint.
Thomas Suozzi.p3: As of 2023, health care and social assistance dominated the district's job base, employing 30.7 percent of workers, a concentration far above the national norm. Other services and real estate also stood out as areas of local specialization. Retail trade and educational services added scale without any particular concentration. Total employment approached 372,400.

Thomas Tiffany.p1: This district is spread thin, just 32.6 people per square mile, the loosest settlement pattern of any comparable seat. The 754,076 residents living across that space earn a median household income of 73,003 dollars, trailing most peer districts, while unemployment stays low. Housing runs cheap relative to pay, a home value to income ratio of 3.6, and homeownership is unusually high, a place built around owning rather than renting.
Thomas Tiffany.p2: Credit unions hold 30.1 percent of retail offices here, a share that stands well above most comparable districts. ROYAL, CONNEXUS and COVANTAGE are the largest names doing that work, against a banking field where BMO Bank National Association books the largest deposits among many separate local competitors. Credit union employment runs more than triple the national norm, a concentration far beyond what the office count alone would predict, meaning these institutions staff their branches much more heavily than their physical footprint implies.
Thomas Tiffany.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing dominated the local economy, employing 21.9 percent of all workers, nearly two and a half times the national norm. Agriculture was similarly concentrated, and public administration added a further specialized layer on top. Overall finance employment ran slightly below the national norm even as the sector grew roughly in step with it nationally. This was an economy built on making and growing things rather than managing money.

Tim Burchett.p1: Joblessness is 3.1 percent, among the lower district rates, across a population of 813,928 with a median age of 40.3. Middle household earnings are 72,659 dollars, lighter than those in peer seats, while owner occupancy is common. The middle home equals about 5.0 times household income, near an ordinary district relationship. Modest pay and widespread ownership coexist in this market.
Tim Burchett.p2: Credit unions operate 33.4 percent of retail offices, a stronger footprint than most districts carry. Knoxville TVA Employees, ORNL, and Y-12 anchor the network amid numerous competing banks. Credit union staffing is more concentrated than the national norm, while the office network is heavier still. Physical reach therefore exceeds staffing weight, giving cooperatives a deep presence among the homeowning households described above. That combination gives credit unions a strong physical role in everyday banking.
Tim Burchett.p3: In the 2023 employment picture, management of companies, wholesale trade, and retail trade each carried more local weight than the national pattern. Health care and retail trade supplied two of the larger job pools, with accommodation and food services close behind. Finance and insurance employment sat near its countrywide baseline, while growth in the broader sector modestly outpaced the nation during the preceding decade. Corporate operations and trade, rather than finance, provide the clearest economic emphasis.

Tim Kaine.p1: Virginia's workforce leans hard into professional and technical work, the kind of consulting and engineering services that run well above the national norm. Households here earn more than most states, and the population is packed in more tightly than most, a settled working population rather than a transient one. Unemployment and poverty both sit well below what most states report, even as home values and rent climb above the norm.
Tim Kaine.p2: Credit unions hold 23.7 percent of the state's retail banking offices, a stronger footing than most states manage, though their office count itself runs close to the national norm rather than ahead of it. Employment in the credit union sector runs far above what the country typically sees, a specialization that outpaces the sector's physical office presence. Navy Federal, Virginia Credit Union and Langley anchor that presence, set against a banking market where Capital One books more deposits here than any other institution under federal reporting rules. That is the base a credit union here draws on, well-paid, densely settled households already used to housing costs above the national mark.
Tim Kaine.p3: Beyond finance, Virginia's 2023 employment picture leaned on health care and social assistance and on retail trade for a sizable share of work, though both ran close to or below the national norm. Professional and technical services and company management pulled the opposite way, running well above that norm. That mix marks Virginia as a place built more on expertise sold to others than on goods made or moved.

Tim Moore.p1: Homes here sell for 4.5 times the typical household's income, a gap wider than most comparable districts see. This district houses 792,862 people earning $78,324 at the midpoint. Homeownership runs above most comparable districts, and poverty sits well below it. Unemployment holds steady at a level unremarkable for the region.
Tim Moore.p2: Credit union offices here are somewhat more common than the national norm predicts, while credit union jobs run thin against that same norm, a gap between storefront presence and payroll worth noting. State Employees', Truliant, and Skyla anchor that presence. Credit unions hold 23.4 percent of retail offices here, near the middle of the range for comparable districts. Wells Fargo Bank leads all institutions by deposits booked locally, one name among many banks serving a district built on homeowners and middle-income earners.
Tim Moore.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing dominated the local job base, employing workers at 1.83 times the national norm, this district's clearest specialty. Wholesale trade added a second, smaller concentration above that norm as well. Finance and insurance jobs overall matched the national norm closely, but grew well faster than the national pace over the prior decade, a period spanning two different maps of this district. That combination of steady manufacturing strength and fast-growing finance work sets the local economy apart.

Tim Scott.p1: South Carolina packs 182.2 people per square mile onto its land, denser than most states manage, with a workforce that leans hard on making things: manufacturing holds 12.6 percent of jobs, well above the national norm. Households earn a median $72,350, trailing most states, yet homeownership sits high at 72.3 percent even as home values and rents run above what comparable places see. Poverty runs above most states too, a harder edge beneath those homeownership numbers.
Tim Scott.p2: Credit unions hold 24.5 percent of the state's retail offices, a bigger share than most states carry, built up through Navy Federal Credit Union, Founders, and South Carolina Credit Union operating alongside Bank of America, the state's largest bank by deposits though hardly its only one. Credit union offices run 1.21 times the national norm, a footprint that has expanded faster than the staff needed to run it. That matters in a state where homeownership is high but income modest, leaving plenty of everyday borrowing for these institutions to carry.
Tim Scott.p3: Finance and insurance jobs overall sit below the national norm here, though the sector added ground against the rest of the country between 2013 and 2023. The real specialization was industrial: manufacturing and utilities both stood out as unusually concentrated that year. South Carolina's economy was built less on finance than on making and moving goods, with retail trade filling out the rest of the workforce.

Tim Sheehy.p1: Montana spreads just under 1.14 million people across wide, thin ground, fewer than eight people per square mile, about as sparsely settled as any state in the country. Jobs concentrate in retail trade, accommodation and food service, and health care, while unemployment stays remarkably low. Households earn a median $75,340, trailing most of the country, yet home values have climbed high enough that the value-to-income ratio now stands at 5.6.
Tim Sheehy.p2: Credit unions hold 29.0 percent of retail offices in Montana, a share few states can match, a foothold built for a population scattered across small towns rather than clustered in one metro. Whitefish Credit Union Association, Clearwater, and Altana carry that presence, alongside Glacier Bank, named the deposit leader by federal rules that count where a bank books its money, not where it operates. Work inside credit unions here is unusually concentrated, well beyond what the national picture would predict, suggesting these institutions employ at a scale that outpaces their share of storefronts.
Tim Sheehy.p3: Mining and oil and gas extraction, measured for 2023, came in far more concentrated here than the country as a whole, alongside agriculture and a public sector swollen by federal and tribal administration. Finance and insurance jobs overall stayed thin against the national picture, even as that broader sector added positions a bit faster than the country did between 2013 and 2023. Employment leaned on tourism-facing trades, resource extraction, and government work rather than a concentrated corporate base.

Tim Walberg.p1: Property remains inexpensive beside earnings. The middle home is worth 228,200 dollars and produces a 3.2 ratio against median household income of 70,684 dollars. Both measures sit toward the modest side of district ranges. Owner occupancy is common, poverty and unemployment are restrained, and population density is low. The result is a household market shaped by small cities and rural areas rather than a major metropolis.
Tim Walberg.p2: Credit unions operate 39.4 percent of retail offices, giving them an unusually large physical role beside banks. TLC Community, United, and True Community anchor that network. Federal records place Huntington National Bank first on the deposit measure attributed locally, within a district containing many bank branches. Credit union staffing exceeds twice the national concentration, confirming that cooperative finance has substantial employment weight as well as storefront reach.
Tim Walberg.p3: In 2021, manufacturing accounted for 22.2 percent of jobs and stood at more than twice the national norm, making it the dominant employment distinction. Utilities employed fewer people but had an even sharper concentration compared with the nation. Finance and insurance employment was below its countrywide baseline despite the strength of credit unions specifically. Purchase lending outweighed refinancing that year. Manufacturing and utilities, not broad financial work, defined the economy.

Timothy Kennedy.p1: This district packs people in tightly, far more densely than most comparable seats, and that crowding shapes daily life more than any other trait here. Household income sits low, at $64,666, and poverty runs deep, touching a larger slice of residents than in most other districts. Home values are modest at $232,800, and homeownership trails most other districts. Unemployment runs higher than in most peer districts too, a sign of an economy still working to keep pace with its population.
Timothy Kennedy.p2: Credit unions hold 38.5 percent of retail offices here, a share among the highest of any district in the country. Broadview, Cornerstone Community, and Niagara's Choice carry that presence, alongside Manufacturers and Trust Company, the largest bank by deposits booked locally. Credit union offices are more numerous relative to the national norm than credit union jobs are, so the physical footprint here outruns the staffing behind it. For an income base and homeownership rate like this district's, that office network carries real weight.
Timothy Kennedy.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance was this district's most specialized sector, employing at a rate well past the national norm, alongside management of companies and other services. Health care and social assistance employed the most people, followed by educational services. Retail trade, by contrast, ran below the national norm. Lenders active here put most originations toward home purchases, while a smaller share of lending reached lower income neighborhoods, evidence of a finance-heavy economy still working to serve a population that is not itself high-income.

Tina Smith.p1: Minnesota spreads its 5,793,151 people thinly across the state, with work concentrated in health care and a manufacturing base that runs well above the national norm. Median household income of 87,117 dollars sits above most states, paired with low unemployment and low poverty. Homeownership is common and housing costs run well below what income alone would predict. This is a state built on steady, specialized production work rather than a dense, service-driven economy.
Tina Smith.p2: Credit unions hold 21.1 percent of retail offices here, a smaller slice than in most states, set against a deep field of competing banks statewide. ENT, Affinity Plus, and TrustOne Financial anchor that presence, working the same manufacturing and health care paychecks that define the state's income base. Credit union employment runs slightly below the national norm even as office presence sits almost exactly at it, so branches here operate leaner than the industry typically does. U.S. Bank National Association books the largest deposit share, a function of reporting rules rather than local branch strength.
Tina Smith.p3: Employment data from 2023 shows the economy leaning hardest on management of companies and enterprises, manufacturing, and health care, the first two far more concentrated than the nation as a whole. Finance and insurance employment also ran above the national norm, though the broader finance sector added jobs more slowly than the country did over the decade prior. The state's distinct strength was corporate management functions, layered onto durable factory and hospital employment rather than retail or tourism.

Todd Young.p1: Indiana runs on making and moving things: manufacturing alone accounts for nearly a fifth of jobs, a heavy concentration against the national norm, with transportation and warehousing adding a second layer of specialization. The state is more densely settled than most of its peers, and unemployment sits at a low 4.1 percent. Households earn a median $71,959, a modest figure next to other states, yet homeownership runs high at 70.7 percent. Rent claims 18.4 percent of median income, a lighter load than most states carry.
Todd Young.p2: Credit unions hold 27.1 percent of retail offices statewide, a share above most peer states, in a market where the largest bank by deposits, JPMorgan Chase, books its lead through reporting rules rather than branch presence among the state's 1,741 bank branches. Everwise, Indiana Members, and Elements Financial anchor the credit union side. Credit union offices run well ahead of the national norm here, more so than credit union employment does, so the physical footprint outpaces the staffing behind it. That footprint matters where manufacturing wages and homeownership, not high income, define what members bring to the counter.
Todd Young.p3: As measured in 2023, finance and insurance jobs overall sat below the national norm even as manufacturing anchored the state's job base, with wholesale trade also running slightly ahead of typical levels. Growth in finance and insurance jobs matched the national pace over the prior decade. Indiana's economy is built to make things and ship them, not to bank them.

Tom Barrett.p1: Pay stretches relatively far into homeownership here. A middle-priced home equals 3.5 times middle household earnings, while the income figure is 80,268 dollars and 73.2 percent of homes are owner occupied. About 792,585 people live across a district with moderate settlement density. These measures describe a stable ownership market rather than a place where shelter runs away from earnings. The combination gives households a comparatively attainable route from income to property.
Tom Barrett.p2: Retail banking has a large cooperative component: credit unions operate 38.2 percent of its offices. MSU Federal, Lake Trust, and LaFCU supply the principal names. First National Bank of America has the foremost deposit amount assigned locally, though numerous banks maintain competing operations. Credit union staffing is much more concentrated than its already substantial office network. For households whose earnings align reasonably with home prices, those institutions function as a familiar part of the financial market rather than a minor alternative.
Tom Barrett.p3: The employment snapshot dates to 2021. Public administration was heavily concentrated, with finance and insurance plus educational services also somewhat more common than their national baselines. Health care and social assistance joined retail trade among the main job fields. Approximately 305,900 positions made up the measured economy. Finance's modest specialization fit a place that also gave credit unions a substantial role in everyday financial service.

Tom Cole.p1: People spread thin across the 4th congressional seat of Oklahoma, just 84.2 residents per square mile, well below most comparable districts. Household income sits at $67,377, and home values follow the same modest pattern, both trailing most peers. A home here costs a stretch over three years of household earnings, looser than the norm, while a month's rent takes a small bite out of that income. Homeownership is the norm across the district, but hardship reaches a larger share of families than in most comparable places.
Tom Cole.p2: Credit union employment here runs thick, 1.39 times the national norm, well ahead of how much retail office space credit unions actually hold, and that mismatch says more about this district's institutions than either figure alone. Tinker, Communication, and Navy Federal Credit Union anchor that presence, even though credit unions hold just 18.2 percent of retail offices. BancFirst books sizable local deposits among a broader field of banks. Together these numbers describe institutions running lean on storefronts but heavy on staffing, matched to the modest incomes and homeownership described above.
Tom Cole.p3: Oil, gas, and mining stood out sharply as of 2023, running well above the national norm despite employing a small slice of workers, a concentrated pocket rather than a broad base. Accommodation and food services employed far more of the district's workforce, and retail trade added a similar share. Overall finance employment ran thin against the national norm, leaving credit unions to carry an outsized part of the district's financial workforce.

Tom Cotton.p1: Arkansas is a lightly settled state, its job base tilted toward factories and company headquarters more than most places. Manufacturing runs well above the national norm, and so does management of companies and enterprises. Median household income sits at 62,106 dollars, among the lowest of any state. Set against a median home value of 215,600 dollars, that puts the ratio at a mild 3.5 to 1, and monthly housing costs stay well under what most states report.
Tom Cotton.p2: Credit unions hold just 10.7 percent of retail offices here, a smaller footprint than in comparable states, and banks otherwise dominate the branch network. Bank OZK carries the largest deposit total, though that reflects deposits booked to an address here rather than a strong local branch presence, and it competes with many other banks across the state. Arkansas, CommunityAmerica, and United carry the credit union name in this market. Credit union employment runs far below the national norm, even as offices hold up better than jobs do, a sign of thin staffing rather than thin reach.
Tom Cotton.p3: As of 2023, Arkansas's economy leaned on manufacturing, health care, and retail trade for its biggest job counts, with utilities and management of companies rounding out its most distinctive sectors. All finance and insurance jobs sat below the national norm, though that sector grew about in step with the country between 2013 and 2023. What sets this state apart is production capacity, an economy built more around making and moving goods than around finance itself.

Tom Emmer.p1: Housing here costs little relative to what people earn, home values sit at 3.6 times median household income and rent takes just 14.9 percent of it, among the lowest housing burdens measured anywhere. Households bring in $105,084 at the median, well above the typical district. Homeownership is common, and both poverty and unemployment run low. Stable, well-paid work and widespread homeownership define daily life here.
Tom Emmer.p2: Credit union offices here outpace credit union jobs by a wider margin than usual, offices run just above the national norm while employment sits below it, a split that deserves attention before anything else. BLAZE, ENT, and St. Cloud Financial are the credit unions with a presence in the district, competing for retail business against Wells Fargo Bank, the largest holder of deposits by federal booking rules among 157 bank branches overall. Credit unions hold just 18.9 percent of retail offices, a smaller slice of the branch network than in most peer districts. Steady household income paired with a light credit union footprint is the mismatch worth watching here.
Tom Emmer.p3: As measured in 2023, manufacturing accounted for 15.3 percent of jobs and ran well above the national norm for the sector, alongside construction and wholesale trade as the district's other specialized industries. Together they mark a district oriented toward producing and shipping physical goods. Most mortgage activity in the district went toward buying homes rather than refinancing, a sign that people here settle in rather than move through.

Tom McClintock.p1: This district spreads its people thinly, well under a hundred per square mile, a settlement pattern far more open than most congressional seats carry. Households here earn above what comparable districts report, and home values sit high to match, with a home value to income ratio of 5.5 that points to real strain for anyone trying to buy in. Ownership is unusually common at 71 percent, but unemployment runs high next to other districts, a harder edge under an otherwise comfortable-looking picture.
Tom McClintock.p2: Golden 1, EEFCU, and Valley First anchor credit union presence here, though credit unions hold just 17.9 percent of retail offices, a thinner share than most comparable districts carry against Wells Fargo and the 156 bank branches operating locally. Credit union employment sits at 0.66 times the national norm, and office presence tracks closely with it, both below typical levels elsewhere. For a credit union, that means working a market of high-earning, mostly-owning households without the office footprint peer districts have built to reach them.
Tom McClintock.p3: Measured in 2023, employment here leaned on farm work, with agriculture running well above the national norm. Health care and social assistance carried an outsized share of work too, alongside accommodation and food services, pointing to a district built on care work and hospitality rather than offices. Arts, entertainment, and recreation also ran ahead of national levels. Finance overall employed below the national rate, a modest slice of an economy oriented elsewhere.

Tommy Tuberville.p1: Manufacturing anchors this state's job base, holding 13.9 percent of employment, a heavier share than the country carries overall. People here live spread across small and mid-sized communities, not clustered around one dominant metro. A typical household brings in 66,659 dollars a year, trailing most of the country, while home values sit well below the national picture too. Homeownership runs high, even as the poverty rate climbs well past the national norm.
Tommy Tuberville.p2: Credit unions hold 30.1 percent of retail offices in this state, a share well above most states, in a market where Regions Bank leads on deposits booked locally among a field of many competing banks. Redstone, All In, and America's First carry the credit union side of that business. Credit union offices run at 1.83 times the national norm and credit union employment at 1.47 times, offices expanding faster than staffing has kept up. That is a heavier credit union presence than most states carry, well suited to a population of homeowners and manufacturing workers who want branches close to home.
Tommy Tuberville.p3: As of 2023, health care and social assistance employed the most people in the state, just ahead of manufacturing, across roughly 1,902,800 jobs statewide. Utilities stood out most sharply against the national norm of any sector measured. Finance and insurance employment overall ran below the national norm, and its growth over the following decade roughly tracked the national pace. This state's real strength lay in production and infrastructure work, not finance.

Tony Wied.p1: Housing here costs little against what people earn, a burden lighter than almost anywhere else measured. A home value to income ratio of 3.6 and rent near a tenth-sixth of income leave room in household budgets that a typical income of $78,966 does not on its own explain. Homeownership is common and poverty rare here. This is a district of settled households and steady work, spread thin rather than crowded.
Tony Wied.p2: Credit unions hold 36.4 percent of retail offices in this district, a share that puts it near the top of the pack. Community First, Capital, and Fox Communities carry that presence, set against a banking sector still led on paper by Associated Bank, National Association, a name that reflects deposits booked to one address rather than branches spread across the district. Credit union employment runs well above the national norm, and office presence further still, a specialization that matches a district full of homeowners with steady paychecks and light housing costs. These are institutions built for exactly the households described above.
Tony Wied.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing anchored the local economy, employing 20.6 percent of the district's jobs, a concentration well beyond what the nation shows overall. Agriculture and wholesale trade added further depth, work tied to the land and to moving goods rather than to any single large employer. Mortgage lending leaned toward home purchases over refinancing, fitting a district built around owning the place you live.

Tracey Mann.p1: Space defines this district before anything else, its population scattered more sparsely than nearly all its counterparts nationwide. Across that expanse live 731,386 residents earning a median household income of 67,677 dollars, on the low side next to other districts. Unemployment runs low, and housing costs far less than typical, with a median home value of 184,200 dollars and rent near 945 dollars a month.
Tracey Mann.p2: Credit unions hold just 15.3 percent of retail offices here, the thinnest presence of any fact measured about them in this place. Navy Federal Credit Union, Golden Plains, and Credit Union of America carry that presence, set against KS StateBank, the name that leads local banks by deposits reported to addresses here. Credit union employment still runs a touch above the national norm, at 1.13 times, and jobs here outpace the office count itself. For an economy this income-constrained and this spread out, that is a real foothold, just not a majority one.
Tracey Mann.p3: Manufacturing anchors the job base, followed closely by health care and educational services, but the sharper signal sits in agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting, which runs at nearly four times the national norm. Extraction work in mining, oil, and gas carries a similarly outsized weight against what is typical elsewhere. Overall finance employment runs below the norm, reflecting how much of this economy sits outside banking altogether. In the working year measured, 2023, this was a district shaped by land based production, not office work.

Trent Kelly.p1: Household income here is among the lowest of any congressional district, at $60,524, and hardship shows up in a poverty rate well beyond what comparable seats post. Even so, unemployment stays low, and most households own rather than rent, at 71.7 percent. Home prices land far under the typical district figure, keeping housing modest against income. With 753,783 people spread across mostly open land, this is rural Mississippi, low-cost and low-wage at once.
Trent Kelly.p2: Credit unions hold just 9.2 percent of retail offices here, a share thinner than nearly every other district measured. Navy Federal Credit Union, CommunityAmerica, and Triangle are the names doing business in a market still dominated by banks, with Cadence Bank booking the largest deposit share among 295 branch offices in the district. Credit union employment runs far below the national norm, even though office presence holds up closer to it. For an institution here, that gap between staff and storefronts is the daily reality.
Trent Kelly.p3: As measured in 2023, manufacturing anchored the district's economy, employing 18.1 percent of workers at a rate that topped the national figure more than twofold. Transportation and warehousing ran even further past the norm, a rare concentration for a district this size. Finance and insurance jobs stayed thin overall, well under the national average, though the sector grew slightly faster than the country as a whole. What this place does well is move and make physical goods, not run financial back offices.

Troy Balderson.p1: Home values in this district run at 3.5 times the median household income of 78,547 dollars, while monthly rent absorbs only 15.2 percent of that pay, a gap between cost and earnings that few other districts can match. Homeownership is common here too, at 74.4 percent of households. Poverty and joblessness both run on the low end. Add a population spread thin across the land rather than packed into it, and this is a settled, affordable place to plant roots.
Troy Balderson.p2: Credit unions hold a thin slice of the retail banking market here, just 11.9 percent of offices, a share few other districts fall below. OUCU Financial Credit Union, TrueCore, and Kemba Financial are the names doing that work, against Park National Bank, which books the largest local deposits. Credit union employment and office presence both trail national norms, with offices holding up somewhat better than jobs. That is a light footprint for an economy this large.
Troy Balderson.p3: As of 2023, manufacturing anchored the district, employing 15.9 percent of its jobs at well above the national norm, with mining and quarrying even more concentrated despite its small size. Transportation and warehousing also ran well above the national norm. Overall finance employment sat below the national norm, even as the finance and insurance sector grew faster than the country as a whole between 2013 and 2023.

Troy Carter.p1: Household income in the 2nd district of Louisiana is among the lowest of any congressional seat, at 58,115 dollars a year, and close to a fifth of residents live in poverty, one of the highest rates measured anywhere. Home values run low next to other districts, yet rent still eats a heavy share of income, a mismatch that squeezes household budgets from both directions. The district counts about 736,000 people, with a median age of 39.6.
Troy Carter.p2: Credit unions hold 34.6 percent of retail offices against banks here, a share far higher than most districts in the country. Credit Human, Navy Federal Credit Union, and OnPath carry that presence, while Capital One, National Association leads only on deposits booked to a single address, not on branches or local customers. Credit union offices run well ahead of the national norm even as credit union jobs sit just under it, so the office network has grown ahead of the staff inside it. That dense office presence carries real weight for households already stretched thin.
Troy Carter.p3: The working economy, measured in 2023, leaned on Accommodation and Food Services, its most specialized sector nationally. Construction followed as a second specialty, also well above the norm elsewhere. Overall finance employment ran well under typical levels, leaving hospitality and building trades as the clearer marks of this district's economy. Mortgage lending favored home purchases strongly, at 61.9 percent of originations.

Troy Downing.p1: Few places in the country settle their population as thinly as this district does, at 5.3 people per square mile, holding 558,158 residents. Household income runs low next to other districts, at 73,599 dollars. Housing costs far less than that income might imply: home values sit near 4.8 times income, and homeownership is unusually common here. Unemployment and poverty both run low as well.
Troy Downing.p2: Retail locations here belong to credit unions at a rate of 31.9 percent, well above most similar areas, in a market where Stockman Bank of Montana leads on deposits even though many other banks operate here too. Altana, Valley Financial, and Montana Credit Union are the names locals would recognize. Credit union staffing runs well ahead of the countrywide baseline, more so than the office count itself, so these institutions do more with each location than elsewhere in the country. For a population spread this thin, with income modest and homeownership high, that footprint carries real weight.
Troy Downing.p3: The working economy here, in 2023, leaned hardest on mining and oil and gas extraction, agriculture, and public administration, sectors far more concentrated than the national picture. Health care, retail trade, and food service employed the most people day to day, only modestly above typical levels elsewhere. Overall finance employment ran just under the countrywide baseline even so, with credit unions carrying unusual weight inside it. Mortgage lending here leaned heavily toward loans for buying homes rather than refinancing them.

Troy Nehls.p1: Household income in the 22nd congressional seat of Texas is among the highest of any congressional district, at $115,961. Home values run near $393,300 against that income, a modest ratio, and the resulting cost burden falls well below what most districts carry. Homeownership and low poverty both stand out here too, a household picture unusually comfortable for its size. Just under 895,000 people call the district home, with a median age of 38.
Troy Nehls.p2: Credit union employment here runs well above the national norm even though credit union offices hold a share of the retail branch network, 22.3 percent, that only matches typical districts. Navy Federal Credit Union, Schlumberger Employees, and First Community anchor that presence. JPMorgan Chase books the largest deposit sum to an address here, but federal reporting rules drive that figure more than any real local dominance, and 170 other bank branches compete for business. The income and homeownership described above give a credit union here a deep, stable base to lend against.
Troy Nehls.p3: Employment in 2023 leaned heavily on classroom and campus work, a specialty found in few other districts, alongside a steady base in health care and retail. Mining and oil and gas extraction made up a small slice of jobs but stood out sharply against the national pattern. Finance and insurance employment overall ran light for a district this size, even as that sector grew faster locally than nationwide. Mortgage lending skewed heavily toward home purchases over refinancing.

Val Hoyle.p1: Space defines this district before anything else does, a mere 61.4 residents per square mile, thinner than most congressional districts manage. A typical household here earns 69,445 dollars a year, while a typical home runs 438,000 dollars, a gap wide enough to sit among the widest home-to-income divides anywhere. Both poverty and joblessness sit far above what a comparable district would usually show. Ownership still holds at 64.2 percent.
Val Hoyle.p2: Credit unions hold 40.8 percent of retail offices here against banks, a share among the highest found anywhere in the country. Oregon Community, First Technology, and SELCO Community carry that presence, sharing the field with Umpqua Bank, a large holder of deposits assigned to addresses here among many separate competing banks. Credit union payrolls dwarf the national norm by a wider margin than even their office count does, a sign of lean branches carrying unusually deep staffing. That is what member-owned lending looks like where distances stretch long and housing has outrun income.
Val Hoyle.p3: As measured in 2023, the job base leaned hardest on agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting, well beyond the national norm, with management of companies and enterprises also notable. Health care and social assistance made up a large slice of the district's roughly 258,000 jobs. Overall finance employment sat below the national norm, leaving credit unions to carry unusual weight in a workforce still rooted in land and caregiving.

Valerie Foushee.p1: Household income in the 4th district of North Carolina sets it apart from comparable districts more than anything else measured here, running well above most. Home values are high too, near $531,100, while rent sits around $1,723 a month against housing costs that otherwise sit right in the middle of the national pack. Poverty and unemployment both run low, and the population is dense for a congressional seat, with people packed in at nearly 764 per square mile.
Valerie Foushee.p2: State Employees', Coastal, and Navy Federal Credit Union anchor the credit union presence here, and together credit unions hold 27.5 percent of retail offices, a share that stands out against most districts. That gives credit unions a real foothold against the district's 115 bank branches, run by many separate banks, including Banc of California, whose reported deposits reflect where they are booked rather than local branch presence. Credit union employment tracks that office footprint closely, running a bit ahead of the national norm. Against the district's high incomes and home values, credit unions here work with a wealthier, more competitive market than most of their peers see.
Valerie Foushee.p3: As of 2023, this district's economy leaned hard into professional and technical services, employing 15.0 percent of workers at a rate far exceeding the national norm. Finance and insurance jobs also ran a touch above that norm, and grew faster locally than the sector did nationally between 2013 and 2023. Mortgage lending skewed toward home purchases over refinancing, with a smaller share reaching lower-income neighborhoods.

Vern Buchanan.p1: Housing here runs 4.7 times the median income, and that gap stands out more than any other measure against comparable districts. Rent takes 26.4 percent of the median household income, and that household earns well above the norm for peer districts. Homeownership is high, at 74.2 percent of housing, while poverty and unemployment both sit low. This is also a denser district than most, filled with working households rather than retirees.
Vern Buchanan.p2: Credit union jobs here run close to the national norm, while credit union offices sit further behind that norm, meaning the branches that do exist tend to carry more staff relative to their numbers. Suncoast, Lake Michigan, and MidFlorida anchor that presence. Together, credit unions hold 16.6 percent of retail offices, a smaller slice than in most comparable districts, competing against a much larger set of bank branches, with Bank of America booking a leading deposit share among them.
Vern Buchanan.p3: As of 2023, this district worked with roughly 216,300 jobs, with retail trade and accommodation and food services each employing large shares of workers alongside health care. Construction ran specialized, and agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting stood out even more, unusual weight for a district this dense. Finance and insurance jobs overall trailed the national norm. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, which made up most originations.

Veronica Escobar.p1: Median household income in the 16th congressional seat of Texas sits at 60,456 dollars, among the lowest of any congressional district in the country. Home values run modest here too, at 212,500 dollars, keeping the gap between pay and housing prices narrower than in most places. Rent runs 1,079 dollars a month, and homeownership trails most comparable districts. Poverty runs unusually deep in this district.
Veronica Escobar.p2: Credit unions hold 45.2 percent of retail offices here, a share that sits above nearly every other congressional district in the country. GECU, Navy Federal Credit Union, and FirstLight carry that presence, serving the same stretched incomes and tight rents described above. WestStar Bank comes out on top of the deposit figures tied to this district, a count driven by where accounts are booked rather than by any lead in branches, since 81 offices belonging to other banks operate here as well. Credit union payrolls carry unusual weight in the local job market, well beyond what the office count alone would explain.
Veronica Escobar.p3: As of 2023, the district leaned hard on administrative and support services, transportation and warehousing, and accommodation and food services, all well beyond typical national employment levels. Health care and retail trade employed the most people, without the same pull above the norm. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases over refinancing.

Vicente Gonzalez.p1: Household income in the 34th district of Texas sits at $54,486 a year, among the lowest figures any congressional district reports, with hardship following close on its heels. Home values are modest too, near a median of $149,700, so what a house costs stays close to what a household earns, a ratio of 2.7. Rent runs $953 a month, a manageable slice of that income. The population sits loosely across a wide expanse, well short of the density found in most districts.
Vicente Gonzalez.p2: Credit union employment here runs well under the national norm even though credit union offices hold close to it, a gap between staffing and storefronts worth carrying into any local meeting. RALLY, Navy Federal, and Security Service anchor that credit union presence, against a retail banking field where International Bank of Commerce books the largest deposits under federal reporting rules. Credit unions hold 21.2 percent of retail offices here. That footprint serves a population with limited income and high poverty, which shapes what lending and services actually get used on the ground.
Vicente Gonzalez.p3: Health Care and Social Assistance carried this economy, at 25.8 percent of jobs, a concentration well beyond the norm, with Educational Services close behind it. Overall finance sector employment stayed well under the national norm. Mortgage lending skewed heavily toward home purchases over refinancing, with a smaller share of loans reaching lower-income neighborhoods.
