Victoria Spartz.p1: Housing here costs far less than income would imply: the median home runs 3.6 times the median household income, and typical rent takes just 17.8 percent of that income. Homeownership runs high at 72.8 percent, and both poverty and unemployment sit on the low side. With a population of 791,265, this is a settled, middle-income district where housing remains inexpensive beside earnings.
Victoria Spartz.p2: Credit union office concentration exceeds staffing concentration, the main split in their local position. Indiana Members, Forum, and Everwise operate a network that gives credit unions 26.6 percent of retail offices, a share above most comparable districts. Merchants Bank of Indiana has the leading deposit position assigned locally, within a field of numerous banks. For a credit union here, physical presence already outruns staffing weight, which ties a substantial storefront network to the homeowning households described above.
Victoria Spartz.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance was a specialized sector for this district, employing 7.1 percent of its jobs, with manufacturing and retail trade close behind. Over the preceding decade, its local expansion outpaced the country. Purchase loans dominated originations that year; lending to lower-income neighborhoods was much less common. This is a place organized around steady finance work and homeownership, not high housing costs.

Vince Fong.p1: Unemployment reaches 7.3 percent, among the higher district rates, while median household earnings are a comparatively strong 90,892 dollars. Housing at the midpoint costs about 436,000 dollars, giving it a 4.8 ratio against income. Residents occupy a broad territory at low density. The contrast is a well-paid but uneven labor market organized around agriculture and energy rather than an urban employment center.
Vince Fong.p2: Credit unions operate 45.4 percent of retail offices, a particularly strong share beside banks. Valley Strong and Navy Federal Credit Union anchor the cooperative network. Federal address reports list JPMorgan Chase ahead on deposits even though its physical network is thin. Credit union staffing and office concentration are both far above the national norm, with locations carrying still more weight than employment. Familiar local financial institutions fit a district of dispersed farm and energy households.
Vince Fong.p3: The 2023 job picture was anchored in agriculture and oil and gas extraction, both far more concentrated than their national baselines, alongside public administration. Health care provided the largest pool of work and also ran above the national mix. Broader finance and insurance employment and growth stayed below national norms, leaving credit unions unusually prominent inside the sector. Purchase mortgages accounted for most lending activity rather than refinancing.

Virginia Foxx.p1: Household income in the 5th congressional seat of North Carolina is among the lowest of any congressional district, at $59,041, and poverty runs well above the typical district. Housing stays within reach of that income anyway, a median home value of $245,700 against rent near $1,007 a month. Home ownership sits at 66.2 percent. The district is thinly settled, far fewer people per square mile than most of its peers.
Virginia Foxx.p2: Credit unions here show an odd split: office presence outruns the jobs behind it, running close to the national norm while employment lags well under it. State Employees', Truliant, and Allegacy anchor a branch presence that claims 25.2 percent of retail offices, a strong share for this kind of district. Truist Bank books more deposits than any other name among the district's many bank branches, though that reflects booking rules more than local reach. A credit union working this district's income and poverty profile is stretching a big office footprint over a thin staff.
Virginia Foxx.p3: Manufacturing employment ran well above the national norm in 2023, alongside strength in transportation and warehousing and in public administration, the mix of freight and government work layered onto factory jobs. Health care and social assistance employed the most people even without any unusual concentration, and retail trade ran slightly above norm too. Mortgage lending that year favored home purchases over refinancing, and only a fifth of loans reached lower-income neighborhoods, a pattern any local lender has to work within.

Warren Davidson.p1: This district's homes run cheap against what people earn here, a mark that separates it from most peers of its kind. Home values land near 3.2 times the yearly earnings of a typical household, and rent absorbs less than a fifth of the $78,375 that household brings in. The population runs to 791,238. Homeownership climbs well past most comparable districts, unemployment stays low, and the overall shape is one of settled, owned housing rather than rented.
Warren Davidson.p2: Credit unions here staff up less than their office count would imply: employment in the industry lags the national norm even though office presence sits slightly above it. General Electric, Kemba, and Telhio carry that presence locally. Credit unions still hold only 18.7 percent of retail offices, a smaller cut than most comparable districts show, which leaves Fifth Third Bank, sizable by deposits booked here among 202 bank branches, and a crowd of other banks running most of the storefronts this district's homeowners and workers use.
Warren Davidson.p3: The working economy here, as measured in 2023, leaned on manufacturing, which employed 16.7 percent of workers at a heavy concentration against the national norm, with wholesale trade close behind on a similarly strong multiple. Transportation and warehousing carried a milder specialization of its own. Health care and retail trade employed more people day to day without matching that concentration. Mortgage lending favored home purchases well over refinancing, fitting a district built around making and moving goods.

Wesley Bell.p1: Median household income in Missouri's 1st is $60,692, among the lowest district figures, and that shortage shapes household choices across the seat. Home values are likewise low at $195,300, but rent still absorbs a heavy part of earnings. Owner occupancy reaches only 54.4 percent. The district is densely urban, concentrating a lower-income population into far less space than the usual congressional seat.
Wesley Bell.p2: Credit union staffing falls below the national norm while office concentration sits slightly above it, so physical access outweighs payroll. First Community, Together, and St. Louis Community anchor that network, which accounts for 20.5 percent of retail offices beside banks. Stifel Bank and Trust has the leading locally assigned deposit position, within a competitive banking field. Against the incomes and rents described above, credit unions maintain more storefront reach than their staffing weight alone would predict.
Wesley Bell.p3: As measured in 2023, the district's economy leaned hardest on management of companies and enterprises, running well over twice the national norm, alongside finance and insurance and wholesale trade. Health care, manufacturing, and professional services rounded out the other major sources of work, drawing on roughly 529,900 jobs total. This is a district built on corporate back-office and finance work, sitting atop a population that has not shared evenly in those sectors' returns.

Wesley Hunt.p1: Household income in the 38th district of Texas sets it apart from most comparable districts, running to 98,753 dollars a year. Home values follow, at 395,700 dollars, roughly four times income by the published middle values, with rent near 1,644 dollars a month. Homeownership lags most peer districts even so. The district packs over 810,000 residents into a dense footprint, skewing toward the middle of working age.
Wesley Hunt.p2: Credit unions hold just 15.7 percent of retail offices here, well below most districts, leaving most branch space to banks. JPMorgan Chase shows the most deposits booked to addresses here among a crowded field of competing banks. Navy Federal, First Community, and Advancial carry the credit union name. Credit union presence in jobs and in office space both fall short of the national norm, jobs the weaker of the two, thin coverage for a district with this much income at stake.
Wesley Hunt.p3: As of 2023, the job market here leaned hardest into mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction, a specialization many times the national norm, alongside real estate and professional, scientific, and technical services. Finance and insurance employment cleared the national norm as well, growing at a similar clip over the prior decade. Home purchases dominated mortgage originations here, while only a slim slice of that lending reached lower income neighborhoods.

William Keating.p1: Homeownership here runs among the highest of any congressional district, at 77.3 percent, and that single fact shapes the rest of the picture. Median household income is high, at 101,312 dollars, and the poverty rate stays low. Home values sit high too, at 645,400 dollars, yet the cost burden that follows from them lands lighter than in most other districts. This is a population settled into owned homes rather than cycling through rentals.
William Keating.p2: Rockland, First Citizens', and St. Anne's are the credit unions with a presence in this district, holding 16.0 percent of retail offices against banks, a smaller share than in most comparable places. Credit union employment here runs below the national norm, and office presence tracks it closely rather than diverging from it. Deposits booked to addresses in this district favor a bank, a reminder that such figures follow where accounts are booked, not where customers actually walk in. The homeowners and high earners described above are the base any credit union here actually works with.
William Keating.p3: The working economy, measured in 2023, leaned hardest on construction, running well above the national norm for the sector. Health care and retail trade carried real weight in the job count too, each mildly specialized rather than dominant. Overall finance employment ran below the national norm, and total employment across the district stood near 264,000 jobs. Home purchases made up much of the year's mortgage originations, a sign of a market built on owning rather than renting.

William Timmons.p1: Density is one feature of this seat, which holds 810,387 residents in a comparatively compact pattern. Its $78,299 middle household income resembles peer levels, while the typical home stays below $310,000. Poverty is less prevalent than across many similar seats. Taken together, those measures describe moderate earnings with housing that remains comparatively reachable. They also create a broad base of households for retail financial institutions.
William Timmons.p2: Credit unions command 24.4 percent of retail banking locations through a network led by Truliant, Founders, and Greenville. Their office concentration sits around the national baseline, but their employment concentration is much smaller, so physical reach exceeds staffing weight. Federal reports assign Truist Bank the foremost local deposit amount within a field of many institutions. Rent absorbs 20.2 percent of median income, connecting that financial footprint to households balancing monthly shelter expenses.
William Timmons.p3: In 2023, manufacturing was the clearest employment specialty and accounted for 14.7 percent of workers. Administrative and support services plus wholesale trade also appeared with greater local weight than their national counterparts. Health care and retail trade supplied other large pools of work. Finance and insurance employment expanded faster than the country during the preceding decade, despite the relatively thin credit union staffing described above. Manufacturing remains the defining difference in the local job mix.

Yassamin Ansari.p1: A home here costs 5.3 times the typical household's income, a ratio among the highest of any district measured, and rent alone runs 28 percent of median earnings. Median household income is $70,539, on the low side for a district like this, while home values land in ordinary territory at $375,800. Homeownership trails well behind renting here. Both poverty and joblessness climb toward the upper end of what other districts report, and the population skews young and packs in tightly, all of it pointing to housing costs that have pulled away from what paychecks can cover.
Yassamin Ansari.p2: Credit unions hold 31.0 percent of retail offices here, a share that stands out clearly against comparable districts, giving them more ground than the many separate bank rivals competing in this market. Desert Financial, Arizona Financial, and Global anchor that presence. Credit union employment sits close to the national norm rather than running thick or thin. For a district stretched this hard between income and housing cost, that office footprint puts credit unions in direct contact with the affordability strain described above.
Yassamin Ansari.p3: As of 2023, transportation and warehousing stood out sharply, employing 11.1 percent of jobs at close to two and a half times the national norm. Public administration and utilities were also unusually concentrated here, well beyond typical levels. Overall finance employment sat almost exactly at the national norm, with little growth over the prior decade. Mortgage lending that year leaned heavily toward home purchases, with a substantial share going to lower-income neighborhoods.

Young Kim.p1: Household income here runs 134,956 dollars, among the highest of any district measured, and that fact colors every other number below it. Home values climb even further out of reach by comparison, with rent taking 24.1 percent of what the typical household earns. Most families own rather than rent, and both poverty and unemployment run well under what comparable districts show. This is also a place packed more densely than most of the West.
Young Kim.p2: Credit union jobs here sit close to the national norm at 0.86 times it, while credit union offices trail further behind at 0.48 times, a gap wide enough that employment is clearly outpacing branch counts. A large statewide credit union, Navy Federal, and Orange County's Credit Union anchor a presence holding 21.3 percent of retail offices against banks. JPMorgan Chase books the largest bank deposits in the district, though plenty of other banks operate here as well. For a credit union, this means serving households that are well off and largely done paying off a house, with borrowing needs pointed elsewhere.
Young Kim.p3: As of 2023, construction and administrative and waste-management services each held 8.8 percent of jobs, both well above the national norm. Wholesale trade followed close behind, another sector this district leans into more than most places do. Health care and retail made up a large share of work too, but held closer to the national average. This is a local economy built on building, moving goods, and business services, rather than finance itself.

Yvette Clarke.p1: This district crowds people into far less space than most comparable districts manage, a dense urban seat in the Northeast holding about 711,601 residents whose median age runs to 38. Incomes trail most comparable districts at a median of $76,531, while home values sit among the highest anywhere. Homeownership is rare here, and rents and other housing costs sit close to the top nationally. Poverty runs higher than most districts see as well.
Yvette Clarke.p2: Just 4.0 percent of retail banking offices here belong to credit unions, a share few other districts fall below. Municipal, SPC Brooklyn, and Berea are the credit unions holding ground in this market, set against JPMorgan Chase, the bank booking the largest local deposits though hardly the only one drawing customers here. Credit union employment and office presence both run well under the national norm and track each other closely. Given the incomes and housing costs residents face here, credit unions have barely gained a foothold.
Yvette Clarke.p3: As of 2023, health care and social assistance dominated the local economy, employing 47.2 percent of workers, nearly triple the concentration seen nationally. Educational services followed as the second-largest and second-most specialized sector. Finance and insurance jobs together grew faster here than nationally over the prior decade, even as overall finance employment stayed well below the national norm. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, with a substantial share reaching lower-income neighborhoods.

Zachary Nunn.p1: Population here spreads thin across the district, well below most comparable seats, with 837,909 people and a median age of 37.2. Household income lands near the midpoint for districts like this one, at $80,284, and housing runs cheaper than most, a home value of $262,600 against income. Unemployment stays low too, pointing to a labor market with little slack.
Zachary Nunn.p2: Credit union employment here falls below the national norm even though credit union offices are specialized and outpace that jobs figure, an imbalance that shapes what follows. GreenState, Veridian, and Community Choice anchor that office presence, which holds 22.1 percent of retail offices. Principal Bank shows up as the top name by deposits, though that reflects deposits booked to an address here rather than branch strength, and it competes with hundreds of bank branches spread across the district. For a district this thinly populated, that combination means credit unions carry real physical presence without a matching local workforce.
Zachary Nunn.p3: As of 2023, finance and insurance dominated the job base, at 2.84 times the national norm, well ahead of any other sector here. Wholesale trade and management of companies added modest specialization on top of that. Growth in finance and insurance together ran just under the national norm over the prior decade. Mortgage lending activity leaned heavily toward home purchases, with the rest split among other loan types.

Zoe Lofgren.p1: Homeownership in the 18th congressional seat of California sits at 50.0 percent, among the lowest shares of any district in the country. That sits oddly against a median household income of $103,010, well clear of most peers, and against home values that climb far above what typical incomes there would support. Rent runs a median $2,136 a month. The district is spread thin, with unemployment running higher than most comparable places.
Zoe Lofgren.p2: Credit unions here include BAY, THE GOLDEN 1, and CITIZENS EQUITY FIRST, operating alongside Wells Fargo Bank, National Association, the largest institution by deposits booked locally among 94 bank branches run by many separate competitors. Credit unions hold 22.8 percent of retail offices, a share close to what similar districts see. Credit union employment here sits well below the national norm, and office presence tracks it closely, meaning the tools those members and that income depend on are thinner on the ground than elsewhere.
Zoe Lofgren.p3: As measured in 2023, agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting dominated the work here, over sixteen times the national norm and a leading share of local jobs. Public administration and information work also stood out well past typical levels, a mix unlike most urban districts. Overall finance and insurance employment sat far under the national norm. Mortgage lending leaned heavily toward home purchases, with a large share of loans reaching lower-income neighborhoods.
